title: Scientists report strong new evidence that specially bred mosquitoes can fend off dengue
summary: There is new evidence that breeding a special kind of mosquito could help fend off dengue infections, rather than solely relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten
story: There is new evidence that breeding a special kind of mosquito could help fend off dengue infections, rather than solely relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten

WASHINGTON -- Children who lived in Brazilian neighborhoods buzzing with a special kind of mosquito were far less likely to catch dengue or another worrisome virus, chikungunya, researchers reported Saturday.

The major study of more than 5,700 children in one of the world’s dengue hot spots offers new evidence that breeding mosquitoes unable to transmit these viruses can be a viable strategy rather than solely relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten.

In neighborhoods populated by these so-called Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes, researchers found about a 69% reduction in dengue and chikungunya infections in schoolchildren compared to similar neighborhoods — an effect sustained even during Brazil’s severe 2024 dengue outbreak, said Dr. Sri Edupuganti of Emory University, part of the international research team.
The researchers reported the findings at a meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene.

“This is really exciting,” said Dr. David Hamer, a global health expert at Boston University who wasn’t involved with the Brazilian study. He predicts that pairing more use of these Wolbachia mosquitoes with existing steps to fight mosquito-borne disease could “knock dengue down to much lower levels” in many places.
The latest research comes as Florida grapples with an unusually large outbreak of the virus, what appears to be the biggest in any U.S. state since at least the 1940s.

Usually in the continental U.S., dengue is found mostly in people who traveled internationally. But as of Friday, Florida health officials had tallied more than 650 locally acquired cases, about three-quarters of them in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa.
Outside the U.S., the nonprofit World Mosquito Program has pioneered the Wolbachia strategy.

How it works: Scientists breed mosquitoes to carry a kind of bacteria called Wolbachia. It is harmless to people and common in many insects, although not dengue-carrying Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. The bacteria dramatically reduce the mosquitoes’ ability to transmit certain viruses. Female mosquitoes spread the bacteria to their offspring, so releasing enough of the specially bred insects — males and females — into an area allows Wolbachia to gradually become established in the local mosquito population.

Field trials and other studies in Indonesia and elsewhere have shown the strategy can significantly lower dengue diagnoses. But because people with mild symptoms may not be diagnosed, the new study in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, went further. Researchers tested blood for signs of dengue, chikungunya or the Zika virus.

The four-year study compared children living in neighborhoods that all got the same pesticide and other mosquito-control interventions, but half were randomly assigned to have Wolbachia mosquitoes released into the area. There were too few cases of Zika to calculate if the special mosquitoes had any effect on that disease.
AP Medical Writer Mike Stobbe contributed to this report.

title: Britain's Princess Catherine reflects on life after cancer diagnosis in a new documentary
summary: The Princess of Wales opens up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary reflecting on life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024
story: The Princess of Wales opens up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary reflecting on life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024
LONDON -- Britain's Catherine, Princess of Wales opens up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary exploring life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024.

“Heal” follows 44-year-old Kate as she attempts the Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours. She completed the feat in June to raise money for the cancer charity of the Royal Marsden Hospital, where she was treated.
In a trailer released Saturday by Prince William and Kate’s Kensington Palace office, the princess reflects on her cancer journey and speaks to others about their experiences.

Kate, who is married to the heir to the British throne, announced in March 2024 that she had cancer and was undergoing chemotherapy following major abdominal surgery. She did not reveal what type of cancer she was treated for.
Kate disclosed in January 2025 that she was in remission and has gradually resumed her public duties, visiting India with William earlier this month.
In the trailer, Kate says cancer changes people profoundly, and “healing is a journey. How to reconnect with the things you once knew, and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty.”
She adds that “it’s clear we’re not meant to carry life’s challenges alone” and “often, it is through pain that we realize there’s a greater beauty that lies beyond that.”

“Heal” will be broadcast by the BBC in Britain on Nov. 29, by NBCUniversal in the United States on Nov. 30, on Australia’s Channel 9 Dec. 1 and Canada’s CTV and Noovo on Dec. 7. Kensington Palace said proceeds from its distribution will go to the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity.

title: South Korea confirms its first case of cholera in 10 years
summary: South Korea has reported its first cholera case in 10 years
story: South Korea has reported its first cholera case in 10 years

SEOUL, South Korea -- South Korea on Friday reported its first case of cholera in 10 years, with health authorities urging people to take precautionary measures, use only safe water and wash their food properly.

The Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency said health workers confirmed cholera from test samples of a person who had visited a hospital emergency room in the southeastern port city of Changwon earlier this month, showing symptoms of vomiting and diarrhea.

The agency said the unidentified person, who recovered and was discharged on Tuesday, had not traveled overseas in the past two months. It said health workers were trying to trace the source of infection and the people the person had been in contact with.

It was the country’s first case of cholera since 2016, when authorities identified three cases suspected to be caused by contaminated seafood. At least 162 people got sick in a larger outbreak in 2001.

Cholera spreads mostly through contaminated water and food and can also spread through contact with an infected person’s stool or vomit, according to the agency. Diarrhea is the most common symptom, and severe illness can lead to dehydration or shock that could potentially be fatal if treatment is delayed.

The agency issued guidance urging people to stick to safe water and cooked food and to wash and peel fruits and vegetables. It also urged medical facilities to promptly test and report suspected cases

title: With measles spreading, do you need a booster shot?
summary: Now that measles is back in the U.S., Mexico and Bolivia, some are asking if adults need a booster shot
story: Now that measles is back in the U.S., Mexico and Bolivia, some are asking if adults need a booster shot
Now that measles is officially back in the U.S., some Americans are asking: Do adults need a booster shot?
Generally, experts say, the answer is no.
“Most people are protected without getting a booster shot” because they’ve either been vaccinated or had measles as kids, said Dr. Richard Martinello at Yale School of Medicine.
The U.S., Mexico and Bolivia lost their measles-free status this week after stubborn outbreaks erased decades of progress. Last year, Canada lost its measles-elimination designation.

Doctors say getting two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine is the best way to protect against one of the most contagious viruses in the world. The vaccine usually protects people for life, as does having had the disease. Americans born before 1957 are considered to have “presumptive evidence” of immunity because almost everyone back then got measles during childhood.
But doctors say certain people should consider getting boosters.

One group is healthcare workers born before 1957 without proof of immunity. They’re more likely than the general public to come in contact with people who have measles, so they may get it or even spread it to vulnerable patients.

Adults vaccinated between 1963 and 1967 also might want to think about boosters. During those years, some children received an inactivated vaccine that uses a killed version of the virus, which was less effective than the current vaccine containing live, weakened virus. Doctors said people who know they got the inactivated vaccine or aren’t sure should get at least one dose of the live MMR vaccine. One dose is 93% effective at preventing measles, while two doses are 97% protective.

Until 1989, only a single dose was standard. Now the recommendation is for adults to have at least one documented dose of MMR. Two doses are recommended for certain people in high-risk groups who don’t have other evidence of immunity.

“People who have had no shots should go get vaccinated, if they weren't born before 1957,” said Dr. Joshua Sharfstein at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. “If they have had only one shot, they may want to consider whether they’re in a risk group for a second shot.”

That risk group, he said, includes people in school, healthcare workers, international travelers or people living with family members who have compromised immune systems. In places with active measles outbreaks, health officials sometimes recommend that everyone have two shots, Sharfstein said.
For people who have only had one shot, especially in an area where measles is circulating, “it’s always a good idea to talk with your physician about whether another shot is needed,” Martinello said.
But what if you don’t know how many shots you received or even if you’ve been vaccinated?

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention suggests asking your parents or doctor, checking with your high school or college health services or reaching out to previous employers that required immunizations. You can also try contacting your state’s health department; some states have registries that include adult vaccines.

If you’re still unsure about your vaccination status, you can talk with your doctor about an MMR immunity blood test that can show whether you have antibodies against measles. But Martinello said this isn't an ideal measure of how safe you are from the virus. Though the test is accurate, he said, scientists don’t know how to link the result perfectly with the level of protection someone might have.
Regardless, doctors said getting a booster just to be safe won’t harm you unless you’re in a group that is not supposed to get the vaccine at all, such as pregnant women.
Now that measles is circulating in the U.S., doctors said it’s crucial to take measures to protect yourself.

“This is a moment to not just check for yourself, but also encourage others to make sure that they are adequately vaccinated,” Sharfstein said. “Too many people took measles for granted … or just didn’t think about measles. But now it’s something to think about.”

title: Palestinians victims of a third of violations against children worldwide, Save the Children says
summary: Save the Children warns that children in the Gaza Strip face severe dangers after three years of war
story: Save the Children warns that children in the Gaza Strip face severe dangers after three years of war

AMMAN, Jordan -- The children of the Gaza Strip face unmatched dangers after three years of war, a prominent non-governmental organization warned Thursday, as they suffer from repeated displacement, loss of family members, lack of healthcare and education, and abysmal living conditions.

Save the Children said almost one third of the tens of thousands of attacks and violations against children recorded worldwide last year took place in the Palestinian territories. The danger was especially high in Gaza, the tiny enclave with a population of 2 million where at least 20,000 children have been killed, according to local health authorities.
The psychological and physical impact on Palestinian children in Gaza will “live for many years to come,” Save the Children Regional Director Ahmad Alhendawi told The Associated Press.

In its annual global report, Save the Children said that one in four children, some 589 million, lived in conflict zones in 2025, the highest number documented since the end of the Cold War in 1990. The vast majority are in the Middle East and Africa.
The number is expected to increase this year with the ongoing war in Iran and the wider Mideast, and renewed war in Lebanon and Yemen in 2026.

Save the Children reported nearly 12,500 cases of violations against children in the Palestinian territories, mostly attacks on hospitals and schools and deprivation of aid. It said the situation was especially critical in Gaza, where Israel continues strikes despite an October 2025 ceasefire agreement with Hamas.
Although the latest report focused on 2025 figures, Alhendawi said conditions have shown little improvement this year.

“Lots of children who have survived themselves are injured themselves and are without surviving parents,” said Alhendawi. “This report is showing very clearly that what happened and what continues to happen in Gaza are violations at a scale that we haven’t seen and needs to be prioritized by the international community.”

Israel launched its war in Gaza in response to Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attacks. It says its ongoing strikes, including one on a hospital in the southern town of Khan Younis last week, target militants and are responses to Hamas violations of the ceasefire agreement.

While Israel has killed most of Hamas’ senior leadership, the conflict has devastated the territory and taken a heavy toll on Gaza’s civilians. The vast majority of people live in crowded tent camps or in the ruins of their former homes, with little access to food, water, or electricity.

“The children of Gaza are deprived of the bare minimum in life,” said displaced Palestinian Riad Abou Shamel, 65, surrounded by children playing in an open lot in Khan Younis filled with rubble and remains of pancaked buildings hit in airstrikes.
“They go to the market and can barely bring back half a cucumber or half an apple.”
Israel's military did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the report.

The report shed light on the surge of cases of abductions, sexual violence, and recruitment of children by armed forces in Africa, in conflict areas in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Nigeria, Sudan, and Somalia, and attacks on hospitals in Ukraine.
The data and figures in Save the Children's report of violations against children and children living in conflict zones come from the United Nations and the Peace Research Institute Oslo.
Chehayeb contributed from Beirut. Associated Press Senior Producer Wafaa Shurafa contributed to this report from Deir al-Balah, Gaza Strip.

title: Scientists are fighting for their halted funds. Trust of Black communities may be harder to win back
summary: In Pittsburgh, a study aimed at understanding why Black Americans are twice as likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease has been abruptly halted
story: In Pittsburgh, a study aimed at understanding why Black Americans are twice as likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease has been abruptly halted

People in a historically Black corner of Pittsburgh took memory tests, tracked their sleep and blood pressure and shared stories of their past to help scientists unravel risks for Alzheimer’s disease.

But they may never get answers. The study was among broader research into why Black Americans are twice as likely as their white peers to develop Alzheimer’s, but the Trump administration abruptly halted it in its final stretch.

Researchers say the move not only wasted more than $8 million in taxpayer money already spent but also is a blow to the hard-earned trust of anxious study participants who won’t even learn if their brain tests showed signs of trouble.

“The community will look like, ’Oh, they came in here, they took all our stuff, they checked us out. Now they’re gonna leave us hanging,'” said Roderick Blair, 70, who had participated in the study for four years.

Trust in U.S. health institutions has long been strained in the Black community, stemming from the nation’s long-standing racial health inequities, unequal access to care and bias within the nation’s medical system. The legacy of the Tuskegee study, which withheld treatment from Black men who had been infected with syphilis in the 1930s, still casts a shadow.

The Pittsburgh study overcame that mistrust. Getting people involved in the city’s Hill and Homewood communities helped get people talking about memory loss, dementia and Alzheimer’s and helped challenge misconceptions about it, according to La’Vette Wagner, the Pittsburgh study’s field coordinator.

Families who once dismissed memory loss as depression began asking about dementia, and people outside the study called her to ask if family members could join, she said. More than half of Black Americans, or 55%, believe that a significant loss of memory or cognitive abilities is a natural part of aging rather than disease, according to the Alzheimer’s Association.
As Blair said, "You start forgetting things and you start to wonder, do you have Alzheimer’s? You wonder, do you have dementia?”

Then the study, which had been near completion in its fifth and final year, was stripped of funding last year by the National Institutes of Health, on the grounds that it was “not science,” according to the study’s researchers, despite a rigorous review and vetting from a community advisory board.
“It wasn’t a Black study or a DEI study,” Wagner said. “It was something that was happening that was real.”

Similar terminations happened all over the country. Negar Fani, a neuropsychologist at Emory University in Atlanta, was two years into a five-year, $2.9 million project on how daily experiences of racial discrimination affect the brain and body of Black Americans when NIH terminated it in July.
While Fani tries to find the roughly $2.3 million she needs to complete the study, she and her team were left to try to explain the situation to participants who feel abandoned.
“It takes a lot to restore trust with the Black community, who has experienced so many different betrayals,” she said.
Like the Pittsburgh study's funding, Fani’s grant had been terminated for being “not scientific” and “subjective” — after the study had been approved and had enrolled 66 of the 220 people it needed.
“It’s simply brain science research,” she said.

In Pittsburgh, study lead researcher Andrea Rosso is one of numerous scientists in a recently filed lawsuit against NIH and its parent Department of Health and Human Services, one of a growing body of legal actions as the administration continues to hunt for and halt medical grants with descriptions that include the words “disparities,” “minority” and “racial.”

Ann Cohen, a director of Pittsburgh’s Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center, also is part of that lawsuit after her separate, complementary study of Alzheimer’s risk also was halted -- after spending $5.2 million over three years. She, too, has a troubling ethics question: What to do with blood samples collected from the participants?
“You lose trust a hell of a lot faster than you build it,” she said.

A spokesperson for HHS said “Massive amounts of DEI grants have failed to translate into better health outcomes for minority populations. Following President Trump’s directives, NIH is shifting money into rigorous research that will help Americans — including minority populations — live longer, healthier lives.”
This year, the NIH has awarded 2,000 fewer grants for multiyear studies worth a total of $200 million compared with 2025, according to an Association of American Medical Colleges report.

“It’s unprecedented. Many of the decisions are based on political biases and based on what politicians think is valuable rather than peer review processes, evidence-based decisions about where to invest our research dollars,” said Jill Rosenthal, the director of public health policy at the Center for American Progress.
“We’re wasting resources, we’re wasting the opportunity to identify cures for diseases,” she said.

Researchers in Pittsburgh are especially concerned that promises made to the community will remain unfulfilled. The study, 15 years in the making, would’ve helped identify participants at a higher risk for Alzheimer’s — and for potential doctor’s visits and care.
Now, Wagner said, the findings are “stuck on a shelf,” and worse, over a decade of trust built with study participants has been breached.
Blair, the study participant, said reinstating trust within their communities will be an uphill battle. “It’s going to take years to reestablish something that was moving pretty good,” he said.

title: Pentagon sharply rebukes Canada over defense spending and the F-35 fighter jet review
summary: The Pentagon has accused Canada of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke to its longtime ally over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets
story: The Pentagon has accused Canada of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke to its longtime ally over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets

TORONTO -- The Pentagon accused Canada on Monday of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke to its longtime ally over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets.
In an unusually blunt fact sheet, the Defense Department accused Ottawa of failing to make the tough decisions needed to modernize its military and meet NATO commitments.
“Canada’s defense shortfalls speak for themselves,” it said. “Canada must get serious and focused.”

The criticism follows a classified directive from U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds said largely restricts officials’ participation in Canadian think tank events and social engagements. Relations have been battered by President Donald Trump’s trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st state.

In May, Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby announced a pause in the Permanent Joint Board on Defense, a bilateral advisory body established in 1940, accusing Canada of failing to make credible progress on its defense commitments.

The rebuke also follows criticism of Washington at the Halifax International Security Forum, where its president, Peter Van Praagh, a former adviser in Conservative Prime Minister Stephen Harper’s government, warned Friday that the United States can no longer be counted on as a predictable leader of the democratic world.

The Pentagon accused Canada of leaving American taxpayers to shoulder the burden of continental defense. It said only 41.9% of Canada’s air force fleet was serviceable in the 2025-26 fiscal year and 53.9% of its naval fleet, while the army’s operational readiness stood at 48%.

“Underinvestment in defense has atrophied the Canadian Armed Forces and limited Canada’s ability to contribute to the defense of North America," the fact sheet said. "Secretary Hegseth is laser focused on incentivizing and enabling Canada’s military modernization after decades of American taxpayers footing the bill for its homeland defense.”

It also criticized Ottawa’s review of its planned purchase of 88 American-made F-35s, warning that a mixed fighter fleet could worsen personnel shortages. The Pentagon accused Canadian leaders of putting domestic economic interests ahead of military effectiveness, creating uncertainty for the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD, which the countries operate jointly.

Prime Minister Mark Carney put the F-35 purchase under review as Trump threatened Canadian sovereignty and imposed tariffs. Canada has examined Swedish-made Gripen fighters, which could bring manufacturing jobs.
Canada’s military did not immediately provide a substantive response to the Pentagon’s criticism.

Carney has acknowledged readiness problems, saying only one of Canada’s four submarines was seaworthy. Ottawa has since named Germany’s Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems as preferred supplier for up to 12 replacements, pending contract negotiations.
“We should no longer send three-quarters of our defense capital spending to America,” Carney said in June.

Canada reached NATO’s previous target of spending 2% of gross domestic product on defense and joined allies pledging to reach 5% by 2035, including related security investments. Its latest budget projects combined defense and security spending of 4.1% of GDP by the 2027-28 fiscal year, but core defense spending of only 2.6%. Canada’s parliamentary budget watchdog says the path to 5% remains unclear.
The Pentagon accused Ottawa of postponing the largest increases until after the 2029 federal election.

Other NATO allies also remain short of the new target. Yet Colby praised Germany’s military buildup Sunday as a “tectonic shift” and called Poland a “true model ally.” He also praised Romania’s plan to reach 5% by 2031.
Speaking Saturday at the Halifax International Security Forum, Rounds said the directive was not expected to affect joint military operations or intelligence sharing.
The Trump administration had already barred Pentagon officials from the Halifax forum under 2025 restrictions on think tank participation.

title: South Korea says several Russian aircraft flew into its air defense zone
summary: South Korea’s military says several Russian aircraft flew inside the country’s air defense identification zone over waters between the Korean Peninsula and Japan
story: South Korea’s military says several Russian aircraft flew inside the country’s air defense identification zone over waters between the Korean Peninsula and Japan

SEOUL, South Korea -- Several Russian aircraft flew inside South Korea’s air defense identification zone Tuesday over waters between the Korean Peninsula and Japan, Seoul's military said, correcting earlier statements that the planes had violated the country’s territorial airspace. An alert for an eastern island was quickly lifted.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff’s statement revised earlier announcements by the Ministry of the Interior and Safety and the local provincial government that said foreign airplanes had violated South Korean airspace and that they were suspected to be Russian or North Korean.

The Safety Ministry ordered Ulleung Island residents to take shelter in underground facilities or buildings around 7:52 a.m., but lifted the order three minutes later, saying the aircraft had left the danger area.

The Joint Chiefs said the country scrambled fighter jets in preparation for contingencies before the Russian aircraft withdrew. It did not immediately say how many Russian planes it detected or what types of aircraft they were.

There were no immediate reports of accidents or major disruptions on the island, which has a population of around 9,000. Ulleung suffered a major scare in 2022, when North Korea fired more than 20 missiles into the sea amid heightened inter-Korean tensions. One missile headed toward the island, triggering air raid sirens and prompting residents to evacuate.

The incident came a week after South Korea scrambled fighter jets to repel several Russian military aircraft that it said temporarily entered the country’s air-defense zone over waters between the Korean Peninsula and Japan last Monday.
Japan the same day protested to Moscow after saying that two suspected Russian aircraft had entered the country’s airspace off its southwestern coast.

title: EU proposes sweeping new Russia sanctions targeting banks, crypto and sports events
summary: The European Commission has proposed new sanctions against Russia, targeting banks, crypto platforms, and sporting teams competing under the Russian flag
story: The European Commission has proposed new sanctions against Russia, targeting banks, crypto platforms, and sporting teams competing under the Russian flag

BRUSSELS -- The European Commission on Monday proposed to target dozens of Russia’s banks, crack down on crypto platforms, and slap bans on sporting teams and athletes from competing under the country’s flag in a new round of sanctions over Moscow's war in Ukraine.

The proposals, put forward by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, must be endorsed by all 27 European Union member countries before they can enter into force. The process can take weeks, and the planned measures are likely to be modified.

The sanctions are intended to keep economic pressure on Russia, almost five years into its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The bloc has already hit more than 4,700 people and entities, including President Vladimir Putin, and several energy companies.

Von der Leyen said the move means the EU will be “striking harder at Russia’s way to finance its war by targeting its banks and crypto platforms,” and will be “shutting the door to its participation to European sports and cultural events.”

She said 60 banks will be removed from the Swift messaging system used for international payments. Countries helping Russia to evade sanctions could be caught by the EU's crypto measures, and a crypto sanctions task force would also be launched, von der Leyen said.

The commission wants to target 70 more vessels from Russia’s shadow fleet, which the Kremlin uses to move illicit oil, and to ban all tanker vessels there from European ports. Europeans would be prevented from occupying top posts of Russian companies.
It’s also proposing a ban on visas for Russians who have fought in the war on Ukraine.

“Russian ex-combatants pose a security risk to Europe,” von der Leyen said. “They cannot be allowed to wander freely across our countries. Therefore, entry into the European Union will be off limits.”
She also said that the EU must ban the display of Russian symbols at sporting or cultural events.

The proposals come just over a month after the EU posted the single biggest listing of sanctions against Russia, targeting almost 1,600 Russian officials and companies linked to its arms industry, notably those suspected of making drone or missile parts.

title: Drone attack on Colombian police base injures civilians and damages homes
summary: Explosive-laden drones have struck a police base in Cúcuta, Colombia, injuring two civilians and damaging 60 homes
story: Explosive-laden drones have struck a police base in Cúcuta, Colombia, injuring two civilians and damaging 60 homes
BOGOTA, Colombia -- Explosive-laden drones struck a police base in the Colombian city of Cúcuta Monday, injuring two civilians and damaging 60 homes, authorities said.
Officials did not immediately say who was responsible for the attack on a base belonging to the Norte de Santander Police.

The attack came as President Abelardo de la Espriella steps up military offensives against rebel groups and drug gangs, increasing air strikes and acting on intelligence that has enabled the military to capture several midlevel commanders.

Armed groups have responded by attacking military bases and police stations with small drones, rockets made with gas canisters and roadside bombs. De la Espriella, a conservative who took office in August, has canceled peace negotiations with rebel groups that were underway with his predecessor Gustavo Petro.

Cúcuta, a city of half a million people a short drive from Colombia’s border with Venezuela, is a major trade hub and an important center for criminal groups that profit from the drug trade and other kinds of smuggling.

Rebel groups including the National Liberation Army and the FARC-EMC also operate in the nearby Catatumbo region, where they tax local businesses and promote the cultivation of coca, the raw material for cocaine.
A 2016 peace deal between the Colombian government and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia led to the demobilization of more than 14,000 fighters.

But violence has increased in some parts of Colombia, including many border areas, as smaller armed groups try to seize territory abandoned by the FARC, where the Colombian state has been slow to provide security and basic services.

A police station in the town of Curumani, in the department of Cesar, was also attacked with drones Monday. On Saturday, one soldier was killed and 12 others were injured during an attack with drones and rockets on a military base in La Jagua de Ibirico, also in Cesar. Officials said that both incidents remain under investigation.

According to the Ideas for Peace Foundation, a group that monitors Colombia’s conflict, illegal armed groups carried out 323 drone attacks during the first nine months of 2026, a 95% increase from the same period last year.
Follow AP’s coverage of Latin America and the Caribbean at https://apnews.com/hub/latin-america

title: WHO director-general visits Cuba as healthcare system breaks down
summary: The World Health Organization's top official is visiting Cuba as the island’s healthcare system crumbles under a spiraling economic crisis and worsening power outages
story: The World Health Organization's top official is visiting Cuba as the island’s healthcare system crumbles under a spiraling economic crisis and worsening power outages
HAVANA -- The World Health Organization's top official is visiting Cuba as the island’s healthcare system crumbles under a spiraling economic crisis and worsening power outages.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus arrived Sunday at the invitation of health authorities in the Caribbean nation for a three-day visit.

Cuban Public Health Minister Dr. José Ángel Portal Miranda welcomed Tedros, saying it was an opportunity for him to see firsthand the reality of the Cuban healthcare system and the challenges that it faces.
Tedros expressed his willingness to listen and understand Cuba's situation and identify ways to provide support, according to state media newspaper Granma.
“I want to use this visit to better understand the challenges you face and would be happy to mobilize the international community to support you,” he was quoted as saying.

Cuba’s once-vaunted system of free universal healthcare has deteriorated sharply. Analysts say the crisis has been compounded by fuel shortages that they blame on tightened U.S. sanctions on the island’s energy sector, worsening an economy that already had been limping for years.
Hospitals across Cuba face shortages of supplies including syringes, gauze, vaccines and anesthetics. They also lack spare parts to repair equipment such as hemodialysis and CT scan machines.

For Cuba, a country with health indicators comparable to those of developed nations — including low mortality, high life expectancy, broad vaccination coverage and widespread prenatal care — the situation “is shocking,” said Mario Cruz Peñate, the Pan American Health Organization and World Health Organization representative on the island.
A government report released in June stated that the survival rate for children with cancer had fallen to 65% from 85% before the energy blockade began in January.
As part of the visit, Tedros is scheduled to visit health and biotechnology institutions, meet with health sector officials, and talk with reporters.
Tedros’ visit marks the second time that he has visited Cuba as WHO director-general.

title: Indonesia names 6 current and former police officials as suspects in an alleged treason plot
summary: Indonesian authorities have named former National Police chief Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo and five other current and former senior officers as suspects in an alleged treason plot against President Prabowo Subianto’s government
story: Indonesian authorities have named former National Police chief Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo and five other current and former senior officers as suspects in an alleged treason plot against President Prabowo Subianto’s government

JAKARTA, Indonesia -- Authorities in Indonesia on Monday named a former National Police chief and five other current and former senior officers as suspects in an alleged treason plot to undermine the government of President Prabowo Subianto.

The move was announced by the National Police Criminal Investigation Agency, known as Bareskrim, at a news conference in the capital, Jakarta. It widened a high-profile investigation that began with allegations of illegal wiretapping targeting the president and other public figures.

The suspects are accused of conspiring to carry out acts of treason in an effort to keep then National Police chief Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo in his position and influence Indonesia’s political landscape.

“The suspects are alleged to have conspired in the preparation and initial execution of acts of treason, motivated by an effort to maintain the position of national police chief for political purposes, by weakening public trust in President Prabowo Subianto’s administration,” Bareskrim chief Asep Safrudin told reporters.
Besides Listyo Sigit, police named Slamet Uliandi, Eko Hadi Santoso, Ahrie Sonta Nasution, Iman Imanuddin and Tedjo Kusumo as suspects.

Safrudin said that the six suspects were being investigated under multiple provisions of Indonesia’s Criminal Code related to treason, conspiracy and preparation to overthrow the government. The offenses carry penalties ranging from long prison terms to life imprisonment or death.

He said the suspects are alleged to have committed criminal acts by ordering, participating in or encouraging others to carry out treason “with the intention of depriving the president of his liberty, rendering the president unable to govern and/or overthrowing the government.”

Investigators have also linked some of the suspects to large anti-government demonstrations held across Indonesia in recent months and confiscated 20 One Piece flags, featuring imagery from the popular Japanese anime and manga franchise that has recently been adopted by some Indonesian anti-government protesters as a symbol of resistance, as well as 735 million rupiah ($45,000) in cash.
When asked whether the protests were connected to the case, Safrudin said that some of the suspects had been involved in organizing or supporting certain activities that are now under investigation.
Safrudin said that investigators were continuing to investigate whether the suspects had supported or influenced other political movements aimed at weakening the government.
“We are tracing what activities they supported, what activities they may have exploited and other related matters,” he said.
Police had seized 39 electronic devices as evidence, including cellphones, laptop computers, central processing units and hard drives, Safrudin said.

Authorities also confiscated hundreds of black T-shirts that investigators said were connected to the case, including 250 shirts bearing an image of a firearm and the slogan “All Cops Are Bastards” and 251 shirts featuring the phrases “Aware of being extorted, aware of being burned, aware of being impoverished,” alongside a three-finger salute and the hashtags #IndonesiaSadar or #AwareIndonesia.

Police didn't immediately provide evidence supporting the treason allegations or explain how the seized items were linked to the alleged conspiracy. It wasn't immediately clear whether the suspects had obtained legal representation. There was also no immediate public response from Listyo Sigit or the other suspects.

The announcement marks a dramatic escalation of the wiretapping scandal that has already led to the dismissal of several senior police officers and prompted parliamentary scrutiny of Indonesia’s law enforcement and intelligence institutions.
Authorities said that the investigation remains ongoing and that additional suspects could still be identified.

title: Bukele reveals circumstances in which 3 Salvadoran soldiers died fighting gangs in Haiti
summary: El Salvador’s president has identified the soldiers from the Central American country who recently died in Haiti as they fight violent gangs
story: El Salvador’s president has identified the soldiers from the Central American country who recently died in Haiti as they fight violent gangs

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele identified three soldiers from the Central American country killed while fighting gangs in Haiti and pledged that troops who want to leave the troubled Caribbean country could do so immediately without facing reprisals.
The three who died Friday are Lt. Cristian Daniel Palacios Santos and corporals Emerson Alexander Zepeda Zelada and Wilber Manuel Serrano Medina.
Bukele wrote Sunday night on X that the two corporals were trying to dislodge a grenade from a drone as its battery was about to run out.

“It was not possible to steer the drone toward a completely safe area for it to crash,” Bukele said, adding that Serrano Medina held the drone off the ground as Zepeda Zelada manually disarmed the grenade.
“They were fully aware of the immense risk they were taking, yet they chose to act to protect others. And they succeeded,” Bukele wrote.
Palacios Santos was killed in the same incident, but Bukele provided no details.
He did say, however, that Palacios Santos was admired after he recently “took control” during a “critical moment” in an operation in which some contractors allegedly retreated.
“He acted with speed and determination, managing to save several lives, including those of his own colleagues,” Bukele wrote Sunday night on X. “We all applaud his bravery.”
He did not identify the contractors.
The Salvadoran soldiers were among 2,500 deployed to Haiti last month after four of their own went missing when they were attacked Oct. 18 deep in gang-controlled territory. They haven't been found.
Bukele said his government would award the families of the three soldiers killed last week $200,000 in addition to a monthly income.

He also stressed that any soldier who wants to leave Haiti immediately may do so “without fear of reprisal and without concern that their return might jeopardize the mission, as many of their comrades have volunteered to relieve anyone who wishes to be relieved.”
Salvadoran troops have come under increased scrutiny as experts and the U.N. note they are operating in a largely unilateral way, but thousands of Haitians recently demonstrated to support Bukele.

The deaths come as local and international forces fight powerful gangs entrenched in Martissant, a community located in a key corridor that links Haiti’s capital to the country’s western and southern regions.
More than 70 suspected gang members have been killed since last week as the battle in Martissant continues, police have said.
It is the first major operation in Martissant in the more than five years that gangs have controlled it.

As Haitian police and others continue to battle gangs in Martissant, a U.N.-backed gang suppression force said it killed several suspected gang members on Sunday as part of ongoing operations in Tabarre and Cite Soleil, located in Port-au-Prince, and in the central town of Gros Morne.
Follow AP’s coverage of Latin America and the Caribbean at https://apnews.com/hub/latin-america

title: Hungary’s Magyar says he will visit Ukraine in a sign of mending relations
summary: Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar plans to visit Ukraine soon, signaling improved relations between the two countries
story: Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar plans to visit Ukraine soon, signaling improved relations between the two countries

BUDAPEST, Hungary -- Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said Monday that he will soon travel to Ukraine in a sign that the icy relations between the two neighboring countries, pushed to the breaking point by former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, are improving.

Magyar's planned visit to the embattled country comes after Kyiv passed a law in October — long demanded by Hungary’s government — that expanded language rights for a Hungarian ethnic minority in western Ukraine.

Speaking to lawmakers on Monday, Magyar did not announce a date for his visit, but said it would take place in the western Ukrainian region of Zakarpattia, home to tens of thousands of ethnic Hungarians. It will be the first visit to the region by a Hungarian head of government since 2015.
Magyar denounced Russian strikes that hit the mountainous region last week and said he would travel there “soon ... to personally deliver the support of the motherland to our Hungarian brethren.”

Before Magyar and his Tisza party won a landslide election in April, Hungary's government under Orbán pursued a hostile approach to Ukraine, repeatedly blocking aid to Kyiv and holding up European Union sanctions against Russia, all while maintaining cordial ties with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Orbán's government had also depicted Ukraine as a threat to Hungary's security, and cast President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as an enemy, using his likeness in taxpayer-funded political campaigns.

Since taking office, Magyar's government has taken a markedly different approach, expressing solidarity with Ukraine and designating Russia a national security threat. In an interview last month with The Associated Press, Magyar said he saw “a chance to open a new chapter in Ukrainian-Hungarian relations.”

On Monday, Magyar expressed his sympathy “to the Hungarians of Zakarpattia and to the entire Ukrainian people, who for nearly five years have been waging a superhuman struggle for their mere survival.”

“I want to make clear what every well-meaning person in the world knows: that Russia is the aggressor and Ukraine, the Ukrainian people, are the victims,” he said. “We stand by our Hungarian compatriots in Zakarpattia and for the Ukrainian people who have come under attack, even if someone in Moscow doesn't like it.”
Magyar also said he would attend negotiations later this week on the EU's next seven-year budget, but that Hungary would insist that the bloc's financial support for Ukraine be handled separately.

title: Greece’s oldest modern-era museum reopens on the Acropolis after major restoration
summary: Greece’s oldest modern-era museum has reopened on the Acropolis in Athens after a seven-year, 6.2 million-euro ($6.8 million) restoration
story: Greece’s oldest modern-era museum has reopened on the Acropolis in Athens after a seven-year, 6.2 million-euro ($6.8 million) restoration
ATHENS, Greece -- A museum that has stood on the Acropolis since 1874, making it the oldest in modern Greece, reopened Monday after a hi-tech makeover.
The squat stone building often goes unnoticed by visitors. It had been closed to the public since 2007, three years before the country was plunged into a massive financial crisis.
The seven-year restoration cost 6.2 million euros ($6.8 million), raised through public funds and private donations, Culture Minister Lina Mendoni said.

The site will host ancient artifacts never before exhibited, digital displays tracing the monuments’ 2,500-year history and a viewing gallery where Culture Ministry technicians will carry out restoration work on ancient objects.
The museum opened in 1874, making it the first museum purpose-built since modern Greece gained independence several decades earlier.
It closed in 2007, becoming an administrative building after cranes carefully lowered its renowned sculptures and other masterpieces to the new Acropolis Museum at the foot of the hill.
“For us, it was inconceivable, almost an affront, that this historic building, with its uniquely privileged location, should be converted into offices and storerooms,” Mendoni said.
“We therefore decided that the museum should reopen in accordance with its original purpose,” she said.
The Parthenon and other temples on the Acropolis remain Greece’s most visited ancient site, with more than 4.6 million admissions recorded last year.
Restoration work continues even during the peak summer months. The Parthenon recently shed its heavy scaffolding for the first time in years.
Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis attended Monday’s inauguration and described the reopening as another milestone for Greece’s cultural heritage.
He used the occasion to restate Greece’s long-running demand for the return of the Parthenon Sculptures held by the British Museum in London.

“The rightful home of these priceless masterpieces is here, beneath the Attic light and in direct proximity to the temple to which they belong,” he said, adding that Greece would not accept the return of the sculptures as a loan.
“No solution and no agreement can be based on the recognition of foreign ownership over our national treasures,” Mitsotakis said.
“I reaffirm my commitment that we will continue this effort with responsibility, seriousness and determination,” he added. “And in the end, we will succeed.”

title: A silver soup tureen once owned by JP Morgan could fetch $8M at a Christie's auction
summary: A massive silver soup tureen once owned by financier J
story: A massive silver soup tureen once owned by financier J
LONDON -- It's a perfect gift for the host with the most.
A huge silver soup tureen once owned by financier J.P. Morgan up for sale, with an estimated price of up to 6 million pounds (almost $8 million).
More than a foot and a half long (46 centimeters) long and weighing in at 44 pounds (20 kilograms), the Meissonnier Tureen is the star of a Dec. 1 auction at Christie’s in London.
Made in the 1730s by the French artist and goldsmith Juste-Aurèle Meissonnier in a flamboyant rococo style, it was “designed to astonish,” according to Christie’s specialist Isabelle Cartier-Stone.

Shaped like a stylized shell, it has a cover encrusted with detailed silver plants and animals, including “a duck, a crab, a fish, an oyster, and a snail among an artichoke and other leafy vegetables,” according to the catalog.

The tureen’s owners have included British aristocrats, Russian statesmen and the American banker John Pierpont Morgan. It is one of a pair split up after they were auctioned together in 1977, with the other in the Cleveland Museum of Art in Ohio.

It is being sold as part of a trove of silver owned by the Blaquier-Arrieta family of wealthy Argentine collectors and has a presale estimate of between 4 million pounds and 6 million pounds ($5.25 million and $7.86 million).

A group of a dozen paintings owned by the same family sold at Sotheby’s last week for $412 million, with the Vincent van Gogh painting “Châtaigniers en fleurs” (Chestnut Trees in Flower) fetching $190.4 million.

title: European Commission warns EU Academy users of data leak after AI-driven cyberattack
summary: The European Commission is warning of a data leak from a major AI-generated cyberattack on its EU Academy website
story: The European Commission is warning of a data leak from a major AI-generated cyberattack on its EU Academy website

BRUSSELS -- The European Commission on Monday warned users of one of its websites that personal data has been leaked in a major AI-generated cyberattack that was launched on the EU institution last month.

The European Union’s executive branch said the EU Academy website had been caught up in the cyberattack. The site offers courses and information about the 27-nation bloc’s policies to people outside EU institutions.

“The exact scale of the data leak remains under investigation as a precautionary measure,” spokesperson Thomas Regnier said. Names and email addresses were among the data taken, he said, but did not specify how many people were affected.
The commission confirmed last week that it had first detected incidents involving its databases on Oct. 22 and that its cyber experts had taken “preventive measures” to limit the damage.
Regnier declined to confirm whether the month-long cyber campaign has been brought under control.
“As long as the investigation is ongoing, I will not make any conclusive statements at this stage on where we are,” he said.

A message on the EU Academy website said that access had been disabled and measures taken to contain the incident and limit its impact. It warned users to watch for suspicious or unsolicited emails and messages and to avoid sharing personal information with anyone contacting them about the website or its activities.
The CERT-EU agency oversees the digital security of the EU institutions, which employ about 40,000 people just in Brussels.

In a Nov. 4 blog post, the agency warned about threats from a specific AI tool called ARTEX. While designed to use AI to identify vulnerabilities in digital systems, it has been linked to recent attacks across the globe.
The agency said it was “highly likely” that ARTEX had been used in AI-driven activities in “its constituency.” It did not confirm any attack on the commission.

“We assess that ARTEX’s public availability will likely accelerate adoption by threat actors, resulting in more frequent, faster, and more scalable automated attacks with a higher success rate,” the agency said.

title: Indonesia’s Prabowo nominates 2 candidates to replace Raka as vice president
summary: President Prabowo Subianto has nominated Agriculture Minister Andi Amran Sulaiman and former Foreign Minister Sugiono to replace Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, who resigned on Nov. 12 over questions about his eligibility for office
story: President Prabowo Subianto has nominated Agriculture Minister Andi Amran Sulaiman and former Foreign Minister Sugiono to replace Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, who resigned on Nov. 12 over questions about his eligibility for office

JAKARTA, Indonesia -- Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto on Monday nominated the agriculture minister and a former foreign minister to replace Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, who resigned earlier this month.

Under Indonesia’s Constitution, the People’s Consultative Assembly, or MPR, the country’s highest legislative body, must elect a replacement within 60 days from two candidates nominated by the president. The winner will serve the remainder of the current term.

MPR Chairman Ahmad Muzani said Prabowo had nominated Agriculture Minister Andi Amran Sulaiman and former Foreign Minister Sugiono in a letter submitted to the assembly’s leadership at the parliament building in Jakarta.

“This is not a situation we expected to face, but this is a reality and Indonesia is a state governed by law,” Prabowo told reporters after formally submitting his letter to parliament. “We will follow our legal procedures and carry out all state responsibilities in accordance with the Constitution.”

Raka, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, submitted his resignation on Nov. 12 amid questions over his eligibility for office after recent court rulings disputed his educational credentials.

Prabowo formally accepted the resignation, saying Raka had chosen to step down “for the greater interest of the nation, the state and the Indonesian people.” He praised the vice president for showing “courage, responsibility and statesmanship.”

Prabowo said he nominated Sulaiman and Sugiono based on their achievements, service, loyalty to the nation and “my confidence that they will serve the state, the Indonesian people and the country to the best of their abilities.”
Muzani previously said the MPR would convene a special plenary session on Dec. 11 to elect and swear in a replacement vice president.

A 36-member verification committee will review the nominees’ qualifications before they can proceed to the selection stage. The panel held its first meeting Friday to discuss procedures for examining their eligibility.
The investigation into Raka’s academic credentials was apparently not related to investigations into allegations that top police officials had been involved in wiretapping targeting the president.

Indonesian authorities on Monday named former National Police chief Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo and five other senior officers as suspects in an alleged treason plot to undermine the government of President Prabowo.

title: Tourists evacuated after fire destroys 6 hotels in Zanzibar's Nungwi Beach area
summary: A fire engulfed six hotels along a popular beach in Tanzania’s Zanzibar archipelago over the weekend
story: A fire engulfed six hotels along a popular beach in Tanzania’s Zanzibar archipelago over the weekend
ZANZIBAR, Tanzania -- Investigations continued Monday into the cause of a huge fire that engulfed six hotels along a popular beach in Tanzania’s semiautonomous archipelago of Zanzibar.
Several hotel workers were injured in the blaze over the weekend. Authorities said about 180 tourists were safely evacuated.

The fire broke out Saturday afternoon at Makofi Hotel on Nungwi Beach, at the northern end of the island, and spread rapidly to neighboring properties, fueled by strong winds and thatched roofs. Firefighters battled the blaze for about three hours before bringing it under control.
Preliminary reports suggest the fire may have started in an oven used to bake bread, though officials have cautioned against speculation.
Tourism Minister Nasra Nassor said Saturday that the government would conduct a rapid assessment and establish the cause of the fire before taking “necessary measures.”

Zanzibar’s white sand beaches and tropical climate draw tourists to the archipelago, where tourism is a major contributor to the economy. Zanzibar sits off the coast of mainland Tanzania, an East African country.

title: Police evacuate 12,000 from rapper Don Toliver concert after substance release
summary: British police have evacuated over 12,000 fans from a Don Toliver concert after an unknown substance was released in the crowd
story: British police have evacuated over 12,000 fans from a Don Toliver concert after an unknown substance was released in the crowd

LONDON -- More than 12,000 fans were evacuated from a concert by American rapper Don Toliver and over 80 were treated by medics after an unknown irritant was released in the crowd, authorities in the English city of Manchester said Monday.

Greater Manchester Police said officers were called around 10 p.m. (2200 GMT) Sunday to the Co-op Live arena after reports of people being affected by a substance, initially believed to be tear gas. Footage shared on social media appeared to show concertgoers coughing and covering their mouths as they left the venue.
The force declared a “major incident,” which allows different emergency services to coordinate their response.
Concertgoer Ben Stevenson told the Manchester Evening News he was in the standing area of the arena when he “started coughing and (my) eyes were kind of itchy.”

He said Toliver left the stage and the venue lights came on, but it was not until almost an hour later that an announcement said, “due to an unforeseen issue, the show is over, and please make your way out at your own pace.”
Joey Howe, a concertgoer, told BBC Radio Manchester that there was a “horrible smell” and people rushed out of the venue.
“People were coming through in wheelchairs, choking. It was really distressing,” he said.
One person was taken to a hospital and more than 80 were assessed at the scene, with some reporting eye and respiratory symptoms, the North West Ambulance Service said.
It said “decontamination is being carried out as a precaution” at the venue.
Police Assistant Chief Constable Steph Parker said: “Anyone who has left the event and since become unwell is advised to attend their local hospital.”
“We will now begin to fully understand what this substance was and how this incident came about,” she said.
Co-op Live, which opened in 2024, is about 2 miles (3.2 kilometers) from Manchester Arena, where 22 people were killed when a bomber blew himself up during an Ariana Grande concert in 2017.
Co-op Live said in a statement that venue bosses were working with police to identify the cause of the incident.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham's spokesman, Tom Wells, said the incident was “deeply worrying” and "many families will understandably be anxious this morning.” He urged people to let police conduct a full investigation.

Grammy Award- nominated trap and R&B rapper-singer Toliver, who features on the soundtrack to the new “Grand Theft Auto” game, is scheduled to perform at London’s O2 Arena on Monday and Wembley Arena on Tuesday as part of his Nitrous tour.

title: India announces a $1.6 billion aid package for Nepal’s flood recovery
summary: India has announced a $1.62 billion aid package to help Nepal rebuild after devastating floods
story: India has announced a $1.62 billion aid package to help Nepal rebuild after devastating floods
NEW DELHI -- India announced Monday a $1.62 billion economic assistance package to help Nepal rebuild areas devastated by floods, providing a major boost to the country’s recovery efforts.

The Aug. 26 floods in Nepal destroyed roads, bridges, power plants, farms and homes, causing an estimated $4.7 billion in losses, according to Nepali authorities. The U.N. Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage has also pledged about $20 million to support Nepal’s recovery.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the aid after meeting Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah in New Delhi. Shah is on his first visit to India since taking office in March, six months after a youth-led uprising over corruption and nepotism forced former Prime Minister K.P. Sharma Oli from power.

Modi said the assistance would help restore infrastructure, rebuild communities and support people who lost their homes and livelihoods. The floods killed 1,500 people and left more than 5,200 missing.
Modi and Shah also virtually inaugurated a hydropower project and an oil storage facility in Nepal, as well as an oil pipeline and a cross-border train service connecting the two countries.

Nepal shares an open border with India, allowing people to cross without passports or visas. India has traditionally wielded considerable influence in the Himalayan nation, but ties have been strained by territorial disputes and accusations of political interference.
China, meanwhile, has expanded its presence in Nepal in recent years, investing in airports, highways and hydropower projects.

Despite growing Chinese influence in Nepal, the landlocked country remains heavily dependent on India for fuel and other essential supplies. At the same time, energy ties have become increasingly reciprocal, with India importing around 1,200 MW of electricity from Nepal.

title: Turkish authorities search for lioness spotted on outskirts of Istanbul
summary: Police and animal welfare teams in Istanbul are searching for a lioness seen prowling the city’s outskirts
story: Police and animal welfare teams in Istanbul are searching for a lioness seen prowling the city’s outskirts
ISTANBUL -- Police and animal welfare teams in Istanbul are searching for a lioness seen prowling the city’s outskirts, Turkish officials said Monday.

A resident spotted the animal Sunday evening in Uskumrukoy, an upmarket neighborhood on the northern edge of Istanbul’s European side, surrounded by forests. The lioness was later captured on security camera footage.
“The location of the lion has been identified, and the necessary care is being taken to capture it alive,” the Istanbul governor’s office said in a statement posted on social media.

Grainy images published by the Demiroren News Agency showed the lioness walking through a grassy area. It was unclear where the animal came from, though some media reports suggested it had escaped from a nearby home. The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office launched an investigation focused on identifying its owner.

The National Parks Directorate said specialist veterinarians and teams equipped with thermal imaging cameras were assisting in the search. More than 70 personnel, supported by drones, were searching in and around the nearby Belgrade Forest, which covers 54 square kilometers north of Istanbul. The forest was closed to vehicles and pedestrians.
Local resident Arda Koc said he saw the lioness after joining the search on Sunday evening.

“I took my car and went out for a drive hoping to see it,” he said in comments reported by the Cumhuriyet newspaper. “While I was driving, it suddenly jumped out in front of me. At first I was scared. After that, I immediately notified the gendarmerie.”

The big cat's appearance has gripped the public’s imagination, drawing people to help with the search. Yusuf Yalcin arrived wearing a lion costume beneath a jersey of local soccer team Galatasaray, nicknamed the Lions.
“Hopefully, the lion will be tranquilized and neutralized without anyone getting hurt,” he told Demiroren.
Residents were warned of the danger, and police were stationed on roads leading into and out of the neighborhood.

Sariyer District Mayor Mustafa Oktay Aksu noted that the lioness had not harmed chickens she passed at night, indicating she had been hand-reared. However, he warned that she should still be treated as dangerous.

Turkey has become a hub for the illegal trade in wild animals as traffickers exploit its air links to Africa and Asia. In December 2024, a young gorilla was rescued after being discovered at Istanbul Airport on a flight from Nigeria to Thailand.

title: Thai court upholds royal defamation conviction for opposition lawmaker and cuts sentence to 3 years
summary: An appeals court has upheld the conviction of an opposition lawmaker for defaming Thailand’s monarchy in social media posts but reduced her prison sentence from six years to three
story: An appeals court has upheld the conviction of an opposition lawmaker for defaming Thailand’s monarchy in social media posts but reduced her prison sentence from six years to three
BANGKOK -- An appeals court Monday upheld the conviction of an opposition lawmaker for defaming Thailand's monarchy in social media posts but reduced her prison sentence from six years to three.

Rukchanok Srinork of the People’s Party was initially charged with lese majeste and violating the Computer Crime Act. In 2023, she was convicted and sentenced to six years in prison over two social media posts.

The appeals court said in a statement that it upheld the conviction in connection with one post but dropped the charges related to the other, halving her sentence. It said the three-year penalty was imposed under the lese majeste law, which carries a heavier penalty than the Computer Crime Act, a broad law regulating online activities.
Rukchanok was accompanied to the hearing by several fellow party members. Supporters greeted her outside the Bangkok court and gave her red roses before she entered.
People’s Party leader Natthaphong Reungpanyawut said the court dropped the charges on one post due to insufficient evidence.

The court later granted Rukchanok's release on bail. If she had been denied bail, she would have been immediately removed from her seat in Parliament. Rukchanok said afterward that she would appeal the ruling with the Supreme Court.

The two posts were shared in 2021 on X, then known as Twitter. One reportedly criticized the monarchy over its links to a coronavirus vaccine, while the other was a repost of an anti-monarchy message. Rukchanok has denied writing the posts herself.

The court’s decision, though expected, underlines that Thailand’s political establishment remains conservative and is sensitive about any perceived threats to the status of the country’s monarchy. The progressive People’s Party is now the main opposition in Parliament after finishing second to the conservative Bhumjaithai Party in this year’s election.

The lese majeste law, also known as Article 112 of the Criminal Code, is controversial not only because it has been used to punish things as simple as liking a post on Facebook, but also because anyone — not just royals or the authorities — can lodge a complaint that most of the time leads to detention during lengthy legal proceedings.
A conviction of defaming the monarchy carries a prison term of up to 15 years, and critics say the law has often been used to quash political dissent.
Student-led pro-democracy demonstrations starting in 2020 sought reforms of the lese majeste law, but the protesters became targets of the law.
Thai Lawyers for Human Rights, a law advocacy group, says more than 290 people, many of them student activists, have been charged with violating Article 112 since early 2020.

title: Indonesian rescuers race to find 34 missing workers after a deadly candy factory fire
summary: Indonesian rescuers are searching for 34 missing workers after a deadly fire swept through a candy factory west of Jakarta
story: Indonesian rescuers are searching for 34 missing workers after a deadly fire swept through a candy factory west of Jakarta
JAKARTA, Indonesia -- Indonesian rescuers searched Monday for 34 missing workers after a deadly fire swept through a candy factory west of Jakarta.

Saturday’s fire broke out at the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia factory in Banten province. Firefighters battled flames for about 14 hours before largely containing the blaze tearing through the three-story building.

About 300 workers were inside the factory when the fire erupted, officials said. Of those, 63 were believed to have been in the hardest-hit area, mostly on the second floor where the flames originated from a cooling unit.

Indonesia’s National Search and Rescue Agency, or Basarnas, did not immediately offer a death toll, but said they collected human remains in 24 body bags for identification through forensic examination.
Meanwhile, rescuers saved 29 workers, five of whom were hospitalized, and continue to search for the missing.

More than 500 rescue personnel, including soldiers, police, Indonesian Red Cross personnel, and volunteers, joined the emergency response, according to Basarnas, to locate the victims within an area of about 2,000 square meters (21,527 square feet), while anxious relatives awaited news.
The factory produces Milkita, an Indonesian brand of milk-based candies and snack products exported to more than 40 countries worldwide.
Indonesia has experienced a series of deadly industrial fires in recent years, raising concerns about workplace safety standards and emergency preparedness at manufacturing facilities.

title: Carney enlists fake Trump for laughs at Canada's annual press gallery dinner
summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney shared the stage with a fake Donald Trump and two versions of himself Saturday, enlisting comedians to help roast the U.S. president and Canadian politicians at an annual dinner with journalists
story: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney shared the stage with a fake Donald Trump and two versions of himself Saturday, enlisting comedians to help roast the U.S. president and Canadian politicians at an annual dinner with journalists

OTTAWA, Ontario -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney shared the stage with a fake Donald Trump and another version of himself this weekend, enlisting comedians to help roast the U.S. president and Canadian politicians at an annual dinner with journalists.
“I am pressing the emergency comedy button,” Carney said Saturday as comedian Mark McKinney appeared impersonating the prime minister, followed by Mark Critch playing Trump.
Critch recreated Trump’s trademark forceful handshake, exchanging grips with Carney and McKinney onstage.
Carney also poked fun at Trump’s lavish makeover of the Oval Office.
“This is a tough room. And I’ve been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator,” Carney said.
Since returning to the White House, Trump has filled the Oval Office with gold accents, gilded decorations and portraits.
The annual Parliamentary Press Gallery dinner is Canada’s version of a Washington political roast, where politicians and journalists trade jokes and insults.

Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre took aim at former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau’s relationship with American pop star Katy Perry, joking that Trudeau was doing to a “faded pop princess” what he had done to Canada during his decade in power.
The remark drew criticism online as sexist and demeaning toward Perry.
Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour, a former Supreme Court justice who represents Britain’s King Charles III as Canada’s head of state, mocked Carney’s extensive international travel.
“Do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he’s supposed to be,” she said.

title: Poland says Russia twice tried to kill a Ukrainian American rapper
summary: Denmark expelled a Russian official after it said it thwarted an alleged plot.
story: Denmark expelled a Russian official after it said it thwarted an alleged plot.

WARSAW, Poland -- Denmark has expelled a Russian official after it said it had thwarted an alleged plot to kill a Ukrainian American citizen on Danish soil. The case took a new twist Sunday when Polish authorities revealed that the same man was allegedly targeted by Moscow's intelligence services last summer in Poland.

Denmark is expected to ask the European Union this week for more decisive action stemming from the case, perhaps restricting Russian citizens from entering and traveling freely within the EU. Poland said it would support such measures.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Russia’s threats were becoming more real, reaching EU soil as the bloc continues supporting Ukraine as Moscow's full-scale invasion nears the five-year mark.
The case involves Albert Vasiliev, a rapper who performs under the name Kyivstoner and holds Ukrainian and U.S. citizenship, according to Danish media.

The assassination attempt in Denmark was planned for Sept. 25 during a concert north of Copenhagen, according to the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, known by its acronym PET. It said the plot was “planned and initiated by Russian intelligence services.”

The plot was thwarted by authorities, the Danish prime minister’s office said Friday. PET said two men were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service in operating in Denmark. They were linked to Loyal to Familia, it said, a banned gang known for “extensive, serious and violent criminal activity.”
Russia dismissed the allegations through its embassy in Copenhagen, saying the accusations were unsubstantiated.
Denmark responded by expelling Russia’s defense attaché.

“In our assessment, the individual concerned was a particular target of the Russian intelligence services," said Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen, director general of PET. “The case demonstrates that Russian intelligence services are both willing and capable of initiating an assassination attempt on Danish soil — at a public event and using individuals from Danish criminal gangs. This is a concrete indication of the heightened threat posed by Russia.”
As Denmark announced the plot against the rapper on Friday, the Polish Foreign Ministry posted on X that it was noting the news with “outrage and concern."

“This is another assassination attempt against this person — the first took place on Polish territory in August 2026 but was thwarted thanks to the efforts of the Polish services and the would-be perpetrator, a Russian citizen, was detained,” the ministry said.
The suspect, who was allegedly recruited by Russia’s secret services, was detained by Polish authorities on Aug. 7.
Maciej Wewiór, a Foreign Ministry spokesman, confirmed to The Associated Press the previous attempt to kill Vasiliev in Poland.

On Aug. 13, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk disclosed the plot to kill a Ukrainian American citizen in Warsaw was thwarted, noting it was the first time that “someone on the order of Russia” sought to attack a U.S. citizen on the territory of another NATO country.
Tusk did not, however, disclose Vasiliev's name, saying only that the target “was uncomfortable” for Russian President Vladimir Putin's government.

Vasiliev was born in Kyiv in 1991, according to Polish media. He posted online comedy sketches and was a former member of the Ukrainian band Hryby. He also was popular in Russia before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
But he left Ukraine after the war broke out and lived for two years in the U.S. before moving to Slovakia. He has expressed his support for Ukraine against Russia.
He performed across Europe this year before his concerts were cancelled for security reasons.

Russia's domestic security service, the FSB, accused Vasiliev of being involved in supplying drones for an alleged Ukrainian attack on a defense enterprise in the Moscow region. It said he was “acting under the patronage” of Ukraine's internal security service, the SBU.
Danish broadcaster DR reported that Vasiliev denied the FSB accusations

He did not comment on social media about the plot against him in Poland, but DR reported that he announced on Instagram that “the intelligence service banned us from holding the concert” referring to the cancellation of his event in Denmark.
Western officials have accused Russia and its proxies of staging dozens of attacks and other incidents across Europe since the invasion of Ukraine.
“Russia’s hybrid threats are becoming less and less hybrid, and more and more real,” said von der Leyen, the EC president, who condemned the alleged plot against Vasiliev in Denmark.

The Polish Foreign Ministry said in a statement that "the events in Denmark are another example of Russia’s criminal activity on the territory of an EU member state, aimed at intimidating and destabilizing our societies.”
Russia has denied accusations by Western officials that it was conducting a sabotage campaign in Europe.
Joanna Kozlowska in London contributed.

title: Suspected Ukrainian sea drones hit Russian warship at Benghazi naval base, Libyan officials say
summary: The sea drone strike triggered an explosion and fire in Benghazi.
story: The sea drone strike triggered an explosion and fire in Benghazi.
CAIRO -- A suspected Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship Sunday at a naval base in Libya, officials said, the latest attack in the North African nation linked to the Russia-Ukraine war.
The strike at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette, and ignited a fire at the facility, two Libyan military officials said.

They said that several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya, according to an initial investigation into the attack. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, they said.
The officials, affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya, spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to talk with reporters.

Libya has been divided since a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime dictator Moammar Gadhafi, who was later killed, in 2011. A U.N.-supported government is based in Tripoli and a rival administration is located in the east. The oil-rich nation remains a focal point for a long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.
The eastern Libya-based government said in a statement that the strike Sunday caused an explosion and fire at the base, which was later extinguished.
