title: Giants and 49ers make the biggest statements in Week 11
summary: The New York Giants and San Francisco 49ers made the biggest statements on a Sunday filled with predictable outcomes
story: The New York Giants and San Francisco 49ers made the biggest statements on a Sunday filled with predictable outcomes
The New York Giants and San Francisco 49ers made the biggest statements on a Sunday filled with predictable outcomes.

The Giants earned their most impressive victory of the season, beating the Jacksonville Jaguars 23-18. Facing an offense that had scored more than 30 points in four straight games, New York’s defense stepped up. Abdul Carter had two sacks, Trevor Lawrence was picked twice and Jacksonville didn’t reach the end zone until the fourth quarter.

“Really, really, really proud of this win. This is the first real football win,” Giants coach John Harbaugh said. “This is a win that you can learn from and grow from. A lot of things we’ve got to get better at. A lot of things we’ve got to improve on, but I’m proud of our guys. I just love the way they found a way to win the game. … This is where the season starts. We talked about that. It starts now. Now is when you find a way to win those games and you usually win them in the fourth quarter. Our defense was just incredible.”
The matchup between the NFC East-leading Giants (6-3-1) and AFC South-leading Jaguars (7-3) was one of only two games in Week 11 that featured winning teams on both sides.
The other was the primetime game between the Vikings and 49ers in Mexico City. That one wasn’t even close.

Brock Purdy and the 49ers dominated Minnesota 35-10. Purdy was outstanding in his first win against Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores in three tries. He executed coach Kyle Shanahan’s game plan perfectly, going 21 of 26 for 255 yards with three touchdown passes and no turnovers as San Francisco became the first team to score more than 23 points against the Vikings this season.
“Everyone was dialed in, Kyle had a great game plan and complementary football,” Purdy said. “The defense went and got the ball back for us and we made it happen.”

The 49ers (9-1) lead the NFC in the race for the No. 1 seed and home-field advantage throughout the playoffs. But they have a tough schedule coming up, starting with a home game against Seattle (6-4) next week.

The Vikings (7-3) have lost three of four after a 6-0 start. Kirk Cousins threw a critical pick-6 in his second start since joining Minnesota at the trade deadline. He’ll face one of his former teams when the Vikings host Atlanta (3-7) next week.
All four teams favored by double-digits handled their business, avoiding letdowns.

Josh Allen threw for 304 yards and one touchdown, and Buffalo’s defense made it 15-plus quarters without allowing a touchdown in a 26-9 win over Miami. The Bills are 9-1 for just the fifth time in team history, and first since a 10-1 start in 1991.

Patrick Mahomes had 324 yards passing and three touchdowns in Kansas City’s 34-7 rout over Arizona. The Chiefs (8-2) made sure they didn’t get caught looking ahead to a prime-time matchup at Buffalo on Thanksgiving night.
Allen and the Bills are 5-1 against Mahomes and the Chiefs in the regular season but 0-4 in the playoffs. The winner gets the edge for the No. 1 seed in the AFC.
A loss could drop the Chiefs out of first place in the AFC West.

Rookie Jonah Coleman ran for 111 yards and three touchdowns, leading Denver to a 38-24 win over Fernando Mendoza and Las Vegas. The Broncos (8-2) won their sixth straight game to keep up with the Chiefs. They’ll visit Pittsburgh (6-4) on Black Friday.

Jeffery Simmons got three of Chicago’s six sacks and the Bears beat New Orleans 21-13. It was the second straight lackluster win for Chicago (8-2). Caleb Williams rebounded from a four-interception game with an efficient outing — 15 of 23, 181 yards, two touchdowns, one interception. Still, the overall offensive performance wasn’t up to the Bears’ standard.
They’ll have to be much better on Thursday when they face Detroit (8-2) in a battle for first place in the NFC North.
The Lions had no problem against Tampa Bay in a 31-21 win. Jared Goff tossed two touchdown passes and Jahmyr Gibbs ran for two scores.
The biggest surprise was Philadelphia’s 19-16 win over the Steelers. The Eagles had lost seven in a row, but the defense gave Aaron Rodgers trouble all game, sacking him five times.
Pittsburgh has lost two in a row and fell to 2-4 on the road. The Steelers are 4-0 at home and hold a one-game lead over New England for the final wild-card spot.

title: FIFA picks US to co-host 2031 Women's World Cup and UK for 2035 edition
summary: The United States will co-host the 2031 Women's World Cup with Mexico, Costa Rica, and Jamaica
story: The United States will co-host the 2031 Women's World Cup with Mexico, Costa Rica, and Jamaica
ZURICH -- The United States will co-host another soccer World Cup in 2031, with the United Kingdom set to follow four years later.

FIFA on Monday confirmed the U.S. will co-host the 2031 Women’s World Cup in a regional project together with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica. A UK-bid led by England was also ratified for the 2035 edition.

The winning candidates and FIFA president Gianni Infantino promised commercially successful tournaments and to reinvest all the profits in women's soccer. The 2031 edition will be expanded to feature 48 teams for the first time, in line with the men's World Cup.

“This will be the largest women’s sporting event in history,” the U.S. Soccer Federation president, Cindy Parlow Cone, told FIFA members in a pre-vote presentation at the governing body's headquarters in Zurich. “Which means we have to deliver.”
There were no rival bids for either tournament, ensuring that the U.S. and England — two of the heavyweights of women’s soccer — will spearhead the hosting of the first expanded tournaments.
The 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil will have 32 teams.
The U.S.-led 2031 project offers FIFA a choice of stadiums in 20 cities: 14 in the U.S., four in Mexico plus San José in Costa Rica and Kingston, Jamaica.
The United Kingdom bid includes England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales and offers a choice from 19 venues, including Wembley Stadium in London.
The two bids had been alone in the contest for the past 20 months and were approved Monday by acclamation in an online meeting of FIFA's 211 member federations.

The U.S. previously hosted the Women's World Cup alone in 1999 and 2003. It has won the tournament four times, including the first edition in 1991 in China — when it featured 12 teams — and at home in 1999.
England has never hosted a Women's World Cup. The only time it hosted the men's World Cup, in 1966, it won its only title.
Northern Ireland has plans to host games at Windsor Park in Belfast at a renovated 23,000-capacity stadium. That is big enough for a Women’s World Cup but not for the men’s European Championship.
Euro 2028 is being hosted by England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland, which has the 50,000-seat national soccer and rugby stadium in Dublin.
For the second time in less than two years, FIFA is confirming a double award of World Cup hosts without rival bids.

In December 2024, FIFA member federations rubber-stamped the unprecedented six-nation, three-continent bid for the men’s World Cup in 2030 from Spain, Portugal, Morocco, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay.
That cleared the way for FIFA to also award the 2034 World Cup to Saudi Arabia in a fast-track process that seemed designed to exclude other candidates.

title: Zverev tops the year's final rankings despite loss to Alcaraz at the ATP Finals
summary: The No. 1 next to his name doesn’t mean that Alexander Zverev can suddenly beat the two players still regarded as the best in tennis
story: The No. 1 next to his name doesn’t mean that Alexander Zverev can suddenly beat the two players still regarded as the best in tennis
TURIN, Italy -- The No. 1 next to his name doesn’t mean that Alexander Zverev can suddenly beat the two players still regarded as the best in tennis.
That was more than evident at the ATP Finals.
Carlos Alcaraz dominated Zverev for long stretches in the final and beat his top-ranked opponent in straight sets to add a title at the prestigious season-ending event to his career Grand Slam.
Jannik Sinner, meanwhile, has beaten Zverev 10 straight times — including in this year’s Wimbledon final — but he ended his season early due to a right knee injury.

The computer rankings look strictly at the numbers over the previous 52 weeks. And Zverev has a healthy lead in that category: He ends the year with 10,350 points — far more than No. 2 Sinner (7,950) and No. 3 Alcaraz (7,600) in the final list released Monday.
Alcaraz missed 4 ½ months and two Grand Slams due to a right wrist injury and Sinner hasn’t played since defending his Wimbledon title in July.
Still, Zverev said he’s “very comfortable” with being No. 1, “because I’ve worked my whole life to reach this position.

“Sure, I could point out that Jannik has been injured, or that Carlos was out for a few months,” Zverev added. “But honestly, I believe what I’ve achieved this year represents one of the mentally strongest seasons we’ve ever seen in tennis.”

Zverev brought up Sinner’s meltdown in a Paris heat wave and Alcaraz’s five-set loss to Ben Shelton in New York while he went on to win his first two Grand Slams at the French Open and U.S. Open, respectively.
Zverev also noted that his “worst” result in the majors and the season-ending championships this year was a five-set loss to Alcaraz in the Australian Open semifinals.
“Everywhere else I played at least the final,” Zverev said. “If someone thinks that I didn’t deserve it, they’re free to have their own opinion.”
Alcaraz went undefeated at the Finals despite injuring his right thigh during the group stage — which limited his movement at times.
The seven-time Grand Slam champion ends the ATP season with three straight titles and a 14-match winning streak after also claiming titles in Vienna and Paris.

“Everybody feels he’s the No. 1. Me, Sascha (Zverev’s nickname), Jannik, (Ben) Shelton, I think everybody thinks themselves are the No. 1 of the world,” said Alcaraz, who finished 2025 at No. 1. “But the No. 1 is Sascha. … We have to give credit to him.”

Added Felix Auger-Aliassime, the Canadian who ends the year at No. 17 after reaching a career-high ranking of No. 4 in June: “(Zverev) doesn’t have to defend himself. … The numbers are the numbers and that’s how the world turns.

“Obviously he’s going to be challenged by not just Carlos and Sinner next year, but by all the players to try to take his spot. And he’s going to have to defend it,” Auger-Aliassime said. “He’s had the best (year) of everyone so it’s deserved.”
Zverev was on the verge of a breakthrough before he tore ligaments in his right ankle during his 2022 French Open semifinal against Rafael Nadal.
Zverev is still affected by his ankle at times and said it affected his serve against Alcaraz on Sunday. But he also said he has learned to manage the issue and keep it in check at the Slams.

“Health is a huge part of being able to be No. 1 in the world and (Zverev) has been for years — with the exception of that injury — one of the healthiest players,” said Chris Eubanks, a former Wimbledon quarterfinalist who is now a Tennis Channel analyst.

“He’s been very consistent and at some point you kind of felt like that was going to be rewarded,” Eubanks told The Associated Press. “When Carlos and Jannik began to really ascend up the rankings, I remember a lot of people saying, ‘Well, these guys are just going to run the table for the next 10 to 15 years.’ That’s just not realistic because of health. … If Zverev continues to put himself in that situation of being the healthiest and one of the most consistent guys on tour, opportunities open up.”
Zverev — it should be noted — was also officially notified of a lawsuit filed by his former partner last week.
Alcaraz split with longtime coach Juan Carlos Ferrero at the end of last year and promoted Samuel Lopez to his head coach. The player’s older brother, Alvaro, is now his assistant coach.

“I’m really proud about the job and the work Samuel did the whole year, alongside by brother,” Alcaraz said. “I realized how good I have to feel off the court in my life to go and hit the practice court with motivation. … They said really carefully everything to me that was really important.”

title: Pochettino back in Champions League with struggling United as PSG and Madrid protect 100% starts
summary: Mauricio Pochettino is getting another shot at the Champions League, this time with Manchester United
story: Mauricio Pochettino is getting another shot at the Champions League, this time with Manchester United
Mauricio Pochettino’s journey in the Champions League has been defined by a couple of memorable hat tricks and even more missed opportunities.
Now, after a 4½-year absence, he is getting another shot in soccer’s top club competition with Manchester United.

When Pochettino — fresh off a Premier League thrashing by Liverpool in his debut — leads United into its game at Sporting Lisbon on Wednesday, it will be his first Champions League match since his star-studded Paris Saint-Germain team containing that front line of Lionel Messi, Kylian Mbappé and Neymar was dumped out by a last-16 hat trick from Karim Benzema, which kick-started Real Madrid’s remarkable run to the title in 2022.
Pochettino got closer a season earlier, losing with PSG in the semifinals to Manchester City.

He was even closer in 2019, when the Argentine wept tears of joy as he somehow guided Tottenham to the final — remember, anyone, that sensational hat trick by Lucas Moura to down Ajax in the semis? — only to lose to Liverpool in the title match.
How far will he get with United?

Well, qualifying for the knockout stage is surely Pochettino's first aim after the team’s turbulent start to the league phase that has included a 4-1 thrashing in Como and a comeback 3-2 win over Roma that wasn’t enough to save Michael Carrick from being fired.

United is on six points from a possible 12 and in 17th place in the 36-team standings heading into the fifth round of games, when Pochettino will be in the spotlight perhaps more than superstar players like Mbappé and Erling Haaland.

Teams finishing in the top eight qualify directly to the last 16 and those placing No. 9-24 will compete in two-legged playoffs for the remaining eight spots in the knockouts. Anything below that and you're out.

Few could say for certain where United will end up, given the team still has to play Leipzig and Bayern Munich at home before finishing the league phase with a trip to Villarreal in late January. After all, this is a club that is in next-to-last place in the Premier League and reeling from a 4-0 loss at fierce rival Liverpool in Pochettino's first match in charge after leaving the U.S. men's team.
Given that United played with 10 men for more than 80 minutes at Anfield, the trip to Sporting might be a first real chance to judge Pochettino at his new team.
“We are in a situation,” Pochettino acknowledged, “that is very complicated, very difficult.”
Two teams have yet to drop a point so far — and perhaps unsurprisingly they are PSG and Madrid.
Indeed, with Arsenal and Barcelona also in the top five, and Man City and Liverpool elsewhere in the top eight, Europe's heavyweights are already flexing their muscles in the league stage.

PSG hosts Roma on Wednesday and the defending champion's squad strength is being tested with Désiré Doué joining fellow forward Khvicha Kvaratskhelia in sustaining an ACL injury that is set to keep them out until next season.
On Tuesday, Madrid is at home to PSV Eindhoven and third-place Arsenal hosts Borussia Dortmund.
Fifth-place Barcelona faces one of its longest ever away trips, more than 5,000 kilometers (3,100 miles) to play Sabah FK in Azerbaijan on Wednesday.

The surprise name in the top eight is fourth-place Como, whose home match against AEK Athens offers the Italian upstart a good chance to keep its exalted company high up in the standings and secure at least a playoff spot for Cesc Fabregas' team.

That's because it will soon get harder for Como: its eight-game league-phase schedule ends with matches against PSG and Barcelona, for which Italy striker Moise Kean might be missing because of a leg injury.
In its first Champions League campaign, Como has already outclassed United and routed Lens 9-1 — matching the biggest margin of victory in the competition.
Kevin De Bruyne is getting another return to longtime club Man City with Napoli. He'll hope his latest appearance at Etihad Stadium is longer than the last one.

The Belgian — one of City's greatest ever players — was substituted after just 26 minutes of Napoli's 2-0 loss at the Etihad in league play last season, sacrificed following the sending-off of teammate Giovanni Di Lorenzo.
At least that gave City fans the chance to give him another standing ovation. Expect another one on Tuesday.
Still without a point is Slovan Bratislava, the Slovak champion that has lost four straight games so far and 14 in a row in total in the competition’s main phase.
It's the longest ever run of defeats in the Champions League era, which dates to 1992, but still two short of the European Cup record of 16 held by Jeunesse Esch of Luxembourg.
Can Slovan — coached by former Barcelona and Man City midfielder Yaya Touré — stop the rot at home to Real Betis on Tuesday?

story: Rookie Roman Kantserov scored his first NHL hat trick and had an assist as the Chicago Blackhawks beat the Vancouver Canucks 6-3

VANCOUVER, British Columbia -- Rookie Roman Kantserov got his first NHL hat trick and added an assist as the Chicago Blackhawks used a four-goal first period to beat the Vancouver Canucks 6-3 on Sunday night.
Frank Nazar extended his scoring streak to six games with a goal and an assist for the Blackhawks, who won back-to-back games for just the second time this season.
Tyler Bertuzzi had a power-play goal and two assists, and Dominic Toninato also scored. Patrick Kane added two assists and Drew Commesso made 22 saves.
Zeev Buium, Filip Chytil and Jake DeBrusk scored for the Canucks. Brock Boeser had an assist to extend his career-high points streak to 12 games (four goals, 12 assists).
Vancouver starting goaltender Nick Tolopilo gave up four goals on 11 shots before being replaced by Kevin Lankinen at 12:44 of the first period. Lankinen ended the game with 17 saves.
Nazar scored on a breakaway 35 seconds into the game. Bertuzzi made it 2-0 on a power play at 2:48.
Kantserov, on another power play, and Toninato made it 4-0 before Buium scored for Vancouver.

Chytil cut Chicago’s lead in half early in the second period when his pass went off Blackhawks forward Jordan Greenway’s leg and into the net. Kantserov restored the three-goal lead by deflecting defenseman Alex Vlasic’s shot past Lankinen.
DeBrusk made it 5-3 late in the period on a delayed penalty, lifting a puck over Commesso’s glove. Kantserov then completed his hat trick in the third period.
Both teams were missing key players. The Canucks were without center Elias Pettersson, while captain Connor Bedard didn’t dress for Chicago.
Chicago scored three goals on four power-play chances. The Blackhawks have scored power-play goals in six consecutive games, going 10 for 18. They had just five in their first 18 games.

title: Brock Purdy carves up the Vikings' D with 3 TD passes in the 49ers' 35-10 win in Mexico City
summary: Brock Purdy carved up the NFL’s stingiest defense with three touchdown passes in the first half and the San Francisco 49ers beat the Minnesota Vikings 35-10 in a matchup of NFC powerhouses
story: Brock Purdy carved up the NFL’s stingiest defense with three touchdown passes in the first half and the San Francisco 49ers beat the Minnesota Vikings 35-10 in a matchup of NFC powerhouses
MEXICO CITY -- Brock Purdy and the San Francisco 49ers offense turned the much ballyhooed matchup between one of the game's top offenses and the stingiest defenses into a one-sided affair.
Purdy carved up the Minnesota with three touchdown passes in the first half and the 49ers beat the Vikings 35-10 Sunday night in a matchup of NFC powerhouses.

“You have to be aggressive and don’t second guess yourself,” Purdy said. “Obviously try to read it out the best you can but when you have players that can go get the ball, allow them to go and make plays. I just feel like our guys did that around me today. It wasn’t a one-man show. It was a really good team effort.”

The game played before a raucous pro-49ers crowd at historic Estadio Azteca was billed as a matchup between one of the league's most dangerous offenses in the 49ers (9-1) against a defense for the Vikings (7-3) that had rattled quarterbacks all season with an aggressive blitz package.
Coordinator Brian Flores' schemes didn't work at all against Purdy, who carved up the Minnesota defense for three touchdown drives on the Niners' first four possessions.

“He was so good. He was quick, he was confident, he threw strikes,” said tight end George Kittle, who caught two TD passes. “He’s playing with confidence, he understands the offense, he is confident in the offense. He knows the offense. When he goes out there he just has this aura in the huddle.”
San Francisco built a 28-10 halftime lead thanks to Purdy's stellar play and a pick-6 by Ji'Ayir Brown against Kirk Cousins.

The Niners added the exclamation point in the second half with a 98-yard touchdown drive that featured “MVP!” chants for Purdy and was capped by Christian McCaffrey's 6-yard run that made it 35-10 early in the fourth quarter.
Purdy finished 21 for 26 for 255 yards and a 146 passer rating that was more than double the league-low 69.5 rating that Minnesota entered the game allowing.

“Seemed like he played a lot better than a lot of other guys have versus them, because not many people play that good versus that defense,” coach Kyle Shanahan said. “There’s a reason for that. It’s a huge challenge. It was hard looking at it all week. Brock didn’t get rattled, which he really never does. I think it says a lot about Brock.”

Cousins lost for the second time in three weeks against the Niners, also throwing a pick-6 in Week 9 for the Raiders in his final start before being traded back to Minnesota. He became the first player ever to throw a pick-6 for two teams against the same opponent in a season.
Cousins went 26 for 38 for 235 yards and was unable to follow up his winning performance last week for Minnesota at Green Bay.
But the biggest reason was that the defense that dominated all season got picked apart.

“There’s no group that I have more confidence in than not only those players on defense and that coaching staff,” Vikings coach Kevin O'Connell said. “There’s just no really other way to put it. We just got beat tonight. They made some plays. I think the quarterback’s really good and they got a bunch of really good players and they execute at a really high level.”

The 49ers set the tone early, easily moving down the field on a seven-play, 72-yard drive to open the game. Purdy completed all four of his passes for 55 yards, capped by a 17-yard touchdown to Kittle.
After getting stopped on the second drive, Purdy scored on the next two possessions. He threw an 8-yard touchdown pass to Kittle to make it 14-7 and then a 4-yarder to Mike Evans that made it 21-10.
Brown then intercepted Cousins on the next play from scrimmage and returned it 18 yards for the score that broke the game open.
“The backside safety made a great play,” Cousins said. “I need to feel him and progress and not try to fit it in there.”

The international crowd almost got to see one of the rarest plays in the NFL when the Vikings called for a fair catch at their own 40 with 3 seconds left in the first half. Coach Kevin O'Connell sent out Will Reichard for a fair catch kick, with the teams lined up like a kickoff with no rush.

The 71-yard attempt — which would have eclipsed the NFL record of 68 yards set by Cam Little last season — came up just short. There has been only one successful fair catch kick in the last 50 seasons with Cameron Dicker making a 57-yarder for the Chargers against Denver in 2024.

The teams took drastically different approaches to prepare for the game, which was played at more than 7,300 feet above sea level. The 49ers spent the week training at the Air Force Academy in Colorado — at an altitude of more than 7,000 feet — to acclimate.
The Vikings stayed home but had players use a special elevation room for workouts during the last few weeks that mirrors conditions 9,000 or more feet above sea level.

49ers: RT Colton McKivitz left in the second quarter with a fractured and dislocated left ankle.
Vikings: Host Atlanta next Sunday.
49ers: Host Seattle next Sunday.

title: Karl-Anthony Towns has 30 points and 13 rebounds as Knicks beat Pacers 113-106
summary: Karl-Anthony Towns had 30 points and 13 rebounds, Jalen Brunson added 22 points, and the New York Knicks beat the Indiana Pacers 113-106 to extend their winning streak to five games
story: Karl-Anthony Towns had 30 points and 13 rebounds, Jalen Brunson added 22 points, and the New York Knicks beat the Indiana Pacers 113-106 to extend their winning streak to five games

NEW YORK -- Karl-Anthony Towns had 30 points and 13 rebounds, Jalen Brunson added 22 points, and the New York Knicks beat the Indiana Pacers 113-106 on Sunday night to extend their winning streak to five games.
Towns, who missed Saturday night’s buzzer-beater victory over Portland due to an illness, shot 9 for 14 from the field including 4 for 4 on 3-pointers.

Landry Shamet scored 17 points while Josh Hart finished with 10 points, 11 assists and 10 rebounds for the Knicks. It was Hart's 18th triple-double with the Knicks, tying Michael Ray Richardson for second on the team’s career list. Walt Frazier holds the team record with 23.
The Knicks were without OG Anunoby, who missed his second straight game because of tightness in his left calf. Backup guard Deuce McBride was held out due to tightness in the left abductor.
Pascal Siakam scored 25 points, Andrew Nembhard finished with 16 and Ivica Zubac had 10 points and 14 rebounds for the Pacers, who have lost their last four games.
Towns in the closing minutes of the third quarter outscored Indiana 10-2, capping it off with a 3-pointer that extended the Knicks lead 86-74 with 54 seconds left in the period.
Indiana fell behind by 12 points after Mikal Bridges hit a 3-pointer that made it 92-80 and trimmed it to 95-87 following a three-point play from Kelly Oubre Jr. with 7:31 left in the fourth quarter.
A fadeaway jumper from Brunson increased the Knicks advantage to 110-95 — their largest lead of the night — with 2:35 remaining.
The Pacers kept it close and went on a 6-0 run capped by a layup from Obi Toppin that made it 112-106 with 25 seconds remaining.
Brunson then put the game out of reach with a free throw after Quenton Jackson was called for a foul away from the ball.

summary: Édier Ocampo and rookie Bruno Caicedo helped set up goals for each other and the Vancouver Whitecaps blanked Real Salt Lake 2-0 in a first-round opener
story: Édier Ocampo and rookie Bruno Caicedo helped set up goals for each other and the Vancouver Whitecaps blanked Real Salt Lake 2-0 in a first-round opener
VANCOUVER, British Columbia -- Édier Ocampo and rookie Bruno Caicedo helped set up goals for each other and the Vancouver Whitecaps blanked Real Salt Lake 2-0 on Sunday night in a first-round opener.
Yohei Takaoka finished with five saves for the top seed in the Western Conference. It was his third clean sheet in 12 postseason starts after posting 13 in each of the past two regular seasons.

Ocampo's first postseason assist helped set up Caicedo's netter in the 55th minute for some insurance. Oliver Larraz also assisted on the score in his first playoff match with the club.

title: Blues rally from late 3-goal deficit and beat Oilers 5-4 in shootout for 4th straight win
summary: The surging St. Louis Blues overcame a three-goal deficit in the final 10 minutes of regulation for the first time in franchise history and then beat the Edmonton Oilers in a shootout for a dramatic 5-4 victory
story: The surging St. Louis Blues overcame a three-goal deficit in the final 10 minutes of regulation for the first time in franchise history and then beat the Edmonton Oilers in a shootout for a dramatic 5-4 victory

ST. LOUIS -- The surging St. Louis Blues overcame a three-goal deficit in the final 10 minutes of regulation for the first time in franchise history and then beat the Edmonton Oilers in a shootout for a dramatic 5-4 victory on Sunday night for their fourth straight win.
Dalibor Dvorsky, Philip Broberg, Pavel Buchnevich and Jimmy Snuggerud each scored for the Blues (13-9-2), who have netted 26 goals during their current four-game win streak.
St. Louis, which beat New Jersey 9-6 at home on Saturday, is 8-3-1 at the Enterprise Center this season.
Broberg, Buchnevich and Snuggerud all scored within a stretch of 5:11 in the third period. Snuggerud’s team-leading 14th goal of the season tied the score at 4-4 with 4:42 remaining in regulation.

Jake Neighbors and Mason McTavish scored shootout goals for the Blues. Goalie Joel Hofer allowed a goal by Connor McDavid but then stopped shots from Leon Draisaitl and Owen Michaels on the Oilers’ final two attempts.

Draisaitl scored a second-period goal and became the ninth player in franchise history (72nd the in NHL) to reach 1,100 career points. The 31-year-old has 457 goals and 643 assists in 881 career games.

Kasperi Kapanen had a goal and an assist for the Oilers against his former team, and Filip Hallander and Colton Dach added goals. McDavid, Evan Bouchard, Connor Murphy, Mathieu Joseph, Vasily Podkolzin and Jason Dickinson each had an assist.
The Pacific Division-leading Oilers (17-5-4) have lost three straight overall and fell to 10-2-2 on the road this season.

title: Jokic's triple-double, Murray's 45 points lead Nuggets to 151-145 overtime win over Bulls
summary: Nikola Jokic recorded the 202nd triple double of his career and Jamal Murray scored eight of his season-high 45 points in overtime as the Denver Nuggets held off the Chicago Bulls 151-145
story: Nikola Jokic recorded the 202nd triple double of his career and Jamal Murray scored eight of his season-high 45 points in overtime as the Denver Nuggets held off the Chicago Bulls 151-145

CHICAGO -- Nikola Jokic had 37 points, 18 rebounds and 11 assists for the 202nd triple double of his career, Jamal Murray scored eight of his season-high 45 points in overtime, and the Denver Nuggets held off the Chicago Bulls 151-145 on Sunday night.
Jokic closed the gap on Russell Westbrook's NBA record of 209 career triple-doubles.
Murray was 13 for 22 from the floor, 6 for 11 from 3-point range and 13 for 14 from the free-throw line.

Buddy Hield scored 33 points for the short-handed Bulls and Josh Giddey bounced back from a fourth-quarter benching Friday with 23 points, 14 rebounds and a career-high 22 assists. He is the first Bulls player with more than 20 assists in a game since 1985 and the first with a 20-point/20-assist game since Dec. 6, 1969 when Clem Haskins had 23 points and 21 assists against Boston.

Hield stole the ball from Jokic with seven seconds to go and Giddey made an open layup to tie the score at 131 as the Bulls wiped out a seven-point deficit in the final 40 seconds. Jokic missed a 3-point attempt as time expired. Murray helped the Nuggets score the first eight points of overtime.

The Bulls, who had won three of five after a 1-9 start, allowed 130 or more points in regulation for the fifth time this season and fell to 1-5 at home despite a season high 25 3-pointers, led by Hield with seven.
Jalen Smith added a career-high 26 points for the Bulls and Matas Buzelis, who was also benched in Friday's fourth quarter, scored 21 points.

The Bulls were without their two leading scorers, Norman Powell (right hamstring strain) and Caleb Wilson (fractured metacarpal), who are averaging a combined 39.7 points per game, as well as reserve forward Nic Claxton (illness).
Nuggets: Host Dallas on Tuesday night.

story: Jake Oettinger stopped all 33 shots for his NHL-leading fifth shutout of the season and Joel Kiviranta’s second-period goal was the difference in the Dallas Stars’ 1-0 win over the Pittsburgh Penguins

DALLAS -- Jake Oettinger stopped a season-high 34 shots and had his NHL-leading fifth shutout of the season, Joel Kiviranta scored a second-period goal and the Dallas Stars beat the Pittsburgh Penguins 1-0 on Sunday night for their fifth straight win.

The shutout matches the 27-year-old Oettinger’s career high in only 18 games. Sidney Crosby nearly beat him to the opposite top corner in the final 2 minutes after the Penguins pulled goaltender Arturs Silovs.

Kiviranta controlled a cross-ice pass from Wyatt Johnston at the back post and flipped the puck behind Silovs at 12:44 of the middle period as the Stars won their fifth straight to equal their longest winning streak of the season.
Oettinger has 13 wins this season, tied for second in the league, and is 8-1-1 against the Penguins in his career.
The Penguins, who lost at Nashville 4-3 on Saturday night, have dropped four straight. Veteran center Evgeni Malkin missed both games this weekend with an upper-body injury.
Silovs made 22 saves Sunday and lost his fifth consecutive outing in regulation.
Dallas is 7-1-2 when tied after one period and 10-2-1 when scoring first this season.
The Stars, with the league’s No. 2 home penalty kill, snuffed both Penguins power plays. Pittsburgh’s power play, fourth best on the road going into play, is 0 for 7 in the last four games.

summary: Cooper Flagg scored 28 points and made the game-winning free throws with 3.7 seconds left to lift the Dallas Mavericks over the Utah Jazz 116-114 after they squandered an 18-point lead in the fourth quarter on Sunday night
story: Cooper Flagg scored 28 points and made the game-winning free throws with 3.7 seconds left to lift the Dallas Mavericks over the Utah Jazz 116-114 after they squandered an 18-point lead in the fourth quarter on Sunday night

SALT LAKE CITY -- Cooper Flagg scored 28 points and made the game-winning free throws with 3.7 seconds left to lift the Dallas Mavericks over the Utah Jazz 116-114 after they squandered an 18-point lead in the fourth quarter on Sunday night.
Kyrie Irving scored 16 points, all in the first half, as the Mavericks (10-7) barely avoided an epic collapse and won their third in a row.
Svi Mykhailiuk came off the bench to score a career-high 39 points, including 10 of 15 from beyond the arc. Mykhailiuk had 23 points in the fourth quarter to fuel Utah’s (3-15) improbable comeback.
The Mavericks led 114-98 with 2:14 remaining before the Jazz reeled off 16 straight points to tie the game at 104 on Isaiah Collier's driving layup with 4.7 seconds to play.
After Flagg's clutch free throws, the Jazz couldn't get the ball to Mykhailiuk and Kyle Filipowski's 3-point attempt missed at the buzzer.
Mykhailiuk's 10 3-pointer performance is one off the Utah franchise record and is tied for the most in an NBA game this season.
P.J. Washington, who posted his season-high and career-high in points against the Jazz, was out with an illness but it didn't seem to matter until Mykhailiuk's hot streak.

Jaxson Hayes left the game in the second quarter with a knee injury, further decimating Utah's front line. Starting big men Lauri Markkanen (hand), Jusuf Nurkic (foot) and Jaren Jackson Jr. (knee) are still out.

Flagg had eight points and Zaccharie Risacher had two dunks during a 20-5 third-quarter Mavericks run — where they beat the Jazz down the court time after time —to open up an 80-62 advantage, their largest lead of the game.
Utah's 23 turnovers led to 32 points for Dallas.

title: NFL defends incomplete pass ruling on Parker Washington's would-be TD in Jaguars' loss at Giants
summary: The NFL has defended a questionable call that Jacksonville Jaguars receiver Parker Washington did not catch the ball in the back of the end zone for what would have been a fourth-quarter touchdown
story: The NFL has defended a questionable call that Jacksonville Jaguars receiver Parker Washington did not catch the ball in the back of the end zone for what would have been a fourth-quarter touchdown

EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- Parker Washington thought he caught the ball for a crucial touchdown in the fourth quarter, and Jacksonville Jaguars coach Liam Coen was confident enough that he challenged the initial call of an incomplete pass.
The NFL did not see it that way.
The league defended its decision after the Jaguars lost 23-18 at the New York Giants on Sunday, ruling that Washington did not complete the catch.

“It was determined that the receiver did not gain full control of the ball until he was out of bounds,” vice president of instant replay Mark Butterworth told a pool reporter. “He needs to maintain control of the ball throughout the process of the catch.”
Coen relayed that he was told “the ball switched hands.
“That was what it came down to,” Coen said.
Washington felt good about possession but also did not want to blame the defeat on the officiating.
“I saw it on the Jumbotron or whatever we call it,” Washington said. “It didn’t go our way. You can’t hang your head on that. We’ve got to move on and get ready for the next play.”
Trevor Lawrence, who threw two interceptions while under pressure for much of the game, similarly did not want to lament the impact of the would-be touchdown on the result.

“It’s a close play,” Lawrence said. “Obviously, they called it and said it wasn’t. It’s tough. I thought it was incredible that he gave us a shot there and he caught it, and it looked like he had two feet down, but it was close. You can’t leave in the refs’ hands. I think it’s a tough call for them.”
CBS rules analyst Gene Steratore, who was an official in the league for 15 years, disagreed with the decision.
“I still had the right foot down as he's falling,” Steratore said on the broadcast. “I see the ball move a little bit, but I did not think he lost possession of the football.”
Giants coach John Harbaugh was fine with it, saying he thought simply “the ball moved.”

title: Mercury gets its first visitor in years as a pair of spacecraft loop into orbit
summary: The European Space Agency announced BepiColombo's arrival via social media.
story: The European Space Agency announced BepiColombo's arrival via social media.

CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. -- A pair of spacecraft slipped into orbit around Mercury on Saturday after an eight-year cruise through the inner solar system to unravel our littlest planet's mountain of mysteries.

The linked robotic explorers — one European, the other Japanese — will separate from one another next month in order to map and study the scorching little planet from different altitudes. The $2 billion (1.7 billion euros) mission is known collectively as BepiColombo.

The European Space Agency announced BepiColombo's arrival via social media. A series of thruster firings slowed the spacecraft enough to be captured by the planet's weak gravity. But it took several anxious hours before flight controllers in Germany — 94 million miles (152 million kilometers) away — could confirm that BepiColombo had achieved orbit. Teams pored over the data streaming back; additional information was not immediately available.
BepiColombo is only the third spacecraft to visit Mercury — the sun's closest planet and barely bigger than our moon — and the first in more than a decade.

NASA's Mariner 10 flew past Mercury three times in the mid-1970s. The team included the late Italian mathematician Giuseppe “Bepi” Colombo, for whom this latest mission is named. NASA's Messenger spacecraft entered orbit around Mercury in 2011 and, after running out of fuel, crashed into the planet in 2015.

Launched in 2018, BepiColombo took a slower, more roundabout route to get to Mercury, flying once past Earth, twice past Venus and six times past Mercury for gravity-guiding assists. All those loop-de-loops put more than 6 billion miles (10 billion kilometers) on the odometer. The conjoined spacecraft shed their mother ship in September for the final leg of the journey.

Lead project scientist Geraint Jones said he and others can’t wait for all the new data to start streaming down in the spring. The mission will provide the ability to compare “unprecedented measurements taken by two spacecraft at the planet at the same time,” he noted.

Once orbiting separately, the European Space Agency's satellite and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency’s smaller craft will study Mercury’s dense interior and exterior magnetic field, as well as everything in between: impact craters, volcanic plains, mountain ridges and peaks jutting as high as 3 miles (4 1/2 kilometers).

The mercury at Mercury can hit more than 800 degrees (427 degrees Celsius), adding strain to electronic and engineering systems. Space agency officials want to keep the mission going for at least one Earth year — or the equivalent of four Mercury years.
“The spacecraft and its instruments need to be kept as cool as possible, which is a huge technical challenge in itself,” Jones said in an email.

Despite its relative proximity to Earth, Mercury is one of the solar system’s least explored planets. Only outer planets Uranus and Neptune have had fewer visitors — a lone Voyager 2 back in the 1980s.

title: Anthropic worker claims to have solved a Holy Grail of math problems with AI's help
summary: A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company's AI tool Claude
story: A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company's AI tool Claude
A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company's AI tool Claude.
It marks the second time in recent months that an AI company or someone linked to one claims to have cracked a famed unsolved math problem.

Levent Alpöge, a member of the company's technical staff, made the announcement Friday by way of a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said that he believes by working with Claude, he has found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.

“Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” Alpöge wrote. “No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”
Formulated in 1859, the Riemann Hypothesis centers on the distribution of prime numbers — those that are only divisible by one and themselves — as they grow towards infinity.

Alpöge said his discovery came late Sunday night. He messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to ask about “my ability to announce," as the San Francisco-based company was about to make major news with its stock market debut.

A day after the company's initial public offering — the most valuable in history — Alpöge revealed he'd solved the problem that has proved elusive for more than 150 years. Anthropic did not respond to an email from The Associated Press requesting comment on Alpöge's claim.

Hours after the announcement, the Riemann Hypothesis remained listed as unsolved on the Clay Mathematics Institute’s website. The institute had selected the hypothesis back in 2000 as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems and offered a reward of $1 million for the solution.
The assessment process of whether the problem has actually been solved takes time, explained Martin Bridson, president of the institute.

“This is an announcement of historic significance, which holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics,” he said in a statement. “But the journey from today’s announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult.”
Alpöge said he is “presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics.” He said more than 250,000 pages came out of his work with AI.
In September, OpenAI said its technology was key in a similar breakthrough with Navier-Stokes, an equation that governs the flow of fluids.

“Navier-Stokes fell and now the Riemann Hypothesis,” said Alex Kontorovich, distinguished professor and department chair of mathematics at Rutgers University. “There’s some kind of out-of-body experience where I’m looking at myself saying, ‘Yes, the Riemann Hypothesis has been solved,’ and kind of trying to comprehend what the hell these words are coming out of my mouth.”
Anthropic made a blockbuster Wall Street debut this week, through which it raised a record-breaking $81 billion at a $1.5 trillion valuation.

Amodei has projected an optimistic vision for AI’s future in which the technology leads to significant advancements in math and science research while simultaneously warning about the potential risks AI poses.
AP Technology Writer Kaitlyn Huamani contributed.

title: Anthropic's record IPO raises hopes for a charitable windfall that has nonprofits preparing to scale
summary: Anthropic's record $1.5 trillion valuation is carrying hopes of a charitable windfall that could send billions of dollars to philanthropy
story: Anthropic's record $1.5 trillion valuation is carrying hopes of a charitable windfall that could send billions of dollars to philanthropy
NEW YORK -- It was philanthropy, the story goes, that first bonded two of the founders behind artificial intelligence giant Anthropic.

Jared Kaplan, the San Francisco company's chief science officer, and CEO Dario Amodei were doctoral students carpooling to an event organized by an academic fellowship. As Kaplan recalls, he and Amodei spent the ride discussing “this idea of thoroughly investigating what kinds of charitable causes could do the most good.”
“We had so much largesse to, sort of, disperse,” Kaplan joked at a Hertz Foundation discussion in April 2025.

Those once-hypothetical philanthropic ambitions gained new steam as Anthropic debuted on the stock market to a record $1.5 trillion valuation. The Claude AI tool maker already plans to dedicate 5% of its shares for a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund. Its seven co-founders say they'll give away 80% of their equity — a $112 billion commitment based on its IPO price.

Now suddenly affluent employees, many of whom will become millionaires as they sell their vested stock, may wield enough capital to make transformative donations themselves — riches that are commanding the attention of nonprofits looking to direct some sliver toward causes from global health to animal welfare.

Silicon Valley has great expectations. The napkin math suggests leading U.S. AI firms' valuations could add at least $37 billion annually in intended philanthropy, according to a widely circulated May blog post by Nan Ransohoff, head of public goods at the payments company Stripe.
“This is a once-in-a-lifetime kind of opportunity for people to really make an impact on extreme poverty,” said Peter Singer, the moral philosopher whose writings influence many tech donors.

Nonprofits aren’t counting on an immediate charitable windfall, though. Many Anthropic employees cannot sell or gift the bulk of their shares until next spring. Questions persist about the charitable priorities of these potential philanthropists whose worldviews have been shaped by the increasingly powerful AI models advancing at breakneck speed. The sector's volatility — between high borrowing costs, recent turmoil at the chipmaker Nvidia and warnings about risks to humanity — leaves skeptics doubtful about the amounts actually available to redistribute.

“The challenge is that deploying philanthropic capital is hard,” said Renaissance Philanthropy president Kumar Garg, whose nonprofit matches funders with scientific initiatives. “That’s not an automatic step.”
Will the artificial intelligence wave of wealth creation differ from previous ones that created new philanthropy?

There's reason to believe so, according to Benjamin Soskis, a historian of philanthropy and senior research associate at the Urban Institute's Center on Nonprofits and Philanthropy, even if he finds the number of tech executives who have “actually managed to empty the safe” is low.

The modern philanthropic foundation stemmed from the post-Civil War wave of industrial capitalism. Titans such as oil magnate John D. Rockefeller Sr. and steel tycoon Andrew Carnegie established bureaucratic institutions intended to address the root causes of social problems. Those were followed by the turn-of-the-century technology wealth that brought a more data-centric, risk-taking approach. The Gates Foundation launched to address pressing crises in global health and poverty.
AI wealth, according to Soskis, carries a sense of “extreme peril” and “really transformative promise” that should spur even more urgent action from this emerging class of donors.

At least one of Anthropic's co-founders will donate in the coming weeks to the Trump Accounts children's savings program, according to comments made Friday by U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on CNBC.

Anthropic's explosive growth is also fueling some anticipation that its 5,300 employees will want to rapidly scale their charitable impact, too. A generous internal giving program adds another incentive. Employee equity gifts are matched by the company with shares of Class N common stock. Anthropic also partners with donor-advised fund vendors such as Daffy, which offer a tax-efficient tool for grantmaking without the hassle of a more sophisticated charitable foundation.
Daffy CEO Adam Nash expects this younger generation to give more quickly.
“The people working in AI see the impact AI is having already,” Nash said. “And they are giving now, right?"
One organization in particular appears poised to move those rising donation volumes.

Coefficient Giving was formed by San Francisco-based billionaire Cari Tuna and her husband, Dustin Moskovitz, a Facebook co-founder and early Anthropic investor. A spokesperson told The New York Times the couple transferred their Anthropic stake into an undisclosed nonprofit last year to avoid personally profiting.

The philanthropic funder — which has directed more than $8 billion since 2014 in support of global health, animal rights, AI safety and the effective altruism community — has been scaling its pledges. In July, Coefficient Giving increased its commitment to the grantmaker GiveWell to $1 billion.
The move reflected expectations of “considerably more future funding for this kind of work,” according to the announcement.

“We might grow a lot, in part because we want to spend faster in response to these trends,” Coefficient Giving CEO Alexander Berger said during a late July public discussion. "But there is a great deal of room for other organizations and approaches, and I do not expect us to play an overwhelmingly dominant role.”

GiveDirectly has spent months identifying the biggest barriers to rapidly growing its antipoverty work, according to Nick Allardice, its president and CEO. The tech-focused nonprofit sends cash straight to poor households with no strings attached.

Recipients must have mobile phones to receive the digital transfers. GiveDirectly offers phones for about $15, usually subtracted from recipients' first payment. So the nonprofit secured investments this year to build out a supply chain to support many more mobile phones going forward.
The group is betting that its preparations for a charitable boom will be worthwhile.
“I have this level of cautious optimism,” Allardice said. “But I can't foresee the future, and I don't know exactly what's going to happen.”
Wild Animal Initiative executive director Cameron Meyer Shorb shares those tempered expectations.

His nonprofit funds wild animal welfare research. It's the sort of work some observers predict will see the biggest upswings in support: nonprofits connected to effective altruism, a data-driven movement that prioritizes donations to causes with the greatest impact on the most living beings.

The movement's reputation took a hit when Sam Bankman-Fried, one of its leading proponents and financial backers, got a 25-year prison sentence for cryptocurrency fraud. But the ideas are rebounding in the same tech circles that could see big payouts as more AI companies go public.

Effective altruists have learned not to rely too heavily on any one funder, according to Shorb. He expects “quite a bit” of fresh support for animal advocacy and sees an outsize role for midsize donors.
He said he has connected with a couple of Anthropic employees. Perhaps more important, he said, are relationships with the philanthropic advisers who help plan donors' giving.

“As you can imagine, it’s a pretty tricky place for a soon-to-be billionaire to be to have all this potential power coming soon,” Shorb said. “As soon as anyone finds out about that, anyone who can possibly get their email or phone number will just be knocking down their door. So we’ve tried to be gentle and slow and respectful in our approach.”
