"There was violence. You can call it what you want. Every American can call it what you want. There was clearly violence," Clayton said.

After a slew of high-profile tech outages, sources told that the FBI and the U.S. Department of Agriculture were hit with cyberattacks late last week. Clayton told "This Week" on Sunday that he could not "get into the specifics" of those incidents.

"We have highly professional people at the FBI who handle both private sector and public sector incidents like this, and I'm sure we'll get the answers in due course, just as we've gotten the answers to the incidents that happened this past week at the NSA, at Microsoft, at other places," Clayton said.
As the Trump administration has explained, many of the outages in recent weeks have come during repairs to infrastructure patches identified by artificial intelligence.

"We have a step change in technology that we're facing with super intelligence and computing power that is expanding exponentially. And we have a dated digital infrastructure. The need to improve our digital infrastructure is clear, and that is the dynamic that we have today," Clayton said.
Clayton maintained that the recent outages were not coordinated or state-sponsored.
"The incidents that we saw during the course of this week, we know that they were not coordinated and that they were not state-sponsored," Clayton said.

"Companies and the government, we should all be transparent with the American people that we have dated systems in a highly-evolving environment where they need to be upgraded in order to have cybersecurity," he added.
Clayton said there has been an increase in cyberattacks, "but this is something that we have had for a long time."

title: Rahm Emanuel: Schumer should commit to stepping down as leader after next Congress
summary: Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, joined "This Week" to discuss what Democrats should do after their historic midterm victory.
story: Democrats should also support Jeffries' House speaker nomination, Emanuel said.

Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel said Sunday that longtime Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer should commit to stepping down from the role after the next Congress, where Democrats are set to hold 56 seats after a strong midterm election showing.

"If I was Chuck Schumer, what I would say is, 'I'm going to secure the majority, I am not going to run for majority leader next cycle, and I'm going to make sure the other -- the young voices and faces of this party grow. That would take that tension out of this," Emanuel, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, said on ABC's "This Week."
"So he should serve as majority leader for these next two years?" co-anchor Jonathan Karl followed up.
"Yeah, just get it over with," Emanuel said. "Chuck Schumer is a friend, as is [Sen.] Chris Van Hollen, but this is not what people voted for. They voted to get their lives better, not yours."

Emanuel, who also served as U.S. ambassador to Japan under President Joe Biden and chief of staff to President Barack Obama, has previously called for instituting a mandatory retirement age of 75 for federal public officials, including members of Congress. Schumer turns 76 on Monday.

Van Hollen announced on Nov. 14 he was officially challenging Schumer for the role of majority leader in the congressional session beginning in January. On last Sunday's episode of "This Week," Van Hollen told co-anchor Martha Raddatz that maintaining the status quo is not how Democrats will "earn the people's trust."
The vote for majority leader, which is a secret ballot, is scheduled for Dec. 1.

While Democrats’ Senate leader is still undecided, House Democrats voted Wednesday to officially nominate Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York to be their candidate for speaker of the House. If he wins a majority of votes among all House members in January, as he’s expected to do, he will become the first Black speaker in U.S. history.

Nearly all Democrats supported Jeffries’ nomination, but there were 11 defectors. Of the eight individuals ABC News has confirmed voted against his candidacy, all were elected for the first time in November.
Emanuel had a message to Jeffries’ naysayers, most of whom identify with the progressive wing of the party, including some who are democratic socialists: “Give me a break.”

“Hakeem Jeffries is history, OK? … First Black speaker, number two in line for the presidency. And as somebody who was chief of staff to President Obama, that is a statement about America that we should take pride in,” Emanuel said. “We're a coalition. You're going to tell the most loyal coalition partner, the African American community, that the moment in history, you're not going to get it?”

"The Black vote is the most significant, most loyal, most dedicated part of the coalition," Emanuel continued. "You voted against Hakeem Jeffries, who made history and earned it when we were in the minority. You just came along and literally hadn't earned this election. He literally over the years built a majority here that should be affirmed and not only affirmed. It tells me when you vote against him, you don't understand the politics of the Democratic Party.”

Emanuel outlined lofty policy goals he thinks the incoming Democratic majorities should try to achieve, including raising the federal hourly minimum wage to $20 by 2030 and reducing or completely undoing tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump. He also called for a major ethics reform package that would impact all three branches of government.

“Ban all stock trading … ban all prediction market participation. Mandatory blind trust, mandatory age and term limit mark out, and what I call the Jared Kushner rule: no foreign money while you're in and for two years out of government,” Emanuel said.

Karl also asked Emanuel what he thinks the next Democratic president should do about the still-under-construction White House ballroom that has been one of the president’s prized projects this term. The White House has said the goal is to finish it before Trump leaves office.

“I think the opening floor should be dedicated to the history of our democracy and what we built: the good, the bad, the ugly,” Emanuel said. “And so you have a version of what the president has done, which is -- I think is horrendous, both substantively and in style that he did, but dedicate a major portion as you walk in, the guests will walk in, to the democracy of this country.”
Emanuel also said that the Rose Garden, which Trump turned into a stone patio, should be reverted back to the design that dates back to the Kennedy administration.
As for whether he'll seek the Democratic presidential nomination for 2028, Emanuel was tight-lipped.
"When do you make this decision-slash-announcement?" Karl asked.
"As soon as I get out of here," Emanuel quipped.

title: Nidal Hasan is set to be executed. The military's other death row cases are in limbo
summary: There are three other former soldiers who are on the military’s death row.
story: There are three other former soldiers who are on the military’s death row.
The U.S. military hasn't executed anyone in 65 years.

Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan is set to be put to death next month. The Army has no immediate plans to carry out any other executions at this time, according to two sources with direct knowledge of the matter.

The Army's three other inmates sentenced to die have spent decades on death row for crimes that include murder, rape and an attack on fellow troops in the opening weeks of the Iraq War. None of them have an execution date. Military courts can impose a death sentence, but the case must go through the Pentagon before the president gives final approval to carry it out.
It's unclear why the Trump administration singled out Hasan, the former Army major who killed 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009.
Both the Pentagon and the White House declined to comment on whether they plan to execute any of the other death row inmates after Hasan.

Hasan is scheduled to face a firing squad Dec. 3 at the same base where he committed the attack, a method the military has not used since 1945. The Army originally planned to use lethal injection, internal documents reviewed by ABC News show.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth initially planned to livestream Hasan’s execution, which would have been the first public execution in the U.S. in nearly a century. Republicans and Democrats questioned the decision to broadcast the shooting death of a prisoner who uses a wheelchair and warned it could fuel anti-American propaganda and ultimately become a spectacle that has been associated with dictatorships in the past century. The plan was scrapped after President Donald Trump intervened.
The four men on the military's death row -- including Hasan -- are imprisoned at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

Ronald Gray, a former Army specialist who served as a cook with the 82nd Airborne Division at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, was convicted in a 1988 military trial on 12 charges, including two counts of premeditated murder and three counts of rape. The attacks involved five women, two of them soldiers. A civilian court separately convicted him on 22 charges and sentenced him to eight life terms.
President George W. Bush approved Gray’s execution in July 2008. It was scheduled for that December, but a federal judge halted it. Another judge lifted the stay in 2016.

Timothy Hennis, a former Army master sergeant who worked on parachutes with the 82nd Airborne Division, was convicted in civilian court in 1986 for raping and murdering a woman and killing her 5-year-old and 3-year-old daughters. His conviction was overturned on appeal, and a second trial ended in acquittal in 1989.

Years later, investigators retested evidence using new DNA tools. The acquittal barred another prosecution, but the Army could bring its own charges. The service recalled Hennis, who had retired in 2004, to active duty. A court-martial convicted him and sentenced him to death.

The fourth inmate, former Army Sgt. Hasan Akbar, attacked fellow soldiers at Camp Pennsylvania, Kuwait, in March 2003, during the opening days of the U.S. invasion of Iraq. Akbar, a combat engineer, wounded 14 soldiers and killed two officers. Akbar was convicted in a military court in 2005 on two counts of premeditated murder and three counts of attempted premeditated murder; he was sentenced to death.
In May, Hegseth awarded Purple Hearts at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, to nine veterans wounded in the attack.
It's unclear whether the other three death row inmates have maintained legal counsel.
Tim Jon Semmerling, the mitigation expert on Hasan’s defense team at his 2013 trial, said he believes the number of people Hasan killed at Fort Hood played a part in why he is being executed.
“If you believe in the death penalty, it's really difficult to argue against so many people being killed by one person,” Semmerling said.

Semmerling said he believes Hasan’s Muslim faith may also have figured into the administration's decision, as may Hasan’s stated motive for the attack, which he described as a protest against the U.S. wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Semmerling, who conducted dozens of interviews with Hasan and his family over four years, described Hasan as a devout Muslim who spends much of his time in prayer and studying the Quran and Muslim scholars.
Hegseth invoked Fort Hood in a 2015 appearance on Fox News where he argued that troops should be allowed to carry weapons on military bases, saying "Islamics are at war with us."
Hegseth told The Hill in September 2025 that he is "100% committed to ensuring the death penalty is carried out for Nidal Hasan" because the "victims and survivors deserve justice without delays."
As Hasan's execution approaches, Army officials say they are revising the outdated firing squad procedures, which date back to 1959.

John Galligan, a retired Army colonel who has long represented Hasan, said officials at the U.S. Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth promised to provide him with the execution protocols, but haven't done so yet. He wants to know how many soldiers will serve on the firing squad and whether Hasan can make a final statement.

“Those kind of details -- details about how you're going to kill someone during their execution -- are important for defense counsel to know -- particularly when, as here, the governing regulation is totally silent on the subject,” Galligan said.
The Army declined to comment when asked detailed questions about how it plans to carry out Hasan's execution.
Hasan could still file a habeas corpus petition, or a judge could delay the execution. It’s unclear whether either will happen.
The Army will have to assemble and train the soldiers who will carry out its first firing squad execution since World War II. It’s unclear what rehearsals they will undergo.

The 1959 procedures allowed prisoners to make reasonable final requests, including a meal, writing materials and access to a chaplain of their faith. On the day of the execution, the prisoner could make a final statement before being hooded and could ask the chaplain to stay until the firing squad was prepared to fire.
Hasan was partially paralyzed after police shot him during the Fort Hood attack. It’s unclear how the Army plans to account for his use of a wheelchair.

In Killeen, Texas, outside of the base where Hasan in set to be executed, officials plan to close city offices and public facilities on the day of the execution as a precautionary measure. Schools will also close, and the city has rescheduled trash collection. It’s unclear whether officials expect any significant protests.
Hasan told a military mental health panel during his trial that he wished he had been killed during his rampage and said he would still consider himself a martyr if the military put him to death.

title: Trump touts relationships with Putin and Xi after historic Asia trip
summary: Trump said the three countries made strides in advancing denuclearization talks.
story: Trump said the three countries made strides in advancing denuclearization talks.

President Donald Trump touted his historic trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday following his trip to Asia earlier this week, claiming that there was "great electricity" between the three leaders of the world’s superpowers.

"I have a fantastic relationships with Putin. That's a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That's a good thing. And our country is safe because of that," Trump said during a Friday news conference.

During the trip, Trump called Putin his "friend." Asked on Friday about whether Putin, who leads a country that is Iran's biggest ally, is a friend to America, Trump said they have a "very good relationship."

Trump has insisted that Putin wants an end to its ongoing war with Ukraine, now in its fifth year, but Russia has continued to launch deadly attacks. Asked by ABC News Senior Political Correspondent Rachel Scott about whether Putin was stringing Trump along, as he has said in the past, the president said "that it's a very hard thing" to end the war.

"To be honest, you have two guys that don't know how to end it. We're trying to help them," Trump said of Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, later adding, "you're very lucky to have somebody that has a relationship with the heads of the most powerful countries."
Trump had promised to end the war within 24 hours of taking office for his second term in 2024.
"It's a tough job. The problem is President Zelensky and President Putin have tremendous hatred, and that's never easy. I thought that would be one of the easier," Trump said Friday.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who delivered brief remarks after Trump and Vice President JD Vance, defended the president’s meeting with Xi and Putin after he garnered criticism for establishing such warm relations with authoritarian leaders.

"These three countries, the United States, Russia, and China, between these three countries, possess the overwhelming majority of nuclear weapons on this planet. The idea that these three leaders should not engage on a regular basis is not just absurd, it's dangerous," Rubio said at the news conference where several other Cabinet members were in attendance. "And if these leaders can't get along and can't engage with one another and don't have a positive relationship, it is impossible to get anything good done for the country and the safety of the world."
Trump said that Russia, China and the U.S. agreed to a "first-of-its-kind trilateral peace declaration."

Trump said that the trilateral meeting made strides in advancing discussions around denuclearization, but he also discussed how "hard" it is for him to give up nuclear weapons. Overall, there appeared to be no major diplomatic breakthroughs.
"I'm the one that keeps talking about the denuclearization of the world, but it's very hard," the president said.

Trump also claimed that he and Xi agreed on "some joint guardrails" on artificial intelligence, despite previously saying this is not something he would do. The president did not offer specifics on what those guardrails entail.

On Sept. 29, Trump declined to partake in a "joint venture" with China on AI despite others encouraging him to do so. He has also been adamant about not curtailing AI, even when some tech CEOs have sounded the alarm on the need for federal guardrails.
Trump also touted trade agreements with Thailand and the Philippines.
The president said he is pushing U.S. tech companies to build controversial data centers in the U.S. -- threatening a "tremendous tax" on those that build in other countries.

"We're not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can. But we're going to put a tremendous tax on them," he said, without offering details about the tax.

Following Republicans' bruising midterm losses, Vance said the Trump administration's ongoing war with Iran was to blame. Asked about Vance's comments on Friday, the president said it was a "very accurate statement," acknowledging the role of rising fuel prices.

"I thought the statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing that if it were asked, I would have said that, 'Would you do it again?' And absolutely. The answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon," Trump said.
Vance was later asked about his previous comments about whether losing the Senate for the next six years was worth the war. The vice president responded that he follows the president's orders.

"I think the president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again," Vance said Friday. "And my view is that my goal is and my job is to support the president of the United States."
A week after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop, Trump said the nation's air traffic control system is "obsolete," but still safe.
"We have an obsolete system. Now, with that being said, it's safe, but it's very safe," he said.

Trump repeated calls from Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy for more funding to fix the air traffic control system they say is broken. Department of Transportation on Thursday officially submitted its $50.1 billion budget funding request -- a marked increase -- to fix the system.
Trump again asserted on Friday that he previously directed the FAA not to spend $12 billion in congressionally appropriated funds.

"Let's not spend the 12, spend as little as you can to keep it going, until we get to 12. So we're asking for $50 billion from the Senate, from government, so that we can have a system better than any system,” Trump said.
Trump made similar comments during his trip to Asia earlier this week, telling reporters in Manilla that he told the agency to save the money.
Trump notably referred to House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries as "smart," despite the president previously calling the Democrat a "thug" with "low IQ."
He also suggested he might prefer working with a Democratic-controlled Congress over his own party.
"But I just want to tell you, he's smart, and your new speaker," Trump said.
He later said Sen. Chuck Schumer, the Senate's top Democrat, is also "smart."

"If they want to get things done, I want to get things done too. You know, there are those that say we might get more done because we had some Republicans that were just impossible to deal with," Trump said.
But the president also said there’s a "real possibility" he can work with Democrats "because of the power of the veto."

"There's a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done, especially on healthcare, I'm open to great healthcare. Now, can it be what they want? No, but it can be a combination of what we all want, and we could end up with great healthcare in our country. We could end up better than dealing with the Republicans,” he said.
Trump also said he is going to wield his veto power to accomplish legislation he wants and that he believes he could use this to reach compromises with Democrats.

"So they're going to send things my way, and I'm going to veto them. And then they're going to send more things, and I'm going to veto them. And they could go two years and one month because that's what we have. And I'm going to veto them," Trump said. "But I think after a month or so, they're going to send things that I'm going to say, 'I'm going to veto unless you want to do this and this and this.'"

title: Democrat Chuck Hubbard wins recount, flips North Carolina US House seat
summary: Democratic Chuck Hubbard will win the election in North Carolina's 5th congressional district, the Associated Press projects.
story: The victory gives Democrats their biggest House majority since 1992.

Democratic Chuck Hubbard will win the election in North Carolina's 5th congressional district, the Associated Press projected on Sunday, flipping the seat held by longtime Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx.
With Hubbard's victory, the Democrats are set to have their biggest majority in three decades in the House of Representatives when the next Congress is sworn in in January.
With 99% of the estimated vote reported, Hubbard leads Foxx 48.7% to 48.6%. Fewer than 300 votes separate the two.
Hubbard wrote in a social media post on Sunday that Foxx, who had requested a recount, called him earlier Sunday to concede.
"Let me be the first to thank Congresswoman Foxx for her decades of service and countless sacrifices," wrote Hubbard, a former local journalist who ran unsuccessfully against Foxx in 2024.

“After a hard-fought and thorough election process, the voters of the Fifth Congressional District exercised their Constitutional rights and made their voices heard," Foxx said in a statement Sunday in part, acknowledging Hubbard's victory. "I recently called to congratulate Chuck Hubbard on his victory in this election, and I sent him my best wishes as he represents this wonderful district in the 120th Congress."
Foxx, first elected to the U.S. House in 2004 after serving in the North Carolina state Senate, is currently the chair of the powerful House Rules Committee.

Democrats have had major successes this year in North Carolina. In addition to Hubbard's win, Democrat Roy Cooper, the former North Carolina governor, flipped the U.S. Senate seat currently held by retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis.

As of Sunday, based on the current ABC News House estimate, which tracks the expected balance of power based on results in U.S. House races, Democrats are on track to have at least 258 members in the U.S. House, with at least 173 for Republicans. Four races have not yet been projected.
Hubbard's win will secure the largest majority Democrats have had in the U.S. House since 1992, when they also elected 258 members, according to U.S. House records.

title: Airline glitches, storms could make for a messy Thanksgiving travel week
summary: It’s shaping up to be a messy time for traveling heading into the Thanksgiving holiday
story: It’s shaping up to be a messy time for traveling heading into the Thanksgiving holiday

Traveling for the Thanksgiving holiday is shaping up to be a bit chaotic, following a cascade of glitches that have upended airlines the past week, the threat of storms on both coasts and soaring airfares.
No wonder Americans are feeling jittery going into the busiest travel week of the year.
On top of all that, there's concern that a big storm brewing along the East Coast could ground the big balloons in the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.
The biggest unknown for travelers is whether airlines will be upended again by new system failures.

First there was the Federal Aviation Administration's network malfunction setting off the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. Then last week, both United Airlines and Delta Air Lines saw their own outages, leading to hundreds of flight delays.
Delta said Monday that its operations were stable Monday, a day after over 1,000 of its flights were delayed after an automated system that calculates aircraft weight malfunctioned.
“Delta teams are focused on keeping the operation moving safely and caring for our customers,” the airline said.
As of Monday morning, the flight-tracking website FlightAware said 7% of Delta’s flights were delayed.
Roundtrip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving are up more than one-third from the same time last year, according to estimates made in late October by the travel-booking company Hopper.

Holiday travelers can expect a rainy week on the East and West coasts and dry conditions in the nation’s mid-section, said Joe Wegman, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service’s Weather Prediction Center.

Many eyes are on an East Coast system. Heavy rain and high winds are expected to start Wednesday night along the coast of the Carolinas, hit the New York City area on Thanksgiving Day and reach Maine by Friday, he said.

The windy forecast was causing concerns about whether the floats will be able to fly during the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York. City law prohibits Macy’s from flying full-size balloons if sustained winds exceed 23 mph (37 kph) or wind gusts are over 35 mph (56 kph).
The weather service said it expected the rain in New York to hold off until after the parade ends, but winds could be an issue.
“This is poor timing with the storm coming up on Thanksgiving Day,” Wegman said. “Perhaps better timing that it’s happening on Thanksgiving Day rather on any of the travel days before and after.”

Rainy and windy weather also was expected on the West Coast. Moderate to major coastal flooding was forecast from Washington state to Southern California because of possible record-breaking king tides.

Rain was forecast for the Pacific Northwest on Monday, and expected to spread to northern and central California by Wednesday morning with snow possible in higher elevations, the weather service said.
Snow was forecast Monday for parts of the Rockies, northern Michigan, western New York state and northwestern Pennsylvania.

“Across the U.S., certainly check with your local airports and airlines for any possible delays,” Wegman said. “I think weather won’t be a significant factor except on Thanksgiving Day itself, and if there are any lingering impacts into Friday morning perhaps from delays that happen on Thanksgiving Day.”
Seewer reported from Toledo, Ohio. Associated Press reporters Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire; and Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, contributed.

title: Immigration officers make arrests at Seattle airport in 'distressing' scene, delaying flight
summary: Masked U.S. immigration officers have detained two people on a jet bridge at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as passengers were boarding
story: Masked U.S. immigration officers have detained two people on a jet bridge at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as passengers were boarding

Masked immigration officers detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, causing what the airline called a “distressing” scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight.
Video of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as a woman screams that her daughter is being taken and she has a work permit.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who “overstayed his visa in violation of our nation’s laws.”

During the confrontation, another passenger “hurled hot coffee on the officers,” the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer.
Online flight data showed that Alaska flight 1306, which had been scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m., was delayed.
Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

“We are concerned by this morning’s law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306,” the airline said. “We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests.”
It added that the airline is committed to “treating every guest with dignity and respect.”
The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The video showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases look on.
ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns “directly with the appropriate authorities.”

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would “engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred.”
Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE's tactics were “deeply un-American” and called for the agency's abolition.

“The video is horrific and it is chilling,” Ferguson said at an afternoon news conference with labor leaders and local elected officials. “We need a system of immigration enforcement and border security that is effective, ethical and humane. And ICE is not it. It is beyond reform.”
Ferguson also said he was looking into how ICE agents accessed the jet bridge and he believes they violated a state law he signed in March limiting facial coverings on law enforcement officers.

April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, representing over 600,000 workers, said union members were aboard the flight. She said the action disrupted travel during one of the busiest times and only days after flights were grounded nationwide due to a communications problem. “Airport workers are already managing extraordinary stress, passengers are already anxious and instead of restoring calm and confidence, federal agents introduced more fear and more chaos,” she said.

title: Pentagon sharply rebukes Canada over defense spending and the F-35 fighter jet review
summary: The Pentagon has accused Canada of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke to its longtime ally over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets
story: The Pentagon has accused Canada of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke to its longtime ally over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets

TORONTO -- The Pentagon accused Canada on Monday of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke to its longtime ally over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets.
In an unusually blunt fact sheet, the Defense Department accused Ottawa of failing to make the tough decisions needed to modernize its military and meet NATO commitments.
“Canada’s defense shortfalls speak for themselves,” it said. “Canada must get serious and focused.”

The criticism follows a classified directive from U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds said largely restricts officials’ participation in Canadian think tank events and social engagements. Relations have been battered by President Donald Trump’s trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st state.

In May, Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby announced a pause in the Permanent Joint Board on Defense, a bilateral advisory body established in 1940, accusing Canada of failing to make credible progress on its defense commitments.

The rebuke also follows criticism of Washington at the Halifax International Security Forum, where its president, Peter Van Praagh, a former adviser in Conservative Prime Minister Stephen Harper’s government, warned Friday that the United States can no longer be counted on as a predictable leader of the democratic world.

The Pentagon accused Canada of leaving American taxpayers to shoulder the burden of continental defense. It said only 41.9% of Canada’s air force fleet was serviceable in the 2025-26 fiscal year and 53.9% of its naval fleet, while the army’s operational readiness stood at 48%.

“Underinvestment in defense has atrophied the Canadian Armed Forces and limited Canada’s ability to contribute to the defense of North America," the fact sheet said. "Secretary Hegseth is laser focused on incentivizing and enabling Canada’s military modernization after decades of American taxpayers footing the bill for its homeland defense.”

It also criticized Ottawa’s review of its planned purchase of 88 American-made F-35s, warning that a mixed fighter fleet could worsen personnel shortages. The Pentagon accused Canadian leaders of putting domestic economic interests ahead of military effectiveness, creating uncertainty for the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD, which the countries operate jointly.

Prime Minister Mark Carney put the F-35 purchase under review as Trump threatened Canadian sovereignty and imposed tariffs. Canada has examined Swedish-made Gripen fighters, which could bring manufacturing jobs.
Canada’s military did not immediately provide a substantive response to the Pentagon’s criticism.

Carney has acknowledged readiness problems, saying only one of Canada’s four submarines was seaworthy. Ottawa has since named Germany’s Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems as preferred supplier for up to 12 replacements, pending contract negotiations.
“We should no longer send three-quarters of our defense capital spending to America,” Carney said in June.

Canada reached NATO’s previous target of spending 2% of gross domestic product on defense and joined allies pledging to reach 5% by 2035, including related security investments. Its latest budget projects combined defense and security spending of 4.1% of GDP by the 2027-28 fiscal year, but core defense spending of only 2.6%. Canada’s parliamentary budget watchdog says the path to 5% remains unclear.
The Pentagon accused Ottawa of postponing the largest increases until after the 2029 federal election.

Other NATO allies also remain short of the new target. Yet Colby praised Germany’s military buildup Sunday as a “tectonic shift” and called Poland a “true model ally.” He also praised Romania’s plan to reach 5% by 2031.
Speaking Saturday at the Halifax International Security Forum, Rounds said the directive was not expected to affect joint military operations or intelligence sharing.
The Trump administration had already barred Pentagon officials from the Halifax forum under 2025 restrictions on think tank participation.

title: Data Centers Flood Black Communities Without Residents Having a Say
summary: Research shows majority-Black communities are over twice as likely to host data centers compared to majority-white ones
story: Research shows majority-Black communities are over twice as likely to host data centers compared to majority-white ones
By the time Zakiya Mabery learned that a $2 billion data center was planned just a 10-minute walk from her house, officials had already approved it.
The 200-acre facility in Augusta, Georgia, was first authorized in 2022 without a public hearing that would’ve allowed the community to voice their concerns.

Just months before the facility known as Project Eisenhower came to be, Mabery bought her home in a new housing development called Hayne’s Station. Since then, two-thirds of the people who’ve moved into the community have been Black.
“We would’ve never purchased a house if we knew a data center was coming,” she said about the project that began construction earlier this year.
Mabery’s experience exposes the racial divide in America’s data center boom — not just in where facilities are built, but in who gets a chance to question them.

Majority-Black communities are more than two times more likely to host a data center than majority-white ones and far less likely to receive the chance to hear about the projects before they’re approved or offer their opinion through public comment.
“It seems like (processes) are being built to silence citizens,” Mabery said at an Augusta Planning Commission meeting this past summer.
In recent years, dozens of AI data centers in communities home to hundreds of thousands of Americans have been approved without a public hearing.
For Black communities, the data center boom is extending a familiar pattern of environmental racism that has plagued families for generations.

Black communities are hosting infrastructure that generates wealth elsewhere. Meanwhile, they live with the pollution and disinvestment that undermines economic opportunity and contributes to poor health outcomes and premature deaths in their neighborhoods.

The stakes are growing as tech companies pour hundreds of billions of dollars into new infrastructure. President Donald Trump has pulled the levers of government in favor of these companies as he’s cast AI dominance as a competition the United States cannot afford to lose to China.

His administration has ordered agencies to exempt data centers projects from federal environmental review and to revise federal rules to accelerate their construction. At the same time, he has pushed federal agencies to limit the opportunities for public comment as the building boom reaches communities already carrying generations of industrial burdens.
The opportunity for residents to speak their mind is consequential to the outcome of a data center project.
On average, communities that have received a hearing before construction are nearly 80% white on average. Those without one are roughly 60% people of color.

When communities have received a public hearing, data centers have been blocked 66% of the time. When they don’t, they’re approved 80% of the time, according to Zoned Out, a tool created by researchers at Harvard University.

“We know disparities already exist in our communities, and now in the case of data centers, we’re seeing the targeting that happens without any say. It is systemic injustice,” said Aino Halonen, a former AI worker who led the Harvard study.

The racial disparities showed up during November’s midterm election. More than 40 jurisdictions nationwide allowed voters to decide if they wanted data centers in their communities via ballot measures. White residents made up an average of over 83% of the population in these places, compared with less than 5% for Black residents.
In Georgia, Mabery and her neighbors want a voice in what happens to their homes, health, and finances.

Data centers have increased PM 2.5 air pollution, which Black Americans die from at the highest rate in the U.S. The pollution can penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream, causing respiratory and cardiovascular disease. It is linked to asthma attacks, strokes, dementia, and cancer.

Carbon emissions from data centers are also connected to the intensification of climate change. America’s largest data centers are responsible for an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of climate change-causing carbon dioxide emissions annually — more than emissions from entire countries like Kenya and Guatemala.

“These are not emotional concerns. This is where we live. We invested here. We live and bear the impact here,” Augusta resident Charles Zabel said about the data center. “We ought to have a voice in this. So far, we have not had a meaningful voice in this discussion. Representation does not mean protecting a project. Representation means protecting the people who already call this place home.”

Researchers at George Washington University Law School joined American University researchers to analyze the placement of more than 5,200 data centers in the U.S., finding the major racial divide in where they’re found.

Researchers accounted for income, population density, home values, and proximity to major power lines, and compared neighborhoods within the same state to test whether economics or geography explained the racial disparities in where data centers were located and the benefits the communities received.
Even after those adjustments, neighborhoods with larger Black, Latino, and Asian populations remained most likely to have these negative experiences with data centers.
“Even when you control for all of that, race stands out,” said Dhanaraj Thakur, director of the Fair Technology Initiative at George Washington University.
“I think it’s important to show that this is not some anecdotal thing that’s happening in a few cities like Memphis or elsewhere,” he added. “It’s actually happening across the country.”

The difference often comes down to zoning. Due to the long tentacles of segregation and redlining, Black people are far more likely to live in communities that are home to tracts zoned for industrial use.

When a data center requires rezoning from, say, commercial to industrial, the approval process generally includes public notice, a hearing, and a vote. But if the land is already zoned industrial, developers can secure permits through an administrative review without requiring opportunities for residents to intervene.

As Capital B has reported, there have been several incidents where developers have pursued projects in poorer, majority-Black neighborhoods with more lax public hearing requirements after encountering opposition in wealthier, whiter areas.

After a data center was proposed in a wealthy, 65% white community in North Carolina, for example, thousands of residents were able to submit signatures and comments against the project. Then, the developer withdrew the project.

Weeks later, that same developer moved the project to another county in North Carolina, where the closest neighborhood was predominantly Black and had a median income that was just one-third of the former community’s. Commissioners in the county quickly approved the project in a 6-1 vote.

Even as data centers are more likely to be in communities of color, these same communities are less likely to receive major economic benefits, Thakur’s study found. Campuses operated by tech giants such as Meta, Google, and Microsoft are more likely to generate property-tax revenue and implement community benefit agreements, but those campuses are more likely to be in majority-white neighborhoods than communities of color.

That pattern raises the prospect that communities of color are shouldering the financial and environmental burdens of data center development writ large without the same potential financial rewards, the researchers wrote.

“A lot of the rhetoric coming from industry is that there are lots of economic benefits from data centers — tax revenue and job creation,” Thakur said. “These are what the industry groups promise, even though we’ve seen a lot of contradictions to that. But even if you do accept that as fact, the research shows that communities of color are less likely to receive those benefits.”
According to some analyses, Black workers make up just 7% of AI workers compared to 13% of the general population.

As for construction, for one week last fall, Capital B spent every morning and evening outside the site for Meta’s data center in northern Louisiana, the largest project in North America. The two closest towns are over 80% Black. None of the workers Capital B spoke to or saw drive off in their Ford F-150s were Black.

As Black communities bear the brunt of this crisis, increasingly, they’ve also been left out of the imagined face of the opposition. Nationwide, roughly 70% of Americans opposed data centers. As such, the fight has been framed by advocates and politicians as one that crosses all racial and political boundaries.
But researchers found that the flattening of data center opposition to an “American problem” has erased the racial injustices permeating the boom.

Communities that have been highlighted via the media in resistance to data centers were about 79% white on average, compared with 53% white in communities without recorded opposition. They said that the disparity reflects unequal media coverage, political influence, and organizing resources.
“It’s interesting that only some communities are being highlighted as opposing it,” Thakur said. “It is erasing the nuance and racial inequality” at the heart of the boom.
At Capital B, we’ve highlighted Black communities fighting data centers everywhere from Memphis to Maryland and Mississippi.

In Augusta, where the community closest to the massive data center site is 67% Black, residents are committed to fighting for a say. This summer, the board of commissioners approved a temporary moratorium on data center development. The $2 billion construction project was not included in the blockage.
“We are asking for respect,” Mabery said.
This report is a collaboration between Capital B, the Pulitzer Center and The Associated Press.

title: Two central Ohio bus drivers killed, nine others injured after head-on crash
summary: Two Columbus transit bus drivers have been killed and nine others injured after their vehicles collided during the morning rush hour in Ohio's state capital and one bus was struck by a third vehicle
story: Two Columbus transit bus drivers have been killed and nine others injured after their vehicles collided during the morning rush hour in Ohio's state capital and one bus was struck by a third vehicle

COLUMBUS, Ohio -- Two transit bus drivers were killed and nine others were injured in Ohio's state capital after their vehicles collided during the morning rush hour Monday and one bus was hit by a third vehicle.

According to Columbus police, the two Central Ohio Transit Authority buses collided head-on on the city's north side at around 8 a.m. The third vehicle collided with the rear or side of one of the buses.
“Early indications are that one of the buses, for reasons unknown, crossed a double yellow line and struck the other bus head-on,” said Columbus Police Sgt. Joseph Albert.
He said the driver of one of the buses was pronounced dead at the scene. The second was transported in critical condition and died later at the hospital. A message was left with COTA seeking comment.

Nine other individuals, either bus riders or passengers in the third vehicle, were transported to area hospitals, Albert said. They were all in stable condition with non-life-threatening injuries. No pedestrians were injured, Albert said.
Columbus City Council President Shannon Hardin and council member Lourdes Barroso de Padilla, who chairs the public service and transportation committee, called the accident “heartbreaking.”

“Our hearts go out to all those impacted by Monday’s accident, especially to the loved ones of those killed,” they said in a statement. “While we try to understand how this tragedy happened, we must not forget the lives lost and the families that will be mourning them just as we enter the holiday season.”

title: Chinese neuroscientist at Princeton is held by ICE after detention at Washington airport
summary: A Chinese neuroscience researcher at Princeton University is in the custody of immigration authorities after she was detained while trying to get on a flight back from Washington
story: A Chinese neuroscience researcher at Princeton University is in the custody of immigration authorities after she was detained while trying to get on a flight back from Washington

WASHINGTON -- A Chinese neuroscience researcher at Princeton University is in the custody of immigration authorities after she was detained while trying to get on a flight back from Washington, marking another instance of federal enforcement at airports.

Eva Yi Xie, a third-year doctoral student at Princeton, was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Thursday as she tried to fly back to New Jersey from a conference in the nation's capital, her university adviser Carlos Brody said in a social media post.
The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, says Xie overstayed her visa and did not have authorization to study in the United States.

“News of Eva’s detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community,” Rodney Priestley, dean of the university’s graduate school, said in a statement. "We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton.”

Two days after Xie was taken into custody in Washington, masked immigration officers detained a father and daughter on an airport jet bridge in Seattle. ICE has ramped up detentions at airports since the summer, especially targeting people it says have overstayed their visas.

Kerry Doyle, Xie’s lawyer, said she came to the U.S. at age 14 with her family from China and has had an asylum application pending for years. Doyle insisted that Xie has permission to live, work and study in the U.S. while her case is pending.
Doyle said Xie is being held in ICE's Caroline Detention Center in Virginia.

DHS said in a statement that Xie came to the United States on a temporary visa on March 16, 2016, but “chose to violate our nation’s laws by refusing to depart by the required date of September 15, 2016.”
The agency said she did not have valid permission to study in the U.S. and “a pending application does not confer legal status.”
“Xie will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending her removal proceedings," the DHS statement said.

On her professional website, Xie said her research at Princeton Neuroscience Institute “seeks to understand the neural basis of decision-making.” She said she graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2024.

title: Miley Cyrus marries rock drummer Maxx Morando in an intimate Palm Springs wedding
summary: Singer Miley Cyrus has married rock drummer Maxx Morando in an intimate ceremony in Palm Springs, California
story: Singer Miley Cyrus has married rock drummer Maxx Morando in an intimate ceremony in Palm Springs, California
Pop culture icon Miley Cyrus married rock drummer Maxx Morando in an intimate weekend wedding in Palm Springs, California, according to a post on the singer’s Instagram account.

The post said Cyrus, 33, and Morando, 28, were wed on Saturday. Photographs show the couple embracing in front of a white backdrop with a palm tree characteristic of the Palm Springs desert in the background, a large dog lying at their feet. In one photo, the couple kisses standing in an aisle of white roses.

The “Party in the U.S.A.” singer wore a long-sleeve silk Saint Laurent gown by Anthony Vaccarello and elegant white silk kitten heels, according to a statement from Saint Laurent. The dress had a low back, and she wore flowers in her hair, which was pulled back into an updo.
Morando wore dark, square shades. His single-breasted tuxedo was also made by the French luxury fashion brand.

The pair have been together since 2021, meeting after they were set up on a blind date, according to an interview Cyrus gave Vogue in 2023. Morando proposed to her while the couple were in Japan late last year, he said in a separate interview with Wonderland Magazine.
“I could feel my heart pounding” before popping the question, Morando said for a profile in the magazine.
Morando is the drummer of the rock band Liily.

title: 9 people shot at a central California concert; 1 in critical condition
summary: Nine people have been shot at a concert in central California, leaving one person critically injured
story: Nine people have been shot at a concert in central California, leaving one person critically injured
Nine people were shot at a concert in central California, leaving one person critically injured with a chest injury, the local sheriff said Sunday.

The shooting broke out around 7:30 p.m. Saturday at a concert attended by about 150 people in Strathmore, a small town in Tulare County, a mountainous region in the center of the state, the county sheriff's department said in a statement. An unspecified number of suspects opened fire on the crowd. No arrests were announced.

One 26-year-old man was shot in the chest and required surgery. He remained in critical condition, the sheriff's department said. Two other victims ages 19 and 22 also required surgery, while six people sustained minor injuries.

Authorities said that they believe the shooting “may be gang-related” but didn't elaborate. The show in the town of roughly 3,000 people featured performers from neighboring states, the department said.
The department didn't immediately respond to emailed questions seeking further details but said there was no longer any immediate threat to the public.

title: 3 killed, 1 wounded in shooting at Ohio baby shower, police say
summary: Authorities say an apparent domestic dispute turned deadly at a baby shower.
story: Authorities say an apparent domestic dispute turned deadly at a baby shower.
PARMA, Ohio -- Three people were killed and one was injured at an Ohio baby shower during an apparent domestic dispute, authorities said.
Officers responded to a shooting Saturday evening at Pandora’s Magical Events Venue in Parma, about 10 miles (16 kilometers) south of Cleveland, a police news release said.

Authorities said one of the shooters, a 29-year-old man, was taken into custody, but he wasn't immediately charged. Detectives were trying to determine whether the man was the aggressor or acting in self-defense, police spokesman Scott Traxler said. A second suspected shooter, a 19-year-old man, was one of the people killed, police said.

Officials have identified two of the victims as 17-year-old Leasia England and 45-year-old Jayson Townsend. Police said Townsend was the father of the woman for whom the baby shower was being held; she was not injured.
Officials haven't released the names of the 19-year-old suspected shooter who was killed, or a 39-year-old woman who was shot in the leg.

Preliminary information indicates that the 19-year-old man was the father of the unborn baby, and witnesses told police that he was not invited to the shower, Traxler said. The man in custody appears to be a relative of the expectant mother.

Both firearms involved in the shooting were recovered by police, officials said. Detectives were reviewing surveillance video and witnesses' statements on Sunday to determine what led to the violent confrontation, Traxler said. Ballistics testing might be required to determine which gun shot each victim.
Prosecutors will eventually determine whether the man in custody should be charged with a crime, officials said.

title: Natural gas pipeline fire shoots flames in Alabama, cause under investigation
summary: A pipeline in rural Alabama sent a column of flames high into the night sky.
story: A pipeline in rural Alabama sent a column of flames high into the night sky.

WARD, Ala. -- A fire on a natural gas pipeline lit up the night sky in rural Alabama late Saturday with a towering column of orange flame, prompting the operator to shut down part of the line but causing no injuries, the company said.
The cause of the fire is under investigation and customer deliveries were not impacted, Southern Natural Gas Company said in a statement Sunday.

Photos and videos posted on social media appeared to show flames rising dozens of yards (meters) above the trees near Ward, with smoke billowing into the air. People said on social media that the fire was visible from miles (kilometers) away across the state line in Mississippi.

Southern Natural Gas said it “experienced a natural gas release and fire” on the segment of the pipeline at around 11:30 p.m. CST Saturday. Emergency responders and company personnel secured the area and the blaze was extinguished, the company said. The impacted part of the pipeline was shut down and depressurized.
The Sumter County Emergency Management Agency did not immediately respond to a voicemail seeking information.

title: San Francisco braces for massive tides, mayor urges residents to reconsider travel
summary: Scattered rain is exacerbating the impacts of historic flooding across central Florida, as Northern California braces for an unprecedented deluge accompanied by high tides ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday
story: Scattered rain is exacerbating the impacts of historic flooding across central Florida, as Northern California braces for an unprecedented deluge accompanied by high tides ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday

Scattered rain continued to exacerbate the impacts of historic flooding across central Florida on Saturday, even as officials in Northern California braced for an unprecedented deluge during high tides heading into the heavy Thanksgiving travel week.

San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie warned that an “extremely serious” situation was about to hit the city, based on National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and National Weather Service forecasts, and urged people to consider not traveling for the holiday.

“We are expecting tides that the National Weather Service told us they have never seen before in recorded history here in San Francisco,” Lurie said via the social platform X. “Take this weekend to get yourself ready, please stock up on supplies, get your shopping done, and know that the city will be out all weekend doing everything possible to protect our residents and our small businesses.”

Storm systems impacting Florida and California are an offshoot of El Niño, the natural warming of the Pacific near the equator that warps weather patterns worldwide. Florida typically experiences its dry season from October to May, for example.

The expected deluge in California coincides with the highest tides of the year, called king tides. Forecasters said up to 2 feet (0.6 meters) of flooding would be likely in low-lying areas near shorelines and tidal waterways through 6 a.m. Monday, and through 4 p.m. Thursday along other areas of the Pacific coast.

Forecasters also warned of dangers Saturday along Florida's Atlantic coast. The weather service issued marine warnings to boaters tied to thunderstorms capable of creating destabilizing waterspouts, and advised beachgoers to beware of rough surf and dangerous rip currents.

NWS meteorologist Melissa Watson in Melbourne said that while the heaviest rains have passed, water levels were expected to continue to rise along the St. Johns River, Florida’s longest, due to continued lighter showers. Near the city of Cocoa, the river rose above a 1953 record Thursday.
“Regardless of any additional rainfall, we are expecting these river floods to continue for an extended period of time,” Watson said.
Heavy rain earlier this week submerged large swaths of Florida’s Atlantic coast, trapping people in floodwaters in the northeastern part of the state.
Associated Press journalist Donna Warder contributed.

title: US senator says Pentagon restrictions on Canada focus on think tanks and social events
summary: A Republican senator says Pentagon restrictions on Canada largely target U.S. military officials’ participation in think tank events and social engagements rather than military operations or intelligence sharing
story: A Republican senator says Pentagon restrictions on Canada largely target U.S. military officials’ participation in think tank events and social engagements rather than military operations or intelligence sharing

HALIFAX, Nova Scotia -- Pentagon restrictions on Canada largely target U.S. military officials’ participation in think tank events and social engagements rather than military operations or intelligence sharing, a Republican senator said Saturday, as Canada’s defense minister described military cooperation as “business as usual.”

The Washington Post reported Friday that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth circulated a classified memorandum last week imposing new restrictions on military cooperation with Canada. The report comes as U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and repeated threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state have strained relations between the longtime allies.

The Trump administration had already barred Pentagon officials from attending the Halifax International Security Forum under restrictions imposed in 2025 on participation in think tank events. Previous Republican and Democratic administrations sent senior U.S. military officials, including defense secretaries.
Republican Sen. Mike Rounds said the latest guidance appeared consistent with existing practices and was not expected to affect joint military operations or intelligence sharing.
Speaking at the Halifax International Security Forum, Rounds said his assessment was based on information from the delegation’s Pentagon liaison.
“They’re basically limiting some social engagements, and they’re asking people to get permission before they come in and do think tanks and so forth,” he said.
“We don’t expect any real changes over the way it has been going for the last year or a year and a half,” he said.
Rounds said the disclosure was unfortunate as Washington sought to reassure Canada and other allies of its commitment to longstanding security relationships.
Canadian Defense Minister David McGuinty said he had not seen the document and had detected no change in military cooperation.
“I’ve seen no evidence of any kind of change. I’ve heard about the existence of a document. I’ve not seen the document,” McGuinty told reporters.

He cited Canadian vessels working alongside American ships to intercept drug trafficking in the Caribbean. “So that cooperation remains ongoing. And as far as we’re concerned, it’s business as usual,” he said.
Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine called the directive’s tone “bad” and “unnecessary,” while Sen. Chris Coons said it risked worsening relations with a close ally.
“The United States should be doing nothing to further aggravate some of the distance and division between the United States and Canada,” Coons said.

title: FBI investigating apparent hack of a key criminal justice information database, AP source says
summary: The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of its National Crime Information Center database
story: The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of its National Crime Information Center database
WASHINGTON -- The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of a national law enforcement database that it maintains, a person familiar with the matter said Saturday.

The National Crime Information Center, known as the NCIC, is a computerized database of criminal justice information that is available to local, state and federal law enforcement agencies and includes records on fugitives, missing persons, criminal history data, stolen property and other topics.

The FBI declined to comment Saturday on the apparent hack, which was first reported by CNN and confirmed to The Associated Press by a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak by name and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
The scope of the problem was not immediately clear.
Asked about the subject on Saturday, President Donald Trump said in a Fox News Channel interview: “We just heard about it and I will say that it’s not good.”

News that the NCIC was targeted comes as the country has encountered a series of digital outages in the government and private sector that Trump administration officials have said were caused by routine efforts to upgrade computer systems and fix vulnerabilities, rather than a cyberattack. There was no immediate indication that the FBI incident was related to those outages.
The bureau has historically been a frequent target for hackers.

In September, for instance, the FBI said it was investigating a hack of its job portal website after a criminal hacking group known as ShinyHunters claimed it had obtained a massive trove of data on bureau employees and applicants.
And in March, the FBI disclosed that it was investigating “suspicious activities” on an internal system that contains sensitive information related to surveillance operations and investigations.

title: Nations at UN talks on AI killer robots agree to more talks but no firm commitment to rein them in
summary: Efforts to establish rules for AI-powered killer robots and drones have run aground
story: Efforts to establish rules for AI-powered killer robots and drones have run aground
GENEVA -- Efforts to set firm rules on AI-powered killer robots and drones ran aground Saturday as U.N.-backed talks in Geneva produced a softened agreement to extend discussions for two more years.

Scores of countries ended the week-long U.N. conference on weapons by agreeing to “elaborate” a possible accord on such lethal autonomous weapons systems by 2028. But they didn’t commit to binding rules sought by U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, many countries, and activists.
The outcome underscored the difficulty of achieving concrete results in diplomacy amid global conflicts and major military powers jockeying for dominance.

Izumi Nakamitsu, the U.N. high representative for disarmament affairs, hailed a “significant achievement” but acknowledged a “glass half full or half empty” scenario, citing Guterres’ hopes for a legally binding deal this year.
Activists accused military powers like Russia and the United States of blocking stronger language.

Stop Killer Robots lamented a “watered-down mandate,” and Beatrice Fihn, founder of international law advocacy group Lex International, said the decision amounts to “pushing the can down the road for two more years."

They noted most countries supported work toward a new treaty, and Max Tegmark, a machine learning specialist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and founder of the Future of Life Institute, said: “States have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about the issue, for the 14th year, while these weapons enable atrocities.”

Before the meeting, seven countries proposed launching negotiations on a rulebook that could prevent or limit the ability of machines to kill without human control or accountability. That effort fell short.

“Technology is moving faster than diplomacy,” said Ambassador Frederico Meyer of Brazil, which joined Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama in proposing such negotiations. “Diplomats are very slow.”

After years of talks on the issue, advocacy groups bemoaned obstructionism largely by Russia, which, like other top AI weapons-developing countries such as the United States, wants a freer hand to develop such high-tech weapons.
Guterres, who leaves office at the end of the year, set a 2026 deadline for launching negotiations toward an agreement on autonomous weapons systems.
Pope Leo XIV and many advocacy and humanitarian groups have framed the issue as an existential debate, urging quick action to rein in AI weapons before they become too commonplace to regulate easily.
Activists say armed drones that can independently strike targets have already been deployed in some select instances in conflict zones, but widespread rollout hasn’t happened.

Talks this week centered on the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, ratified by 128 countries, where decisions are made by consensus. That means any single country can thwart an agreement, and that any deal was likely to be based on a low common denominator.

title: Famed Marine Corps veteran under federal investigation over undisclosed allegations
summary: The Naval Criminal Investigative Service says it is investigating a famed Marine Corps veteran over undisclosed allegations
story: The Naval Criminal Investigative Service says it is investigating a famed Marine Corps veteran over undisclosed allegations

LAS VEGAS -- A celebrated Marine Corps veteran who became famous for his heroism during the Iraq War is under criminal investigation for undisclosed allegations, the Naval Criminal Investigative Service confirmed Friday.

CBS News first reported that retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal is under investigation over allegations stemming from his time as an ROTC assistant at a high school in Henderson, Nevada. The Naval Criminal Investigative Service, which is the Navy’s lead for felony-level criminal investigations, declined to provide further details to The Associated Press.

Kasal is a well-known veteran who earned the Navy Cross — the second-highest award for heroism for members of the Navy and the Marines — for his actions during combat operations in Fallujah, Iraq. Kasal was wounded in 2004 while fighting and shielding an injured Marine from a grenade. An iconic photo capturing the moment that soldiers helped carry Kasal inspired sculptures that were displayed at Marine Corps base camps.

The Clark County School District, which oversees hundreds of schools in the Las Vegas area, confirmed that Kasal worked at the Basic Academy of International Studies as an ROTC assistant. He was hired in August 2018 and resigned in August 2025, the district said.

In an email to Basic Academy families, the district said it was aware of the investigation into the former employee and said the former employee is no longer on campus. The district added that it will “cooperate fully with any investigation.”
The AP left text and voicemail messages Friday at a cellphone number for Kasal. CBS News said he did not respond to its own attempts to seek comment.

Some former students interviewed by CBS News praised him as a caring instructor who devoted time, energy and resources to his students. Other cadets claimed to the outlet that Kasal would take a select group of female cadets to get Starbucks.

Damien Greenwell, a 22-year-old who participated in the program from 2018 to 2022, told CBS News that he questioned some of Kasal’s conduct over the years and his behavior toward students could be interpreted as inappropriate by an outside observer.

Estella Deleon, a cadet who graduated in 2022, told the AP she was “baffled” by the investigation into Kasal and she never witnessed inappropriate behavior by him. Kasal always made himself available to cadets if they needed someone to talk to, she said, and he taught them important life lessons she still thinks about.

Deleon, 22, said Kasal would take everyone to get coffee or bring it to cadets if they were staying late after school or arriving early in the morning. One day he brought everyone in the class tamales, she said.
Deleon said she can understand the thinking that he should have kept a more professional relationship, “but he was like a father figure to a lot of us, and he was a great role model.”

title: Leaders of Mexican drug cartel and 19 others indicted for smuggling guns, drugs and people
summary: A federal grand jury in Texas has indicted the leaders of a powerful Mexican drug cartel and 19 others
story: A federal grand jury in Texas has indicted the leaders of a powerful Mexican drug cartel and 19 others

A federal grand jury indicted the leaders of a powerful Mexican drug cartel and 19 others Wednesday, accusing them of a range of crimes, including drug trafficking and smuggling firearms from the U.S. into Mexico.

The indictment accuses Mexican nationals Johnny Hurtado Olascoaga, alias “El Pez,” and Jose Alfredo Hurtado Olascoaga, alias “El Fresa,” of leading La Nueva Familia Michoacana cartel. The two are currently at large.

La Nueva Familia Michoacana, or LNFM, is one of nearly two dozen Latin American and Caribbean gangs designated by the Trump administration as a foreign terrorist organization. The cartel, founded in 2006, operates in the Mexican states of Michoacan and Guerrero, and authorities say it produces and distributes drugs. The brothers took control of the cartel in 2011.

The brothers are charged with conspiring to distribute and import cocaine, heroin, and methamphetamine, trafficking firearms — including .50-caliber rifles — international money laundering and human smuggling. The brothers, along with 14 others accused in the case, are at large and believed to be in Mexico, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas. The U.S. is offering rewards of $5 million and $3 million for information leading to the brothers' capture.

The indictment, which was filed in federal court in Western Texas, also accuses 19 others of being members or associates of the cartel and committing related crimes. All 21 are charged with racketeering.

Edgar Aguilar Cruz of Mexico, for instance, orchestrated the purchase of firearms “by numerous straw purchasers throughout Texas and the Southeastern United States,” according to the indictment. The guns were eventually transported to Mexico by couriers. He is also accused of overseeing the cartel's human smuggling operations.

U.S. citizens are among the accused, including a 23-year-old man who is alleged to have been a “mid-level drug trafficker who coordinates drug trafficking logistics” for the cartel, primarily in Texas and North Carolina. Another U.S. citizen, a 35-year-old man, recruited people to buy firearms for the cartel, authorities said.

Cash profits from drug trafficking and human smuggling were often transported together with firearms back to the cartel in Mexico, according to the indictment. Members and associates of the cartel discussed obtaining military-grade weapons, such as rocket-propelled grenades, and cartel leaders customized their guns with gold plating and cartoon and religious figures, authorities said.

Only five of the accused are in federal custody, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas. Gregory Torres, an attorney for Rogelio Ponce Esquivel, a 33-year-old Mexican national who is charged in the indictment and is in custody, declined to comment. It is unclear if the other four who were detained have lawyers.

In addition to its drug and firearm trafficking operations and for-profit human smuggling, the cartel has expanded to control mines and barter with Chinese companies to trade Mexican minerals for chemicals used in drug distribution, the indictment said. ___
Kelety reported from Phoenix. Associated Press writer Fabiola Sanchez in Mexico City contributed.

title: Federal judge denies a request to release man shot by immigration agents in New York
summary: A federal judge has denied a request to release a man shot and wounded by immigration officers in New York
story: A federal judge has denied a request to release a man shot and wounded by immigration officers in New York
NEW YORK -- A federal judge on Friday declined to release from custody a man who was shot and wounded by immigration officers as they arrested him in New York last month.

U.S. District Court Judge Hector Gonzalez said in a written ruling that agents may have made a procedural error in serving an arrest warrant on Oscar Belgal before he was given a notice to appear in immigration court. However, he wrote, that was merely a technical error that does not require Belgal to be released from federal custody pending deportation proceedings.

Belgal, a 28-year-old Dominican national, entered the U.S. illegally in 2021, and about two years later he was arrested on robbery and other charges and eventually pleaded guilty to grand larceny. He was given a sentence of probation, and in 2025 he was arrested again, this time on allegations that he attempted to sell controlled substances. That case remains pending.
On Oct. 8, amid President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents found him as he was driving his 5-year-old son home from school.

Security camera footage released by New York City police shows an officer dressed in plainclothes running up to the car with his gun pointed at Belgal, then immediately using the barrel of his gun to bash the driver’s side window. A second officer then draws his gun as Belgal pulls out, away from the two officers. The chase ends moments later, with Belgal’s bullet-riddled car coming to rest.
Belgal was struck in the shoulder and neck. His son was not injured. His attorneys said he didn’t learn the men were ICE officers until he awoke later in the hospital.

“It is unconscionable that Mr. Belgal should have to endure another day in detention, separated from his family, particularly given everything he has already suffered,” The Legal Aid Society, a nonprofit law firm that represents him, said in a written statement.

Federal officials maintained that ICE officers fired their weapons because they believed their lives were in danger. They said Belgal smashed his car into two government vehicles and “accelerated toward other officers.”

His attorneys said the agents did not have a valid warrant and never identified themselves before running up to Belgal’s car, smashing a window and firing several shots inside. The lawyers also argued in their filings that Belgal's due process rights were violated because he was subjected to “unreasonable use of extreme force” during his arrest.

The judge disagreed that the agents did not have a valid warrant. And the petition Belgal filed for release from custody was not an appropriate venue for arguing that the agents used excessive force, he said.
Gonzalez noted that Belgal can still ask the immigration court to release him on bond.
Johnson reported from Seattle. Associated Press writer Michael R. Sisak in New York contributed.

title: House to debate slightly tweaked version of Protect College Sports Act
summary: The House of Representatives will soon consider a slightly tweaked version of a bill already passed in the Senate that needs to be signed by the end of the year to become law
story: The House of Representatives will soon consider a slightly tweaked version of a bill already passed in the Senate that needs to be signed by the end of the year to become law
The House of Representatives will soon consider a slightly tweaked version of a bill already passed in the Senate that needs to be signed by the end of the year to become law.

One key change in the House version of the Protect College Sports Act released Friday would allow conferences to expand to as many as 22 teams — two more than allowed in the Senate version. The bigger number appears designed to cater to teams in Florida and the Carolinas that play in the Atlantic Coast Conference.
The House version would also forbid schools with $50 million or more in media-rights revenue from using student fees to subsidize sports.
The NCAA sent a letter to members pushing them to advocate for the bill, which it said could start to be considered as soon as Nov. 30.
