“Given the short time period, it is imperative member schools contact their representatives as soon as possible,” the letter said.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Republican colleagues Tim Walberg and Brett Guthrie released a statement saying, “Congress needs to pass strong antitrust protections to end the Wild West atmosphere that exists today.”
In a news conference, President Donald Trump reiterated his support for the bill, saying without it, “you’re going to have these colleges all go bankrupt.”
The bill, which among other things locks in rules that regulate how athletes are paid and builds in protections for Olympic sports, passed the Senate 77-22 last month.

But it faces a tougher road in the House where Democrats have expressed several concerns, including over athletes' rights in the face of the bill's proposed antitrust exemption. That exemption would prevent many lawsuits, including those over eligibility, the likes of which have been streaming through courts around the country since the start of this school year.
See AP’s full sports coverage here

title: A California billionaire tax proposal faced a major setback despite big wins for progressives
summary: A first-in-the-nation effort to pass a billionaire tax in California faced a major setback when voters rejected the measure and passed a policymaking it much harder to enact such a tax in the future
story: A first-in-the-nation effort to pass a billionaire tax in California faced a major setback when voters rejected the measure and passed a policymaking it much harder to enact such a tax in the future

SACRAMENTO, Calif. -- In an election with major wins for Democrats and progressives nationwide, California voters not only rejected the biggest test yet for a state wealth tax, they also approved a measure making it much harder to enact one in the future.

Proposition 40 would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion, with most of the money dedicated to healthcare. Just more than half — 52% — of voters rejected it. Meanwhile, they narrowly approved Proposition 42, which bans the state from enacting future taxes on people’s financial assets. State lawmakers can't override that; it can only be undone by voters with a future ballot measure.

“I don’t think you’re going to see such a good Democratic electorate in the near future,” said Wesley Hussey, a political science professor at California State University, Sacramento. “This was the time to pass something that was pretty lefty and progressive and had a lot of opposition.”

Nationally it was a good year for so-called “tax the rich” measures in other states, including Washington, where voters upheld a 9.9% tax on household income over $1 million. But California's measure was different because it would have taxed the assets, not the income, of the ultrarich.

And it targeted billionaires, who are significantly wealthier than millionaires and have far more assets to spend. A committee that opposed Proposition 40 and backed Proposition 42 raised more than $333 million, including large donations from tech billionaires such as Google co-founder Sergey Brin and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. Collectively, the fight over taxing billionaires was one of the most expensive ballot battles in state history.

Outside observers say the fact that it failed in California, a heavily Democratic state often viewed as a liberal leader, is not surprising because of the sheer amount of money spent opposing it and the big-name Democrats who lined up against it. Gov. Gavin Newsom was among those warning it was a bad financial deal for the state. Opponents outspent supporters by 10 to 1.

But proponents of the wealth tax, which included SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna, are trying to frame the loss as progress toward holding billionaires accountable in the future. They have teased bringing the idea before voters again in 2028.
“The game is up, people have had it and this election is just the beginning,” Khanna said on election night.

Faced with pushback from Newsom, SEIU UHW offered to scale back its proposal in June just before it qualified for the ballot. The union proposed a 2% levy, down from 5%, but Newsom's office said the proposed tax remained fundamentally flawed. Efforts to make a deal fell apart, and the union proceeded despite a growing coalition of groups opposing the tax.

Opponents of the tax said its failure affirmed that voters understood the risks associated with it. They warned it would have driven billionaires and their tax money out of state, causing budget problems down the road. California relies heavily on the rich for its income tax revenue.

“We were hopefully optimistic based on the polls that voters would agree with us that Prop. 40 was just a horrible idea for the state and Prop. 42 provides some important protections going forward," said David Kline, a spokesperson for the California Taxpayers Association.

California voters didn’t completely repudiate the concept of taxing the wealthy at higher rates in this year’s election. They approved a measure to indefinitely extend a tax increase on individual incomes exceeding $371,000 to raise money for education.

Besides Washington, Colorado voters adopted a graduated income tax that imposes higher rates on people with higher income, including an 8.4% tax on income over $1 million. The revenue from both states' taxes will go toward education, healthcare and other services. Spending on the Washington and Colorado measures paled in comparison to the billionaire tax battle. Legislatures in Hawaii, Maine and Rhode Island also approved new taxes this year on people with incomes over $1 million.
California has a 1% income tax on millionaires that voters approved in 2004 to raise money for mental health services.

Carl Davis, research director at the nonprofit Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, said the results indicated “a really good batting average” for backers of higher taxes for the wealthy. California's billionaire tax effort was hurt by divisions among organized labor over the measure, he said.
“I think the pendulum is swinging toward increased interest in taxing the rich,” he said.

Advocates for higher taxes on the wealthy plan to expand their push next year in a half-dozen states where Democrats recently won control of both legislative chambers and the governor's office, said Amber Wallin, executive director of the State Revenue Alliance, a nonprofit advocacy group for progressive tax policies.
“I think that the movement will only continue to grow,” Wallin said.

California's Proposition 42 bans new taxes on people's financial assets, business interests and intellectual property, as well as taxes that apply retroactively. The billionaire tax, for instance, would have applied to people living in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026, even though it would have taken effect the following year. That will now be prohibited.

California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who will take over from Newsom in January, opposed the billionaire tax. But he said recently that the amount of support it received sent “a clear signal” that people “don’t believe everybody in California is paying their fair share.” He said he wanted to correct that but didn’t specify how.

Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions, which supported Proposition 40, said opposition from groups like the California Teachers Association and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California made it harder to pass the measure than if supporters had been fighting billionaires alone.
But she said this year’s ballot fight was just the start.
“We have to go back to the ballot,” Gonzalez said. “We’ve got to keep fighting.”
Associated Press writer David A. Lieb in Jefferson City, Missouri, contributed.

title: Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
summary: The man accused of sparking last year’s deadly Palisades Fire has been found guilty of arson charges
story: The man accused of sparking last year’s deadly Palisades Fire has been found guilty of arson charges
LOS ANGELES -- The man accused of sparking last year’s deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.

Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.

Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges.
With little apparent reaction, Rinderknecht gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. The verdict was delivered on the third day of deliberation.

Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in LA, said the verdict was a “testament of the hard work” his team put into the case. He said he was “intimately familiar” with the strength of the evidence and was happy with the jury that convicted Rinderknecht.
Rinderknecht’s attorney Steve Haney said in a statement they were disappointed in the verdict but respected the jury process.
“After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration,” Haney said. Regarding an appeal, he said they would review all the options at the right time.
Rinderknecht is set to be sentenced March 17, 2027. Each count carries a mandatory minimum of five years and a maximum of 20 years in federal prison.

Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht’s first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial. Essayli said he believed the first jury acted improperly and appeared to consider things in their decision that weren’t presented as evidence during the trial.

Juror No. 3, who only wanted to be identified by his first name Cameron, said he was the only person who felt Rinderknecht was not guilty at the start of deliberations. Another person was undecided, and the rest of the 10 jurors believed Rinderknecht was guilty.
“It took a lot for me to be convinced otherwise,” he said. “After listening to every single point, I do now agree that he’s guilty.”

Cameron said he initially had concerns about a technical review conducted by a defense expert witness, who argued the government had gotten the origin area of the fire wrong. He said there was a “lack of information” presented to the jury about the technical review.
In the end, it was Rinderknecht’s own testimony that was the strongest piece of evidence pointing to a guilty verdict, he said.
“Stating that he was up on the hill, didn’t smell a fire, didn’t see fireworks … no one else was on the hill that night,” Cameron said.

During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organized case that presented digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht’s state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. They did not focus as much on his resentment toward the rich and powerful to present the crime as arson motivated by “societal revenge” like they previously did.

Prosecutors zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire’s origin area, such as photographs that showed his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and cellphone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks.
They established that Rinderknecht was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.
“He was mad at everything, and frustrated,” said Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams.

After the fire began, Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times as he walked down the hill. Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: “Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?”
These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said.
They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was a holdover fire from the initial blaze Rinderknecht sparked.
Haney cast doubt on the government’s case, saying the fire scene could have been compromised because the area was publicly accessible until the Palisades Fire started Jan. 7.
The defense called their own expert witnesses, including a retired fire investigator for the U.S. Forest Service who argued the fire origin area was different from what the government concluded.

Prosecutors attacked the fire investigator during cross examination and at one point accused him of perjury, alleging he did not disclose all records related to the case. The judge ultimately rejected prosecutors’ request to strike his testimony.

Haney argued the government could not conclusively say there was no one else by the fire ignition point that night because of missing cell data records, and pointed to a neighbor’s testimony that he saw a group of teenagers running away from the direction of the trailhead.
He told jurors to disregard any evidence related to Rinderknecht’s character, such as his angry text messages, because they were “evidence of the man, not evidence of the act.”

Finally, Haney presented an alternate explanation for what ignited the fire — fireworks. Multiple witnesses, including two neighbors and a local firefighter, all said they heard a loud bang or explosion from the direction of the hill the fire purportedly started on.
In the thousands of images of the evening collected from cameras in the area, none showed fireworks in the sky above the hill where the fire started, prosecutors said.

title: Officials: Washington pulp mill violated safety standards before deadly tank rupture
summary: State investigators have revealed that a Washington pulp mill, where a chemical tank ruptured in May killing 11 people, had a history of severe safety violations
story: State investigators have revealed that a Washington pulp mill, where a chemical tank ruptured in May killing 11 people, had a history of severe safety violations

SEATTLE -- The Washington state pulp mill where a chemical tank ruptured in May, killing 11, had an extensive track record of egregious and willful safety violations, including failure to inspect or repair more than a dozen other tanks at the facility, state investigators said Friday.

Nippon Dynawave Packaging Co. faces more than $10 million in state fines, including the largest employer safety fine in state history, and investigators plan to refer their findings to prosecutors for possible criminal charges.

“Without repair or replacement, the tank walls were a ticking clock,” Dan Pitts, state Labor and Industries compliance manager, said during a press conference in Longview to announce the findings. "It was a question of time, and time ran out."
Nippon did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment about the state’s findings.

Nippon plans to restart operations in December. Officials said the company has an obligation to fix any hazards that have been identified, and the state will be closely monitoring to ensure that happens.

Besides the 11 who were killed, 12 were injured on May 26 when the tank holding more than 900,000 gallons (3.4 million liters) of “white liquor,” a highly corrosive chemical used in paper manufacturing, ruptured. The flood of caustic material was powerful enough to blow out building walls and overturn pickup trucks at the site.

“Nippon’s decision to keep G-10 operating when they knew it was not safe contributed to the death of 11 workers," said Labor and Industries Director Joel Sacks. "Because of that, we will be referring this case to prosecutors to consider criminal charges.”
The state Ecology department also announced that it has issued 34 violations that impacted air and water, and is seeking $961,000 in penalties and costs for responding to the emergency.

Most of the environmental violations were due to the impact of the white liquor that spread across the site, officials said. It reached storm drains and a wastewater treatment system, with some discharging into the Columbia River and a nearby ditch, killing fish.

State investigators said Friday the company failed to take appropriate action to address the issue in violation of state law, and similarly failed to inspect or address deficiencies in 13 other tanks at the site.

Officials also said Nippon's emergency response and planning fell short of state requirements. The company had not effectively prepared its staff to respond to an emergency, and there was no employer-led incident command for several hours after the tank failed, Pitts said.
“We believe failures in the response were a contributing factor in serious injuries to four of 12 workers who were hurt that day," Pitts said.

The state investigation mirrored an August report by the U.S. Chemical Safety Board that revealed inspectors hired by the company in 2025 found the tank that ruptured was “not fit for continued service” due to deteriorating thickness in the tank walls.

An AP review of inspections and safety complaints at the plant prior to the tank collapse found that Labor and Industries had investigated more than a dozen safety complaints at the plant since 2018 and issued almost $7,000 in fines for violations. Ecology had issued 54 environmental violation notices against the company since 2016 and fined them $41,500 for eight serious offenses.

More than $2.4 million in workers’ compensation claims have been paid for 169 employees injured on the job since 2015, the agency reported, including for injuries related to exposure to caustic substances.
After the May tank collapse, the state’s Department of Ecology filed a violation notice against the company listing 35 citations.

Nippon Dynawave said in an email Wednesday that they have remained engaged with the government agencies that are investigating the tank collapse. They said the mill has hosted hundreds of visits by regulators and investigators.

“The full deconstruction, forensic examination and technical analysis needed to determine the root cause have not yet been completed,” the company said. “The tank is currently being deconstructed, with great care being taken to log and retain portions of the tank to determine the root cause.”

Among workers killed in the rupture were brothers Tyler and Brad Covington. Their mother, Sheri Lynn King, has filed a wrongful-death lawsuit against Nippon Dynawave, saying her sons were burned and crushed by the white liquor and debris. The lawsuit claims the company failed to maintain and inspect equipment, failed to properly train and supervise employees and failed to implement safety policies and emergency response procedures.

title: 2 men cleared in South Carolina road rage shooting now face charges after family finds new evidence
summary: Two men initially cleared in a South Carolina road rage shooting three years ago now face murder charges
story: Two men initially cleared in a South Carolina road rage shooting three years ago now face murder charges

COLUMBIA, S.C. -- Two men initially cleared of criminal charges in a South Carolina road rage shooting three years ago now face murder charges after the victim's family uncovered evidence of police officers influencing the investigation.
Two of the Horry County officers also were indicted this week on obstruction of justice and misconduct charges for their role in investigating the shooting of Scott Spivey in September 2023.
The charges came after another independent look at the case pushed by Spivey's family. After prosecutors first decided not to charge Weldon Boyd and Kenneth Williams, they filed a civil lawsuit.

The family received recordings Boyd made of his own phone calls where he bragged about the shooting and asked a police officer friend to intervene. It also got body camera footage of another officer writing a note to the men the day of the shooting that said “act like a victim camera.”

The case started with Boyd and Williams chasing Spivey for several miles after Spivey pulled a gun on them in a road rage incident, authorities said. Both pickups reached speeds over 100 mph (160 kph) before Spivey pulled off a side road and got out of his truck with a gun and told the men to stop following him, investigators said.
The men shot through the windshield of the pickup, hitting Spivey in the right side of his back near his armpit, authorities said.

The local prosecutor in the case turned it over to the South Carolina Attorney General's Office after Boyd posted a message on Facebook thanking police and prosecutors for their work on the case a week after the shooting.

The Attorney General's Office decided not to prosecute Boyd and Williams in the shooting seven months later, ruling they were threatened and therefore justified to fire on Spivey under the state's stand your ground law.

That led to the civil lawsuit, which unearthed Boyd's phone calls. In one, he talks to Williams about them getting teardrop tattoos since they killed a man. In another, he told someone Spivey figured out during the chase he could drive faster than them and was terrified. In another, he said about the shooting, “I know it’s (expletive) up to say, but I had a (expletive) blast."

The officers were fired after the new evidence and the Attorney General's Office brought in prosecutor Barry Barnette from Spartanburg to review the case. He called for another grand jury that led to Thursday's indictments.

Lawyers for all four men charged said publicity has tainted the case. They all said their clients were innocent and Boyd's lawyer Shaun Kent said the charges should be dropped in part because the evidence from the civil case was used to build criminal charges — a tactic that led to the dismissal of sexual assault charges against Bill Cosby.
There are reasons prosecutors initially cleared the men including findings that Spivey had alcohol in his system, Kent said.
“He was intoxicated. He had a firearm. He was pointing it at other individuals," Kent said in court Thursday.

Boyd and Williams were both indicted on murder charges, while former Horry County Deputy Chief Brandon Strickland and Sgt. Damon Vescovi were charged with misconduct in office and obstruction of justice.
Boyd called Strickland several times from the scene and after, and Strickland told his friend he talked to investigators and prosecutors, according to Boyd's phone calls.
Strickland's lawyer said at a Thursday bond hearing that his comments may have been inappropriate but there is no evidence he influenced the investigation.
Vescovi passed along the note about the camera. His lawyer said he made a poor choice but at that point he thought Boyd and Williams were victims of a road rage incident.

Jennifer Spivey, who pored over the evidence in her brother's killing until she found the note and heard Boyd's phone calls, was at Thursday's hearing and asked the judge to make sure justice is finally served.
"Scott tried desperately to escape the violence that ultimately took his life," she said.

title: Fans near and far mourn Fiona the hippo
summary: Fans of the Cincinnati Zoo’s beloved Fiona the hippo are mourning
story: Fans of the Cincinnati Zoo’s beloved Fiona the hippo are mourning

CINCINNATI -- Fans of Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo's hippo, draped a hippo statue with flowers and notes written in crayon Friday, a day after she died from complications caused by swallowing a knit hat accidentally flung into her enclosure.
A little girl held up a drawing of Fiona while a woman left behind a watermelon, one of Fiona's favorite treats.
“She brought so much love in her lifetime,” said one note.

Born prematurely almost a decade ago and given slim odds of survival, Fiona became not only a source of hometown pride but also a worldwide symbol of hope and inspiration for many — from teachers to parents to children.

“I have never known an animal so beloved in all my life. From the day she was born, she was like lightning in a bottle,” Thayne Maynard, the zoo board's executive chair, said in a statement. “And, she will be remembered and beloved many years from now.”
Zoo officials have yet to release the specific medical cause of Fiona's death or details surrounding her final hours. Fiona was 9 years old.
“Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn’t fight anymore,” zoo director Dave Jenike said.
At first, Fiona showed no signs of distress after swallowing the hat 11 days before her death. A zoo visitor tossed the hat, which a ceiling fan caught and flung into the hippo habitat.
But a few days later, her appetite started to decline, zoo officials said. By Monday, the zoo announced Fiona was undergoing veterinary care.
The zoo's animal care team gave her fluids through an IV, conducted a colonoscopy and tried to shake the obstruction loose with a vibration table borrowed from a horse farm.
They said they were cautiously optimistic she could pass the hat.
“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome,” the zoo said.
The zoo's director said Fiona's death came as a shock. “We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn’t anymore,” Jenike said.
Fiona captured the hearts of millions in her first months and final days, uniting people across all boundaries and political spectrums.
Usha Vance, the wife of Vice President JD Vance, posted a photo of one of their children face-to-face with Fiona through the glass wall of her enclosure.
Former first daughter Chelsea Clinton posted photos of her behind-the-scenes encounter with Fiona, writing that she would treasure “the smiles she gave me.”
Speaking outside the zoo Thursday, Amy Haacke, a teacher from Dayton, said that she was a “huge fan” of Fiona because she likes underdogs. She said she uses the Fiona book series in her classroom.
“It kind of means a lot to be here,” she said.
Fiona was born six weeks premature, weighing just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms), far below the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at the time.
The zoo's staff went to extraordinary lengths to keep her alive, raising her by hand. She couldn't nurse, so a zoo staffer hand-milked her mother to feed her.
She became a celebrity during her nine years. Hippos typically live 40 to 50 years in zoos.

Her story marked an uplifting turn for the Cincinnati Zoo after months of backlash over the 2016 shooting of Harambe. The gorilla became a pop culture phenomenon after he was killed because a child got into his enclosure.

title: NYC Mayor Mamdani is injured in soccer match against journalists
summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani says he tore his Achilles tendon while playing in a soccer match against the City Hall press corps
story: NEW YORK -- New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Friday that he tore his Achilles tendon during a pickup soccer match against the City Hall press corps and will have to wear a medical boot for the next several weeks.
Mamdani, 35, hobbled into a news conference on crutches and, when a reporter asked about his injury, explained that he got it in Thursday night's game.
As for why it happened, the millennial leader of America's biggest city identified a possible culprit in the form of a neglected pre-game warmup: “I did not stretch."
Still, the avid soccer fan appeared happy to report that he scored a goal “soon after getting on the pitch” but said he “forgot that I was 35.”
He was also quick to note that his team wound up beating the journalists' squad.
The mayor, known for a busy schedule, said he'll be wearing the medical boot for six to eight weeks and will be back on the pitch in about nine months.

title: ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ sets record with $3.79B in first-day retail sales, Rockstar Games reports
summary: Rockstar Games announces that “Grand Theft Auto VI” has generated a record $3.79 billion in first-day retail sales
story: Rockstar Games announces that “Grand Theft Auto VI” has generated a record $3.79 billion in first-day retail sales

NEW YORK -- Sales of “Grand Theft Auto VI” generated a record with $3.79 billion in first-day retail sales, maker Rockstar Games said Friday, underscoring the enormous demand for the first new installment in the blockbuster series in 13 years.

The worldwide figure was based on company estimates through the end of the day Thursday, the day the game launched. Rockstar also said in a release that it sold 32.5 million units prerelease, setting a record across platforms.

“We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you,” Sam Houser, Rockstar’s president and founder, said in a release.
The launch far eclipsed that of its predecessor.

“Grand Theft Auto V,” released in 2013, generated $1 billion in retail sales in its first three days. It went on to become one of the bestselling video games of all time, accounting for more than 230 million of the franchise's more than 470 million units sold globally, according to publisher Take-Two Interactive.

Earlier Friday, market research firm Sensor Tower estimated “GTA VI” had generated $2.36 billion in revenue on approximately 24.6 million units sold. Rockstar's figures, released later in the day, were based on the company's own estimates of worldwide, day-one retail sales.
The standard edition of the game retails for around $80 in the U.S.

Earlier this month, the PlayStation blog said that “GTA VI” was the most preordered game in the history of its namesake store. Due to the demand, PlayStation said that it was teaming with Rockstar Games to allow players to start preloading the game nine days early, so that they'd be ready to play on launch day.

“GTA VI” is the latest installment in the hyperviolent, open-world video game series that has skewered American culture with fictionalized versions of New York and Los Angeles and is now returning to its sun-baked version of Miami — Vice City.

It's the first new “GTA” game in 13 years, with the story of “GTA VI” centered on Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple trying to improve their circumstances through crime across the fictional state of Leonida.
Early reviews for the game have noted a greater emphasis on relationship building that goes beyond the violent stickups, bank robberies and mayhem that have long defined the franchise.

The game's release also ended years of secrecy around its cast. Manni L. Perez plays Lucia and Dylan Rourke portrays Jason, while Bobby Moynihan, Stephen Root, Taryn Manning, Roselyn Sanchez and rapper Denzel Curry are among the familiar names in Rockstar’s sprawling credits.
The enormous launch comes after more than a decade of anticipation around a series that has become one of the biggest properties in entertainment. ___
This story has been corrected to show that Sensor Tower on Friday estimated “GTA VI” had generated $2.36 billion in revenue, not $2.36 million.
Jonathan Landrum Jr. is an Entertainment Writer reporting from Los Angeles.

title: Northeastern Florida faces flood threats from devastating storms
summary: Heavy rains that left large swaths of Florida’s Atlantic coast under water and led to dozens of rescues moved further north on Friday
story: Heavy rains that left large swaths of Florida’s Atlantic coast under water and led to dozens of rescues moved further north on Friday

Heavy rains that left large swaths of Florida's Atlantic coast under water and led to dozens of rescues moved further north on Friday as forecasters warned flooding threats could stretch into next week when a major river is expected to crest well above record levels.

The National Weather Service posted flood warnings and watches stretching around 200 miles (320 kilometers) from just south of Melbourne to the Jacksonville area. Additional rainfall of 2 to 6 inches (5 to 15 centimeters) was expected through Saturday, while some areas could see an extra 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 centimeters).

“Severe, widespread flash flooding is expected,” the weather service said in a Friday morning forecast. “In addition, areas that normally do not experience flash flooding will flood. Furthermore, lives and property (are) in great danger.”

The St. Johns River, Florida's longest, rose above a record level Thursday near Cocoa that was set in 1953. The river is forecast to stay at least 2 feet (61 centimeters) above flood stage through early next week, the weather service said.

Also Friday, a nontropical low-pressure system was expected to form and could become a subtropical or tropical storm along the southeastern U.S. coast, the National Hurricane Center in Miami said. The southeast and mid-Atlantic coasts should expect strong winds, dangerous surf and coastal flooding into early next week ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

Parts of Florida's east coast have been deluged with rainfall totaling more than 17 inches (43 centimeters) in some spots since Tuesday, according to preliminary totals by the weather service. That's in addition to heavy rains that fell earlier this month. Several places have already seen their wettest November on record.

The storms shifted north to the Space Coast on Thursday, sending rivers over their banks and prompting water rescues of people and horses during what is supposed to be Florida's dry season that runs from October to May.
“Never seen such a thing like this in Florida,” said Jazmin Foster, whose Melbourne home was inundated with water for the second time in two weeks.

In Brevard County on Thursday, people with trailers braved knee-deep water to rescue dozens of horses and other animals at the Blue Lake Equestrian Center, an animal hospice and boarding facility in Cocoa. The animals were taken to a dry pasture elsewhere.

First responders conducted nearly 100 high-water rescues across the county, and those numbers continued to climb, Sheriff Wayne Ivey said. The city of Palm Bay conducted mandatory evacuations for some residents of a mobile home community. Shelters were opened for residents forced from their homes.

Nearly 200 Florida National Guard personnel with 50 high-water vehicles have been deployed to help up and down the coast, the Division of Emergency Management said. Other responding agencies included about 235 officers with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission.

This week’s storms have been fueled by persistent high pressure over Virginia and a low-pressure system and an associated stationary front in the Gulf, which together have pushed a steady onshore flow across the Florida Peninsula. They're an offshoot of El Niño, the natural warming of the Pacific near the equator that warps weather patterns worldwide.
Forecasters said El Niño conditions are expected to persist through the spring, meaning the soggy extreme weather in Florida and California will likely continue through the winter.

The California coast, from the Los Angeles to San Francisco areas, was also swamped with flooding in many areas this week, leaving neighborhoods under water and forcing some drivers to abandon stalled vehicles in floodwaters. A long stretch of the coastal Highway 1 was closed south of the Monterey Peninsula due to rock and mud slides.
Associated Press writers Amy Taxin in Santa Ana, California, and Jessica Hill in Las Vegas contributed to this report.

title: Trump administration use of encrypted messaging apps like Signal is scrutinized by House Democrat
summary: A Democratic lawmaker is investigating the use of encrypted messaging apps by Justice Department employees for official business
story: A Democratic lawmaker is investigating the use of encrypted messaging apps by Justice Department employees for official business

WASHINGTON -- A top House Democrat is demanding that multiple government agencies preserve communications created on nongovernment messaging apps and investigate whether any records related to official business have been deleted.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee and the panel's incoming chairman, said in a series of nearly identical letters made public on Friday that he was concerned that President Donald Trump's administration was circumventing record-keeping requirements by using apps like Signal that can be configured to automatically delete messages after a certain time period.

Raskin noted in the letters, which were sent to top officials at the FBI, the Justice Department, the Department of Homeland Security, the Bureau of Prisons and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, that the agencies were legally required to preserve all records related to their official business, policies and decisions.

But he said: “There is significant evidence that Trump Administration officials have engaged in the widespread destruction, mutilation, and concealment of government records, seemingly with the express purpose of circumventing federal record preservation laws. This attempt to evade transparency extends to the highest levels of federal agencies, including top-ranking law enforcement officials.”

The Maryland Democrat cited as an example a Signal exchange that he said he had obtained between the FBI’s general counsel and an associate of the Republican president's oldest son, Donald Trump Jr., in which a potential or ongoing healthcare fraud investigation was discussed.

The Justice Department said in a statement Friday that it “follows all legal requirements for the management of federal records involving its official functions and decisions.” The other agencies cited by Raskin did not immediately return messages seeking comment.

Signal is an app that can be used for direct messaging and group chats as well as phone and video calls. It uses end-to-end encryption for its messaging and calling services that prevents any third party from viewing conversation content or listening in on calls.
Encrypted messaging apps are increasingly popular with government officials, an Associated Press review from last year found.

Their prevalence was demonstrated in vivid fashion last year when journalist Jeffrey Goldberg revealed that he had been inadvertently added to a Signal group chat of U.S. national security officials coordinating plans for airstrikes.

The White House and the Pentagon have said that disgruntled former employees were spreading false claims about the use of Signal, a commercially available app not authorized to be used to communicate sensitive or classified national defense information.

title: Don Toliver concert in U.K. evacuated due to mystery substance
summary: Some 12,000 fans of American rapper Don Toliver had to evacuate his concert in Manchester, England, after a noxious substance spread through the arena.
story: More than 12,000 people were evacuated from an arena in northern England Sunday night after the crowd at American rapper Don Toliver's concert suddenly started screaming, choking and coughing when a powerful smell spread through the venue.
Police said the Co-op Live arena in Manchester was evacuated at about 10 p.m. (5 p.m. Eastern).
There's been speculation online that the mysterious substance that spread through the air in the arena was tear gas, but authorities have not confirmed that.
Don Toliver, who is set to end a world tour with a Tuesday night show in London, left the stage in Manchester and police declared it a major incident.
One person was hospitalized and dozens were assessed for eye and respiratory symptoms according to the local ambulance service.
The arena was being fully decontaminated as a precaution, the emergency medical service said.
Ben Stevenson told the Manchester Evening News newspaper that he was in the audience standing section when he "started coughing and (my) eyes were kind of itchy."

He said the lights came on as Toliver left the stage, but that everyone remained in the venue for almost an hour before an announcement asking people to make their way out was heard over the loudspeaker.
"We will now begin to fully understand what this substance was and how this incident came about," Police Assistant Chief Constable Steph Parker told reporters.
The venue opened in 2024 and is only about 2 miles from the Manchester Arena, where 22 people were killed in 2017 by a suicide bomber who blew himself up during an Ariana Grande concert.

title: Tony Shalhoub on food, family, and his book, "We Thought They'd Never Leave"
summary: For the award-winning star of "Monk," food had always been an integral part of family. And now he's teamed with daughter Josie Adams to write a food memoir: "We Thought They'd Never Leave," the story of their family reunions - and their recipes.
story: He was a detective with a quirk in "Monk," and played an alien opposite the "Men in Black." But if you really want to feel the soul of Tony Shalhoub, this character might be it: the stubborn chef Primo in "Big Night," his 1996 film with Stanley Tucci about food, family and … even more food.

Shalhoub is himself an investor in a New York City restaurant, Massara, where he invited us last week to break bread with his daughter, Josie Adams. The act of breaking bread, he said, is very important: "It's part of the family tradition, really. Having bread at the center of the table, it's how we were formed."
He's even made a TV series, "Tony Shalhoub Breaking Bread," about different types of bread from different places.

For him and his family, the passion for food can be traced back to a time when there wasn't any. Shalhoub's father, Joseph, was born in war-torn Lebanon. Orphaned at a young age, he faced hunger and food shortages as a child. "A lot of his early memories were about that hunger," he said, "so that ties into our current family situation and our appreciation for and devotion to preparing food and feeding each other."
The Shalhoubs settled in Green Bay, Wisconsin, and by the time Tony came along in 1953, there were a lot of mouths to feed; he was one of ten children.

The family was close, and stayed that way. Every summer, the entire extended Shalhoub clan – more than 50 in all – gathers in Wisconsin for a reunion. It's a week of big, homecooked meals and intense family bonding. And when the party's over, everyone gets a traditional Shalhoub family send-off: "At the end of the week," Tony said, "as people are loading up their cars, everyone else who's remaining gathers in a line in the drive and raises their hands," and a chorus cries out: "We thought they'd never leave!"
"We Thought They'd Never Leave" became the title of a book Shalhoub co-wrote with Josie, the story of their family and its recipes.

She actually started it during the pandemic, when both of her parents (Tony and actor Brooke Adams) were sick with COVID, and she feared that their memories and recipes would be lost forever. So, she gave them both journals to write it all down. "My dad was like, 'Do you think we're going to die? Why are you giving us this right now?'" Josie said. "He's like, 'I'm better now!' So I said, 'OK, well, will you maybe work on this cookbook with me? I'd like to do the family cookbook for real.' And he said yes."

Shalhoub and his wife raised two daughters in Los Angeles as he navigated the feast-or-famine life of a Hollywood actor. But for every Emmy-winning success like "Monk," there were lesser roles. "Sometimes there were jobs that I did that were just for the money," he said. "Do I regret doing those jobs? Not really. I mean, maybe one or two, but sometimes you just got to eat."
In 2016 he said he wanted to take a break from screen acting, move to New York, and just do live theater. He won a Tony Award for best lead actor in a musical for "The Band's Visit."
But then he got a job offer that was irresistible. As family patriarch Abe Weissman in "The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel," Shalhoub won his fifth Emmy.

In real life, Shalhoub has been married to Brooke Adams for 34 years, and he actually does a lot of the cooking at home. Josie said, "Yeah, you cook for Mom a lot. Every morning my dad wakes up before my mom and makes her a cappuccino and brings it to her in bed. Every single morning."
"Except when I'm not there!" he laughed.
And that's the Shalhoub family's love language: cooking and serving each other, whether it's one loved one, or a crowd of 50.

Josie said, "It's really easy to send a text and say, 'I love you, thinking about you.' But it's a lot harder to do something for someone else. And that's what this whole reunion is about: getting together and showing the people that you love, that you love them."

title: Kwame Onwuachi's culinary journey
summary: The New York Times named the award-winning chef's Tatiana the best restaurant in the city two years in a row. Kwame Onwuachi discusses his Afro-Caribbean menu, and his path to becoming one of today's brightest culinary stars.
story: New York City's famed Lincoln Center is a dream destination for ballerinas, baritones, and one award-winning chef. As a youngster, Kwame Onwuachi sat on the steps in the plaza, taking a break from selling candy on the subway. "I never thought that one day ... I would have my sister's name on the side of the building," he said.

Onwuachi's restaurant Tatiana, located right on the renowned plaza, is one of the hardest reservations to book. The New York Times named Tatiana the best restaurant in New York City two years in a row; Time magazine put Onwuachi on their list of Most Influential People; and the James Beard Foundation gave him the Rising Star Award.

For Onuwuachi, now 37, he's just cooking what he knows. Asked to characterize the food he makes, he replied, "I would say Afro-Caribbean. The technical term is African people who came through the Caribbean. You're going to see a couple different things from these different regions, but they're all tied together. Jambalaya and joloff rice, gumbo and okra stew, right? Barbecue and suya. Like, these things are connected."
Onwuachi's love of food started early. He grew up in the Bronx. His mother was a caterer, his father an architect.

Asked his first memory of food, Onwuachi said, "Oh man, I remember very, very vividly being on my grandmother's hip, and her putting this piece of bread, this thin bread with, like, this electric, almost like a muted electric green sauce into my mouth. And it was curry goat with roti. And I remember the explosion of flavors. It was very vivid."

As a teenager, he found himself working a variety of jobs, but always had an appetite for the kitchen. He enrolled at the Culinary Institute of America in Hyde Park, New York. On a return visit, he said, "It's always feels good to be back here. So many memories, so many, like, defining moments for me, like truly becoming like a leader – that happened here."

He's a star there now, mentoring students at the school that gave him direction and purpose, when he was one of the few Black students in his class. "I think there was two of us in my class," he said. Asked how it made him feel, he said, "I'm a chef, for God sakes! I took it out on the lobsters.

"I focused on my studies at the end of the day," he said. "It's reflective of the industry, too, in the fine dining sense. There's not a lot of people of color in that. I didn't focus on this, but I knew I wanted to use my platform to help amplify my culture."

Onwuachi has a lot on his plate. Over the past decade, he's been everywhere from bookshelves to competing on shows like "Top Chef." He now has three restaurants, including Dogon in Washington, D.C., and his latest, Maroon, which opened last April on the Las Vegas Strip.

For Kwame Onuwachi, success never gets stale. And we witnessed him receive Maroon's first big review last month, when the Los Angeles Times called his restaurant "the best steakhouse in Las Vegas, and beyond."
But the chef says he's cooking up more than just food.
"I think if a dish tells a story, it has a soul," Onuwachi said. "You're not just cooking for perfect seasoning, you're cooking to share something with someone."

title: Princess Kate announces she's in remission from cancer
summary: Princess Kate made the announcement on social media after visiting the London hospital where she received treatment.
story: Catherine, the Princess of Wales, said Tuesday her cancer is in remission, about 10 months after announcing her diagnosis. Princess Kate made the announcement on social media after visiting the London hospital where she received treatment.

"It is a relief to now be in remission and I remain focused on recovery," she said in her post on Instagram after visiting the Royal Marsden Hospital in London. "As anyone who has experienced a cancer diagnosis will know, it takes time to adjust to a new normal."
The princess had announced last March that cancer was discovered following an abdominal surgery and she was undergoing preventative chemotherapy.

In September, she said she had finished chemotherapy. She spoke about receiving the cancer treatment during her visit Tuesday. "It's really tough,'' she said, according to the Associated Press. "It's such a shock."

Kate spoke with patient Katherine Field about the chemotherapy port that's used to deliver the treatment, saying, "I got so attached to it," and joking that she was almost reluctant to have it removed, according to the AP.
On social media Tuesday, Kate said she visited the hospital to thank the staff "for looking after me so well during the past year."

"My heartfelt thanks goes to all those who have quietly walked alongside William and me as we have navigated everything," she said, referring to her husband, the Prince of Wales. "We couldn't have asked for more. The care and advice we have received throughout my time as a patient has been exceptional."
Kensington Palace also announced that she and William have become patrons of the hospital.

"My hope is, that by supporting groundbreaking research and clinical excellence, as well as promoting patient and family wellbeing, we might save many more lives, and transform the experience of all those impacted by cancer," Kate said on social media.

Since 2007, William has held the role of the hospital's president. His mother, Princess Diana, also held that position, according to the palace. The hospital is known as a world-leading cancer center with three sites in London.
Kate spoke with other patients as well as doctors and nurses during Tuesday's visit, according to Britain's Press Association news agency.
"The body is amazing at telling us 'you need to take time out,'" she said after learning about a man's diagnosis.
She also talked about receiving her cancer diagnosis, according to the news agency.

"It's the uncertainty of that initial diagnosis," she said. "It's such a wealth of information. Understanding the diagnosis, it's a massive amount of information to take on as a patient. Having that continuity, in the clinical setting and outside in the home setting, is so important."

title: Book excerpt: "We Thought They'd Never Leave" by Tony Shalhoub with Josie Adams
summary: The Emmy- and Tony Award-winning actor and his daughter collaborate on a book featuring reflections on food and extended family, including their yearly ritual of a week-long summer reunion.
story: We may receive an affiliate commission from anything you buy from this article.

Emmy- and Tony Award-winning actor Tony Shalhoub's new book, "We Thought They'd Never Leave: Musings on Food and Family" (written with daughter Josie Adams, and published by Gallery Books), offers reflections on food and his extended family, including their yearly ritual of a week-long summer reunion.
Read an excerpt below, and don't miss Tracy Smith's interview with Tony Shalhoub and Josie Adams on "CBS Sunday Morning" November 22!
Prefer to listen? Audible has a 30-day free trial available right now.
Origin Story
What kind of lunatic family willingly gathers fifty-plus people in one place for seven days straight with no catered food, no outside help, and no exit strategy? Mine.

Every July, we converge in Wisconsin like salmon returning to spawn. Only with more card games, more garlic, and slightly less grace. Outsiders never believe it when I explain it to them. Nearly all my relatives, across four generations, cooking every meal from scratch, cleaning up the fallout, negotiating sleeping arrangements, and arguing over who's on the hook for Tuesday breakfast. No, we don't get paid. Yes, we do it every year. And the most bewildered question I'm always asked is ... Why?!

I used to respond with logistics. I'd explain how each family takes a night to cook, how we rotate the duties—head chef, sous chef, cleanup crew—as if we were on a ship, alone at sea with no port in sight. I'd describe how the menu is posted months in advance, how someone inevitably forgets the garlic, how someone else then inevitably overbuys the garlic, how someone else altogether inevitably burns the garlic, and how, miraculously, it all gets eaten anyway.

I'd outline the sleeping arrangements: the cousins packed in bunk beds like sardines, the uncles snoring in recliners, the blow-up mattresses that never survive the week. But logistics only explain how it works, not why it works. And that's the real question, isn't it? Because if you drill down, this reunion is objectively insane. Most sane people spend their summers escaping family obligations—jetting off to beaches, renting cabins far away from their in-laws, finding any excuse to avoid the awkward conversations and mismatched expectations that come with extended kin. We, on the other hand, run toward them—voluntarily spending seven days each summer marinating in each other's quirks, grievances, and toum sauce.

Truth is, a reunion should not be confused with a vacation. It's work. It's heavy lifting—sometimes literally, when you're carrying cases of tomatoes up the steps or hauling coolers of ice across the lawn. It's emotional labor, too: smoothing over past grudges, refereeing card games, and determining which conversations are "on the table" and which are simply "tabled."

Which is why, to explain why we do this, to understand this ritual of ours—the chopping and bickering and feeding of too many people until the table groans—I need to go back a hundred years, to another table on another continent, where the question wasn't how to make food for fifty, but whether there would be bread enough for one.

title: Here are the GTA 6 songs you'll hear cruising around Vice City
summary: Grand Theft Auto 6 players carry out missions to songs by artists such as Cardi B, Lana Del Rey and Travis Scott.
story: Grand Theft Auto 6 relies on a murderer's row of musical hitmakers to provide the backbeat for cruising around Vice City.

The latest installment in the video game franchise, which officially launched on Thursday, features 34 original songs from a range of artists, including Cardi B, Lana Del Rey, Travis Scott and Morgan Wallen. The game's official album was created in partnership with Atlantic Records, and will be available on music platforms such as Spotify and Apple Music beginning on Nov. 20.
Rockstar Games, the company behind the GTA series, is also offering fans limited-edition vinyl and CDs featuring the original tracks.
Music is an essential part of the GTA experience for players like 34-year-old Kansas City resident Cameron Logan Cox, who credits the game's music over the years with helping springboard his career.
"I went on to become a filmmaker and director for a hip-hop label," he told CBS News. "I really don't think I would have had that musical affinity if not for GTA."

In addition to the official GTA 6 soundtrack, gamers will be exposed to countless other tracks through "in-game radio," a feature in GTA 6 that allows players to listen to songs from fictional radio stations while they carry out their missions. They can turn on a station while they drive through Vice City, or via their phone.
"My favorite thing in GTA has never been a mission," Cox told CBS News. "It's the car, the radio and nowhere I have to be."

GTA 6 offers 22 stations, according to industry media outlet GameStop. Some have DJ personas, such as the Cocoteo FM station, which is hosted by characters voiced by Puerto Rican singers Bad Bunny and RaiNao, according to Rolling Stone.

GameStop has a list of some of the songs in Vice City. Among the hundreds of tracks are old hits like "Let Your Love Flow" by the Bellamy Brothers and "Pour Some Sugar on Me" by Def Leppard, as well as more recent hits like Chappell Roan's "HOT TO GO!".

title: Gamers, start your engines. Grand Theft Auto 6 is ready to roll.
summary: The latest, long-awaited version of the hit video game franchise launches at midnight local time on Nov. 19 in countries worldwide. Here's what to know about GTA 6.
story: In the immortal words of Carl "CJ" Johnson from an earlier edition of Grand Theft Auto, "Ah s***, here we go again." After 13 years and two delayed launches, video game fans are finally getting their hands on Grand Theft Auto 6.

GTA, as it's widely known, has evolved since its launch in 1997 into one of the biggest franchises in entertainment and one of the few sure hits in the ferociously competitive video game world. Tens of millions of people globally are expected to pick up their joysticks as Rockstar Games, the company behind the series, rolls out GTA 6 on Nov. 19 in countries around the world.

As fans eagerly await the latest GTA installment, Rockstar has whipped up interest with a series of trailers and even an extended look on Netflix. In typical fashion, however, the company has kept the hype simmering by withholding key information about the game ahead of its official launch this week.

"Having been over a decade since the last full release of a Grand Theft Auto game, all that energy just keeps getting bottled up and bottled up, and people are reading into every tweet and every little piece of news that's coming out of Rockstar to try and glean all the details of this game," Andrew Marok, director of equity research for digital media at financial firm Raymond James, told CBS News.
Here's what to know about the long-awaited release of GTA 6.
What is GTA 6 about?

The latest GTA installment centers on the stories of Lucia Caminos, the game's first-ever female protagonist, and Jason Duval. Jason, who has been working for drug runners, craves a quieter life but keeps getting dragged back into crime, according to Rockstar's synopsis of GTA 6. Lucia, meanwhile, has recently left Leonida Penitentiary, where she landed after "fighting for her family."

When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair becomes entangled in a wider conspiracy. The series is based in Vice City, inspired by Miami, in the fictional state of Leonida. Rockstar has touted the location as the most detailed version of the game yet, with architecture, beaches, roads and bars all inspired by South Florida.
There's "this concept of GTA 6 being just bigger than the game," Marok said.  "It's also about the immersion in the world of Vice City."
What equipment do I need to play the game?

Players will need a PlayStation 5 or an Xbox Series X/S console to play GTA 6. Rockstar told players who are preloading the game to plan ahead, as they may need up to 212 GB of storage space, depending on their device.
When can people start playing?

The game officially debuts worldwide on Thursday, Nov. 19. Rather than a single launch time, GTA 6 is rolling out at midnight local time in countries around the world, giving some users access before others. This website shows the countdown time by country.

Pre-orders for the game began back in June. But users weren't allowed to start pre-downloading on their PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S consoles until Nov. 10, according to Rockstar. Gamers were also able to purchase a "code-in-box" version, a physical case that contains a code users can input to download the game from the PlayStation Store or Xbox.
How much does it cost?
Grand Theft Auto 6 costs $79.99 for the "standard edition" and $99.99 for the "ultimate edition." The latter contains an exclusive collection of cars, weapons and apparel.
What are players saying?

New Zealand was among the first countries where players could access the game. One 25-year-old told CBS News he set up his PlayStation account to appear as if he were in New Zealand — where the game is already live — rather than his home in the United Kingdom, to access it as soon as possible.
"It's definitely more immersive than previous entries," he told CBS News, requesting anonymity because he is taking a day off from work to play GTA 6. "Visually, it's incredible."
Other gamers were also quick to praise GTA 6's visual quality and action-packed plot.

"The gameplay dynamics are just amazing, and the graphics are great, and you can tell that the storytelling is really deep, which is impressive," Adam Simmons, a 50-year-old in Wellington, New Zealand, where the game has already rolled out, told The Associated Press.

On Metacritic, a review aggregator website, players gave GTA 6 a score of 99 out of 100. "Grand Theft Auto VI, against all odds, has somehow managed to not only meet but surpass all my expectations," one user wrote.
How long does it take to play?
Insider Gaming, a website focused on the video game industry, said it takes an average of roughly 50 hours to complete all of the missions in GTA 6.
When will online play launch?

The online, multiplayer version of the game introduces new missions and allows players to stay immersed in the world of GTA after completing the more linear single-player version. It's free with the option of in-game purchases, according to Marok of Raymond James.
Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar's parent company, hasn't confirmed GTA Online's availability, though it seems likely given its enormous revenue potential.
"That's where GTA 5 made so much of its money," Marok said.
Will there be a PC version?

Rockstar Games did not respond to a request for comment about whether it will release a desktop version of the game. Historically, a PC version has been released about 12 to 18 months after the console version, according to Marok. However, the company could decide to launch it sooner.

"I think that there are reasons why Rockstar and Take-Two would want the PC version of the game out sooner than usual, and a lot of that has to do with the Grand Theft Auto Online component of the game, which is the multiplayer, ongoing monetization piece of it," he told CBS News.
Who plays GTA?
Male millennials and Gen Zers represent the key demographic playing GTA 6, according to a recent report from Sensor Tower. The company estimates 72% of players are male, while 57% are under 35.
What music is featured in the game?

GTA 6 features an original adaptive score from Justice, the Grammy-winning French electronic duo featuring Gaspard Augé and Xavier de Rosnay. The music is "dynamically tuned to the different ways players engage with the world of Vice City and Leonida throughout Jason and Lucia's story," Rockstar Games said on its website.
The 30-track "Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score" is scheduled for release Dec. 11 and includes collaborations with Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein.
Who are the voice actors?

Rockstar has not disclosed the full voice cast. However, actress Manni Perez was nominated for her voice acting in the "Best Performance" category at The Game Awards, an annual ceremony that celebrates the video game industry. Actor Stephen Root has also confirmed to the AP that he appears in the game, though Rockstar has not publicly disclosed his participation.
How many GTA 6 units have already been sold?

The company had sold 19 million units, including pre-order copies, and generated $1.84 billion in revenue by Thursday, according to Sensor Tower. The market intelligence and digital analytics platform said earlier this month that GTA 6 is the "most pre-ordered game in history."
Raymond James projects that Rockstar will sell 50 million units of the game from launch through the end of Take-Two's fiscal year 2027, which runs until March 31.
"That would be by some distance the biggest launch in video gaming history," Marok said.

GTA 5, released in 2013, has sold nearly 235 million copies, according to Take-Two. The game has generated more than $10 billion in revenue over the last 13 years, according to Victor Matheson, an economist at the College of the Holy Cross who studies sports and major events.
How much did GTA 6 cost to make?
Rockstar hasn't disclosed the exact figure, but analysts estimate GTA 6 cost upward of $1 billion to produce, which would make it the most expensive video game in history.
"I would be shocked if it was under a billion dollars because they've been working on this for the better part of a decade," Marok said.
Asked about the price tag during a recent Wall Street Journal event, Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick didn't offer an exact figure, saying only, "It was expensive, and it took a long time."

title: CBS to air Kennedy Center Honors in December
summary: CBS has reached a one-year deal to air the awards ceremony next month, sources said.
story: The Kennedy Center Honors may have left the Kennedy Center itself, but the annual awards gala isn't leaving its longtime broadcast home. CBS has reached a one-year deal to air the awards ceremony next month, according to sources familiar with the arrangement.

This year's event, scheduled to be taped on Sunday, Dec. 7, and aired on Dec. 27, will be held at Capital One Arena in downtown Washington. Honorees include musicians Paul Anka and Barbara Mandrell, composer David Foster, actor Andy Garcia and playwright David Mamet.

In September, the Kennedy Center board voted to close the performing arts center amid a legal dispute over building upgrades and attempts to add President Trump's name to the facade. Mr. Trump said he would only help fundraise for renovations if his name was added to the facade. A federal judge in Washington, D.C., however, ruled that only Congress had the authority to change the building's name.

While modest maintenance projects continue, planning for the major renovations are underway and a construction schedule cannot be set until an ongoing federal court case halting construction is resolved. A court hearing is set for Thursday.

CBS has broadcast the Kennedy Center Honors each year since 1978. The multiyear contract lapsed after the 2025 show, but the arts center and the network reached a short-term deal for this year's show last week. The program will also stream on Paramount+.

President Trump co-hosted the show in 2025, punctuating artistic performances with several speeches throughout the evening. The White House did not respond to a CBS News inquiry on whether the president would attend this year.

title: Bezos says he was "heavily involved" in casting Pattinson as 007
summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos says "it was obvious" to him and others that Robert Pattinson should be the next James Bond.
story: Amazon founder and executive chairman Jeff Bezos said Tuesday that he was "heavily involved" in casting Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond.

Speaking at Semafor's Silicon Valley and The World forum in California, the head of the retail and entertainment giant that now owns the rights to the 007 franchise spoke about what he called the "real old-fashioned screen tests" for five Bond finalists, complete with "full costume, real sets."

On Friday, the team of selectors spent several hours going over the screen tests of each actor, Bezos said in remarks reported by Semafor, adding that while they were all "extraordinarily talented … there was something special about Rob."
Bezos said the group was initially biased against Pattinson, "because he's already so famous," and they had been inclined to choose someone "a little more unknown."
The role of the iconic British spy has historically gone to lesser-known actors, who have then made their name doing the Bond movies.
"But in the screening tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond," Bezos said of Pattinson, who shot to fame with his starring role in the "Twilight" vampire movies.

Amazon bought MGM, which co-owns the rights to the Bond franchise, in 2022. Pattinson will be the first Bond not forged under the creative stewardship of the Broccoli family, who had run the franchise since 1962, when the first movie featuring 007, "Dr. No," was released.

"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement after he was unveiled as the seventh actor to take on the role. "To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

He will step into the shoes of Hollywood leading men Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig to star in the 26th Bond movie, which will be directed by Denis Villeneuve. It is expected to hit screens in 2028.

title: Can Anthropic win hearts and minds by curing hearts and minds?
summary: Anthropic says Claude Science can drive breakthroughs in drug discovery. It could also open lucrative commercial opportunities, experts say.
story: Fresh off its record-setting initial public offering, Anthropic now must show investors that it can sustain growth and generate profits. The company has a plan for that: curing some of the world's gnarliest diseases.

In its IPO prospectus, Anthropic states that AI holds the potential to "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine, potentially curing diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia, including cancer, Alzheimer's disease, heart disease, rare genetic diseases, and the major infectious diseases."

Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei said in a post on X in August that he believes "it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!)."
Speeding in the right direction

Developing breakthrough drugs is among the most promising avenues of research for AI, potentially bringing treatments for a range of conditions to market much faster than is currently possible, according to scientists and industry analysts.

"AI can accelerate research. It will help you get there faster, but it's not just speed — it's directional speed," Neerav Kaushal, an AI and molecular biology expert at Michigan Technological University, told CBS News. "Let's say you're at the top of the mountain and your aim is to find a drug for cancer that lies in the valley. AI will not just help you get down there faster — it will help you get down to the right valley where the drug is."

For Anthropic, meanwhile, developing drugs could open up potentially enormous commercial opportunities. The company has partnered with biotech and pharmaceutical companies that use its Claude Science model for various purposes. Anthropic also operates its own AI-powered biology wet lab in San Francisco that has already made scientific discoveries.
"If you can use a large language model to condense any part of the timeline, it is very economically valuable," Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan told CBS News.
The challenge for Anthropic will be how it turns its life sciences research into profits. That could take time, Khan told CBS News.

"How this becomes lucrative for Anthropic is a very important question, and I think it's a question Anthropic hasn't figured out yet," Khan said. "Coding is its best-proven use case, followed by cybersecurity applications, then financial and legal research."
But the potential to move the needle for both Anthropic and its pharma partners is significant.

"If you improve your drug's efficiency by a couple of percentage points, that can make a world of difference," Khan added. "You'll get asymmetric payouts in the sense that if a model can help with any part of the process, it's very economically valuable."

For example, he expects a drug developer like Eli Lilly and Co., which partners with Anthropic to give its employees access to Claude, would be willing to pay "hundreds of millions or billions of dollars to make its arthritis drug 2% better than it is."
A way to win hearts and minds by curing them?

Developing potentially lifesaving drugs could have other benefits for Anthropic. By applying tools to the life sciences and using them to improve human life, the company could help shift the narrative around AI to a more positive one, according to experts.

"If you are the AI company that helps advance some kind of cure or solution to a sickness or illness that's prevailed for quite some time, I think that gets you a ton more trust with consumers and end users," Khan said. "Because you end up becoming the company that is actually improving the quality of life for humans at large."

title: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
summary: Nvidia said Monday that it has restored Jensen Huang as the chipmaker's chief executive, calling him the "right person" to lead the company.
story: Nvidia's board of directors said on Monday that it has reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO.

The action comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned amid a scandal over an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of spying for China. China has denied it. Huang also had an extramarital affair with a subordinate at Nvidia, according to a New York Times report.

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Board Chair Harvey C. Jones said in a statement on Monday.

"In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk," the company added.

Eleven days after his resignation, Huang said in a statement that he is "honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution." He also thanked the company's board, interim CEO Colette Kress, and Nvidia staffers and shareholders.
"I can't wait to get back to work," Huang added.
The decision to restore Huang to his position came as a major surprise. In a company earnings call last week, Jones said the company "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

Huang's affair with a woman believed to have links to China's Ministry of State Security has put a spotlight on Nvidia's business in the People's Republic, with lawmakers questioning whether the company's AI chips were winding up in China in violation of U.S. export rules.
Push for his return

Huang last week underlined his eagerness to return to the chip company he co-founded in 1993, saying that if the "board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."

Numerous business leaders and thousands of Nvidia employees had signed a petition urging the chipmaker to rehire Huang. President Trump had also suggested that he would support the leader's return to Nvidia. "I would not mind seeing that," Mr. Trump said last week.
In a social media post on Monday, Mr. Trump cheered Nvidia's move.

"The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO," Mr. Trump said on Truth Social. "The Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy. The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security."
Mr. Trump also told CNBC that he had spoken directly to Nvidia's board about reinstating Huang.
Too big to fail?

Dan Ives, a tech analyst with Yorkville Ives, told CBS News that the board "had no choice" but to bring Huang back as CEO, saying that the executive's shock resignation earlier this month was becoming an "economic and global markets issue."
Nvidia makes advanced chips and other components that help power AI, which is driving economic growth in the U.S. and until recently had fueled record stock market gains.
"Nvidia is the linchpin to the global economy," Ives said.
Gil Luria, lead tech analyst at investment adviser D.A. Davidson, attributed Nividia board's U-turn to White House pressure to reinstate Huang.

"Because there is so much concern about the health of the overall economy and ability for the U.S. to continue to grow the AI investment cycle, which was accentuated by stock market declines last week, the White House wanted to put him back in his seat to move the economy forward," Luria told CBS News.

Nvidia's stock soared more than 30% on news of Huang's reinstatement. The news also buoyed other stocks, with the Nasdaq Composite Index erasing all of its losses in early trading after a steep sell-off on Friday.
Other Wall Street analysts who follow Nvidia expressed surprise at the company's sudden turnaround, but said the executive's return bolsters the company and the broader AI sector.

"Jensen was a singular CEO who built Nvidia into an AI juggernaut and maintained an extremely flat corporate structure, making him difficult to replace," Adam Crisafulli of Vital Knowledge told investors in a report.

Under Huang, Nvidia has emerged as a pillar in the growing AI industry, not only through its technology prowess but also for its role in financing the purchase of advanced chips and striking other deals to stoke demand for its products.
