title: Ossoff's broad and decisive Senate win fuels 2028 speculation
summary: Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff's commanding victory in Georgia relied on a broad coalition, and this is fueling 2028 presidential interest in him, even though he says he'll be in the Senate for the next six years.
story: Washington — Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff's commanding reelection victory in Georgia is drawing renewed attention to his potential as a 2028 presidential contender, as election data shows how he assembled a broad coalition of voters in the pivotal presidential battleground state.

Despite the growing speculation, Ossoff, 39, is for now dismissing the possibility of a White House bid. During a debate in October, Ossoff said he had "zero interest in running for president" in 2028.

Some early polls place him at the top of a hypothetical 2028 primary field. A post-election Emerson College survey showed Ossoff with the support of 17% of respondents — narrowly ahead of former Vice President Kamala Harris and New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, with former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and California Gov. Gavin Newsom rounding out the top five.

Ossoff has attracted interest from both centrists and progressives while delivering a decisive victory in a closely divided presidential battleground state. At Crooked Con, a primarily progressive gathering in Washington after the midterms, Ossoff received 38% of first-choice votes in its straw poll, ahead of Ocasio-Cortez and Buttigieg.

"I think he would make an attractive presidential contender on the Democratic side," said Jerry Gonzalez, CEO of GALEO Impact Fund PAC, a Georgia-based Latino political action committee that endorsed Ossoff in his Senate race. "He is not afraid, he won't shy away from holding the Trump administration accountable, but in a way that works towards actually building coalitions to get something done."
Democrats who can win statewide in conservative or swing states tend to be moderate, and that's true of Ossoff, too.

"He comes across, and tries to present himself, as a moderate, and he talks about issues which moderate conservatives could get behind," said Charles Bullock, a longtime political science professor at the University of Georgia. "The issues he stresses are things which are within the broad mainstream of 'These would be good things.'"

It's unclear how well a moderate would fare in the early nominating states. What is effective in a Georgia general election may be a tougher sell in a Democratic primary, where voters often reward ideological purity over swing-state caution.
"Obviously, he's successful here in Georgia," Bullock said. "How would he play elsewhere?
"I think what we will be seeing is preparation, maybe for a later run," Bullock speculated.

Ossoff's record gives rivals on both flanks openings to attack: progressives have criticized his vote for the Republican-backed Laken Riley Act and his reluctance to embrace "Medicare for All," while his votes to restrict certain weapons sales to Israel and his criticism of its military conduct in Gaza have drawn objections from some pro-Israel Democrats and donors.
All of those issues are certain to be part of the 2028 primary contest. For example, Rep. Ro Khanna, another potential 2028 candidate, last week tried to restart the debate over universal healthcare.

"Medicare for All means healthcare for everyone, like public school is free for every kid," Khanna wrote on X, arguing, "'Medicare for All who want it' is pablum. It's telling parents they have to pay for public school."

In his reelection this month, Ossoff defeated GOP opponent Mike Collins by around 18 points, two years after President Trump defeated Harris by around two points in 2024. It was a much wider margin than his last Senate election, which he won by just over one percentage point.
Powering Ossoff's win this year was a broad coalition of voters, including some swing constituencies that Democrats have struggled with in recent years, CBS News' exit polling shows.
Ossoff maintained strong support among Black voters, winning 93% of the group, which make up almost one-third of the state's eligible voters according to Pew Research Center.

He did not win the White voters who make up just over half of Georgia's electorate, but he did make significant inroads, winning 40% — after Harris had won just 28% two years earlier. He also notched some improvement in groups that have shifted hard against Democrats: He won 29% of White voters without college degrees (compared to Harris' 18%) and 19% of White evangelical or born-again Christian voters (compared to less than 10% for Harris).
Ossoff also won men by nine points after Harris lost them by 13 points.

Both Ossoff and Harris won younger Georgians, but Ossoff won them by a larger margin, securing 85% of voters ages 29 and under. Ossoff also split the 45-and-older vote roughly in half, while Harris lost that age group by a 15-point margin.

And Ossoff made gains with Hispanics — a group that makes up less than 10% of Georgia's eligible voters but which has grown rapidly and has become a swing demographic that could decide a close race in the perennial battleground. In his reelection victory, he won around two-thirds of Latino voters, up seven points from Harris' performance two years earlier.
A comparison of 19 Georgia precincts where at least 30% of active registered voters identify as Hispanic or Latino shows substantial Democratic improvement.

Ossoff won those precincts by a combined 49 points in the two-candidate vote, compared with an eight-point advantage for Harris in the 2024 presidential election and an 18-point margin for fellow Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock in 2022.
The changes were significant in areas that had supported Mr. Trump just two years earlier.

In six heavily Latino precincts in Whitfield County, the combined results shifted from a 12-point Trump advantage in 2024 to a 37-point Ossoff victory in 2026. Three similar precincts in Hall County shifted from an 11-point Trump edge to a 33-point Ossoff victory.

Those figures reflect the voting behavior of entire precincts rather than individual Latino voters, and comparisons between presidential and midterm electorates are not exact. Still, they underscore how dramatically the environment changed in places with large Latino populations.
Gonzalez attributed the shift in part to concerns over affordability and immigration enforcement, two issues he said weighed heavily on Latino voters in Georgia.

"Things are really expensive," Gonzalez told CBS News. "The price and affordability were a big driving issue." He also pointed to the Trump administration's immigration crackdown and its impact on Latino communities in Georgia. Ossoff has investigated allegations of abuses in federal immigration detention facilities as part of his Senate oversight work.
Gonzalez also credited Ossoff's success among voters across the political spectrum to his accessibility and constituent outreach.
"His office is accessible to all Georgians, and that's part of the reason why he won."

In this wave election, Ossoff wasn't the only Democrat to pick up ground in the midterms. Latino and Black voters, men, voters without college degrees and younger voters moved back toward Democratic candidates nationwide, a reversal after all four groups had shifted rightward in 2024.
In 2028, those groups could once again play a central role in both the Democratic Party's nominating process and the general election.

States with large Black and Latino populations will lead the Democratic primary calendar after the party rearranged its schedule, and Ossoff, with his strong support from both groups, would likely stand to benefit if he were to decide to run. South Carolina — where Black Democratic voters have long played an influential role in choosing the party's presidential nominee — will go first, followed by Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia.
The DNC says approximately 4.2 million Latinos live across the six early nominating states, a major increase from the party's previous early-state lineup.

In the general election, maintaining a strong lead with Black, Latino and younger voters — and preventing too much slippage among White and non-college-educated voters — will also be a core task for Democrats, as they seek to prevent the GOP's first non-Trump presidential candidate in over a decade from reassembling the Trump coalition.
Though Ossoff says he doesn't plan a White House bid in 2028, his performance in Georgia has provided an early measure of what an electoral coalition for him could look like.
"He has mentioned that he was focused on winning reelection, which he has done, so I think that gives him a little bit of latitude to think about it a little more seriously," Gonzalez said.

title: Bessent: We "need answers" on Nvidia role in sending China AI chips
summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says the government wants to know if Nvidia had "malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for the noncompliance" with chip export controls.
story: Washington — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that the administration needs answers from Nvidia as questions swirl about whether it has complied with export restrictions, after revelations surrounding its CEO's alleged affairs sent the chipmaker into crisis.
"We do need answers," Bessent said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

After Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO amid revelations about extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged spy, the U.S. is investigating how Nvidia may have given China access to advanced AI computer chips, despite government restrictions.

Last week, Bessent referenced a possible "culture of noncompliance" at Nvidia, questioning whether the company was "pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings." In an interview on Fox News, Bessent said he needed answers from Nvidia on its compliance with export restrictions within 10 days. On Sunday, he told Brennan the administration has not yet received those answers.

"We've been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers," Bessent said. "It behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was."

Nvidia's CFO, Colette Kress, has taken the helm after Huang's departure. But Bessent has urged the company to bring someone in from the outside to run the company. The treasury secretary said Sunday, "We do need to see who was in charge of compliance there."

Asked how challenging it could be to get to the bottom of what Jensen Huang was doing, given reporting about Nvidia's "handshake" business approach, Bessent said, "For deals that size, there's no such thing as an untraceable handshake deal."
"There are bills ablating that movement, there are money movements," he said. "They may not be the 100-page documents, but it will be possible to understand what has gone on here."
On his call for an inquiry into whether Nvidia had a culture of noncompliance, Bessent said that it's simply a possibility that the dynamic was at play.
"We will see, and that's why I think the board is moving very quickly to establish whether this did or did not exist," Bessent said.

The comments come as President Trump has called for Jensen Huang to return as CEO of Nvidia. Asked whether the president understands the risks that Bessent has pointed to, Bessent replied that it remained to be seen "which level of the business knew about this."

"Was it at the lower levels? Was it at the middle levels? Did it go all the way to the top? And I have confidence that the Nvidia committees are moving very quickly on this and will come up with some very fulsome and robust answers," he said.

When pressed on whether he thinks it would be a good idea for Jensen Huang to return, Bessent said, "I think we have to see where the buck stops — Were these malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for the noncompliance?" He also drew a distinction between this possible dynamic, and Jensen Huang's alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang.
"I think that is kind of a canard," Bessent said. "Was there a culture of compliance versus one person's foibles?"
Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee and will also be interviewed by House panels in early December.

title: Jeffries talks about where Democrats may be able to work with Trump
summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries outlined areas where Democrats "can explore coming together" with President Trump.
story: Washington — Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who's set to become House speaker when his party takes control of Congress next year, outlined areas on Sunday where he said Democrats "can explore coming together" with President Trump.
"Let's see what's possible in terms of what the president has said with respect to healthcare," Jeffries said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

As Democrats are poised to take control of both the House and Senate in the new year, following a slew of victories in the midterm elections, Mr. Trump expressed openness to working with Democrats in recent days — citing healthcare as a possible area for compromise.

"I'm open to great healthcare," Mr. Trump said at a press briefing on Friday. "Now, can it be what they want? No. But it can be a combination of what we all want, and we could end up with great healthcare in our country. We could end up better than dealing with the Republicans."

Jeffries identified a couple of areas where Democrats and Republicans might come together, pointing to lowering the age of Medicare eligibility, expanding healthcare coverage to include vision, hearing and dental, and making sure that children get coverage, "so that every single child and young American in this country can afford to go see a doctor when they need one."

"That's a place where we can explore coming together," Jeffries said. "I know it has strong support amongst Democrats in the House and the Senate, and let's see what's possible in terms of what the president has said with respect to healthcare."

The New York Democrat repeatedly emphasized the need for action, saying, "Can you imagine how angry the American people will be with Washington if, over the next two years, we fail to do anything about affordability, fail to do anything about healthcare, and fail to do anything about immigration?"
"The economy is broken — life is not working for far too many Americans, and it's clear we can't simply return to the status quo," he said.
Jeffries said Democrats are "committed to bringing about the type of dramatic change the American people are demanding."

Beyond healthcare, where Democrats more broadly would like to see a reversal to the Medicaid cuts in the GOP's One Big Beautiful Bill last year, Jeffries said the two other key areas of focus in the next Congress will be the high cost of living and the immigration system.
"Those are three possible areas to explore whether we can work together with the president and our colleagues on the other side of the aisle," Jeffries said.

Jeffries also highlighted combating corruption as an early focus, saying that Democrats have promised the American people that "we need to deal with accountability" among lawmakers, the Supreme Court and members of the administration.
"No one is going to get a pass," he said.
Jeffries said stock trading by lawmakers will be high on the Democrats' agenda.
"Very early on in the new Congress, House Democrats are going to move to ban members of Congress from trading stock," adding, "we will see if that gets the bipartisan support needed."

The president's relationship with Jeffries still remains to be defined. But Mr. Trump has already cast doubt on his ability to work with Jeffries' expected counterpart on the other side of the Capitol, Sen. Chuck Schumer.

"It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader," Mr. Trump said in a post on Truth Social earlier Sunday. "He failed badly as 'Leader' once before, one of the worst in history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again. All he did was perpetuate the Russia, Russia, Russia Hoax, and many other Hoaxes and Scams, making my victory in 2024 an easy and glorious one. Here we go again!"
When asked whether impeachment efforts would be a focal point for the House Democrats in the new Congress, Jeffries said, "We haven't ruled anything in, and we haven't ruled anything out."

"We're focused on actually delivering and keeping our commitment. And it's my expectation that with respect to the accountability agenda, that everyone involved in whatever investigations are unveiled, they're going to follow the facts," Jeffries said. "They're going to apply the law. They're going to be guided by the Constitution, and they're going to let the chips fall where they may."

title: Marine Corps hero under federal investigation
summary: Retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal, whose bloodied visage was depicted in an iconic Iraq War photo, is under investigation stemming from his tenure as a high school JROTC instructor.
story: Henderson, Nevada — One of the most celebrated Marine Corps veterans, whose heroism during the Iraq War earned him the nation's second-highest award for combat valor and a place in military history, is the subject of a criminal investigation over allegations stemming from his tenure as a high school instructor for a Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps, CBS News has learned.

Retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal, who served in the Marine Corps for 34 years, is under investigation by the Naval Criminal Investigative Service, the primary federal law enforcement agency for matters involving the Navy and Marine Corps.

The allegations against the highly decorated Marine veteran have not been disclosed by the law enforcement agency. However, federal agencies told CBS News that the investigation concerns the period of time when he worked as a JROTC instructor at the Basic Academy of International Studies. The academy is a public high school in Henderson, Nevada, operated by the Clark County School District.

The federal investigation marks a dramatic turn for a Marine whose actions on the battlefield made him a symbol of military courage. Kasal's heroism was captured in a 2004 photograph showing him in the Second Battle of Fallujah. His uniform was soaked in blood, and he was being helped out of a building by two Marines. His right leg was shattered, and his body riddled with gunshot wounds and grenade fragments, but he still gripped a pistol and combat knife. The scene was later immortalized in statues installed at two Marine bases. He retired after 34 years of service and was the recipient of two Purple Hearts and the Navy Cross, the second-highest decoration for combat valor, behind the Medal of Honor.

On Wednesday, the Marine Corps told CBS News that the service is "aware of the allegations against a retired Marine Sergeant Major which occurred while he was employed as a civilian JROTC instructor by the Basic Academy of International Studies."
The Marine Corps also said that the Naval Criminal Investigative Service "is actively investigating the allegations, as the Department of the Navy's lead for felony-level criminal investigations."
Separately, Denise Caskey of NCIS confirmed that its field office at Camp Pendleton in California is conducting the investigation.

NCIS does not typically confirm active investigations, making this an unusual case. The agency commonly investigates matters of homicide, sexual assault, fraud and even terrorism and espionage cases. The agency also conducts counterintelligence investigations, working with other federal agencies to identify threats to national security.
Kasal did not reply to CBS News' multiple attempts to contact him.

CBS News traveled to Henderson, Nevada, and over the course of the last two weeks spoke to nearly 40 people, including former students, school district employees, city officials, parents, U.S. military service members and Marine veterans who served with Kasal. Some asked for anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly or feared reprisal.

The cadets CBS News spoke to alleged Kasal often gave rides home to a select group of female cadets. He would take them to Starbucks and spend time with certain students outside of school-sponsored functions. Some also described instances when he was alone with a cadet in a room.

A former school district employee told CBS News that Kasal was advised on several occasions about the perceptions surrounding his relationships with students and was warned against putting himself in potentially compromising situations, including being alone in a room with a cadet.

One former female cadet described developing an unusually close relationship with Kasal after meeting him in 2020, when she was 14. She said she confided in him about difficulties at home and personal matters, including her relationships with boys. After knowing her for barely a year, Kasal offered to adopt her, saying in a text message, "I'm not asking as charity. I'm asking because your [sic] wanted."

When her family members learned of Kasal's offer, she said, they made it clear that adoption was not an option. She said that her relationship with Kasal continued, and she remained comfortable confiding in him about deeply personal matters. The cadet alleged some of their conversations involved sexual rumors that had been spread about her and why Kasal believed some of the problems she was experiencing stemmed from her relationship with her father. In retrospect, she said she realizes that those conversations were inappropriate for an instructor to have with a teenage student.

She now says she thinks Kasal crossed other boundaries, alleging that Kasal invited certain cadets to spend time at his home and at his cabin, she said, including for at least one birthday celebration. He did not extend invitations to everyone in the program. She also claimed that Kasal drove one student home nearly every day.

The Clark County School District told CBS News Kasal was hired by the school district three months after he retired from the Marine Corps, in August 2018. He resigned in August 2025, the school district said.
Enrollment in Basic Academy's JROTC program fluctuates from year to year, averaging roughly 135 students. The program is overseen by a senior Marine instructor and a senior enlisted leader.
When Kasal transitioned from the Marine Corps to the high school JROTC program, he sought to restructure it to more closely resemble the military service.

Some former cadets described him as professional and organized, crediting him with establishing strict standards and bringing a sense of discipline to the program. They also praised the time, energy and personal resources he devoted to his students.

Samantha Francisco, 22, who was in the program from 2018 to 2022, said, "I can't say enough about how amazing he was," and that "he genuinely cared about everybody and taught us incredible lessons." She added that she and her husband, who was also in the JROTC program, still talk weekly about Kasal or something he taught them.

Ashley Vazquez Romo, 22, another cadet from that period, said Kasal "poured his heart and soul into the program." She recalled that he sometimes helped pay for program outings and purchased equipment, including a CPR training mannequin, so students could practice.

Damien Greenwell, 22, who participated in the JROTC program from 2018 to 2022, told CBS News that he deeply respects Kasal for his military service and mentorship, especially to cadets with a troubled home life. But Greenwell also said that over the years he questioned Kasal's conduct on several occasions, adding that even if the decorated Marine's intentions were innocent, his actions could appear inappropriate to an outside observer.

"He would mentor us on how to be a proper leader — which is his job — but he would go a bit beyond this. Sergeant Major [Kasal] helps people in a time of need and that's very honorable," Greenwell said.

"If someone couldn't eat, he would pay for their food. If someone didn't have a ride home, he would help them out. It's awesome, it's great and very commendable," Greenwell said. "But if you're regularly getting Starbucks for a girl … it looks kind of weird … and with driving people home on a consistent basis, it looks bad. You need to have a certain kind of boundary between you and students."
Greenwell told CBS News he remembers a night that still "shocks him a little." It happened in 2024, two years after Greenwell graduated.

Greenwell claimed he went to Lowe's home improvement store around 9 p.m. and saw Kasal's truck in the parking lot. In the store, he observed Kasal walking with a student who he believes was a senior at the high school or a newly minted graduate.

"It was just really weird to me," Greenwell said, recalling that he briefly exchanged greetings with Kasal and the student before the two continued down the aisle. CBS News is withholding the student's name for privacy reasons.

Greenwell said over the years of observing Kasal, he developed doubts about him. He believed the optics could be interpreted as inappropriate, but at the same time wonders if Kasal could just be trying to help students navigate the difficulties of life. But even if he found a relationship between Kasal and a student odd, he was "not gonna say anything. Like, who am I to tell [a] sergeant major?"
Daniel Gillan, who participated in the program from 2018 to 2022 and later enlisted in the Marine Corps, said JROTC was good for him and that Kasal was part of the reason he ended up joining.

The program "gave me a lot of structure and discipline," Gillan said, adding that Kasal helped him "become a better person overall, and once you become a better person, things will fall into place for you."

Gillan said he never witnessed Kasal engage in inappropriate behavior. He sees Kasal as having made an effort to create memorable experiences for students by organizing group hikes, camping trips and other activities outside the classroom. He said Kasal recognized that some students did not have a good home life, and he wanted to make the JROTC program enjoyable and inclusive, emphasizing that all cadets were invited to participate.

Still, he acknowledged that Kasal appeared to favor certain cadets, sometimes buying them coffee, for instance. Gillan said Kasal had also bought coffee for him, but he didn't think it was inappropriate, describing him as a "nice guy."

Gillan also alleged Kasal would take cadets on hikes without seeking permission from the school, but he said this was more a matter of convenience. The hiking trail was only a few minutes away from Basic Academy.
"It was about a 10-minute drive from Basic, and [about] 20 cadets would go. Whoever wanted to go, they would go. We would all carpool," Gillan said, and the hikes were just about an hour.

"Legally, you gotta get [trips] ran through the school, and they gotta approve of it, … but [Kasal is] not gonna wait for [the school] to take two weeks to [approve] an event that takes one day to get back."
One former male cadet, who joined the program in 2019 and now serves in the U.S. military, alleged that Kasal invited him to visit his cabin in Iowa over the summer.

The trip was not school-sponsored, he said, and "it was just going to be the two of us." He says he declined the invitation because he was playing a sport that summer. At the time, he said, he did not consider the invitation to be inappropriate, believing Kasal had extended it because they shared an interest in the sport.

Greenwell said that at one point, he heard a rumor that Kasal was trying to adopt a fellow cadet but that he didn't believe it was true. When CBS News told him that Kasal had offered to adopt a former female cadet, Greenwell said he was "very surprised, shocked and disappointed."
"Even if you have the best intentions in the world, it still looks bad, no matter how you put it, because she's a minor," said Greenwell.

The Defense Department and local school districts share responsibility for overseeing JROTC programs because they are federally sponsored and operate in high schools nationwide. Although instructors are employed by school districts, they must also be certified by their respective military branches, which are responsible for monitoring their professional conduct and ensuring compliance with military standards.
The military services certify and oversee instructors, while school districts handle employment decisions, classroom supervision and compliance with local education policies.

JROTC instructors must acknowledge in writing that they will not engage in prohibited activities between JROTC instructors and students. The rules ban instructors from developing personal, intimate or sexual relationships with cadets, engaging in inappropriate communications and attending social gatherings with students on a personal basis. The restrictions apply from an instructor's first contact with a cadet until six months after the student leaves the JROTC program.

Under the rules, instructors are generally not allowed to give students rides in their personal vehicles, including rides home from school. Exceptions may be made when a student's safety or welfare is at risk or for official school functions involving multiple students. The rules specifically prohibit an instructor from transporting a single student in their personal vehicles.

Instructors are also not allowed to have cadets or other students in their homes. Other interactions, such as purchasing coffee or refreshments for students, are not explicitly prohibited. But such interactions could raise questions about compliance with the rules.
Instructors must sign the acknowledgment before beginning their duties as JROTC instructors and recertify it annually.
When CBS News received the initial news tip regarding Kasal, the Marine Corps said it was aware of allegations and of an investigation, but made no mention of NCIS' involvement.

The Henderson Police Department initially said it had no record of a complaint about Kasal. The Clark County Detention Center and the Clark County District Attorney's Office also did not have any complaints about Kasal on file when contacted some two weeks ago.

Later, during that same period, a spokesperson for the Henderson Police Department said the Clark County School District Police Department was handling the matter. Multiple calls and emails to the Clark County School District and the school district's police department went unanswered. Lt. Bryan Zink of the Clark County School District police department referred inquiries to the school district.
Last week, when CBS News emailed to check in on its inquiry, an email sent in error to CBS News asked a human resources manager to "disregard the request."
When CBS News asked why the request for information was being disregarded, Bryan Callahan, the district's public information officer, emailed for the first time: "We are looking into your request."

When questioned by a CBS News reporter in Henderson earlier this week, Callahan said he was not aware of an investigation of Kasal by the Clark County School District or the school district's police department.

Before he retired from active duty, Kasal reflected on his time in Iraq. The Second Battle of Fallujah in November 2004 was the bloodiest battle involving U.S. Marines since the Vietnam War, marked by brutal house-to-house fighting against Iraqi insurgents.

In 2018, Kasal told CBS News' David Martin that he had entered the building to rescue fellow Marines trapped by insurgent gunfire during one of the war's bloodiest battles. By the time he emerged, Kasal had been shot seven times, shielded a wounded Marine from an exploding grenade and refused medical treatment until others received care.
His actions earned him his second Purple Heart and the Navy Cross.
The photograph of Kasal became an iconic symbol of Marine resilience and sacrifice. The Marine Corps Heritage Foundation named a photojournalism award for Kasal.

The photograph inspired a bronze statue called the "No Man Left Behind" monument, which is installed at both Camp Pendleton in California and Camp Lejeune in North Carolina, according to the Marine Times. The sculpture was the work of John Phelps, a Navy Vietnam veteran whose son Chance was killed in Iraq in 2004, the newspaper reported.

When CBS News first learned about the criminal investigation into Kasal earlier this month, the retired sergeant major was in New York as the guest of honor at an event hosted by the NYPD Marine Corps Association to commemorate 251 years since the founding of the U.S. Marine Corps and honor Marines who also serve as New York City police officers. The New York Post reported that Kasal was presented a framed retirement shadowbox by NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch at police headquarters in Manhattan.
James LaPorta reported from Henderson, Nevada. Julia Kimani Burnham and Eleanor Watson reported from Washington, D.C.

Editor's note: For the past three years, James LaPorta has served as a judge for the Marine Corps Heritage Foundation annual awards program. He has never judged the award category named for retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal.
Editor's note: An earlier version of this article misspelled former JROTC cadet Daniel Gillan's name. The article has been updated.
This story published first on CBS News at 9:28 p.m. on Nov. 19, 2026.

title: Army delays detonation in Iowa that could send toxic dust into Illinois
summary: The U.S. Army has delayed plans to detonate unstable explosives at a munition plant in Iowa, amid concerns about the risks of a plume of dust containing toxic lead particles that could spread across parts of Iowa and Illinois.
story: The U.S. Army has delayed plans to detonate unstable explosives at a munition plant in Iowa, after elected leaders and environmental groups raised concerns about the risks of a plume of dust containing toxic lead particles that could spread across parts of Iowa and Illinois.
The dust plume is expected to spread across portions of eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois, potentially settling on farmland, playgrounds and other surfaces.

The detonation was originally scheduled for noon CT Friday, Nov. 20, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, a small community of 360 people, four hours west of Chicago, near the Mississippi River. However, on Thursday evening, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle announced the explosion would be delayed until Monday.

"Public safety is the Army's top priority, and I have directed Army Materiel Command to postpone tomorrow's controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa until Monday, November 23. This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material," Telle wrote in a post on X.

The Army plans two controlled detonations involving 68 barrels of lead azide, a highly sensitive explosive used in military ammunition since World War I. The Associated Press reported the material totals about 5 tons. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, the material has deteriorated during storage, allowing lead azide to recrystallize and become increasingly sensitive to friction and shock.

"In March of this year, the Army uncovered degrading Lead Azide housed in bunkers at the installation and immediately began communicating with stakeholders and the public in Middletown and the modeled impact area about the danger it posed," Telle wrote in a post on X. "In coordination with the Environmental Protection Agency, experts, and the local community, it was determined that a controlled detonation was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area. Public communication is essential to public trust. Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information."
In a statement after the Army postponed the detonation, U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois) wrote on X, "The American people deserved better than this."

"This whole operation was poorly planned and poorly communicated. Families were abruptly told to avoid the area, unsure if they would return to broken homes and whether their air and water could be at risk due to toxic lead exposure. This was unacceptable and a failure of leadership of epic proportions," Duckworth wrote. "Moving forward, I will continue to demand answers about how we even got to this point and accountability to make sure the Army never allows unsafe conditions to get this dire again."
U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois) called on the Army to hold a community town hall meeting on Saturday to answer questions from the public before proceeding with the demonstration on Monday.

Thursday afternoon, two environmental groups filed a lawsuit in the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to block the detonation. Earthjustice, a nonprofit public interest environmental law organization, filed the suit on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter. They are challenging the validity of the emergency permit granted by the EPA.

"We were very concerned about the very short notice that people in Iowa had to prepare," said Kerri Johannsen, senior director of policy and programs with the Iowa Environmental Council. "We also have not seen the evidence that the EPA used to determine that this was the best course of action, in terms of safety and health."
Michael Schmidt, general counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council, noted in a news release that the EPA itself says there is no safe level of exposure to lead.

"When our federal government makes decisions that result in a potentially toxic plume of lead dust that could cover much of southeastern Iowa, Iowans deserve to know that every available alternative was considered before choosing this method of disposal," Schmidt said.
Iowans protested and some made plans to fortify their homes or leave the state.
"I called my daughter and said, 'I'm coming to Chicago,'" said Pam Munce, who lives in Burlington.
Garrett Anthony, who also lives in Burlington, said he plans to put a tarp over his air conditioner.
"And I'm going to try and seal up windows as best I can," he said.

The barrels had been stored at the plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers, sitting in a bath of ethanol and water to keep the material stable, said Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist at Army Sustainment Command. A routine check earlier this year found that some of the water had evaporated, Barati said.

The Army said moving or transporting the material now poses an unacceptable risk of accidentally detonating it, potentially even killing the explosives technicians handling it. After evaluating alternative disposal methods, military officials determined that detonating the explosives in place was the safest available option. Barati said the risk of accidental detonation increases in cold weather. "We're really concerned that it will detonate on its own," Barati said.
The Army describes such operations near populated communities as highly uncommon, it told CBS News Chicago.

"A team of experts from around the nation got together to figure out what the best and safest disposal method was, and they determined that the safest method would be to detonate it in place," Barati said.

The Army says it is taking several steps to limit the amount of lead-containing dust released during the explosions, including earthworks, soil wetting and air monitoring. According to the AP, the barrels are surrounded by concrete and buried under soil, with sand barriers stacked two stories high around them. Barati said the soil will be sprayed with water and the air misted to try to keep the majority of the lead on Army property. EPA's permit also requires environmental monitoring at the installation and off-site locations, along with post-detonation sampling and cleanup measures.

With the detonation delayed until Monday, the winds are expected to be different than Friday, meaning that plume of lead dust could impact a completely different group of people as it moves in a different direction.
Residents urged to evacuate as explosions could shatter windows

The planned detonations are powerful enough that the Army is warning of possible damage to nearby buildings, including shattered windows. Residents in Middletown's City Park neighborhood are being asked to temporarily evacuate their homes from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. Friday. Residents who can't leave should stay inside with windows and doors closed, officials said.

In its Nov. 15 public advisory, the Army says residents should expect loud explosions, ground vibrations and a visible dust plume. Temporary accommodations will be available at the Armed Forces Reserve Center in Middletown.

A group of Democratic and Republican elected officials from Illinois and Iowa had urged the Pentagon and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to delay the planned detonation and seek safer alternatives.

"While we understand the urgent need to address these volatile materials, their detonation has the potential to spread lead contamination in and around the region. We call on you to consider delaying this detonation until there is an opportunity to explore safer alternatives," they wrote to Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle and U.S. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin. "Iowa and Illinois residents understandably are concerned about the potential health impacts of the scheduled detonation."
The elected officials who signed the letter include:

U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois)U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois)U.S. Rep. Darin LaHood (R-Illinois)U.S. Rep. Mary Miller (R-Illinois)U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen (R-Illinois)Illinois Gov. JB PritzkerU.S. Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton (D-Illinois)U.S. Sen.-elect Josh Turek (D-Iowa)
U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois)
U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois)
U.S. Rep. Darin LaHood (R-Illinois)
U.S. Rep. Mary Miller (R-Illinois)
U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen (R-Illinois)
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker
U.S. Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton (D-Illinois)
U.S. Sen.-elect Josh Turek (D-Iowa)
They also raised concerns about communication with the public before the detonation.

"Our offices have received reports of poor communication from the Army and EPA about the detonation plans and anticipated monitoring after the detonation. In addition, there are significant concerns about appropriate Army and EPA oversight of this contractor-operated facility, the site of which remains on a Superfund list. We urge you to examine the contractor's handling of this and other hazardous material to prevent any future issues," they wrote.
Toxic lead dust could travel miles downwind

Following the initial blast, airborne toxic dust becomes the main concern. According to the Army's published plume forecasts and public safety advisory, the explosions are expected to release particles containing lead into the atmosphere.

The preliminary maps show a potential airborne plume stretching northward across eastern Iowa, the Mississippi River, and potentially into far northwest Illinois. The Army notified communities as far as 100 miles away Sunday, the AP reported, and thousands of people live along the plume's projected track.

In addition to airborne dust, toxic dust particles are expected to settle on surfaces. That raises concerns about possible lead contamination on agricultural land, residential properties, playground equipment and other outdoor surfaces.
Actual exposure levels and the extent of any contamination will depend on the amount of lead released, atmospheric conditions and how much material settles out of the plume.
Lead is a toxic heavy metal that does not degrade naturally over time. Once deposited, it can persist in soil for decades and may be transported through erosion or runoff into waterways.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warns that no safe blood lead level has been identified in children. Even relatively low levels of lead in the blood have been linked to learning difficulties, developmental delays and behavioral problems. Lead exposure is also especially dangerous to pregnant women.

Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a professor at the University of Iowa's Department of Occupational and Environmental Health, told the AP it is encouraging that the Army and EPA are working to minimize the dust, but it's still unknown how much will end up in the air and on surfaces. He said he is particularly concerned about toddlers who put everything in their mouths. Andrew Whelton, an environmental engineering professor at Purdue University who has helped communities recover from chemical disasters, told the AP that high doses over a short period can cause lead poisoning and make people feel sick.

The Army's forecasts do not establish that harmful exposure will occur at every location within the projected plume. The Army says extensive modeling predicted that lead particle levels in the air may be elevated but still well below the level at which the EPA would require protective action, according to the AP. Environmental sampling will be needed to determine where lead was deposited and at what concentrations.
Weather conditions will determine where the plume travels

Wind direction, speed and vertical motion in the atmosphere will play critical roles in determining the plume's eventual path. Officials expect the dust to linger for no more than an hour, depending on wind speed, according to the AP.

Current forecast guidance suggests gusty southerly winds of 20 to 30 miles per hour Friday will carry the plume northward through eastern Iowa, keeping it well west of the Chicago metropolitan area. Communities closer to the Mississippi River and the Illinois border could be more relevant to potential downwind exposure. The exact path remains subject to change as the detonation approaches.

Under the EPA's emergency permit, the operation cannot proceed if certain unfavorable weather conditions are forecast, including surface winds below 1 mph or above 15 mph, strong winds aloft, thunderstorms, precipitation or temperature inversions. There is no word yet on whether Friday's gusty winds could cancel the detonation.
The Army is required to update its plume forecasts six hours before the operation, and hourly thereafter until the detonations are completed.
Army promises environmental monitoring and cleanup

The permit requires soil and surface-wipe sampling to begin within 24 hours in accessible public and consenting private areas where modeled lead-dust deposition meets a specified threshold. The Army must also submit environmental findings and proposed remediation plans to EPA.

For residents potentially affected by dust deposition, the Army recommends wet-cleaning surfaces that people frequently touch, including outdoor toys, playground equipment, patio furniture and windowsills. However, questions remain about the extent of contamination that could occur beyond the ammunition plant, the effectiveness of cleanup efforts and how residents will know whether their properties are safe.
EPA issues emergency permit for detonation

On Nov. 13, the EPA issued an emergency permit allowing the Army to detonate the lead azide at a location not authorized for the activity under the facility's existing hazardous-waste permit. In its Nov. 16 public notice, EPA said the emergency authorization was necessary to address an imminent threat to public safety posed by the unstable explosives.

The detonation is being regulated under the federal Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, or RCRA, which governs the treatment, storage and disposal of hazardous waste. However, federal emergency-permitting provisions allow greater flexibility than ordinary permitting procedures. Under 40 CFR § 270.61, applicable environmental requirements must be incorporated into emergency permits to the extent possible and consistent with the emergency situation.

The emergency permit issued for Middletown includes specific environmental safeguards and incorporates applicable federal hazardous-waste regulations. It remains unclear whether EPA modified or omitted any requirements that would ordinarily apply to this operation because of its emergency designation.
The EPA's authorization does not mean the detonation will produce no environmental contamination.
CBS News Chicago has sought additional information about the EPA's environmental risk assessment and the standards that would trigger cleanup of affected properties.

The Illinois Department of Public Health referred CBS News Chicago's questions about potential health impacts back to the EPA. Environmental and public health officials in Illinois have urged the military to conduct comprehensive sampling in that state after the detonations, the AP reported.

Iowa Health and Human Services told CBS News Chicago it was made aware of the planned detonation only very recently and is coordinating with other state agencies as they assess and respond to the public health concerns. The agency said the Army released two maps showing possible exposure but did not say what conditions the modeling included.
Community concerns grow ahead of detonation

Some residents and environmental advocates are questioning whether the planned detonation has received sufficient independent scrutiny. Protest organizers have called for greater transparency, independent environmental review and assurances that any contamination resulting from the explosions will be properly addressed.
U.S. Sen.-elect Josh Turek was among those calling for the detonation to be delayed, arguing the public needs a better understanding of the potential health impacts, the AP reported.

Middletown residents learned in March that the Army needed to dispose of the degraded lead azide, after the plant paused operations for a review and the material was discovered, the AP reported. The Army previously held a public open house on Oct. 15, where military officials discussed the safety operation and answered residents' questions.

Some schools in the region canceled classes Friday before the detonation was delayed, including in Danville, a few miles from the plant. Superintendent Pat Wallace said his initial intention was to keep schools open, but the uncertainties made closing "the most responsible decision." He wrote that he is not suggesting the detonation will create unsafe conditions: "The reality is that we simply do not know exactly what conditions will look like Friday afternoon," the AP reported.

In Mediapolis, less than 20 miles northeast of the plant, city officials learned of their potential exposure Sunday, when the Army's map put the town in the center of the dust exposure area, the AP reported. The school district announced Tuesday it will close Friday with no events or sports practices, and the public library will also close. The local fire department plans to hose down playgrounds that could be covered in lead particles. City officials said the EPA will have a command center in Mediapolis to sample air, soil and water during and after the detonation, and the city plans to do its own testing.
"The biggest issue we're having is the lack of information," Deputy City Clerk Amy Stucker told the AP. Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds' office said it was first briefed on the public advisory Monday.

The Iowa Department of Agriculture advised bringing animals, bales of hay and water indoors. Staff at the Iowa State University Extension office in Des Moines County fielded calls Thursday from residents "deathly afraid" for their animals and vegetable gardens, staff member Morgan Hoenig told the AP. "We ran out of soil test kits yesterday," she said.

The Army recommends that those within the projected exposure area consider avoiding outdoor activities, remaining indoors with windows closed and setting ventilation systems to recirculate air until officials announce that the exposure period has ended.
The latest official plume forecasts, public advisories and safety instructions are available on the U.S. Army's Iowa Army Ammunition Plant information page.
Residents can sign up for toxic plume forecast updates from the U.S. Army by sending an email request with the subject line "IAAAP Environmental Updates" to usarmy.ria.asc.list.pa@army.mil.

title: Voyager 1 sets distance record of 1 "light day" from Earth
summary: Voyager 1 and its sister ship Voyager 2 are still beaming back data from interstellar space as they near their 50th anniversary next year.
story: NASA's Voyager 1 probe, launched nearly a half century ago in 1977 to provide the first close-up views of Jupiter, Saturn and their assortment of moons, reached a distance from Earth early Wednesday of one light day — more than 16 billion miles — the farthest any human artifact has ever ventured from the home planet.

Its sister ship Voyager 2, on a different trajectory, added Uranus and Neptune to the outer planets "Grand Tour" before following its sibling out of the solar system and into interstellar space in 2018, six years after Voyager 1.

Both spacecraft continue to beam back data about the magnetic fields, charged particles and plasma waves in the space between the stars as their power steadily declines and their signals grow weaker and weaker.

As of 5:16 a.m. EST Wednesday, Voyager 1, sailing through space at nearly 38,000 mph, was expected to pass the one-light-day milestone, so far away that radio signals, traveling at 186,000 miles every second, need 24 hours to reach flight controllers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
That means the 13-member team will have to wait until Thursday for Voyager 1's first post-light-day signal to confirm the achievement.

And what an achievement it is: No other space agency in the world has matched or even attempted a mission rivaling Voyager, one that many believe ranks with the Apollo moon landings as one of the greatest feats of American space flight.

"It's difficult to describe, difficult to put into words," said Voyager Interstellar Mission Manager Kareem Badaruddin, one of just three full-time team members keeping the aging Voyagers healthy and their antennas aimed at Earth. "I feel like this mission is one of the great things that people have ever done, that humans have ever done.
"All of us, every person, whether they've worked on this mission or not, can take some pride in it and can feel like this is a part of what our civilization has accomplished."

It's not known how long the Voyagers will continue to function as the plutonium in their nuclear power packs steadily decays. With luck and clever management, engineers hope to keep the data flowing for several more years before the signals finally stop.

Voyager 1 started out with about 470 watts of power. That's down to a little more than 210 watts now, enough to run just two of its 10 instruments while keeping the spacecraft properly oriented so it can beam magnetometer and plasma wave data back to Earth. Voyager 2 has a slightly more powerful generator and is operating on a bit more than 230 watts, enough to keep three instruments running.

But even after the power is exhausted, both Voyagers will continue on their way, expected to remain roughly intact, if powerless, for a billion years or more, almost certainly outlasting human civilization.

On the remote chance any aliens might one day stumble upon a Voyager in the cold reaches between the stars, both spacecraft are carrying what amount to messages in a bottle, gold phonograph records encoded with the sights and sounds of planet Earth.

The records include greetings in 55 languages, 115 photos of Earth's people, wildlife and technology, representative natural sounds and carefully selected art and music from multiple cultures, everything from J.S. Bach to Navajo chants to Chuck Berry singing "Johnny B. Goode."

"If Voyager should, sometime in its distant future, encounter beings from some other civilization in space, it bears a message, a phonograph record ... with instructions for use," Carl Sagan, the late astronomer who led the golden record project, said in the 1980 "Cosmos" television series.

"And on this record are a sampling of pictures, sounds, greetings and an hour and a half of exquisite music, the Earth's greatest hits, a gift across the cosmic ocean from one island of civilization to another."

Now beyond the confines of Earth's solar system, the stream of ones and zeros describing the interstellar environment leaves Voyager 1's 12-foot-wide dish antenna with less than half the power used by a typical 40-watt refrigerator bulb.

By the time the signal reaches Earth 24 hours later, its strength is a tiny fraction of a trillionth of a watt, vastly less than the power needed to run a wristwatch — a signal so weak that giant 230-foot-wide antennas in NASA's globe-spanning Deep Space Network are needed to pull in the faint whispers.

Commands from flight controllers at JPL now take a full day to reach the spacecraft with another 24 hours required to find out if the commands were received and acted upon. Fixing a problem is a glacial, nail-biting affair.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," Suzanne Dodd, the Voyager project manager at JPL, said in a web posting.
Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 are powered by electricity generated through the decay of radioactive plutonium 238 in compact nuclear power plants known as radioisotope thermoelectric generators, or RTGs.

Both spacecraft have slowly but steadily lost power as the plutonium in their RTGs has decayed. Flight controllers closely manage the available power and the resulting heat needed to keep fuel lines from freezing so thrusters can fire when needed to keep the spacecraft — and their dish antennas — locked onto Earth.
Badaruddin said the small flight control team feels the weight of responsibility for keeping the Voyagers alive.

"If ever you get that sense that oh, I made a mistake, I'm the one who caused a problem for the spacecraft, that's crushing," he said. "Every one of the team members feels they're committed to doing everything in our power to do our best for these spacecraft. We're doing everything we can to keep them going for as long as we can."

Only three of the 13 Voyager team members are full-time JPL employees. Two are retirees who worked on the project at launch and came back to help during the interstellar voyage while the rest split their time between Voyager and other projects.

"I've been at JPL for 32 years, and everybody loves their spacecraft, and everybody feels like it's a family member and gives everything they've got for it," said Badaruddin. "And Voyager is no different in that regard. And these two retirees have come back and given a tremendous amount of effort and time."

The Voyager program was approved in the early 1970s when the outer planets were lined up in a way that would permit a so-called "Grand Tour" of them, enabling spacecraft to make velocity-boosting flybys to jump from one planet to the next, shaving years off the time needed to explore them all.
But to reduce costs, the project was only funded for flybys of Jupiter and Saturn. Voyager 2 was launched first, on Aug. 20, 1977. Voyager 1 followed on Sept. 5.

Voyager 1 was on a faster trajectory and reached Jupiter first as planned, flying past the giant planet in 1979, sending back spectacular images of its Great Red Spot — a storm that has been churning for centuries, the planet's turbulent atmosphere and its major moons, including detailed looks at Europa, where an icy crust is thought to shield a global ocean, and Io, found to be the most volcanic world in the solar system.

It then flew on to Saturn, wowing astronomers with fantastically detailed photos of the solar system's most spectacular planet, sending back never-before-seen views of its rings, small moons that shepherd the ring particles along, the planet's atmosphere and, as it departed, cloud-shrouded Titan.

With the successful Titan flyby and the completion of the mission's major objectives, NASA approved sending Voyager 2 on a gravitational slingshot past Saturn and on to Uranus and Neptune in 1986 and 1989, respectively.

On Valentine's Day 1990, Voyager 1's cameras were used a final time to take a family portrait of the six largest planets — Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — from a distance of 3.7 billion miles. Earth appeared as little more than a blue dot in the pinkish glow of reflected light within the camera.

"Consider again that dot. That's here. That's home. That's us," Sagan said of the photo. "On it everyone you love, everyone you know, everyone you ever heard of, every human being who ever was, lived out their lives ... on a mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam."

He concluded by saying "there is perhaps no better demonstration of the folly of human conceits than this distant image of our tiny world. To me, it underscores our responsibility to deal more kindly with one another, and to preserve and cherish the pale blue dot, the only home we've ever known."
Voyager 1's cameras have been powered down ever since.

In 2012, Voyager 1 flew through the outer edge of the bubble around the solar system defined by the solar wind and the sun's magnetic field, sailing out into interstellar space. It is now in what Carolyn Porco, a well-known planetary scientist and member of the Voyager imaging team, calls "the realm of deep time."

In about 18,000 years, she writes on her Substack page, Voyager 1 will reach another major milestone: passing through a distance of one light-year from Earth, roughly 5.8 trillion miles, only a quarter of the way to the nearest star and "still well within the zone where the sun is the dominant gravitational influence."

But in a million years, the silent spacecraft will have passed well beyond the confines of the solar system, reaching a distance of 56 light-years while "remaining within the sun's local interstellar neighborhood — a low density region filled with diffuse hydrogen and helium gas and scattered stars: most are very dim, some are sun-like, and comparatively few are luminous."

In 100 million years, Voyager 1 will be about 2,000 light years from Earth as the spacecraft and the distant solar system are carried along by the galaxy's rotation. "Still not very far," Porco writes. "But at this time, it will find itself among cold, dense molecular clouds, star-forming regions and nebulae and supernova remnants formed by the deaths of stars."

Finally, 1 billion years from now, the spacecraft will have sailed about 20,000 light-years from home, making four trips around the galactic core in the process. "By then, the sun's growing luminosity will have sufficiently heated the Earth to destroy atmospheric carbon dioxide, halt oxygen production and exterminate plant life and the complex lifeforms that depend on it."
"By that time, both robot and maker will be extinct."

The cosmic travelogue concludes with a personal observation: "The foretelling of Voyager's galactic wanderings leaves one to contemplate the impermanence of all existence and the preciousness of life. And that just might be Voyager's greatest gift of all."

title: 2,000-year-old bog woman was beheaded in possible ritual killing
summary: The "Ballymacombs More Woman," whose body lay in a Northern Ireland bog for 2,000 years, was beheaded, possibly in a "ritualized killing," researchers say.
story: London — An investigation into the death of a young Iron Age woman whose remains were preserved in a Northern Ireland bog for more than 2,000 years has found that she was beheaded, possibly in a "ritualized killing," when she was between 15 and 22 years old.

The enquiry into the remains known as the "Ballymacombs More Woman," discovered in a peat bog in central Northern Ireland in October 2023, determined that she was decapitated from behind, most likely with a bladed weapon.

"While the precise circumstances surrounding her death remain unknown, the evidence suggested that she may form part of a wider tradition of ritualized killing and sacrifice," said the Ulster Museum, which hosted a coroner's investigation into the two-millennia-old killing. It said the woman's death appeared similar to others documented among  Iron Age bodies discovered in bogs across northwest Europe.
The More Woman's body dates from between 343 to 1 B.C., from the prehistoric Iron Age period.

"Finds like this that are women are incredibly rare," Hannah Crowdy, head of curatorial for Northern Ireland's National Museums, told CBS News partner network BBC News. "She's the first of her kind in Northern Ireland."

"This helps us piece together a part of history that is quite mysterious," Crowdy added. "There's been a really intensive period of research … To honor her, it's important to tell her story and bring that to the fore."

The team that carried out what the Ulster Museum called a "unique public event modelled on a modern coroner's investigation into the remains" used scientific mapping techniques, 3D imaging and analyses of bone, hair, skin and nails to gain evidence of the woman's age, health, diet, physical condition and the injuries that led to her death.

Niamh Baker, the Ulster Museum's curator of archaeology, told the BBC that an osteoarchaeologist — someone who studies archaeological human bones —   reviewed the remains and found cut marks on the woman's neck.
"It would appear she was intentionally decapitated in the bog," said Baker. "No skull was recovered with further investigation."

"There are examples of some Iron Age remains in the Republic of Ireland that are male that similarly met violent deaths and some of those are thought to be associated with kingship and sovereignty," said Baker. "Was she a female sovereign? Or it may be that it was related to an agricultural or weather issue at the time."
Residents of the nearby town of Balleghy have named the woman Aine.

"We feel that Aine is one of our own," said Séamus Mac an Fhirléighinn, from the town's historical society, who attended the coroner's investigation."This is her inquest. She needed her people, her family there with her to act on her behalf as advocates."
"Local people are very interested," he said. "We wanted to know who this person was, how she died, how she lived."

"By that time, both robot and maker will be extinct."

The cosmic travelogue concludes with a personal observation: "The foretelling of Voyager's galactic wanderings leaves one to contemplate the impermanence of all existence and the preciousness of life. And that just might be Voyager's greatest gift of all."

title: Can Anthropic win hearts and minds by curing hearts and minds?
summary: Anthropic says Claude Science can drive breakthroughs in drug discovery. It could also open lucrative commercial opportunities, experts say.
story: Fresh off its record-setting initial public offering, Anthropic now must show investors that it can sustain growth and generate profits. The company has a plan for that: curing some of the world's gnarliest diseases.

In its IPO prospectus, Anthropic states that AI holds the potential to "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine, potentially curing diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia, including cancer, Alzheimer's disease, heart disease, rare genetic diseases, and the major infectious diseases."

Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei said in a post on X in August that he believes "it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!)."
Speeding in the right direction

Developing breakthrough drugs is among the most promising avenues of research for AI, potentially bringing treatments for a range of conditions to market much faster than is currently possible, according to scientists and industry analysts.

"AI can accelerate research. It will help you get there faster, but it's not just speed — it's directional speed," Neerav Kaushal, an AI and molecular biology expert at Michigan Technological University, told CBS News. "Let's say you're at the top of the mountain and your aim is to find a drug for cancer that lies in the valley. AI will not just help you get down there faster — it will help you get down to the right valley where the drug is."

For Anthropic, meanwhile, developing drugs could open up potentially enormous commercial opportunities. The company has partnered with biotech and pharmaceutical companies that use its Claude Science model for various purposes. Anthropic also operates its own AI-powered biology wet lab in San Francisco that has already made scientific discoveries.
"If you can use a large language model to condense any part of the timeline, it is very economically valuable," Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan told CBS News.
The challenge for Anthropic will be how it turns its life sciences research into profits. That could take time, Khan told CBS News.

"How this becomes lucrative for Anthropic is a very important question, and I think it's a question Anthropic hasn't figured out yet," Khan said. "Coding is its best-proven use case, followed by cybersecurity applications, then financial and legal research."
But the potential to move the needle for both Anthropic and its pharma partners is significant.

"If you improve your drug's efficiency by a couple of percentage points, that can make a world of difference," Khan added. "You'll get asymmetric payouts in the sense that if a model can help with any part of the process, it's very economically valuable."

For example, he expects a drug developer like Eli Lilly and Co., which partners with Anthropic to give its employees access to Claude, would be willing to pay "hundreds of millions or billions of dollars to make its arthritis drug 2% better than it is."
A way to win hearts and minds by curing them?

Developing potentially lifesaving drugs could have other benefits for Anthropic. By applying tools to the life sciences and using them to improve human life, the company could help shift the narrative around AI to a more positive one, according to experts.

"If you are the AI company that helps advance some kind of cure or solution to a sickness or illness that's prevailed for quite some time, I think that gets you a ton more trust with consumers and end users," Khan said. "Because you end up becoming the company that is actually improving the quality of life for humans at large."

title: How Huang's resignation and return unfolded at Nvidia
summary: Jensen Huang's shocking exit as CEO of Nvidia unspooled suddenly, yet signs of trouble had emerged much earlier.
story: Nvidia's board of directors announced on Monday, Nov. 23, that it is reinstating Jensen Huang as the chipmaker's CEO. The move marks an abrupt shift from board members' position only last week that they had no plans to rehire the billionaire entrepreneur at the company he co-founded more than 30 years ago.

Huang's departure from Nvidia on Nov. 12 capped a tumultuous week for the chipmaker, with his resignation coming less than a week after his extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy became public. The woman with whom he had a relationship, Alice Huang (no relation), arrived on the tech scene in 2023, when she became the managing director of Singapore-based data center Megaspeed International.

Megaspeed, which says it has complied with U.S. laws, would proceed to buy billions of dollars in Nvidia chips and servers. Over the past two years, Alice Huang, also known by her Chinese name Huang Le, has been photographed and recorded socializing with Jensen Huang, prompting questions in May from one quizzical investor about their "uncomfortably close relationship."

In a statement on Sunday, Nov. 15, Megaspeed said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025, and it denied any wrongdoing, saying it "conducts legitimate and lawful business." "Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters," the company's statement said.
Below is a timeline of events that led to Jensen Huang's startling resignation, and the board's decision to rehire him:
November 2015

Alice Huang, a former television reporter in China, joins investment firm Shanghai Hexi Investment Management as deputy general manager, according to social media posts and records from Simuwang, a Chinese private equity database. Shanghai Hexi was founded by Kang Wei, who became her husband, according to The Wall Street Journal.
March 2023

7Road International, originally incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International, is renamed Megaspeed, and ownership of the "neocloud" company is transferred to Huang Le Ltd., an enterprise controlled by Alice Huang. She becomes its managing director.
June 2023
Cloud-computing company Shanghai Century Litong is founded. A company linked to Alice's sister, Huang Yu, held an ownership stake.
October 2023
Nvidia designates Shanghai Century Litong as a preferred cloud partner, giving the Chinese company priority access to Nvidia's chips, according to The Information.
Around November 2023
Megaspeed's shares were transferred to another Singapore company, Swiftdata, and Alice Huang ceased to be listed as a director of the company, according to news site Caixin Global.
June 7, 2024
Information technology firm NetThunder posted a picture on social media of Alice Huang and Jensen Huang with other tech executives at a bar in Taipei, Taiwan.
End of 2024
Megaspeed's assets exploded from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024, according to financial filings reviewed by Reuters.

Shipment records from December 2024 through early 2026, analyzed by short-selling firm Culper Research, suggest that Megaspeed's Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix, imported about $4 billion in products from a company that builds equipment with Nvidia chips.
Early 2025

Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, jointly pitched Chinese investors on a Southeast Asia data center project, reportedly telling them they had "no problem securing GPUs" — the graphics processing units Nvidia specializes in — and citing Alibaba as a customer, according to the Financial Times.
Jensen Huang meets with President Trump at the White House. It marks their first of many White House encounters in Mr. Trump's second term.
February 2025
Singapore opens an investigation into Megaspeed and several other companies over suspected false declarations related to the purchase of servers and other offenses, according to Bloomberg News.
Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are recorded on video together at a dinner at San Liu Shi Fu restaurant in Taipei, around the time of the Computex tech conference in Taiwan.
July 2025

Jensen Huang says the technology giant has won approval from the Trump administration to sell its advanced H20 computer chips, used to develop artificial intelligence, to China, a reversal of prior administration policy.
"It's so innovative and dynamic here in China that it's really important that American companies are able to compete and serve the market here in China," Huang said at the time.
That same month, Nvidia becomes the first public company to be worth $4 trillion.
February 2026
Chinese police detained Kang Wei, Alice Huang's husband and business partner, in connection with suspected stock manipulation, sources told Caixin.

That same month, Singapore barred Alice Huang from re-entering the country after she downplayed her role at Megaspeed amid the country's investigation into its operations, according to a Bloomberg News report.
Jensen Huang boards Air Force One in Alaska to accompany Mr. Trump on a two-day trip to Beijing.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefed Mr. Trump about the counterintelligence risk posed by Jensen Huang's affair with Alice Huang, according to The New York Times. The briefing, which occurred before Jensen Huang joined the trip, was the second briefing Mr. Trump had received from U.S. intelligence about the Nvidia CEO's relationship, the Times reported.
Jensen Huang attends Mr. Trump's state dinner for China's Xi Jinping at the White House.
Jensen Huang attends an AI event at the White House and signs a set of voluntary AI safety standards amid calls for tighter guardrails on the technology.

Jensen Huang writes a message to Nvidia employees admitting that he had an extramarital affair. The same day, Nvidia's board said it had launched an independent investigation amid reports that its CEO was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort."
The New York Times on Nov. 8 reported that U.S. government surveillance suggested Alice Huang was feeding information directly to Beijing.

At an impromptu press conference at the White House, Mr. Trump said he had spoken to Jensen Huang and that the tech exec had indicated he was unaware of Alice Huang's links to China's intelligence services. Mr. Trump also described the Nvidia CEO as an "honorable man" who's "definitely suffering."
Mr. Trump didn't address questions about when he first learned about the spy allegations, only saying "not too long ago" and that "it didn't make much of an impact on me."
The New York Times reports that Jensen Huang had an affair with Kimberly Powell, a subordinate at Nvidia.
Nvidia's board of directors announces that Jensen Huang has resigned, effective immediately.

Nvidia reports its third-quarter earnings, with interim CEO Colette Kress hosting the call following Huang's resignation. Nvidia Board Chair Harvey Jones said the company "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

Nvidia reverses course on Huang's exit, announcing his reinstatement as CEO effective immediately. "In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk," the company said in a statement.
