title: Trump, tech CEOs cheer Huang's return, but lawmakers question board
summary: President Trump and prominent tech figures applauded Huang's reinstatement as CEO, though some lawmakers criticized the move as "reckless."
story: President Trump and high-profile business leaders applauded Nvidia's shock move to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after the billionaire entrepreneur's resignation from the chipmaker.
In a post on social media platform Truth Social on Monday, Mr. Trump cheered the board's move, calling it "an absolutely GREAT decision" that would benefit the U.S. economy.

Mr. Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had spoken to Nvidia's board members to encourage them to reinstate Huang. "We have to protect our geniuses, and he is certainly a genius," he told the media outlet.

SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, another prominent supporter of Huang's, said in a post on X that "The mistake has been corrected," referring to the Nvidia co-founder's Nov. 12 resignation following revelations that he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy.

Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair and apologized to his family. Huang also had a relationship with a subordinate at Nvidia, the New York Times reported last week, while Reuters reported that he had an intimate relationship with a second employee at the company.

Nvidia Board Chair Harvey Jones on Monday announced that Huang's "reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers." Last week, during a quarterly earnings call discussing Nvidia's latest financial results, Jones said the board had no intention of rehiring him.
Sam Altman, CEO of ChatGPT developer OpenAI, in which Nvidia has pledged to invest up to $100 billion, issued a one-word post on X on Monday. "Jensen!" he wrote.
For their part, investors also seem heartened by Huang's return. Nvidia's stock soared $39.80 per share, or 32%, on Monday, quickly adding more than $1 trillion to the company's market value.
Lawmakers keep heat on Nvidia

Not everyone cheered Huang's return to the world's most valuable AI chipmaker. In a statement, Sen. Elizabeth Warren called the Nvidia board's decision to reinstate Huang "reckless." The Massachusetts Democrat also pressed Nvidia's board to offer more details on its decision to rehire Huang.

"Jensen Huang's return only increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law and making sure Nvidia does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk," she said.

Lawmakers have moved to strengthen controls around U.S. exports to restrict China from gaining remote access to the most powerful chips and chipmaking equipment. On Nov. 16, the U.S. Commerce Department issued a new rule to close a loophole to protect sensitive American technology.

"Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain," Sen. Charles Schumer, a Democrat from New York, said in a social media post. "We'll also work on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries."

Sen. John Cornyn, a Texas Republican, also expressed concern on social media about Nvidia's decision to restore Huang, questioning the board's conclusion that rehiring him posed no national security risk.

In addition to existing license requirements for advanced semiconductors, the rule adds new license requirements for exporting, re-exporting or transferring advanced semiconductors to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore or Thailand. The department said such nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion."

Despite Huang's resumption of his duties at Nvidia, the House Intelligence Committee plans to carry on with a closed-door hearing with the executive next week, sources told CBS News. Huang and Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter were also expected to appear before other congressional panels in early December to answer questions about the company's export practices, among other issues.
Huang has long lobbied for the federal government to allow Nvidia to sell its most powerful AI chips to China.

title: Anthropic's IPO set for blastoff in key test for AI boom
summary: Anthropic's stock is poised to start trading on Nasdaq Thursday in one of the largest IPOs of all time. The AI world is watching.
story: Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering is set to launch on Thursday, a milestone that will test investor enthusiasm for the company behind the popular Claude chatbot and the burgeoning artificial intelligence sector.

"This is a case where the deal is so large and important, so central to the AI thesis, that it's going to be a turning point for the AI sector," Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at Renaissance Capital, told CBS News. "Even non-AI companies are going to feel the ripple effects, especially in the IPO market."
Anthropic shares are scheduled to start trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol "ANT" sometime after markets open Thursday at 9:30 a.m. ET.
Anthropic increases stock price amid high demand

In an announcement on Wednesday night, San Francisco-based Anthropic said it will offer 980 million shares of Class A common stock priced at $83 each. The initial public offering raised around $81 billion and valued Anthropic at $1.5 trillion, making it the largest public offering in history. Elon Musk's SpaceX raised $75 billion when it went public in June.
Anthropic is selling 956.3 million shares, although only 7.4% will be available for public trading (up to 9.8% including Class A shares held by nonfounder employees), according to Renaissance.

The company plans to raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, all of which have a stake in the AI race.

Kennedy thinks Anthropic shares could reach $100 by the end of their first day of trading, an increase that would represent a "solid pop," he said. If the stock rises closer to $140, "that would tell me that AI enthusiasm has come roaring back," he added.
Great expectations
Although many investors appear eager to own a piece of Anthropic, the IPO comes amid growing concerns about whether the torrid spending on AI will deliver the expected productivity and profit boom.

AI-related stocks have fluctuated in recent weeks following subpar earnings and the mountainous debt companies are taking on to finance data center construction. Jensen Huang's shock exit from Nvidia last week has also rattled investors, with the chipmaker's stock now down more than 35% from its October all-time high.

"The whole AI sector has sold off from its July peak. Investor enthusiasm was greatest then," Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business, told CBS News.

Although Anthropic has yet to turn a profit, the company has shown explosive revenue growth over its short time in business. Anthropic raked in nearly $17 billion in the third quarter this year, up 45% from the second quarter, a recent regulatory filing shows. Given that heady rate of expansion, Ritter expects Anthropic to reach profitability quickly.

To justify its projected trillion-dollar valuation, however, the company will need to sustain that momentum while operating under Wall Street's unsparing gaze. Compounding the challenge is how quickly the AI landscape itself is changing. For instance, Anthropic could struggle to maintain its growth rate as consumers shift from pricier AI models like Claude and ChatGPT to cheaper open-source models, Ritter noted.

Anthropic also will have to spend heavily to keep developing its AI models and stay ahead of rivals, from OpenAI, Alphabet and Meta to Chinese platforms. Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is "substantial." Meanwhile, the company has committed to spending nearly a trillion dollars on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045, according to a securities filing.

Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a national backlash against data centers, giving new impetus to a congressional effort last year to enact a national moratorium on new ones.
"The company is likely to be very successful, but the market is pricing in very lofty expectations," Ritter said. "It could be hard for management to execute."
Wall Street analysts said Anthropic's share offering has broader ramifications for the AI sector, with the IPO's pricing setting a benchmark for other tech companies planning to go public.
Even if Anthropic's stock soars on the first day of trading, it won't necessarily create a swarm of IPO activity, Kennedy said. Still, it could reinvigorate markets, he added.

Meanwhile, by going public, Anthropic is effectively asking investors to discount the threats that Anthropic founder Dario Amodei himself has identified as posed by AI. In September, he called for an industrywide slowdown in AI development after a former Anthropic researcher warned of the existential threat AI poses to humanity.

title: Anthropic shares jump in Nasdaq trading debut after record IPO
summary: Anthropic raised a record $81.3 billion, catapulting it past SpaceX, which raised $75 billion​ when it went public in June.
story: Anthropic's stock soared in early trading on Nasdaq Thursday before partly shedding those gains in the afternoon, as the artificial intelligence developer completed the largest initial public offering in history.

Trading under the ticker "ANT," Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, up 34% from the $83 offer price, and rose as high as $114.99, valuing the company at more than $2 trillion at the peak. The stock pared those gains over the course of the day, closing at $97.17, a rise of 17%.

"Both the jump from the offer price and the high volatility are not surprising, given the enormous potential of the company and the wildly different opinions about how profitable the company will become," Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business, said in an email.

Anthropic shares rose on a day when the rest of the stock market took a dive. Late in Thursday's session, the Nasdaq dropped 550 points, or 2.3%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled more than 1,100 points, or 2.2%, and the S&P 500 sank 2%.
"Seminal" moment
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei celebrated Anthropic's market debut at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York City on Thursday.
"The goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time," Dario Amodei said Thursday in an event to mark the IPO.
"The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history, and we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better," he added.

San Francisco-based Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in its IPO, catapulting past SpaceX, which raised $75 billion when it went public in June. The IPO values the company behind the Claude chatbot at roughly $1.5 trillion, more than companies such as Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway, JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Walmart.

Anthropic's IPO represents an "A-plus success," Dan Ives, a tech analyst and partner of Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News. "I think it's a vote of confidence for the market relative to the tech trade," he added.
The public offering delivered a huge payday to the seven Anthropic co-founders, boosting their worth on paper to around $20 billion each. It will also turn many Anthropic employees into millionaires.

Anthropic said Wednesday that it would offer 980 million shares of Class A common stock priced at $83 per share, allowing it to raise a record-breaking amount. Anthropic originally priced its shares in a range of $70 to $78, but raised its per-share IPO price amid strong investor demand.

The IPO price of $83 a share is what Anthropic insiders and other early investors pay to receive an allocation of stock. According to Renaissance Capital, which tracks IPOs, 7.4% of Anthropic shares are available for public trading (or up to 9.8% if Class A shares held by non-founder employees are included).
Even if Americans don't buy shares, Anthropic's IPO could still affect their 401(k), given how exposed the stock market is to AI stocks.

Anthropic has previously said it will raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, bringing its fundraising total to around $107 billion.
Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at Renaissance Capital, thinks Anthropic shares could reach $100 by the end of their first day of trading.

However, like many companies that go public in a blockbuster, and perhaps overhyped, share offering, Anthropic's stock could well waver in the months to come. In a Truist study of 32 of the biggest ever IPOs, more than half saw their shares slide by at least 50% at some point during their first year of trading.

Anthropic announced its plans to go public in October, inviting investors to be part of what it called one of the "seminal moments in human history." The company is the first frontier AI lab to go public.
Critical time for AI trade

Anthropic's IPO comes at a critical time for the AI industry, as investors are asking harder questions about the sector's growing losses, capital investments and returns, Sam Grelck, an equity strategy analyst at Truist Advisory Services, a unit of Truist Financial, told CBS News.
"I wouldn't view Anthropic's IPO as a verdict on AI, but the reception can give us another indication of investors' appetite for the AI theme after what's been a challenging few weeks," he said.

AI-related stocks have swung sharply in recent weeks as concerns mount about the mountainous debt companies are taking on to finance the data center buildout and a potential Democratic-led crackdown on the AI boom following the midterms. Jensen Huang's shock exit from Nvidia last week has also rattled investors.
At a time when investors are skittish, the robust demand for Anthropic shares suggests there is still faith that lofty investments in AI will pay off.
"Anthropic's IPO is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning," Ives said in a research note.
Financing its future

The IPO provides Anthropic with cash to finance its AI development plans. The company, which is yet to turn a profit, has said it wants to use its technology to "improve how humans live" by providing tailored financial and legal advice and speeding up scientific discovery.
"I believe sufficient and powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of medical and scientific progress into a decade," Amodei said at Nasdaq in New York on Thursday.
While the IPO will boost its coffers, Anthropic could quickly burn through cash as it works to keep its AI models on the cutting edge and stay ahead of rivals like OpenAI.

As of Sept. 30, the company had $6.2 billion in debt, according to its regulatory filing. At the same time, it has committed to spending nearly $1 trillion on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045.

title: Stocks enter correction territory, driven by deepening tech rout
summary: The tech-heavy Nasdaq tumbled more than 1,200 points, putting it on track for its second-worst day of the year.
story: Technology stocks plunged on Friday, dimming investor cheer over Anthropic's high-profile IPO this week amid mounting concerns about the health of the artificial intelligence sector.

The Nasdaq Composite Index fell 1,261 points, or 5.3%, to close at 22,618, the tech-heavy index's second-worst day of 2026 and erasing all of its gains for the year. The S&P 500 declined 3.7%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.9%.

Both the  S&P 500 and Dow entered "correction" territory, meaning the indexes have fallen more than 10% from their most recent highs. The S&P 500 is set for its seventh consecutive day of losses, its longest losing streak since February 2020, when the pandemic caused investors to sell in a panic.

Investors are fretting over the value of AI stocks, which drove much of Wall Street's gains earlier this year but are now driving the slide. Microchip companies like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom led Friday's losses over concerns about a possible slowdown in data center construction and over tighter federal policies on exporting chips outside the U.S.

"The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. "But I don't think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over."

The S&P 500's decline into correction territory was largely driven by investors selling AI-related companies, but the underlying U.S. economic and business fundamentals remain solid, said Chris Larkin, managing director of trading and investing at E*TRADE from Morgan Stanley, in an email.

"It's impossible to know when any selloff will run its course, but history shows most moves like this don't turn into bear markets —only five of the past 15 corrections from all-time highs since 1983 have done so," he said, referring to when stocks decline 20% or more from the market's most recent peak.
Anthropic can't buck the market

Thursday's big market debut for Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI chatbot, fizzled on Friday, along with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.3% to $88.14, although it remains above its IPO price of $83 per share.

As of early afternoon trading on Friday, Anthropic's stock had fallen about 23% from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That's an even bigger drop than the dive Facebook (now Meta) saw shortly after its May 2012 IPO.
Shares of Nvidia, considered practically synonymous with the AI boom, are falling for the ninth day in the last 10, down 13% in late Friday trading.

The chip company's stock was caught up in the market's anxiety about the strength of the AI buildout, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its co-founder and former CEO. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has shed more than 25% of its value.
Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills jumped 4.4%, and homebuilder Lennar rose 2.5%.

title: White House national cyber director leaving his post
summary: White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross will be leaving his position, a White House official told CBS News.
story: White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross will be leaving his position, a White House official told CBS News.
Cairncross was fired, multiple sources told CBS News.

White House chief of staff Stephen Miller — who took over for Susie Wiles earlier this month — had long wanted Cairncross out of the job, sources said, telling people he didn't think Cairncross had the expertise needed to be national cyber director.

Miller immediately teed up a search process for a replacement and selected Kirsten Davies, currently the Pentagon's chief information director, to replace Cairncross, the sources said. On Friday, the White House announced President Trump had named her the new White House cyber director. She will, however, require Senate confirmation to serve in the role permanently.
Axios was first to report that Cairncross would leave.

Cairncross' departure comes as the U.S. reels from a series of technological outages over the last week that have hit Microsoft services, air traffic control systems, banks and the National Security Agency's internal network.

Authorities investigating the outages have "seen nothing that would indicate that they are related," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told lawmakers this week. He said he is "98% confident" the outages are not the result of malicious foreign activity, though he acknowledged that he had "absolutely not" seen so many outages in a short period of time.
The national cyber director advises the president on cybersecurity and coordinates cyber strategy across the federal government. An attorney, Cairncross has served in the role since August 2025.
The job was created in 2021. In recent years, the U.S. has faced a series of cyberattacks linked to actors in Iran, Russia, China and other U.S. adversaries.

The Trump administration released its cyber strategy in March, which Cairncross' office oversaw. The seven-page document vowed to "detect, confront, and defeat cyber adversaries before they breach our networks and systems," harden critical infrastructure, maintain a U.S. edge in artificial intelligence and modernize federal tech systems.
In a November 2025 appearance at the Aspen Cyber Summit, Cairncross said one of the administration's primary goals is "introducing costs and consequences" on adversaries.

"I think, as a country, we have not done a terrific job of sending a signal to our adversaries that this behavior is not consequence-free," he said. "And we need to do that because it is scaling and it is becoming more aggressive every passing day."
In a statement, Cairncross called the role "the honor of a lifetime."

"I leave my role as Director of Cyber incredibly proud of our work to strengthen America's cybersecurity, protect our critical infrastructure, confront foreign threats, and position America to lead the world in Super Intelligence. None of it would have been possible without President Trump's extraordinary leadership," he said.

title: NSA network outage linked to software vulnerability
summary: The director of national intelligence and multiple sources said the National Security Agency's network outage stemmed from the patching of vulnerabilities in the programming language, PHP.
story: The National Security Agency's network outage Tuesday has been linked to an urgent patching of vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language that powers the majority of all websites, multiple sources told CBS News.

The NSA's internal network, which is used to store and share classified information, went offline Tuesday, prompting the agency to stagger arrival times for some personnel at its headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland.
Artificial intelligence helped uncover a pair of critical security vulnerabilities, triggering a global scramble last month to update software used by much of the internet, including the NSA.

The flaws, collectively known as PHP2Shell, affect PHP, which is a programming language used by roughly 70% of websites. The race to patch vulnerable systems may help explain some of the recent technology disruptions.

The PHP2Shell threat was so serious that the FBI, NSA and CISA issued urgent warnings just under a month ago, on Oct. 21, directing organizations to immediately patch vulnerable systems. The three agencies also advised those unable to install the fixes to take affected systems offline altogether until they could be secured.

Speaking on Fox Business Tuesday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton directly linked the NSA's classified network outage to urgent software updates following the discovery of critical vulnerabilities in PHP.

"If you go back about 10 days ago, we had what was labeled as PHP, an update to a web interface system," Clayton said. "And the patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected. That is what has happened at the NSA today."

According to two sources familiar with the system, NSA Net as of right now is back up and running. Nonetheless, staggered arrival is continuing as fears persist that the system might not be able to handle everyone signing on at the same time. There is no word yet on how long the agency will continue the staggered arrival schedule, known as "Code Gray."

NSA maintains that mission critical information sharing has not been impacted, while it asks personnel to delay nonessential tasks, according to sources. The NSA said Tuesday the agency had experienced a "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance," adding that its mission/critical capabilities were still fully operational. The NSA is responsible for collecting and analyzing foreign signals intelligence, identifying and countering cyber threats and protecting U.S. government communications.
The agency has not yet responded to a CBS News request for an update on Wednesday.

One U.S. intelligence official described the broader challenge of updating infrastructure that was originally designed for an earlier internet era. The volume and speed of changes can overwhelm aging equipment. The official's assessment reflects a growing concern among intelligence and Homeland Security officials that modern technology is advancing faster than the systems that support it.

Speaking about PHP vulnerabilities, Clayton also pointed to the growing role of AI in speeding up both those kinds of discoveries and the pressure to respond. He described PHP as a "legacy vulnerability" that has been successfully patched across systems globally, adding, "This type of identification of vulnerabilities and patching goes on all the time."

Unlike the NSA outage, Friday's FAA nationwide ground stop involved a hardware problem, rather than a software vulnerability. Routine telecommunications maintenance triggered excessive network traffic that overwhelmed older routers, creating a cascading disruption across much of the air traffic control system. It is not yet clear whether the banking, airline or technology companies' outages shared the same cause.

title: Largest U.S. data centers use as much power as some countries
summary: Hyperscale data centers used almost 2% of all U.S. electricity between 2024 and 2025, a Harvard study shows.
story: The largest U.S. data centers collectively consume roughly as much energy as some individual states and even some countries, according to new research from Harvard University.

Researchers found that so-called hyperscale data centers, which occupy as much space as several football fields, consumed 82 terawatt-hours of electricity, or 1.8% of all U.S. electricity, between 2024 and 2025. That's roughly the equivalent of what a state like Missouri uses or a nation like Denmark. Combined, the facilities also produced 26 metric tons of carbon dioxide.

Harvard scientist Gianluca Guidi, the lead author of the paper published in Nature Sustainability this week, told CBS News that it took two years to analyze the electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions of 403 hyperscale data centers between May 2024 and April 2025. The study likely understates the centers' estimated energy consumption, given the swift pace of AI construction across the U.S., he added.

"The data stops in April 2025, which in AI time is basically ancient history," Guidi said. There are now more than double that number of large-scale facilities operating in the U.S., with an additional 2,000 planned or under development.
"The industry is growing faster than anyone can track it," Guidi added.
Factories that never sleep
The study highlights AI's dependence on data centers and their outsized impact on the environment. Guidi explained why the facilities are such heavy electricity users.

"Every email you send, every photo you post, every show you stream, every question you ask of any generative AI software goes through a building like this," he said of the windowless facilities housing tens of thousands of computers that run around the clock.
The machines generate a lot of heat and require constant cooling. "So it's basically a factory that never sleeps," Guidi said.

Although he's excited about AI's capabilities and considers himself a proponent of the technology, Guidi called for more transparency in assessing when and how facilities are built, along with their impact — before data centers are built.

"The evidence shouldn't show up after the buildings do, and neither should the public's voice," he said. "There are better ways to build this, maybe that cost more, maybe they take longer. So we have to ask ourselves: Are we confusing what's possible or what's profitable with what's actually good for society?"
To that end, he issued a challenge to hyperscalers like Amazon, Meta and Microsoft. "We've proven we can build AI really fast. Now, let's prove that we can build it right," he said.
Negotiators at the United Nations COP31 climate talks in Turkey earlier this week launched a voluntary pledge calling on companies and governments to power AI with cleaner energy.

"We cannot ask people to accept higher bills, more planet-heating pollution and deeper inequality today in exchange for promises of a better tomorrow," United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said Monday during the pledge's launch. "Claims about future emissions savings cannot excuse rising pollution now, making climate disasters even worse."
So far, the pledge has failed to attract signatures from the U.S. tech companies that are driving the AI buildout.

title: Nvidia says it will stop selling some data center chips to China
summary: Nvidia's sales to China are facing heightened scrutiny after revelations that former CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
story: Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday that the company has stopped shipping artificial intelligence chips from its Hopper series to China, despite earlier U.S. approval to sell the technology there.
The Hopper line, designed to speed training of AI models, includes the powerful H200 chip, which the U.S. Department of Commerce approved for sale in China in January.

Kress didn't provide a reason for the decision, but the strategic shift comes amid heightened scrutiny of Nvidia's sales in China following revelations that former CEO and cofounder Jensen Huang had a relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Huang, who successfully lobbied the Trump administration to ease export controls on its advanced chips, had agreed to give the U.S. government 15% of revenue generated by sales of its AI chips in China.

Kress said that sales of licensed Hopper products to China totaled $2.4 billion in the third quarter, or about 2% of its total revenue. But "our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China," she said in a call with Wall Street analysts to discuss Nvidia's latest financial results.
Dilin Wu, a research strategist at Pepperstone, told Agence France-Presse that "the timing says quite a lot."

"We don't know exactly what prompted the decision to stop shipments, but it certainly looks like Nvidia is trying to draw a clearer line around its China business and reassure regulators that compliance comes first," Wu said.

Nvidia also said on Tuesday that its board has formed a panel to oversee its national security policies and compliance with U.S. export controls. Washington still bans exports of Nvidia's more advanced Blackwell and Rubin GPUs to China, citing security concerns over AI's use in military applications.

Nvidia reported robust growth as Kress hosted her first earnings call since Huang resigned last week after it emerged that he had at least extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. authorities have linked to Chinese intelligence and a direct subordinate at Nvidia.

The chipmaker reported fiscal third-quarter profits of $65.3 billion, topping analyst forecasts and up 105% from earnings of $31.9 billion in the year-ago period. Nvidia's revenue rose to $115.8 billion, compared with $57 billion a year ago.

title: Apple restores services after internal update caused outages
summary: The company's system status shows that all Apple services, including iCloud sign-in, have been restored after experiencing issues earlier Tuesday.
story: Apple said it has restored all services after users reported issues with Apple Pay, Apple Support, iCloud and other products on Tuesday.
A spokesperson for the company told CBS News in an email that its services are "green across the board," referring to the System Status page on Apple's website, as of approximately 5:46 p.m. ET.

Thousands of people reported issues with Apple services on Tuesday, according to the tracking site Downdetector.com. The reports started to spike before noon ET and lasted several hours before tapering off in the afternoon, the site shows.

By 4:45 p.m. ET, Apple's system status page showed problems with iCloud sign-in and "AppleCare on device" had been resolved. However, some services, including Apple Business and Apple School Manager, were still experiencing issues, according to the tech giant.
The issues were not the result of a cyberattack, according to the spokesperson.

Apple is the latest company to experience service disruptions following a string of outages that affected everything from air travel to Microsoft email. On Monday, customers at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and other major financial institutions also reported service issues affecting bank deposits and Zelle transfers.

Users also reported issues accessing Gmail on Tuesday. In a statement shared on X, Google said it isn't "currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption" and encouraged users to check its workplace status dashboard for updates.

title: Can Anthropic win hearts and minds by curing hearts and minds?
summary: Anthropic says Claude Science can drive breakthroughs in drug discovery. It could also open lucrative commercial opportunities, experts say.
story: Fresh off its record-setting initial public offering, Anthropic now must show investors that it can sustain growth and generate profits. The company has a plan for that: curing some of the world's gnarliest diseases.

In its IPO prospectus, Anthropic states that AI holds the potential to "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine, potentially curing diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia, including cancer, Alzheimer's disease, heart disease, rare genetic diseases, and the major infectious diseases."

Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei said in a post on X in August that he believes "it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!)."
Speeding in the right direction

Developing breakthrough drugs is among the most promising avenues of research for AI, potentially bringing treatments for a range of conditions to market much faster than is currently possible, according to scientists and industry analysts.

"AI can accelerate research. It will help you get there faster, but it's not just speed — it's directional speed," Neerav Kaushal, an AI and molecular biology expert at Michigan Technological University, told CBS News. "Let's say you're at the top of the mountain and your aim is to find a drug for cancer that lies in the valley. AI will not just help you get down there faster — it will help you get down to the right valley where the drug is."

For Anthropic, meanwhile, developing drugs could open up potentially enormous commercial opportunities. The company has partnered with biotech and pharmaceutical companies that use its Claude Science model for various purposes. Anthropic also operates its own AI-powered biology wet lab in San Francisco that has already made scientific discoveries.
"If you can use a large language model to condense any part of the timeline, it is very economically valuable," Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan told CBS News.
The challenge for Anthropic will be how it turns its life sciences research into profits. That could take time, Khan told CBS News.

"How this becomes lucrative for Anthropic is a very important question, and I think it's a question Anthropic hasn't figured out yet," Khan said. "Coding is its best-proven use case, followed by cybersecurity applications, then financial and legal research."
But the potential to move the needle for both Anthropic and its pharma partners is significant.

"If you improve your drug's efficiency by a couple of percentage points, that can make a world of difference," Khan added. "You'll get asymmetric payouts in the sense that if a model can help with any part of the process, it's very economically valuable."

For example, he expects a drug developer like Eli Lilly and Co., which partners with Anthropic to give its employees access to Claude, would be willing to pay "hundreds of millions or billions of dollars to make its arthritis drug 2% better than it is."
A way to win hearts and minds by curing them?

Developing potentially lifesaving drugs could have other benefits for Anthropic. By applying tools to the life sciences and using them to improve human life, the company could help shift the narrative around AI to a more positive one, according to experts.

"If you are the AI company that helps advance some kind of cure or solution to a sickness or illness that's prevailed for quite some time, I think that gets you a ton more trust with consumers and end users," Khan said. "Because you end up becoming the company that is actually improving the quality of life for humans at large."

title: Husband of woman arrested by ICE at airport calls it "unjust"
summary: Jose Castillo told CBS News he felt "useless" seeing his wife and father-in-law be taken into federal custody at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport.
story: The husband of a woman whose arrest by immigration agents inside a jetway at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport gained national attention says he felt "useless" when seeing his wife and father-in-law be taken into federal custody, calling the episode "unjust."

Jose Castillo, an American citizen, teared up when recounting the moment on Saturday when masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers detained his wife, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, and his father-in-law, Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza.

"You black out. You don't even know what's going on. You don't even know what's happening. Everything is moving so fast. Trying to protect your wife and they're taking your father-in-law," Castillo told CBS News in an interview Monday. "As a U.S. citizen, you feel useless."
Castillo said he felt "disgusted."
"How can you sit with yourself and strip somebody away like that in broad daylight, in front of families?" Castillo added.
The arrest was captured on videos that have gone viral. Hernandez Mejia is heard wailing and saying she has a valid work permit, while bystanders demand answers from the federal agents.

Department of Homeland Security officials identified Hernandez Mejia and Larrondo Mendoza as Mexican nationals living in the U.S. illegally after overstaying their visas. The agency said ICE officers were targeting Larrondo Mendoza for arrest when "other passengers began obstructing federal officers."
DHS accused Hernandez Mejia of assaulting agents, alleging she threw hot coffee on them. Castillo pushed back on the allegations.
"There was no assault on her end," Castillo said. "She did nothing. She was being shoved. They came directly at us."
"When you're coming at me and my wife and you're shoving us, obviously coffee's going to be spilled," he added.
DHS has said Hernandez Mejia "will be charged with assaulting a federal officer."

Castillo said he was traveling with his wife and father-in-law to a family event when they were approached by ICE agents in plainclothes on the jetway to an Alaska Airlines flight. The flight was delayed by over two hours, and the flight crew had to be replaced, the airline said.
Officials at Alaska Airlines and the Port of Seattle, which runs the airport, said they were not given prior notice of the ICE operation. The Port of Seattle said it was "outraged."
Hernandez Mejia and her father remain in ICE custody in Tacoma, Washington, according to their attorney. Castillo pleaded for their release.
"They don't deserve to be in there," he said. "It was done in such an unjust manner."

The incident is the latest in a string of ICE operations that have gone awry in recent weeks, even after President Trump acknowledged to 60 Minutes that his crackdown on illegal immigration may have been "too tough."

Last week, video captured ICE agents pushing a pregnant woman and U.S. citizen to the ground in Modesto, California. ICE accused her of interfering with the arrest of a man with a criminal record. In Texas, an ICE agent is facing criminal charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon after allegedly striking a Mexican immigrant with an unmarked SUV. His attorney has called the incident an "accident."

The detention at Sea-Tac airport is part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to send ICE officers to major airports across the country to arrest travelers who are in the U.S. illegally or with a tenuous legal status. Those arrested have included travelers with pending legal immigration applications but whose underlying permission to be in the U.S. expired.

Olia Catala, who is representing the father and daughter detained at Sea-Tac, said her clients entered the U.S. as tourists and that both have pending immigration applications. Hernandez Mejia, Catala said, applied for a green card as the spouse of a U.S. citizen.
She said the family was trying to follow the immigration process prior to being arrested.

"Congress created legal pathways and Sofia and her father were using them," Catala said. "We can't tell immigrants to use the legal pathways, to follow the law and then punish them for doing just that."

title: 9th measles death recorded in Pennsylvania amid ongoing outbreak
summary: Pennsylvania's outbreak is the largest in the country​, with over 1,600 cases reported, and the deaths this year are the Keystone State's first from measles in 35 years.
story: Pennsylvania on Monday announced its ninth measles-related death this year as cases continue to surge across the U.S., reaching their highest mark in decades.

The death was reported in Centre County, in the middle of the state. The Pennsylvania Department of Health did not provide any further information about the patient. The announcement came just three days after Virginia reported that a child under the age of 5 had died after testing positive for measles. It was Virginia's first measles-related death this year, the state's Health Department said.

Pennsylvania's outbreak is the largest in the country, with over 1,600 cases reported, according to the state Department of Health, and the deaths this year are the Keystone State's first from measles in 35 years.
In Lancaster County, one woman told CBS News her three children all have measles.

The U.S. had eliminated measles by the year 2000, but last week the country lost that status. A country is considered to have eliminated measles if there are "no locally transmitted measles infections or outbreaks lasting 12 months or longer," according to the World Health Organization.

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data show that about a quarter of this year's measles cases are linked to outbreaks that began in 2025, when the U.S. saw a 30-year high of 2,289 cases, and that the virus continued to spread. As of last week, there have been 5,838 confirmed measles cases in the U.S. this year, according to the CDC.
Dr. Evan Shirey, an infectious disease specialist, said he went from seeing no measles cases to dealing with them "almost every day."
He blames misinformation for vaccine hesitancy.
"The manifestations of that can just be horrible to see," he said. "Children gasping for air. Seeing a child who is altered, confused, unable to recognize their own mom."

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has long been criticized for casting doubt on vaccine safety, said in the wake of the U.S. losing its measles elimination status, "I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles."
Kindergarten vaccination rates have fallen below the 95% needed to protect the immunocompromised and infants too young to be vaccinated. Among the latter group: Shirey's 3-month-old son.
"I'm absolutely counting down the days," he told CBS News. "I'll have him in there on the date to make sure that I'm doing what I can for him to protect him."
The first dose of the MMR vaccine is usually given at 12 to 15 months of age, but can be given as early as 6 months in high-risk cases, such as during an ongoing outbreak.

                                  Grace  Manthey

title: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
summary: Nvidia said Monday that it has restored Jensen Huang as the chipmaker's chief executive, calling him the "right person" to lead the company.
story: Nvidia's board of directors said on Monday that it has reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO.

The action comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned amid a scandal over an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of spying for China. China has denied it. Huang also had an extramarital affair with a subordinate at Nvidia, according to a New York Times report.

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Board Chair Harvey C. Jones said in a statement on Monday.

"In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk," the company added.

Eleven days after his resignation, Huang said in a statement that he is "honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution." He also thanked the company's board, interim CEO Colette Kress, and Nvidia staffers and shareholders.
"I can't wait to get back to work," Huang added.
The decision to restore Huang to his position came as a major surprise. In a company earnings call last week, Jones said the company "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

Huang's affair with a woman believed to have links to China's Ministry of State Security has put a spotlight on Nvidia's business in the People's Republic, with lawmakers questioning whether the company's AI chips were winding up in China in violation of U.S. export rules.
Push for his return

Huang last week underlined his eagerness to return to the chip company he co-founded in 1993, saying that if the "board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."

Numerous business leaders and thousands of Nvidia employees had signed a petition urging the chipmaker to rehire Huang. President Trump had also suggested that he would support the leader's return to Nvidia. "I would not mind seeing that," Mr. Trump said last week.
In a social media post on Monday, Mr. Trump cheered Nvidia's move.

"The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO," Mr. Trump said on Truth Social. "The Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy. The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security."
Mr. Trump also told CNBC that he had spoken directly to Nvidia's board about reinstating Huang.
Too big to fail?

Dan Ives, a tech analyst with Yorkville Ives, told CBS News that the board "had no choice" but to bring Huang back as CEO, saying that the executive's shock resignation earlier this month was becoming an "economic and global markets issue."
Nvidia makes advanced chips and other components that help power AI, which is driving economic growth in the U.S. and until recently had fueled record stock market gains.
"Nvidia is the linchpin to the global economy," Ives said.
Gil Luria, lead tech analyst at investment adviser D.A. Davidson, attributed Nividia board's U-turn to White House pressure to reinstate Huang.

"Because there is so much concern about the health of the overall economy and ability for the U.S. to continue to grow the AI investment cycle, which was accentuated by stock market declines last week, the White House wanted to put him back in his seat to move the economy forward," Luria told CBS News.

Nvidia's stock soared more than 30% on news of Huang's reinstatement. The news also buoyed other stocks, with the Nasdaq Composite Index erasing all of its losses in early trading after a steep sell-off on Friday.
Other Wall Street analysts who follow Nvidia expressed surprise at the company's sudden turnaround, but said the executive's return bolsters the company and the broader AI sector.

"Jensen was a singular CEO who built Nvidia into an AI juggernaut and maintained an extremely flat corporate structure, making him difficult to replace," Adam Crisafulli of Vital Knowledge told investors in a report.

Under Huang, Nvidia has emerged as a pillar in the growing AI industry, not only through its technology prowess but also for its role in financing the purchase of advanced chips and striking other deals to stoke demand for its products.

title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang still testifying before Congress next week
summary: Jensen Huang is still set to testify before lawmakers next week, congressional panels confirmed, after he was reinstated as Nvidia's CEO Monday, after resigning earlier this month amid allegations of affairs.
story: Washington — Jensen Huang is still scheduled to testify before lawmakers next week, congressional committees confirmed, after he was reinstated as Nvidia's CEO following his resignation earlier this month.

After Huang stepped down less than two weeks ago, amid reports of extramarital affairs — including one with an alleged Chinese spy — Nvidia's board of directors said Monday that it had reinstated Huang as president and CEO. The board's move, for which President Trump claimed some credit, sent shockwaves through the political sphere, with lawmakers on both sides of the aisle expressing concern, and threw into question whether the congressional hearings would proceed.

Huang is set to appear for a transcribed interview with a trio of panels on Dec. 1, including the House Intelligence and Foreign Affairs committees, along with the Select Committee on China. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter voluntarily agreed to appear before the committees on Dec. 2. A spokesperson for the House Intelligence Committee told CBS News that the reinstatement "changes nothing."

"When Jensen was CEO, our three committees were demanding answers. When he was removed and no longer CEO, we were still pursuing the facts," the spokesperson said. "The fact that he has been reinstated as CEO, changes nothing. There are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers. Seems like the only thing that is consistent these days on this issue is our three Committees' commitment to oversight."
Rep. Jim Himes of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, added, "We expect to see him on Capitol Hill next week."
The Senate Banking Committee also sent out a notice Monday announcing that Huang would still appear before the panel to testify on Dec. 3.
Lawmakers from both parties expressed alarm Monday about Huang's reinstatement, which is taking place as the focus shifts to questions about the chipmaker's compliance with export restrictions.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer vowed that Democrats "will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives." And Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, the top Democrat on the Banking Committee, said in a statement that Huang's reinstatement "does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers."

She went on to say that Huang's return to Nvidia's top job only "increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law and making sure NVIDIA does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk."

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who's set to become House Speaker in the new Congress next year, called Nvidia's decision to reinstate Huang "indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible" and vowed a "swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation" into any potential misconduct by the company and by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Rep. Robert Garcia of California, who is set to chair the House Oversight Committee in the new Congress, argued that President Trump's alleged involvement in Huang's reinstatement "raises serious national security and corruption questions," which he said must be investigated.

"No president who has invested in a private company should be involved in their board decisions," Garcia said in a statement. "Congress must come together in swift bipartisan action and demand answers immediately."

On the GOP side, Sen. John Cornyn of Texas questioned the rationale behind the Nvidia board's conclusion that Huang's return poses no national security risk, as did Sen. John Curtis of Utah, who pointed to the board's claim that it received input from "senior levels of the United States government."

"I have some questions," Curtis said in a post on X. "Mr. Huang was right to step down when the affair came to light. Just 11 days after Nvidia announced his departure, the board brought him back while its own independent investigation was still underway. Last week, the board said it didn't intend to reinstate him. I'd like to know what changed."

Sen. Kevin Cramer of North Dakota said the "risk of extortion by a Chinese asset who's been banned by Singapore is risk enough to not rehire Huang," while urging Congress to "immediately pass the strictest export controls possible."

"The legal and reputational risk of hiring a CEO who may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws is now born by the board of Nvidia, but the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens," Cramer said.
Sen. Pete Ricketts of Nebraska argued that Huang's behavior "does not support reinstatement," citing his own experience serving on a public company board.

"Nvidia's decision today doesn't excuse Jensen Huang from testifying before Congress," Ricketts added. "It also doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips. I look forward to Mr. Huang coming to the Senate in December."
A representative for Huang declined to comment about Huang's appearances before Congress.

Caitlin  Yilek
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: Huang's return at Nvidia puts spotlight on chipmaker's board
summary: Nvidia directors' decision to rehire Jensen Huang shows a "lack of courage," according to one prominent governance expert.
story: Nvidia's stunning about-face on Monday to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO undermines the credibility of its board of directors and raises questions about its commitment to enforcing the company's own rules, according to corporate governance experts.

Huang resigned from Nvidia on Nov. 12  after revelations that he had an extramarital affair with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence suspects of spying for China. In announcing its decision to rehire Huang, the company's board said it had concluded that reinstating him "poses no national security risk," citing input it had received from senior U.S. officials.

Yet in reversing itself, Nvidia is undermining its own corporate code of conduct and could expose the company to potential legal liability, Charles Elson, founding director of the John L. Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware, told CBS News.
"It shows a weakness, and I think, frankly, a lack of courage to stand behind the correct decision they made to suggest he resign. That was the right decision," he said.

Nvidia's code of conduct stipulates that personal relationships can create a conflict of interest and instructs employees to ask themselves whether they could defend an action if it were made public on social media or known to colleagues. If not, the policy states, "do not proceed."
"A company culture that allows this sort of stuff to occur ultimately will kill the company itself,"  Elson said.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In announcing Huang's return, Nvidia Board Chairman Harvey Jones said the board "believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers."
Bowing to political pressure?

Technology industry leaders and President Trump celebrated Huang's return. Investors also cheered the return of the man who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and whom many view as synonymous with the burgeoning artificial intelligence sector. The company's stock price surged more than 31% on Monday, quickly bolstering its market value by $1 trillion.

At the same time, the move drew swift condemnation from Democratic and Republican lawmakers, who said the board's decision could put America's national security at risk by undermining efforts to strengthen chip export controls to China.

Despite Nvidia's stock market gain on Monday, governance experts said Nvidia directors failed to live up to their fiduciary duty to act in the best interest of shareholders, including ensuring the company's long-term value.

"They are there for the difficult times. They are the shareholders' fiduciary and lifeboat pick to navigate through a crisis," said Betsy Atkins, who has served on dozens of private and public company boards. "That's their job — deliberate and make the right business judgment."

President Trump told CNBC in a phone interview on Monday that he spoke to Nvidia's board and convinced directors to reinstate Huang, raising questions about whether the board may have bowed to political pressure.

Shiva Rajgopal, a Columbia Business School professor who studies corporate governance, said Mr. Trump's move put Nvidia directors in a difficult position, given the U.S. government's importance as a stakeholder in the company.
"I don't know whether any board would have been able to say no to the president," he told CBS News.
Nvidia's 10-person board, which includes the former president of Taco Bell and a former vice chairman of Goldman Sachs, was lacking in critical ways even before bringing Huang back, Rajgopal added.
"I don't see a whole lot of expertise in, say, export controls, chip architecture, or foundry supply chain," he said.

Several high-profile CEOs have been ousted after their relationships with employees and customers came under scrutiny, such as former McDonald's CEO Steve Easterbrook. But it's rare for a CEO to exit under a cloud only for the board to swiftly bring them back.

The only other high-profile case cited by experts was in 2023, when OpenAI's board decided to rehire CEO Sam Altman just days after pushing him out over questions about his ability to lead the AI startup.

Huang's reinstatement is noteworthy given allegations that he violated Nvidia's code of conduct at least twice, Elson said. Huang allegedly had a relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence has linked to China's Ministry of State Security. At the time, Alice Huang was an executive at an Nvidia customer, Singapore data center Megaspeed.

The Trump administration on Monday formally restricted Megaspeed from buying advanced semiconductor chips. Megaspeed has been accused of transferring high-tech Nvidia chips that power AI to China, a charge the company denies. China also denies targeting Jensen Huang in an intelligence operation.

Huang also had an extramarital affair with a subordinate at Nvidia, according to The New York Times, while Reuters reported that he had an intimate relationship with a second employee at the company. Huang's connections to Alice Huang (no relation) have raised concerns that Nvidia was providing its AI chips to China in violation of U.S. export rules.

title: Nasdaq gains 6.5% after Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO
summary: The Nasdaq Composite closed 6.5% higher, erasing all of its losses from Friday, when the index suffered its second-worst day of 2026.
story: U.S. stocks made a comeback on Monday, with Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO boosting financial markets after Friday's sell-off plunged the S&P 500 and Dow into correction territory.

The Nasdaq Composite jumped 1,472 points, or 6.5%, to close at 24,090, regaining ground after the tech-heavy index on Nov. 20 suffered its second-worst day of 2026. The S&P 500 rose 4.7%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 3%.

Huang resigned less than two weeks ago amid scandal over an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of spying for China. On Monday, the board said it believes Huang is the "right person to lead Nvidia" and that it has "every confidence" in him as he resumes his leadership role at the company. Huang's reinstatement is "effective immediately," the board said.
"The company reported fantastic numbers last week, but the uncertainty of their leadership was like a huge overhang," eToro investment analyst Bret Kenwell told CBS News.
"Now that uncertainty suddenly is not only removed, but it's replaced with the very familiar leadership of Jensen," he added.

Nvidia shares surged more than 31% on Monday, adding roughly $1 trillion to its market value. Shares of CoreWeave, a cloud computing company and Nvidia customer, shot up 22%. The PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index, which tracks 30 of the largest companies involved in the design, distribution, manufacture and sale of chips, rose 14%.

"I believe the White House leaned hard on the board, and the message is crystal clear. America needs Jensen Huang leading Nvidia and, therefore, the wider AI industry," Nigel Green, CEO of investment advisory firm deVere Group, said in an email. "His return hands him more control than ever. He's got the backing of the board, the U.S. president and the market, and that's a phenomenal platform to take Nvidia to another level."
Not out of the woods
Despite Monday's market exuberance, some Wall Street analysts said investors remain on edge amid concerns that the artificial intelligence sector is unraveling.

"Stocks in the U.S. are staging a large rebound rally so far this morning, although, just to put things into context, the S&P futures aren't even reclaiming their loss from Friday, much less the entire week," Vital Knowledge analyst Adam Crisafulli said in a note to investors on Monday before Nvidia announced it was reinstating Huang.
"Sentiment remains pretty bleak — most people are looking at this [Monday] uptick as nothing more than technical in nature, a partial reversal of extremely oversold conditions," he added.

Financial markets tumbled Friday as concerns swelled about a possible slowdown in data center construction across the U.S. and tightening restrictions on chip exports, both of which could hurt corporate profits.

The losses were led by microchip companies like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom, which shed 13.3% and 12.2%, respectively. Both recovered Monday, with AMD gaining 6.9% and Broadcom rising 3%. Anthropic, which made its public market debut on Thursday, sank 1.4%.

Kenwell said financial markets still face headwinds, including a more hawkish Fed, high inflation and investor uncertainty over the AI trade. However, corporate profits remain strong, he said, citing Nvidia's robust earnings last week and bullish financial markets.
"That's not a today story," Kenwell said. "That was true a week ago, true a month ago, and it'll be true at the start of next month."

title: Appeals court clears way for Army to detonate Iowa explosives
summary: A federal appeals court on Monday declined to block the Army from detonating explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Iowa.
story: A federal appeals court on Monday declined to block the Army from detonating five tons of explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Iowa.
President Trump has said the government won't move forward unless Iowa's incoming Democratic governor signs off, although technically the governor-elect's input is not required.

The court's ruling came after environmental groups warned the planned detonation could send a plume of toxic lead particles into the surrounding area, and argued the Environmental Protection Agency hadn't given enough notice or weighed the risks before giving the Army permission to move forward. The government has argued the detonation is necessary because the lead azide has become unstable and could unexpectedly explode.

The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily blocked the detonation last week to give itself time to issue a longer-lasting ruling. On Monday, the court said the environmental groups that challenged the plan had failed to show they are likely to succeed.

"We are mindful of the very real risks presented by the Army's planned detonation of the stores of degraded lead azide," the ruling said. "However, we must acknowledge the realities of the situation: the degraded explosives present a risk of an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion, which would occur without the benefit of the safety measures that the Permit puts in place."

Mr. Trump said earlier Monday the government would not carry out the detonation, which the Army said over the weekend was scheduled for Wednesday, until the appeals court ruled and unless Democratic Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand signed off. Mr. Trump added that government experts felt detonating the material was the best option.

"If [Sand] or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation," the president said on social media.

Sand said on social media the Trump administration "should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks."
"Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward," Sand said.

The government has argued that even if the appeals court had stayed its EPA permit, the Army has the legal right to move forward without a permit to "respond to the immediate threat of an uncontrolled explosion." The Army has warned that it needs to act before cold weather causes lead azide crystals to break down, making a spontaneous explosion more likely.

The Army has stored the lead azide in earthen-covered containers for decades at its ammunition plant in Middletown, a small town located near the Mississippi River in southeastern Iowa. The EPA has said the government discovered earlier this year that the material deteriorated over time, risking explosion if it is moved or disturbed.

As part of an earlier detonation plan slated for Friday, the Army asked some Middletown residents to temporarily evacuate their homes for six hours, and said people could expect loud noises, vibrations and a dust plume.

Environmental groups and Iowa and Illinois politicians from both parties criticized the plan, arguing the detonation could lead to widespread lead contamination in both states and pressing the EPA and Army to consider other options.

The Sierra Club and the Iowa Environmental Council asked the federal appeals court to step in and review the EPA's permit last week, arguing the plan would create "a plume of lead dust that will blanket homes and communities, possibly as far away as 100 miles or more."

The environmental groups said the EPA failed to fully assess the risks of the detonation or consider alternatives, and argued the Army was operating on an "extraordinarily rushed timeline" that prevented residents from getting enough notice.

On Monday, a panel of three appellate judges sided with the federal government. The court found that the EPA "adequately incorporated safeguards" to mitigate the risks, including barriers and plans for environmental monitoring, and the Army considered a range of alternatives.

title: Trump tells Army to halt detonation for now in Iowa this week
summary: President Trump said he will wait for the courts and Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand to agree with the Army's plan.
story: Update: A federal appeals court on Monday declined to block the Army from detonating the explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Iowa. Read earlier developments below.

Washington — President Trump says he has ordered the U.S. military to hold off for now on detonating an explosives site in Iowa, deferring the decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit and Iowa's Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand. The Army had planned to carry out the detonation this week.

The president made the announcement on Truth Social, after the U.S. Army said it planned to move forward with the detonation of tons of unstable explosives at a munitions plant in Middletown, Iowa. That Army decision came in spite of a federal court order pausing it indefinitely, which the Army said it didn't need to follow, citing risks associated with the possibility of the explosives detonating spontaneously. Community members in the small southeastern Iowa town have voiced concerns about the risk of toxic particles spreading across Iowa and neighboring Illinois.

Last week, two environmental groups filed a lawsuit to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit to block the detonation, challenging the validity of the emergency permit granted by the Environmental Protection Agency. The appeals court issued a stay on Thursday pending a final decision on the validity of the permit.

On Truth Social, Mr. Trump wrote that there is a "substantial chance that this material will explode on its own volition," and he thinks the safer option is to detonate now. But, he said he will follow what the courts and Sand wish to do. The president called Iowa a "very special place" to him.

"I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation," the president wrote. "If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation."
The federal government told the court over the weekend that it needed to conduct the controlled detonation by Tuesday, before the temperature is expected to drop below freezing.
Earlier this year, the Army said dozens of drums of lead azide started recrystallization. The lead has been stored in bunkers in the munitions plant, which was built during World War II.
CBS News has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.

Sand said on social media the Trump administration "should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks."
"Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward," Sand said.

title: Why the Army says it needs to detonate unstable explosives in Iowa
summary: The U.S. Army plans to detonate 68 drums of lead azide in Iowa despite local leaders and residents raising concerns.
story: The U.S. Army's plan to detonate several tons of unstable explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa has been delayed multiple times amid a court battle and community outcry about the risk of toxic lead particles spreading in a dust plume for miles.
The Army said the controlled detonation of lead azide is necessary due to the public safety risks associated with the possibility of the explosives detonating on their own.

"Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized," the Army said in a statement.

President Trump said Monday that without the demolition, "a very dangerous situation exists," but ordered the Army to defer its plans until a ruling came down from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit. The court ruled Monday evening that it can go forward.
So why exactly does the Army need to detonate the chemicals and what are the risks to the public?
Why does the Army need to detonate lead azide in Iowa?

In March of this year, the Army said it discovered that 68 drums of lead azide at the site had started "recrystallization." The lead was stored in bunkers at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, a munitions plant built in 1941, which produces quality medium- and large-caliber munitions.
Lead azide is a highly sensitive primary initiating explosive. Due to its extreme sensitivity, even minor external triggers, such as sparks, open flames, friction or pinpricks, can detonate it.
The recrystallization of lead azide can have a high risk of spontaneous explosion, which the EPA said creates a highly unstable and dangerous situation.

Additionally, cold weather would further destabilize the explosive materials. Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist at Army Sustainment Command, told CBS News Chicago that the risk of accidental detonation increases in cold weather.
Military officials said it's not safe to relocate the explosive materials.
The Army said it modeled four different ways to try to neutralize the chemicals, and concluded that a controlled detonation was the best method available.

"It was determined that a controlled detonation was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area," Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a statement.

Army officials said they connected with stakeholders and the public in Middletown and the surrounding area about the approved plan. Critics, however, contend they weren't made aware of the plan to detonate the lead azide until just days before the scheduled controlled explosion.
Local politicians said the decisions were made at the federal level, and poor communication contributed to the outcry and confusion from residents concerned about toxic chemicals.

"The safety of Iowans now and in the future should be the government's top concern. An unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation," Sand said.
What are the risks to residents?
One of the main concerns is that lead particles would be scattered in the dust plume created by the explosion. Lead in any amount is dangerous for humans, and in particular for young children.
"Lead is a really challenging contaminant," said David Cwiertny, a professor at the University of Iowa and director of its Environmental Policy Research Program.
He said there are essentially two ways the lead could be released: moving freely in the air and collecting on the ground.
"We do expect that air to dissipate fairly quickly as it moves with the wind," Cwiertny said.

Lead can enter the body through contaminated food, water or through dust or fumes, according to the U.S. National Institutes of Health, leading to health issues for adults and children. It can impede growth, contribute to learning disorders and damage the brain and nervous system. Children under age 6 are most susceptible to lead poisoning, the CDC says, as their bodies and brains are still developing.

Residents were told to evacuate the immediate area ahead of the planned explosion. But some are worried that afterward, lead would contaminate the environment and infiltrate their groundwater, rendering their communities unsafe.
Middletown resident Sean Byers, whose house is across from the munitions plant, pointed down the street and said, "There's a playground back over there where kids in the community play all the time."
Byers, who has three young children, said he's worried about contamination.
"It's going to linger probably for decades," he said. "It's going to affect everyone."
Are there any steps to reduce the risk?
The Army said it planned to take a number of steps to reduce the risk in a controlled detonation.

The lead azide drums would be detonated inside earth-covered magazines made of concrete, and surrounded with Hesco barriers full of sand, which are approximately two stories high. Before and during the detonation, explosive experts would saturate the soil above with water. Water misters would also be spraying, the Army said.

Residents would be asked to vacate the area at that time, as the controlled detonation "will cause temporary noise, ground vibrations, and a dust plume that will contain some lead," the Army said in a statement.

Byers said he found out about the planned explosion through his neighbor a few days before the planned explosions — not from the U.S. Army. He said he plans to evacuate with his family to Branson, Missouri, where they'd stay for three or four days.
He said the Army told them it would be safe to return to their homes after six hours, but he "highly doubts" that.
Notices were sent out by the Army saying residents' windows could potentially break, and if they do, they'd be replaced by the ammunition plant.

Byers said he got the notice, but says, "The damage at that point has already been done, because it's going to let all that lead enter the house. And the question is, are they going to come in and decontaminate that? Are they going to, you know, are they going to do that? Probably not."

The Army said that due to its mitigation efforts, while there will be some lead particles in the air after the detonation, the levels will be well below the level at which the EPA requires protective actions.
