title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns in wake of affair, spy scandal
summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned effective immediately, the company's board of directors announced Thursday.
story: Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of AI tech giant Nvidia effective immediately following a scandal involving an alleged spy, the company's board of directors announced Thursday.

The decision came amid an investigation into Huang's affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspect was spying for China. President Trump said this week the FBI is investigating romantic and business ties between Huang and suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. The two aren't related.
Nvidia's board had been preparing to oust Huang, two sources familiar with the matter confirmed to CBS News on Wednesday night, plans that were first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

Huang's departure also follows a New York Times report Wednesday that five employees at Nvidia came forward alleging Huang was romantically involved with a subordinate, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare.

The Times also reported Huang and Powell, who are both married to other people, were caught on video being affectionate at a conference in March, according to two Nvidia employees. The Times has not seen the video and CBS News has not verified the report.

After Huang's resignation was announced Thursday, the Reuters news agency reported that Huang also had an intimate relationship with a second employee, according to two people familiar with the matter. The agency only identified the employee as a woman.
The company's interim CEO will be Colette Kress, who is currently Nvidia's chief financial officer and will continue in that role.

"The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," Harvey Jones, who was announced as the company's first board chair, said in a statement.
Kress has been Nvidia's CFO since she joined the company in 2013. She previously worked in finance roles at tech companies like Cisco and Microsoft for nearly 25 years.

Nvidia was co-founded by Huang in 1993. It became one of the most valuable companies in the world by designing the powerful semiconductors that fuel many of the world's leading AI firms, making its technology highly sensitive and subject to export controls limiting sales to China.
Nvidia's stock plunged as news emerged of the company's turmoil, potentially erasing almost $500 billion in value. In Thursday's trading, the stock price closed down 4.3% at $166.19.
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was an executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data center company whose website touts its partnership with Nvidia.

Megaspeed grew with the help of access to Nvidia's restricted AI computer chips. According to U.S. investigators, Alice Huang was able to gain access to 240,000 chips that were banned from being exported to China. Megaspeed is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China.
In Washington, top Democrats on Capitol Hill have expressed concerns over whether Jensen Huang's ties to Alice Huang may have compromised U.S. national security.
Following Jensen Huang's resignation, Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts said his departure doesn't absolve him or the company from the scandal.
"Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Warren said in a statement.
Before Huang resigned, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News the departure could help China in the competition between Beijing and the U.S.

"With him out as CEO, China could significantly narrow the gap versus the U.S.," Ives said. He added: "The problem now is that there's no replacement for Jensen. It's a black eye moment for him, for Nvidia, and actually the U.S. tech industry. I'd say it's dark day for, you know, U.S. technology."
Following Thursday morning's announcement, Mr. Trump said on his Truth Social platform that there was "only one man" who could replace Huang: former Apple CEO Tim Cook.

Mr. Trump had a close relationship with Huang, who has attended AI-focused White House events and traveled with Mr. Trump to China. Late last year, Mr. Trump granted Nvidia the right to sell advanced H200 chips to "approved customers" in China, with the U.S. government getting a 25% cut — a major coup for Huang, who has long sought to sell more technology to the Chinese market. The deal did not cover Nvidia's even more advanced Blackwell and Rubin systems.

In a radio interview Thursday, Mr. Trump brought up that he gave Huang a National Medal of Science earlier this year. "What a horrible thing that is," he said of the situation involving Huang, adding, "That's so sad to see that happen."
The president also said in an interview: "What a horrible thing that is
In a statement accompanying her appointment as interim CEO, Kress said that the company's focus will be on "serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders."

"NVIDIA's strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years," Kress said.
The board said it will be conducting a search for a permanent CEO and will consider internal and external candidates.

title: How Huang's resignation and return unfolded at Nvidia
summary: Jensen Huang's shocking exit as CEO of Nvidia unspooled suddenly, yet signs of trouble had emerged much earlier.
story: Nvidia's board of directors announced on Monday, Nov. 23, that it is reinstating Jensen Huang as the chipmaker's CEO. The move marks an abrupt shift from board members' position only last week that they had no plans to rehire the billionaire entrepreneur at the company he co-founded more than 30 years ago.

Huang's departure from Nvidia on Nov. 12 capped a tumultuous week for the chipmaker, with his resignation coming less than a week after his extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy became public. The woman with whom he had a relationship, Alice Huang (no relation), arrived on the tech scene in 2023, when she became the managing director of Singapore-based data center Megaspeed International.

Megaspeed, which says it has complied with U.S. laws, would proceed to buy billions of dollars in Nvidia chips and servers. Over the past two years, Alice Huang, also known by her Chinese name Huang Le, has been photographed and recorded socializing with Jensen Huang, prompting questions in May from one quizzical investor about their "uncomfortably close relationship."

In a statement on Sunday, Nov. 15, Megaspeed said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025, and it denied any wrongdoing, saying it "conducts legitimate and lawful business." "Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters," the company's statement said.
Below is a timeline of events that led to Jensen Huang's startling resignation, and the board's decision to rehire him:
November 2015

Alice Huang, a former television reporter in China, joins investment firm Shanghai Hexi Investment Management as deputy general manager, according to social media posts and records from Simuwang, a Chinese private equity database. Shanghai Hexi was founded by Kang Wei, who became her husband, according to The Wall Street Journal.
March 2023

7Road International, originally incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International, is renamed Megaspeed, and ownership of the "neocloud" company is transferred to Huang Le Ltd., an enterprise controlled by Alice Huang. She becomes its managing director.
June 2023
Cloud-computing company Shanghai Century Litong is founded. A company linked to Alice's sister, Huang Yu, held an ownership stake.
October 2023
Nvidia designates Shanghai Century Litong as a preferred cloud partner, giving the Chinese company priority access to Nvidia's chips, according to The Information.
Around November 2023
Megaspeed's shares were transferred to another Singapore company, Swiftdata, and Alice Huang ceased to be listed as a director of the company, according to news site Caixin Global.
June 7, 2024
Information technology firm NetThunder posted a picture on social media of Alice Huang and Jensen Huang with other tech executives at a bar in Taipei, Taiwan.
End of 2024
Megaspeed's assets exploded from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024, according to financial filings reviewed by Reuters.

Shipment records from December 2024 through early 2026, analyzed by short-selling firm Culper Research, suggest that Megaspeed's Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix, imported about $4 billion in products from a company that builds equipment with Nvidia chips.
Early 2025

Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, jointly pitched Chinese investors on a Southeast Asia data center project, reportedly telling them they had "no problem securing GPUs" — the graphics processing units Nvidia specializes in — and citing Alibaba as a customer, according to the Financial Times.
Jensen Huang meets with President Trump at the White House. It marks their first of many White House encounters in Mr. Trump's second term.
February 2025
Singapore opens an investigation into Megaspeed and several other companies over suspected false declarations related to the purchase of servers and other offenses, according to Bloomberg News.
Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are recorded on video together at a dinner at San Liu Shi Fu restaurant in Taipei, around the time of the Computex tech conference in Taiwan.
July 2025

Jensen Huang says the technology giant has won approval from the Trump administration to sell its advanced H20 computer chips, used to develop artificial intelligence, to China, a reversal of prior administration policy.
"It's so innovative and dynamic here in China that it's really important that American companies are able to compete and serve the market here in China," Huang said at the time.
That same month, Nvidia becomes the first public company to be worth $4 trillion.
February 2026
Chinese police detained Kang Wei, Alice Huang's husband and business partner, in connection with suspected stock manipulation, sources told Caixin.

That same month, Singapore barred Alice Huang from re-entering the country after she downplayed her role at Megaspeed amid the country's investigation into its operations, according to a Bloomberg News report.
Jensen Huang boards Air Force One in Alaska to accompany Mr. Trump on a two-day trip to Beijing.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefed Mr. Trump about the counterintelligence risk posed by Jensen Huang's affair with Alice Huang, according to The New York Times. The briefing, which occurred before Jensen Huang joined the trip, was the second briefing Mr. Trump had received from U.S. intelligence about the Nvidia CEO's relationship, the Times reported.
Jensen Huang attends Mr. Trump's state dinner for China's Xi Jinping at the White House.
Jensen Huang attends an AI event at the White House and signs a set of voluntary AI safety standards amid calls for tighter guardrails on the technology.

Jensen Huang writes a message to Nvidia employees admitting that he had an extramarital affair. The same day, Nvidia's board said it had launched an independent investigation amid reports that its CEO was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort."
The New York Times on Nov. 8 reported that U.S. government surveillance suggested Alice Huang was feeding information directly to Beijing.

At an impromptu press conference at the White House, Mr. Trump said he had spoken to Jensen Huang and that the tech exec had indicated he was unaware of Alice Huang's links to China's intelligence services. Mr. Trump also described the Nvidia CEO as an "honorable man" who's "definitely suffering."
Mr. Trump didn't address questions about when he first learned about the spy allegations, only saying "not too long ago" and that "it didn't make much of an impact on me."
The New York Times reports that Jensen Huang had an affair with Kimberly Powell, a subordinate at Nvidia.
Nvidia's board of directors announces that Jensen Huang has resigned, effective immediately.

Nvidia reports its third-quarter earnings, with interim CEO Colette Kress hosting the call following Huang's resignation. Nvidia Board Chair Harvey Jones said the company "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

Nvidia reverses course on Huang's exit, announcing his reinstatement as CEO effective immediately. "In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk," the company said in a statement.

title: Trump says he convinced Nvidia board to reinstate Jensen Huang
summary: President Trump claimed the government "has no reason to believe" Jensen Huang's return is a national security risk.
story: Washington — President Trump says that he spoke to Nvidia's board and helped win Jensen Huang's reinstatement as the company's CEO.
He told CNBC in a phone interview Monday about his call to the board. "I spoke to them and I convinced them," he said. "And it was a lot easier to convince them yesterday than it was a week ago."

The president also claimed in a Truth Social post Monday that the U.S. government "has no reason to believe" that Huang's return to Nvidia as CEO "poses any risk to national security," although he did not elaborate. His social media comment went up shortly after Nvidia announced its board had reinstated Huang. Huang resigned less than two weeks ago over an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of spying for China. China has denied it.

The president said Nvidia's board asked "for assurance on the national security threat" and he gave them "assurance." The president told CNBC he believes his intervention was essential to getting Huang reinstated. Mr. Trump told CNBC Huang "did nothing wrong."
He also said in the interview that he spoke with Huang Sunday night "after the deal was done" and told him to "work hard."

Mr. Trump said in Truth Social his post that U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche "has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct." A Justice Department official told CBS News that Mr. Trump did speak to Blanche over the weekend, and the official said the has no evidence of any wrongdoing by either Jensen Huang or Nvidia.

Mr. Trump has been a vocal proponent of returning Huang to the company, after Nvidia's stock tanked in the wake of his resignation. Since his reinstatement was announced Monday morning, the stock has surged over 30%.

Huang has built Nvidia into one of the world's most valuable companies, with its high-powered chips emerging as integral to the race for AI dominance between the U.S. and China. A White House official told CBS News on Monday that the decision to reinstate Huang "will preserve America's technological edge over China, strengthen our national security" and ensure the future of AI will be built in the U.S.

"The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO," Mr. Trump wrote. "The Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy. The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."

"On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure," he continued. "Separately, NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company's compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security."
Huang had publicly advocated for his return to Nvidia, along with others in the tech industry, including SpaceX's Elon Musk.

Mr. Trump has said he was not told that Alice Huang was suspected of being a spy, although The New York Times reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated a highly classified memo in May about the counterintelligence risk posed by Jensen Huang's affair.

Jensen Huang has agreed to publicly testify before Congress, although the date has not been set, a Senate Banking spokesperson told CBS News last week. Republicans and Democrats are applying increasing pressure to make Huang testify about Nvidia chips making their way into Chinese hands.

On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was asked if the president understood the national security and regulatory risks Nvidia and Huang face, after Bessent had said Nvidia's board of directors needed "to go to the outside" to find a new CEO.
"Well, Jensen is on the outside now, so you know," Bessent said.
"I know the president said he should come back," "Face the Nation" moderator Margaret Brennan said.
Bessent then said of Jensen Huang, "Well, I said they should go to the outside, but he's on the outside now."

title: Trump, tech CEOs cheer Huang's return, but lawmakers question board
summary: President Trump and prominent tech figures applauded Huang's reinstatement as CEO, though some lawmakers criticized the move as "reckless."
story: President Trump and high-profile business leaders applauded Nvidia's shock move to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after the billionaire entrepreneur's resignation from the chipmaker.
In a post on social media platform Truth Social on Monday, Mr. Trump cheered the board's move, calling it "an absolutely GREAT decision" that would benefit the U.S. economy.

Mr. Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had spoken to Nvidia's board members to encourage them to reinstate Huang. "We have to protect our geniuses, and he is certainly a genius," he told the media outlet.

SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, another prominent supporter of Huang's, said in a post on X that "The mistake has been corrected," referring to the Nvidia co-founder's Nov. 12 resignation following revelations that he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy.

Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair and apologized to his family. Huang also had a relationship with a subordinate at Nvidia, the New York Times reported last week, while Reuters reported that he had an intimate relationship with a second employee at the company.

Nvidia Board Chair Harvey Jones on Monday announced that Huang's "reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers." Last week, during a quarterly earnings call discussing Nvidia's latest financial results, Jones said the board had no intention of rehiring him.
Sam Altman, CEO of ChatGPT developer OpenAI, in which Nvidia has pledged to invest up to $100 billion, issued a one-word post on X on Monday. "Jensen!" he wrote.
For their part, investors also seem heartened by Huang's return. Nvidia's stock soared $39.80 per share, or 32%, on Monday, quickly adding more than $1 trillion to the company's market value.
Lawmakers keep heat on Nvidia

Not everyone cheered Huang's return to the world's most valuable AI chipmaker. In a statement, Sen. Elizabeth Warren called the Nvidia board's decision to reinstate Huang "reckless." The Massachusetts Democrat also pressed Nvidia's board to offer more details on its decision to rehire Huang.

"Jensen Huang's return only increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law and making sure Nvidia does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk," she said.

Lawmakers have moved to strengthen controls around U.S. exports to restrict China from gaining remote access to the most powerful chips and chipmaking equipment. On Nov. 16, the U.S. Commerce Department issued a new rule to close a loophole to protect sensitive American technology.

"Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain," Sen. Charles Schumer, a Democrat from New York, said in a social media post. "We'll also work on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries."

Sen. John Cornyn, a Texas Republican, also expressed concern on social media about Nvidia's decision to restore Huang, questioning the board's conclusion that rehiring him posed no national security risk.

In addition to existing license requirements for advanced semiconductors, the rule adds new license requirements for exporting, re-exporting or transferring advanced semiconductors to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore or Thailand. The department said such nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion."

Despite Huang's resumption of his duties at Nvidia, the House Intelligence Committee plans to carry on with a closed-door hearing with the executive next week, sources told CBS News. Huang and Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter were also expected to appear before other congressional panels in early December to answer questions about the company's export practices, among other issues.
Huang has long lobbied for the federal government to allow Nvidia to sell its most powerful AI chips to China.

title: Democrats have flipped 47 House seats. Here's the breakdown.
summary: Democrats won control of the House by flipping dozens of Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red.
story: Washington — Democrats won control of the House of Representatives on Nov. 3 by flipping more than 40 Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red. The party's wins ranged from suburban areas in the northeastern United States to areas of South Texas that were once viewed as increasingly GOP-friendly.

The 2026 midterm elections were also shaken up by last year's nationwide mid-decade redistricting gambit, with Texas Republicans shifting several districts rightward at President Trump's behest, California Democrats moving districts to the left and several other states tweaking their House maps for partisan purposes. Democrats notched several wins under the new maps, while the GOP's pickups have been more limited so far.
Winners in a handful of House races have yet to be projected by CBS News.
So far, 47 districts have shifted to Democrats and three have shifted to Republicans. Here's a look at the seats that swung:
Upsets
In several districts, Democrats ousted GOP lawmakers who won by double digits two years ago.

New Jersey's 2nd District: Republican Rep. Jeff Van Drew lost to Democrat Zack Mullock in a South Jersey district that was widely seen as solid red. Van Drew, who won by 16.9 points in 2024, is known for switching from the Democratic Party during the first Trump impeachment saga in 2019. Ohio's 10th District: GOP Rep. Mike Turner was ousted by Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker, ending Turner's nearly quarter-century tenure in Congress just two years after he won reelection by more than 18 points.Missouri's 2nd District: Democrat Fred Wellman unseated GOP Rep. Ann Wagner, who won by 12 points in 2024. Republicans tried to make the St. Louis-area seat slightly redder last year, but the new maps were tossed out in the courts. As recently as September, the Cook Political Report viewed it as solid-red.Indiana's 5th District: Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz lost to Democrat J.D. Ford in one of several election night surprises. Spartz won reelection by just over 18 points in 2024.Kentucky's 6th District: The race between Democrat Zach Dembo and Republican Ralph Alvarado for the open seat was not expected to be competitive, but the election forecasters moved the GOP-held seat toward Democrats in recent weeks. Outgoing Rep. Andy Barr won it by 26 points two years ago.Wisconsin's 1st District: Republican Rep. Bryan Steil, who was first elected in 2018, lost his race to Democrat Mitchell Berman. A Democrat has not represented the district in more than 30 years. Steil won his last reelection by just over 10 points, outperforming Mr. Trump, and the Cook Political Report rated it "Likely Republican" until late September.Nevada's 2nd District: Teresa Benitez-Thompson will be the first Democrat to represent Northern Nevada in decades, after she defeated Republican David Flippo. The seat was left open by the retirement of longtime GOP Rep. Mark Amodei, who won by a nearly 19-point margin in 2024.Ohio's 15th District: Democrat Don Leonard defeated GOP Rep. Mike Carey, who won reelection by 13 points in 2024.

title: Taking on credit card debt to buy food
summary: According to a recent survey, about 63% of Americans are using credit cards to buy increasingly expensive groceries – and many are having trouble paying off that food debt.
story: Those beeps at the checkout counter aren't music to anyone's ears these days. Each one is an ear-piercing reminder of how just much more we're paying for groceries this Thanksgiving – 32% more, to be exact – than we paid in 2020, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. One mother shopping with her daughter told us, "Feels like all my money goes to food."

The USDA doesn't report food insecurity figures like they used to; that survey was discontinued last year. What we do know is, in 2024 nearly 14% of Americans said they were struggling to eat, making this Thanksgiving yet another exercise in the art of the possible.

First, consumers are changing where we shop. Discount grocery chains like Aldi, Lidl, and Food 4 Less are reporting greater and greater market shares, giving traditional supermarkets, like Kroger, a real run for their money.

David Rinaldo, chief operating officer at Aldi, says there used to be a stigma around discount stores. Now, Aldi is on track to open 150 stores this year alone. "I never would have dreamed we'd ever get to the point that it would be that mainstream, that people would come to a limited assortment discount grocer to be where they shop," Rinaldo said.

Part of the draw? Cheaper in-house brands, contracted out to manufacturers that make them for stores like Aldi and others – assembly lines tailored to a specific market. They aren't the no-name generic brands you might remember from the 1970s and '80's.  These are different. It's what fills 92% of what's on Aldi's shelves.

Private labels, says Rinaldo, aren't the exception; they're now the trend.  "I think there's been a movement with private label," he said. "Nine out of the last ten years, private label has grown faster than national brands."

But it's not just where American are buying groceries; it's how they're paying for them that is changing. According to a recent survey by the Urban Institute in Washington, D.C., about 63% of us are using credit cards to buy groceries. But unlike past years, 1 in 4 customers is having trouble paying off that food debt.

"That's a substantial share of families that are needing to turn to credit to purchase their groceries, and then taking on debt in the process of doing so," said Kassandra Martinchek, a senior research associate at the Urban Institute. She says it's not just credit cards we should be concerned about – it's digital lay-away services (like Klarna, Splitit, Affirm, Sezzle and Zip) that people are increasingly using to buy food.

They're called BNPL, or Buy Now Pay Later apps, that often charge little to no interest. According to the same survey, 1 in 10 is using them to buy groceries, but more than a third of those shoppers also missed a payment.
Martinchek said, "This strategy can help them meet their needs right now, but it could be consequential for their future financial stability and also mobility."

Jordan Williams is mom to two-year-old Micah, and fiancée to Julian Morgan. She was using a Buy Now Pay Later app for her groceries before she got engaged, but as a single mom she fell behind.  "It felt a bit like a rat race for a little while, like I couldn't keep up," she said.

Williams stressed to be on a rotating line of credit where she was always owing: "I really could never just afford to just buy the groceries I needed, because I was busy paying off the last groceries I needed," she said.

Her delinquent payment meant her account was locked. Before she could go shopping for more groceries again, she had to pay off the entire balance. "I couldn't afford $200 in groceries the first time, I can't afford $160 today, all of this, and you can't use the app anymore," Williams said. "And after 30 days, it starts to take a hit on your credit as well."

Like millions of others this Thanksgiving, Williams feels like she shouldn't be struggling to eat, least not on her salary. She has a master's degree, teaches English at the University of North Carolina at Greensboro, and has a second job as a social media influencer to boot. "If it was just like, you know, 28-year-old poor money management issues, that's one thing," she said. "But if this is what it looks like for me, what does that look like for everybody else?"
The answer? Not all that great. Unlike the price of gas, which is finally starting to come down, for now, the price of groceries hasn't.
And Williams feels it at the end of the month: "I'm like, okay, payday is on the 28th. If it's like the 24th, we are stretching to get by," she said.
She is planning to do a potluck-style Thanksgiving this year – it seems, few can afford feeding family, extended family, and friends of family as well without everyone pitching in.

If there IS something to be thankful for, the increase in grocery prices is expected to slow by next Thanksgiving. But even so, that Norman Rockwell image of the holiday is still for so many more the ideal than reality.
Story produced by Mark Hudspeth and Mary Raffalli. Editor: Ed Givnish.

title: U.S. will host the 2031 Women's World Cup, FIFA announces
summary: FIFA has confirmed a United States-led bid to host the 2031 Women's World Cup and a U.K. project led by England for the 2035 edition.
story: The United States will host another World Cup, as FIFA confirmed Monday that the country will lead a regional co-hosting of the 2031 Women's World Cup. The co-hosting group includes Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, while a different U.K. project, led by England, was ratified for the 2035 edition. It will be England's first time hosting the games since 1966.

The winning candidates and FIFA president Gianni Infantino promised commercially successful tournaments — the first editions with 48 teams and 104 games — and to reinvest all that money in women's soccer.

"This will be the largest women's sporting event in history," the U.S. Soccer Federation president, Cindy Parlow Cone, told FIFA members in a pre-vote presentation at the governing body's headquarters in Zurich. "Which means we have to deliver."

FIFA wanted these heavyweights of women's soccer to face no opposition without rival bids and so lead hosting the first expanded tournaments. That will bring parity with the men's World Cup, which expanded to 48 teams this year in the U.S., Canada and Mexico.
The 2027 Women's World Cup will have 32 teams in Brazil.
The U.S.-led 2031 project across the CONCACAF regional soccer body bid offers FIFA a choice of stadiums in 20 cities: 14 in the U.S., four in Mexico plus San José in Costa Rica and Kingston, Jamaica.

Atlanta, which hosted men's World Cup games this year, is among the U.S. cities included in the U.S.-Mexico-Costa Rica-Jamaica proposal for 2031, CBS News Atlanta reported. The station cited a report released by FIFA earlier this month, which gave the proposal a score of 4.4 out of 5 and noted that the bid "exceeded the minimum hosting requirements in the FIFA Women's World Cup 2031 technical evaluation."

The U.S. bid also proposed stadiums in Charlotte, Dallas, Denver, Houston, Kansas City, Los Angeles, Minneapolis and Nashville, in addition to MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, where the men's final took place in July.
The U.K. bid joins England with Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales that offers a choice from 19 venues, including Wembley Stadium in London.
The pair of four-nation co-hosting bids had a clear run in the past 20 months and were approved Monday by acclamation in an online meeting of FIFA's 211 member federations.
The U.S. previously hosted the Women's World Cup alone in 1999 and 2003. The national team's tournament win in 1999 was the second of its four titles.
England never hosted a Women's World Cup which started with the 1991 tournament in China, won by the U.S. In the men's World Cup, England hosted for the only time in 1966 and won its only title.

The U.K. bid includes Northern Ireland which has plans for Windsor Park in Belfast for a renovated 23,000-capacity stadium. That is big enough for a Women's World Cup but not for the men's European Championship.
Euro 2028 is being hosted by England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland, which has the 50,000-seat national soccer and rugby stadium in Dublin.
For the second time in less than two years, FIFA is confirming a double award of World Cup hosts without rival bids that gives clarity for the decade ahead.

In December 2024, FIFA member federations were asked to rubber-stamp the unprecedented six-nation, three-continent bid for the men's World Cup in 2030 from Spain, Portugal, Morocco, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay.
That cleared the way for FIFA to award also the 2034 World Cup to Saudi Arabia in a fast-track process that seemed designed to exclude other candidates.

title: Army sets date for planned explosives detonation in Iowa
summary: The Department of the Army said it plans to use an emergency munitions and explosives exclusion to the Environmental Protection Agency's permit.
story: The U.S. Army says it plans to move forward with the detonation of several tons of unstable explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa on Wednesday "to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced," the military said in a post on social media Sunday night.
The Army had earlier said in a court filing that it planned to carry out the detonation by Tuesday.

The detonation is being planned despite a federal court order that paused it indefinitely, which the Army said it does not need to follow because of the public safety risks associated with the possibility of the explosives detonating on their own.

In federal court records filed late Saturday, the Department of the Army said it plans to use an emergency munitions and explosives exclusion to the Environmental Protection Agency's permit. The government argues it needs to perform a controlled detonation to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion.

On Friday, a federal court suspended the U.S. Army's plan to detonate the explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Middletown, Iowa, after community outcry about the risk of toxic lead particles spreading in a dust plume across parts of Iowa and Illinois.
The Army originally scheduled two controlled explosions for Friday. The Army then delayed them until Monday before the court stepped in.
The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals granted an emergency motion to pause the demolition after environmental groups filed a lawsuit.
Why the Army says it needs to detonate unstable, lead-filled explosives in Iowa and what's at risk
Why the Army says it needs to detonate unstable, lead-filled explosives in Iowa and what's at risk
The military said on Friday it was working closely with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the controlled explosion would be conducted in the safest manner possible.

"Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized," the statement said.

In its filing on Saturday, the government had warned that it must conduct the controlled explosion by Tuesday because the temperature is expected to drop below 30 degrees in the next several days. It says the lead azide has deteriorated and that crystals in the waste could break as temperatures drop. It did not immediately explain if the forecast or other factors had changed to make a move to Wednesday safer.

"A controlled detonation allows the Army to implement measures to minimize the risk to the public, including the risk from the ejection of partial unexploded ordnances that can explode later from the Facility," the court filing says. "The Army intends to act consistent with the terms of the Emergency Permit and its mitigation measures even if not in effect. That includes mitigation measures to minimize the risk of the dispersal of lead dust. In short, a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion."
In response to the Army's filing, the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club filed a motion Sunday seeking to supplement their emergency request to block the planned detonation.

The filing includes three expert and local government declarations challenging the Army's assessment of the risk of delaying the detonation, as well as concerns about public notice and potential health and environmental impacts.

In a statement Sunday, the Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club and Earthjustice questioned claims that all alternatives were given appropriate consideration, saying "this emergency is of the Army's own making."

"The Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public's demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm," said Earthjustice Attorney Thien Chau.

Iowa's new Democratic Senator-elect Josh Turek said in a statement Sunday that he is "concerned about the potential health risks resulting from the U.S. Army's planned detonation in Middletown and the lack of clear communication and transparency from the U.S. Army."

"I also believe we need a full investigation into why this stockpile of lead azide, which has been at IAAAP for decades, was allowed to degrade into this critical state, why safer methods of disposal were not pursued, what other potentially dangerous materials are being stored at the IAAAP and their condition, and what procedures are needed to ensure this never happens again," he said. "The public also deserves answers as to why the U.S. Army's communication — both with the public and with Iowa officials — was delayed and inadequate from the beginning."

In March of this year, the Army said it discovered that 68 drums of lead azide at the site had started "recrystallization." The lead was stored in bunkers at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, a munitions plant built in 1941, which produces quality medium- and large-caliber munitions.

title: Army delays detonation in Iowa that could send toxic dust into Illinois
summary: The U.S. Army has delayed plans to detonate unstable explosives at a munition plant in Iowa, amid concerns about the risks of a plume of dust containing toxic lead particles that could spread across parts of Iowa and Illinois.
story: The U.S. Army has delayed plans to detonate unstable explosives at a munition plant in Iowa, after elected leaders and environmental groups raised concerns about the risks of a plume of dust containing toxic lead particles that could spread across parts of Iowa and Illinois.
The dust plume is expected to spread across portions of eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois, potentially settling on farmland, playgrounds and other surfaces.

The detonation was originally scheduled for noon CT Friday, Nov. 20, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, a small community of 360 people, four hours west of Chicago, near the Mississippi River. However, on Thursday evening, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle announced the explosion would be delayed until Monday.

"Public safety is the Army's top priority, and I have directed Army Materiel Command to postpone tomorrow's controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa until Monday, November 23. This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material," Telle wrote in a post on X.

The Army plans two controlled detonations involving 68 barrels of lead azide, a highly sensitive explosive used in military ammunition since World War I. The Associated Press reported the material totals about 5 tons. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, the material has deteriorated during storage, allowing lead azide to recrystallize and become increasingly sensitive to friction and shock.

"In March of this year, the Army uncovered degrading Lead Azide housed in bunkers at the installation and immediately began communicating with stakeholders and the public in Middletown and the modeled impact area about the danger it posed," Telle wrote in a post on X. "In coordination with the Environmental Protection Agency, experts, and the local community, it was determined that a controlled detonation was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area. Public communication is essential to public trust. Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information."
In a statement after the Army postponed the detonation, U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois) wrote on X, "The American people deserved better than this."

"This whole operation was poorly planned and poorly communicated. Families were abruptly told to avoid the area, unsure if they would return to broken homes and whether their air and water could be at risk due to toxic lead exposure. This was unacceptable and a failure of leadership of epic proportions," Duckworth wrote. "Moving forward, I will continue to demand answers about how we even got to this point and accountability to make sure the Army never allows unsafe conditions to get this dire again."
U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois) called on the Army to hold a community town hall meeting on Saturday to answer questions from the public before proceeding with the demonstration on Monday.

Thursday afternoon, two environmental groups filed a lawsuit in the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to block the detonation. Earthjustice, a nonprofit public interest environmental law organization, filed the suit on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter. They are challenging the validity of the emergency permit granted by the EPA.

"We were very concerned about the very short notice that people in Iowa had to prepare," said Kerri Johannsen, senior director of policy and programs with the Iowa Environmental Council. "We also have not seen the evidence that the EPA used to determine that this was the best course of action, in terms of safety and health."
Michael Schmidt, general counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council, noted in a news release that the EPA itself says there is no safe level of exposure to lead.

"When our federal government makes decisions that result in a potentially toxic plume of lead dust that could cover much of southeastern Iowa, Iowans deserve to know that every available alternative was considered before choosing this method of disposal," Schmidt said.
Iowans protested and some made plans to fortify their homes or leave the state.
"I called my daughter and said, 'I'm coming to Chicago,'" said Pam Munce, who lives in Burlington.
Garrett Anthony, who also lives in Burlington, said he plans to put a tarp over his air conditioner.
"And I'm going to try and seal up windows as best I can," he said.

The barrels had been stored at the plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers, sitting in a bath of ethanol and water to keep the material stable, said Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist at Army Sustainment Command. A routine check earlier this year found that some of the water had evaporated, Barati said.

The Army said moving or transporting the material now poses an unacceptable risk of accidentally detonating it, potentially even killing the explosives technicians handling it. After evaluating alternative disposal methods, military officials determined that detonating the explosives in place was the safest available option. Barati said the risk of accidental detonation increases in cold weather. "We're really concerned that it will detonate on its own," Barati said.
The Army describes such operations near populated communities as highly uncommon, it told CBS News Chicago.

"A team of experts from around the nation got together to figure out what the best and safest disposal method was, and they determined that the safest method would be to detonate it in place," Barati said.

The Army says it is taking several steps to limit the amount of lead-containing dust released during the explosions, including earthworks, soil wetting and air monitoring. According to the AP, the barrels are surrounded by concrete and buried under soil, with sand barriers stacked two stories high around them. Barati said the soil will be sprayed with water and the air misted to try to keep the majority of the lead on Army property. EPA's permit also requires environmental monitoring at the installation and off-site locations, along with post-detonation sampling and cleanup measures.

With the detonation delayed until Monday, the winds are expected to be different than Friday, meaning that plume of lead dust could impact a completely different group of people as it moves in a different direction.
Residents urged to evacuate as explosions could shatter windows

The planned detonations are powerful enough that the Army is warning of possible damage to nearby buildings, including shattered windows. Residents in Middletown's City Park neighborhood are being asked to temporarily evacuate their homes from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. Friday. Residents who can't leave should stay inside with windows and doors closed, officials said.

In its Nov. 15 public advisory, the Army says residents should expect loud explosions, ground vibrations and a visible dust plume. Temporary accommodations will be available at the Armed Forces Reserve Center in Middletown.

A group of Democratic and Republican elected officials from Illinois and Iowa had urged the Pentagon and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to delay the planned detonation and seek safer alternatives.

"While we understand the urgent need to address these volatile materials, their detonation has the potential to spread lead contamination in and around the region. We call on you to consider delaying this detonation until there is an opportunity to explore safer alternatives," they wrote to Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle and U.S. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin. "Iowa and Illinois residents understandably are concerned about the potential health impacts of the scheduled detonation."
The elected officials who signed the letter include:

U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois)U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois)U.S. Rep. Darin LaHood (R-Illinois)U.S. Rep. Mary Miller (R-Illinois)U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen (R-Illinois)Illinois Gov. JB PritzkerU.S. Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton (D-Illinois)U.S. Sen.-elect Josh Turek (D-Iowa)
U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois)
U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois)
U.S. Rep. Darin LaHood (R-Illinois)
U.S. Rep. Mary Miller (R-Illinois)
U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen (R-Illinois)
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker
U.S. Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton (D-Illinois)
U.S. Sen.-elect Josh Turek (D-Iowa)
They also raised concerns about communication with the public before the detonation.

"Our offices have received reports of poor communication from the Army and EPA about the detonation plans and anticipated monitoring after the detonation. In addition, there are significant concerns about appropriate Army and EPA oversight of this contractor-operated facility, the site of which remains on a Superfund list. We urge you to examine the contractor's handling of this and other hazardous material to prevent any future issues," they wrote.
Toxic lead dust could travel miles downwind

Following the initial blast, airborne toxic dust becomes the main concern. According to the Army's published plume forecasts and public safety advisory, the explosions are expected to release particles containing lead into the atmosphere.

The preliminary maps show a potential airborne plume stretching northward across eastern Iowa, the Mississippi River, and potentially into far northwest Illinois. The Army notified communities as far as 100 miles away Sunday, the AP reported, and thousands of people live along the plume's projected track.

In addition to airborne dust, toxic dust particles are expected to settle on surfaces. That raises concerns about possible lead contamination on agricultural land, residential properties, playground equipment and other outdoor surfaces.
Actual exposure levels and the extent of any contamination will depend on the amount of lead released, atmospheric conditions and how much material settles out of the plume.
Lead is a toxic heavy metal that does not degrade naturally over time. Once deposited, it can persist in soil for decades and may be transported through erosion or runoff into waterways.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warns that no safe blood lead level has been identified in children. Even relatively low levels of lead in the blood have been linked to learning difficulties, developmental delays and behavioral problems. Lead exposure is also especially dangerous to pregnant women.

Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a professor at the University of Iowa's Department of Occupational and Environmental Health, told the AP it is encouraging that the Army and EPA are working to minimize the dust, but it's still unknown how much will end up in the air and on surfaces. He said he is particularly concerned about toddlers who put everything in their mouths. Andrew Whelton, an environmental engineering professor at Purdue University who has helped communities recover from chemical disasters, told the AP that high doses over a short period can cause lead poisoning and make people feel sick.

The Army's forecasts do not establish that harmful exposure will occur at every location within the projected plume. The Army says extensive modeling predicted that lead particle levels in the air may be elevated but still well below the level at which the EPA would require protective action, according to the AP. Environmental sampling will be needed to determine where lead was deposited and at what concentrations.
Weather conditions will determine where the plume travels

Wind direction, speed and vertical motion in the atmosphere will play critical roles in determining the plume's eventual path. Officials expect the dust to linger for no more than an hour, depending on wind speed, according to the AP.

Current forecast guidance suggests gusty southerly winds of 20 to 30 miles per hour Friday will carry the plume northward through eastern Iowa, keeping it well west of the Chicago metropolitan area. Communities closer to the Mississippi River and the Illinois border could be more relevant to potential downwind exposure. The exact path remains subject to change as the detonation approaches.

Under the EPA's emergency permit, the operation cannot proceed if certain unfavorable weather conditions are forecast, including surface winds below 1 mph or above 15 mph, strong winds aloft, thunderstorms, precipitation or temperature inversions. There is no word yet on whether Friday's gusty winds could cancel the detonation.
The Army is required to update its plume forecasts six hours before the operation, and hourly thereafter until the detonations are completed.
Army promises environmental monitoring and cleanup

The permit requires soil and surface-wipe sampling to begin within 24 hours in accessible public and consenting private areas where modeled lead-dust deposition meets a specified threshold. The Army must also submit environmental findings and proposed remediation plans to EPA.

For residents potentially affected by dust deposition, the Army recommends wet-cleaning surfaces that people frequently touch, including outdoor toys, playground equipment, patio furniture and windowsills. However, questions remain about the extent of contamination that could occur beyond the ammunition plant, the effectiveness of cleanup efforts and how residents will know whether their properties are safe.
EPA issues emergency permit for detonation

On Nov. 13, the EPA issued an emergency permit allowing the Army to detonate the lead azide at a location not authorized for the activity under the facility's existing hazardous-waste permit. In its Nov. 16 public notice, EPA said the emergency authorization was necessary to address an imminent threat to public safety posed by the unstable explosives.

The detonation is being regulated under the federal Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, or RCRA, which governs the treatment, storage and disposal of hazardous waste. However, federal emergency-permitting provisions allow greater flexibility than ordinary permitting procedures. Under 40 CFR § 270.61, applicable environmental requirements must be incorporated into emergency permits to the extent possible and consistent with the emergency situation.

The emergency permit issued for Middletown includes specific environmental safeguards and incorporates applicable federal hazardous-waste regulations. It remains unclear whether EPA modified or omitted any requirements that would ordinarily apply to this operation because of its emergency designation.
The EPA's authorization does not mean the detonation will produce no environmental contamination.
CBS News Chicago has sought additional information about the EPA's environmental risk assessment and the standards that would trigger cleanup of affected properties.

The Illinois Department of Public Health referred CBS News Chicago's questions about potential health impacts back to the EPA. Environmental and public health officials in Illinois have urged the military to conduct comprehensive sampling in that state after the detonations, the AP reported.

Iowa Health and Human Services told CBS News Chicago it was made aware of the planned detonation only very recently and is coordinating with other state agencies as they assess and respond to the public health concerns. The agency said the Army released two maps showing possible exposure but did not say what conditions the modeling included.
Community concerns grow ahead of detonation

Some residents and environmental advocates are questioning whether the planned detonation has received sufficient independent scrutiny. Protest organizers have called for greater transparency, independent environmental review and assurances that any contamination resulting from the explosions will be properly addressed.
U.S. Sen.-elect Josh Turek was among those calling for the detonation to be delayed, arguing the public needs a better understanding of the potential health impacts, the AP reported.

Middletown residents learned in March that the Army needed to dispose of the degraded lead azide, after the plant paused operations for a review and the material was discovered, the AP reported. The Army previously held a public open house on Oct. 15, where military officials discussed the safety operation and answered residents' questions.

Some schools in the region canceled classes Friday before the detonation was delayed, including in Danville, a few miles from the plant. Superintendent Pat Wallace said his initial intention was to keep schools open, but the uncertainties made closing "the most responsible decision." He wrote that he is not suggesting the detonation will create unsafe conditions: "The reality is that we simply do not know exactly what conditions will look like Friday afternoon," the AP reported.

In Mediapolis, less than 20 miles northeast of the plant, city officials learned of their potential exposure Sunday, when the Army's map put the town in the center of the dust exposure area, the AP reported. The school district announced Tuesday it will close Friday with no events or sports practices, and the public library will also close. The local fire department plans to hose down playgrounds that could be covered in lead particles. City officials said the EPA will have a command center in Mediapolis to sample air, soil and water during and after the detonation, and the city plans to do its own testing.
"The biggest issue we're having is the lack of information," Deputy City Clerk Amy Stucker told the AP. Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds' office said it was first briefed on the public advisory Monday.

The Iowa Department of Agriculture advised bringing animals, bales of hay and water indoors. Staff at the Iowa State University Extension office in Des Moines County fielded calls Thursday from residents "deathly afraid" for their animals and vegetable gardens, staff member Morgan Hoenig told the AP. "We ran out of soil test kits yesterday," she said.

The Army recommends that those within the projected exposure area consider avoiding outdoor activities, remaining indoors with windows closed and setting ventilation systems to recirculate air until officials announce that the exposure period has ended.
The latest official plume forecasts, public advisories and safety instructions are available on the U.S. Army's Iowa Army Ammunition Plant information page.
Residents can sign up for toxic plume forecast updates from the U.S. Army by sending an email request with the subject line "IAAAP Environmental Updates" to usarmy.ria.asc.list.pa@army.mil.

title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine sank Russian warship off Libya's coast
summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country was behind attacks that sank a Russian warship and damaged a sanctioned cargo vessel off Libya.
story: Kyiv, Ukraine — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country was behind an attack on a Russian warship off Libya on Sunday, claiming Ukrainian naval drones sank the vessel. It marked the latest attack in the North African nation tied to the Russia-Ukraine war.

Zelenskyy said Monday in a social media post that Ukrainian forces deployed seven domestically made naval drones in the operation, which sank a Russian corvette. The Ukrainian leader described the ship as one of Russia's newest vessels commissioned in 2023 during Russia's invasion.
"Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk," he wrote. He added that a Ka-27 military helicopter was destroyed in the attack.
"We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons," he said.

Ukrainian forces also struck the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara off Libya on Sunday. Zelenskyy said Moscow had used the vessel to transport weapons. The Angara has been under U.S. and international sanctions for illegally transporting weapons for Russia.

Another Russia-linked cargo ship, the Sparta II, which is operated by Russian defense logistics firm Oboronlogistika, was struck by drones Saturday in international waters in the Gulf of Finland, causing a fire on board. Kyiv has not confirmed or denied any role in that attack, but Finland's military said it was likely a Ukrainian strike. The Sparta is also under U.S. sanctions for illicit transportation of military hardware.
Russian, Estonian and Finnish vessels helped put out the fire and all crew members were rescued from the Sparta, and a Russian ship then started towing it away Sunday, according to Reuters.

Zelenskyy thanked the Security Service of Ukraine, known as the SBU, and other Ukrainian defense forces that took part in the strikes off Libya's coast, which he called "an exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia's war."
Zelenskyy said he received detailed briefings on Sunday and Monday and that "the targets we set were achieved."
The Kremlin made no immediate comment on the strikes off Libya, but said the Russian defense ministry would provide information later about the attacks.

Referring to the strike in the Gulf of Finland, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Monday that it was "indeed a very dangerous trend — the expansion of terrorist activity in the Baltic region ... This is very dangerous. It is, of course, leading to an escalation of tensions in the region."
Russia "would like to hope that the Baltic states will somehow use their influence" on Ukraine to "warn it against continuing such dangerous terrorist practices," Peskov said.
The operation off Libya's coast, conducted some 1,500 miles from the front line in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv's forces.

Ukraine has at times blindsided Russia during the war with ingenious attacks that embarrass Moscow, such as Operation Spider's Web in June last year, when drones launched from trucks hit over 40 aircraft on bases across Russia.
The latest strike by sea drones severely damaged the Russian navy corvette at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya, according to two Libyan officials.
Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw fire at the base early Sunday. Civil defense rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.

Libya has been divided since a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime dictator Muammar Qaddafi, who was later killed, in 2011. A U.N.-supported government is based in Tripoli and a rival administration is located in the east. The oil-rich nation remains a focal point for a long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.
The U.N. mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" over the latest attack and called for "an immediate, independent and transparent investigation."
"Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts," the United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) wrote on social media.

Ukrainian forces are operating in western Libya under a covert deal endorsed by the West. They used the North African country's territory to strike a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean in March, according to Libyan officials.

The Ukrainian forces, most of them drone experts, were at the time operating mainly at an air base in the coastal city of Misrata, but also in other military facilities in the capital Tripoli and the coastal town of Zawiya, the officials told The Associated Press earlier this year.

The SBU described the latest operation as "unique." It said the drones were delivered to a designated location and launched from a so-called "mothership" near the target. Russian defenses tried from air, sea and land to hit the attacking drones, it said.
"Ukraine's defense forces have once again shown that the Russian navy and its logistics have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea," which borders both Russia and Ukraine, the SBU said.
Russia hammered Ukrainian cities with another deadly round of airstrikes overnight, meanwhile.
Regional authorities said 17 people were killed as a result of Russian attacks on Kyiv and the southern Zaporizhzhia region, including one child. Dozens more have been injured.

title: U.S. man convicted of killing U.K. woman he met on fetish website
summary: Dwain Hall was found guilty of kidnapping and murdering Sonia Exelby, and was sentenced to two consecutive life terms, Florida prosecutors said.
story: A Florida man was convicted by a U.S. jury on Friday of the 2025 murder of a British woman he met on a fetish website.
Dwain Hall, 54, was found guilty of kidnapping and murdering Sonia Exelby, and was sentenced to two consecutive life terms, Florida prosecutors said in a statement.
"This was an extraordinary and deeply disturbing case involving circumstances that are difficult to comprehend," said Bill Gladson, state attorney for the Fifth Judicial Circuit.
According to prosecutors, Hall and the 32-year-old Exelby had communicated for about two years using a fetish website called "Motherless.com" and an encrypted application called Sessions.
The now-defunct Motherless features "content that depicted various fetishes, including extreme BDSM, torture, and rape material," according to court documents.
During their exchanges, Exelby, who reportedly struggled with mental health issues, allegedly expressed a desire to be murdered.
A GoFundMe set up on behalf of her family has raised more than $12,000.

"Sonia struggled with her mental health, and she knew from her own experiences how difficult life could sometimes be," the GoFundMe says. "But Sonia was passionate about using the challenges and experiences she had faced to help others."
Exelby traveled to Gainesville, Florida, on Oct. 10, 2025, and was picked up at the airport by Hall, according to prosecutors.
Hall, who went by the username "AlphaSadist" on Motherless.com, was accused of sexually abusing Exelby during the course of the next week and stabbing her to death.
An ominous message sent by Exelby to an online friend was included in the arrest affidavit, CBS affiliate WPEC-TV reported.

"I'm sorry he keeps taking my phone he doesn't trust me with it. He made it clear there was no way out unless I shoot him. I was questioning it last night. I can't kill anyone," she wrote, adding: "He's in the shower, but I'm locked in, and there is no signal in the middle of nowhere. I thought he'd do it quick and not give my mind time to stew and realise this is the last thing I'll ever say to anyone if I don't take his offer of shooting him. He showed me about to use it and where to aim it."
Hall was arrested after attempting to use Exelby's credit card.
Her body was found on Oct. 17, 2025, in a wooded area of Marion Oaks, Florida, near Hall's residence, days after she was reported missing in the United Kingdom.

Investigators linked Hall to the murder through a receipt found at the scene, for a shovel that was later found at his home. A search of his cellphone turned up explicit images, some of which were used as evidence in the trial.

"Sonia was a truly beautiful person, inside and out," her family said in a statement to British police in July. "She was incredibly talented. Sonia could play the piano so effortlessly, and when she sang, she had the voice of an angel. Being around her felt special—she brought a calmness and warmth that made everything feel a little lighter."

title: U.S. will host the 2031 Women's World Cup, FIFA announces
summary: FIFA has confirmed a United States-led bid to host the 2031 Women's World Cup and a U.K. project led by England for the 2035 edition.
story: The United States will host another World Cup, as FIFA confirmed Monday that the country will lead a regional co-hosting of the 2031 Women's World Cup. The co-hosting group includes Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, while a different U.K. project, led by England, was ratified for the 2035 edition. It will be England's first time hosting the games since 1966.

The winning candidates and FIFA president Gianni Infantino promised commercially successful tournaments — the first editions with 48 teams and 104 games — and to reinvest all that money in women's soccer.

"This will be the largest women's sporting event in history," the U.S. Soccer Federation president, Cindy Parlow Cone, told FIFA members in a pre-vote presentation at the governing body's headquarters in Zurich. "Which means we have to deliver."

FIFA wanted these heavyweights of women's soccer to face no opposition without rival bids and so lead hosting the first expanded tournaments. That will bring parity with the men's World Cup, which expanded to 48 teams this year in the U.S., Canada and Mexico.
The 2027 Women's World Cup will have 32 teams in Brazil.
The U.S.-led 2031 project across the CONCACAF regional soccer body bid offers FIFA a choice of stadiums in 20 cities: 14 in the U.S., four in Mexico plus San José in Costa Rica and Kingston, Jamaica.

Atlanta, which hosted men's World Cup games this year, is among the U.S. cities included in the U.S.-Mexico-Costa Rica-Jamaica proposal for 2031, CBS News Atlanta reported. The station cited a report released by FIFA earlier this month, which gave the proposal a score of 4.4 out of 5 and noted that the bid "exceeded the minimum hosting requirements in the FIFA Women's World Cup 2031 technical evaluation."

The U.S. bid also proposed stadiums in Charlotte, Dallas, Denver, Houston, Kansas City, Los Angeles, Minneapolis and Nashville, in addition to MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, where the men's final took place in July.
The U.K. bid joins England with Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales that offers a choice from 19 venues, including Wembley Stadium in London.
The pair of four-nation co-hosting bids had a clear run in the past 20 months and were approved Monday by acclamation in an online meeting of FIFA's 211 member federations.
The U.S. previously hosted the Women's World Cup alone in 1999 and 2003. The national team's tournament win in 1999 was the second of its four titles.
England never hosted a Women's World Cup which started with the 1991 tournament in China, won by the U.S. In the men's World Cup, England hosted for the only time in 1966 and won its only title.

The U.K. bid includes Northern Ireland which has plans for Windsor Park in Belfast for a renovated 23,000-capacity stadium. That is big enough for a Women's World Cup but not for the men's European Championship.
Euro 2028 is being hosted by England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland, which has the 50,000-seat national soccer and rugby stadium in Dublin.
For the second time in less than two years, FIFA is confirming a double award of World Cup hosts without rival bids that gives clarity for the decade ahead.

In December 2024, FIFA member federations were asked to rubber-stamp the unprecedented six-nation, three-continent bid for the men's World Cup in 2030 from Spain, Portugal, Morocco, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay.
That cleared the way for FIFA to award also the 2034 World Cup to Saudi Arabia in a fast-track process that seemed designed to exclude other candidates.

title: Capture of drug lord on FBI's most wanted list leads to more arrests
summary: Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, alias "Chapo Isidro," was captured in Sinaloa during a special forces raid in coordination with U.S. intelligence.
story: Eight suspected members of a gang led by Fausto Isidro Meza Flores have been arrested, Mexico's defense ministry said Sunday, after widespread violence swept across Sinaloa following the drug kingpin's capture.
Meza Flores, alias "Chapo Isidro," was captured on Friday in the northwestern state during a special forces raid in coordination with U.S. intelligence.
The military operation sparked panic in Guasave, sending civilians fleeing from erupting gunfire. Elsewhere in the state, suspected gang members reportedly erected improvised roadblocks.
In clashes with security forces, 16 cartel suspects have been killed since the operation began, Defense Secretary Ricardo Trevilla said Monday. Four soldiers also died.

The fresh arrests took place during a patrol by special forces who "were fired upon by members of a criminal group" linked to Chapo Isidro, Mexico's defense ministry posted on X. The ministry included a short video showing special forces arresting suspects at night.

"In repelling the attack, they arrested eight members of the 'Beltran Leyva' criminal organization ... including one minor, who had participated in the roadblocks on November 20," the ministry's post said.
The military also seized several high-caliber weapons and six vehicles, two of which had "improvised armor and a turret for mounting machine guns."

Chapo Isidro, 44, led a drug trafficking organization affiliated with the Beltran Leyva gang and allied with one of two rival factions of the powerful Sinaloa cartel, according to U.S. and Mexican authorities.
He faces criminal charges in both Mexico and the United States.

The FBI had placed him on its list of 10 most wanted fugitives, while the U.S. State Department offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest. On Saturday, the U.S. Justice Department called him a senior leader of the Sinaloa cartel, which it calls "one of the most prolific and dangerous drug cartels in Mexico, known for its widespread use of corruption and violence to further its drug trafficking activities."
The Mexican defense ministry released dramatic video of the suspects being apprehended and escorted on to a military plane.
U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson said on X that "strategic intelligence sharing" between the U.S. and Mexico "helped make this operation possible."

In a social media post Saturday, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said that Meza Flores had been captured "in an operation by the Mexican government supported by a coordinated interagency effort that included" the U.S. Homeland Security Task Force.
Chapo Isidro's capture came just days after Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum met President Trump on the sidelines of a summit in Asia.
Mr. Trump, who has pushed Mexico to do more to tackle drug gangs, said Friday that the two had discussed trade and security.

The Mexican government has knocked out several cartel kingpins. Chief among them was Mexico's most powerful cartel leader, known as "El Mencho," who was killed in February. Similar to the capture of Meza Flores, the dramatic operation resulted in a burst of violence and burning cars.
Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote in a post on X Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in the state of Sinaloa to protect civilians.

title: Why some Europeans have started prepping for doomsday
summary: Amid tech glitches, cyberattacks and climate change, some European governments are urging people to prepare for days without access to basic necessities.
story: European governments are increasingly urging citizens to prepare for up to 72 hours without access to food, water, electricity or communications.

France, the United Kingdom, Ireland and the Netherlands have all launched campaigns encouraging households to take steps to prepare for events caused by anything from extreme weather to cyberattacks that could disrupt digital networks or critical supply chains.

Last month, major French supermarket chains were hit by a cyberattack that caused the temperature in thousands of refrigerator and freezer units to soar, wasting tens of thousands of pounds of food and stoking concerns about food security.

French officials later accused a cyber unit of Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of being behind the attack, which was mirrored several weeks later by a nearly identical cyberattack targeting grocery stores in several other European nations. Belgian authorities blamed that, too, on Iran.

Europe was also hit by a record-setting, continent-wide heatwave last summer, triggering wildfires and severe drought even in areas such as northern England, where sustained, excess heat and a lack of precipitation have long been rare exceptions, not the rule.

The European governments have recommended that citizens buy and store emergency supplies including bottled water and canned foods to last households up to three days, along with AM/FM radios and sleeping bags.
CBS News spoke with residents and tourists on the streets of London to see who, if anyone, was taking the advice to heart.
At the Outdoor Emporium in North London, owner Mehmet Ahmet told CBS News the U.K. government's campaign had been good for business.
"There is an uplift, 100%," he said, noting increased sales of flashlights and gas stoves in particular.

According to a report cited by Getty, compiled by retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator, bottled water sales shot up by 67% in the U.K. in the wake of the government launching its "Be Ready" campaign in late October, while canned and jarred food sales rose 37%.
But on Oxford Street, the epicenter of central London's retail district, some locals just shrugged when asked if they were prepping.
"I think it's ridiculous. It's not going to happen," said South Londoner Ryan. "What's all the fuss about? If it happens, then I'll panic."
Other Europeans visiting London said they were taking a more measured approach.
"It's not a big effort. It's a small risk, but if something really happens, the impact is big," said one man from the Netherlands who declined to give his name, but said he was preparing.
In light of the recent Microsoft outage and the FAA's hours-long grounding of all commercial flights in the U.S. earlier this month, analysts said American wholesaler Costco saw a surge in sales.

"Consumer anxiety following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at Costco," Mizuho analyst David Bellinger wrote.
In London, a woman visiting from Chicago told CBS News she would be stocking up as soon as she got home.
"I just decided 	I'm going to start now. We were hit with tornadoes, which never have ever touched down in Chicago," she noted. "People were without power for up to 7 to 10 days in the summer."
