title: Don Toliver concert in U.K. evacuated due to mystery substance
summary: Some 12,000 fans of American rapper Don Toliver had to evacuate his concert in Manchester, England, after a noxious substance spread through the arena.
story: More than 12,000 people were evacuated from an arena in northern England Sunday night after the crowd at American rapper Don Toliver's concert suddenly started screaming, choking and coughing when a powerful smell spread through the venue.
Police said the Co-op Live arena in Manchester was evacuated at about 10 p.m. (5 p.m. Eastern).
There's been speculation online that the mysterious substance that spread through the air in the arena was tear gas, but authorities have not confirmed that.
Don Toliver, who is set to end a world tour with a Tuesday night show in London, left the stage in Manchester and police declared it a major incident.
One person was hospitalized and dozens were assessed for eye and respiratory symptoms according to the local ambulance service.
The arena was being fully decontaminated as a precaution, the emergency medical service said.
Ben Stevenson told the Manchester Evening News newspaper that he was in the audience standing section when he "started coughing and (my) eyes were kind of itchy."

He said the lights came on as Toliver left the stage, but that everyone remained in the venue for almost an hour before an announcement asking people to make their way out was heard over the loudspeaker.
"We will now begin to fully understand what this substance was and how this incident came about," Police Assistant Chief Constable Steph Parker told reporters.
The venue opened in 2024 and is only about 2 miles from the Manchester Arena, where 22 people were killed in 2017 by a suicide bomber who blew himself up during an Ariana Grande concert.

title: Search on for lioness seen roaming Istanbul's outskirts
summary: Police and animal welfare teams in Istanbul are searching for a lioness seen prowling the city's outskirts, Turkish officials say.
story: Istanbul — Police and animal welfare teams in Istanbul are searching for a lioness seen prowling the city's outskirts, Turkish officials said Monday.

A resident spotted the animal Sunday evening in Uskumrukoy, an upscale neighborhood on the northern edge of Istanbul's European side, surrounded by forests. The lioness was later captured on security camera footage.
"The location of the lion has been identified, and the necessary care is being taken to capture it alive," the Istanbul governor's office said in a statement posted on social media.

Grainy images published by the Demiroren News Agency showed the lioness walking through a grassy area. It was unclear where the animal came from, though some media reports suggested it had escaped from a nearby home. The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office said it launched an investigation focused on identifying its owner.

The National Parks Directorate said specialist veterinarians and teams equipped with thermal imaging cameras were assisting in the search, which was focused on the wooded area. A drone was being used as well, the Anadolu state news agency reported.
Local resident Arda Koc said he saw the lioness after joining the search.

"I took my car and went out for a drive hoping to see it," he said in comments reported by the Cumhuriyet newspaper. "While I was driving, it suddenly jumped out in front of me. At first I was scared. After that, I immediately notified the gendarmerie (police)."
Residents were warned of the danger, and police were stationed on roads leading into and out of the neighborhood.

The search sparked numerous memes on social media, French news agency AFP noted, including one widely shared image showing a lioness sitting outside a gate with the logo of Besiktas FC, one of Istanbul's three major football clubs (soccer teams).

"The lion being sought is under our protection ... it will be tamed and handed over on Monday evening," read a social media post in a Besiktas fan account, referring to the lion being the the symbol of Galatasaray, the club's fierce rivals.

Turkey has become a hub for the illegal trade in wild animals as traffickers exploit its air links to Africa and Asia. In December 2024, a young gorilla was rescued after being discovered at Istanbul Airport on a flight from Nigeria to Thailand.

title: Pro golfer, chef arrested for 111 pounds of alleged drugs in luggage
summary: Officials said Grobler and a pro golger and his alleged accomplice, a 25-year-old chef, swapped luggage tags to conceal ownership of the cannabis.
story: Nigeria's anti-narcotics agency Sunday said it had arrested a South African professional golfer with 50.4 kilograms (111 pounds) of cannabis in his luggage on arrival at Lagos airport.
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency said 37-year-old Henlo Grobler was arrested on Oct. 11 after arriving from South Africa.

The agency said Grobler and his alleged Kenyan accomplice, a 25-year-old chef named Faiza Njambi Abubakar, swapped luggage tags to conceal ownership of the cannabis. Officials said the golfer traveled in business class while his accomplice flew economy.
While Grobler carried bags tagged in the Kenyan woman's name, she collected two bags bearing his tags and left the airport.
The bags found with Grobler contained 46 parcels of a "strong strain of cannabis," the NDLEA said.
Grobler told investigators he was recruited by a South African associate and was promised $280 upon successful delivery of the drugs.
Abubakar, who was arrested on Oct.15 as she prepared to board a flight to Kenya, told investigators she had been offered $8,000 for her role in the operation.
"Both suspects identified each other during an identification parade," NDLEA spokesman Femi Babafemi said in a statement.
The agency said tracking devices were installed on the luggage and Grobler's mobile phone, allowing the syndicate to monitor its couriers and consignments.

Similar devices were also found in bags abandoned by an American professional basketball player arrested at the same airport on Nov. 11 with 34 kilogrammes of cannabis. Officials said the player, DaMonte Greene, claimed he was visiting Nigeria to "build networks for his basketball career" but examination of his mobile phone showed information suggesting his "knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity."
PGA South Africa lists a player by the name of Henlo Grobler.
Nigeria is considered a trafficking and production hub for drugs destined for other countries, but researchers say the contraband also finds its way into local markets.

Recent discoveries of industrial-scale methamphetamine production laboratories have raised concerns among authorities that Mexican cartels are establishing links in Nigeria to produce and ship the drug abroad.

title: U.N. climate summit ends without deal after contentious fossil fuel debate
summary: COP31, the latest installment of the United Nations' annual climate conference, ended Sunday without a final agreement after days of contentious talks collapsed.
story: COP31, the United Nations' annual climate conference, ended Sunday without a final agreement after days of contentious talks collapsed, mainly because of disputes between nations pushing to phase out fossil fuel use and others opposed to doing so.

The breakdown capped two weeks of negotiations in Antalya, Turkey, between delegations from nearly 200 countries. Their debates ran into overtime, becoming the longest COP summit in history, at a moment that U.N. officials and many scientists have called decisive for the trajectory of global warming and climate change.
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said in a statement that Sunday he was "deeply disappointed" by the outcome of the summit.

"I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands," he said. "But this setback does not change the facts. There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science."

The United States sent no representatives to the climate conference for the second year in a row, following the Trump administration's withdrawal from the 2015 Paris Agreement. That accord set a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, a target that has anchored every U.N. climate summit since and that the world is now poised to overshoot.
Talks reached an impasse Sunday, as the European Union opposed a draft agreement that failed to mention fossil fuels and which, its delegates argued, placated countries that export them.

"We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuel, which is the key driver of climate change," said Ireland's climate minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking for the EU in Antalya. "And we will not accept negotiating backward in time, and we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel."

The EU joined a group of smaller nations facing heightened threats of climate extremes and challenged oil producers, like Saudi Arabia, that staunchly rejected their views. The finale came after days of tense discussions over some of the core topics at issue during the summit, including whether to establish new rules and goals around transitioning away from coal, oil and natural gas in favor of renewable energy.

COP31 President Murat Kurum, who is Turkey's environmental minister, said in televised comments from Antalya on Sunday that a draft had not been adopted due to a lack of consensus. The conference rules require unanimous agreement to reach a deal, so even a single nation's dissent can derail the process.

"We have always emphasized that this process is one that respects the will of the parties. We did everything we could," Kurum said. "In the end, we did not impose this text on anyone. We did not pressure anyone with a take-it-or-leave-it approach. There are parties in the hall that oppose this text, and we see that there is no agreement on it. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted."

Australia's climate and energy minister Chris Bowen, who shared the COP31 presidency with Kurum as Turkey and Australia jointly hosted this year's summit, said Sunday that talks broke down because of "unbridgeable red lines" and added that "the situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory," reported CBS partner BBC News.

On Friday, the scheduled final day of the conference, a coalition led by France and Panama and including countries from Europe, Africa, Latin America and the Pacific rejected the latest draft agreement as too weak, according to the U.N. The group demanded explicit language on fossil fuels and stronger commitments on climate finance.

"We cannot continue to be held hostage by petroleum producers," said Panama's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, at a news conference last week. He also vowed that Panama would formally object to any deal omitting issues related to fossil fuels.

An initial draft of negotiators' agreement had called for "accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels," a recurring goal at these summits, and urged an end to inefficient fossil fuel subsidies. It also resolved to bring warming back below 1.5 degrees as early as possible this century. But that language was gone days later, reflecting deep divisions over timelines and financing.

Later drafts still did not contain language about fossil fuels, although they did include proposed targets to capture billions of tons of carbon dioxide annually from the atmosphere by 2035, using technology that critics have said distracts from the need to cut fossil fuel use. They also called for electricity to supply more than a third of the world's energy by the same deadline, alongside goals around renewable energy and energy efficiency.

Negotiators had expressed "deep concern" in drafted text over global warming, which at its peak is projected to exceed 1.5 degrees. They also reaffirmed the need "for deep, rapid and sustained emissions reductions," warning that every increment of additional warming will increase the frequency and intensity of climate-related loss and damage. If current international climate plans were fully implemented, they noted, the world would be on track for just over 2.5 degrees of warming, down from projections of more than 4 degrees before the Paris accord.

The COP31 summit unfolded in a year marked by deadly disasters, record heat, destructive wildfires, tumultuous surf and other anomalies, which meteorologists have largely tied to a powerful El Niño. Scientists say its effects are amplified by climate change.

Speaking in Antalya last week, Guterres urged governments to move away from fossil fuels, triple adaptation funding by 2035 and tax fossil fuel companies' windfall profits to help vulnerable nations recover from disasters. "Polluters must pay," he said. At a press conference two days later, he linked the climate crisis to deeper social and political instability.

"You cannot eradicate poverty when climate disasters keep throwing people back into it," Guterres said. "You cannot promise young people a better future while destroying the natural systems on which that future depends. And you cannot speak seriously about justice when those who did least to cause the crisis suffer first and worst."
Some environmental advocates felt the conference proposals didn't go far enough to meet the needs of communities that are already facing real consequences of the climate crisis.

Ellen Dorsey, named this month to the TIME100 climate list, told CBS News after leaving Antalya over the weekend that she hadn't expected substantial action from COP31, despite clear signs of urgency.

"The time for simply talking about phasing out fossil fuels is over. Governments need to act," Dorsey told CBS News. "That means no fossil fuel expansion, an end to fossil fuel subsidies, and an equitable phaseout that protects workers and communities."

Dorsey said fossil fuel lobbying has grown over the past decade, as has the presence of industry interests in national delegations at U.N. climate talks, including this one. Still, she sees promise in efforts pushing back, from grassroots movements to the Santa Marta process, a coalition using diplomacy to drive a transition away from coal, oil and gas.
"Momentum is building beyond the negotiations," said Dorsey, who called this "a historic inflection point" for climate policy. "The opportunity for real systemic change is here."

title: Russian warship struck by suspected Ukrainian drones at Libya naval base
summary: Libyan officials say a suspected Ukrainian drone strike has hit a Russian warship at a naval base in Libya.
story: A Russian warship was struck by a suspected Ukrainian drone at a naval base in Libya's Benghazi, Libyan officials said. It marked the latest attack in the North African nation tied to the Russia-Ukraine war.
The strike at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette, and ignited a fire at the facility, two Libyan military officials said.

They said that several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya, according to an initial investigation into the attack. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, they said.
The officials, affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya, spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to talk with reporters.

Satellite imagery appeared to show a boat on fire at the Benghazi port on Sunday, and images captured several hours later appeared to show the same boat partially submerged, CBS partner BBC News reported.

Libya has been divided since a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime dictator Muammar Gaddafi, who was later killed, in 2011. A U.N.-supported government is based in Tripoli and a rival administration is located in the east. The oil-rich nation remains a focal point for a long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.
The eastern Libya-based government said in a statement that the strike on Sunday caused an explosion and fire at the base, which was later extinguished.

The vessel had docked at the base for refueling and supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said, without providing details on the vessel or its cargo.
A joint investigation was launched with Russia to "uncover the circumstances of the attack, its source, and the party behind it," the statement said.
No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack. There was no immediate comment from either Russia or Ukraine.

On Sunday evening, local media said that another sea drone hit a commercial vessel off the port of Benghazi in a separate attack. No further details were given. The Almasar satellite television channel said that naval and air forces destroyed at least 12 other sea drones off the Mediterranean city.
The western Libyan government expressed concerns about "dragging Libyan ports and civilian facilities into external conflicts," in an apparent reference to the war in Ukraine.
"The government reaffirms its categorical rejection of turning Libya into an arena for international conflicts or a theater for external powers to settle scores," it said in a statement.

In March, Ukrainian forces operating in western Libya under a covert deal struck a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean in a suspected sea drone attack near Maltese waters, Libyan officials said at the time.

The Ukrainian forces, most of them drone experts, operated mainly at an air base in the coastal city of Misrata, but also at other military facilities in the capital, Tripoli, and the coastal town of Zawiya, the officials told The Associated Press.

title: Athlete swims Strait of Hormuz to highlight Iran war's wildlife toll
summary: British endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh has swum the Strait of Hormuz to highlight environmental threats during ongoing conflict.
story: British endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh has swum in the North Pole and Antarctica to draw attention to environmental causes. But battling freezing waters and extreme conditions hasn't prepared him for his latest challenge: swimming the Strait of Hormuz while tankers are attacked and blown up nearby.
Pugh, who is a United Nations Patron of the Oceans, spent three days this week swimming parts of the dangerous waterway to highlight how the war with Iran threatens the area's habitat and wildlife.

Wearing only swimming trunks, goggles and a cap bearing the U.N. logo, the athlete started from the Musandam Peninsula, on the southern tip of the strait, and ended by rounding the Cape of Hormuz, completing about 9.3 miles in total. Pugh is believed to be the first person to undertake a long-distance swim there since the war started.
The swimmer said that minutes after he entered the water on Monday, he heard two loud explosions that rocked the sea.

"I looked up and I could see that an oil tanker about four kilometers away had been hit," he told The Associated Press after he returned to London. "The explosion was so loud, two booms, and then fighter jets coming in. And at that moment I realized we have to get out of here right now."
Pugh, 56, managed to finish his feat after more stops and starts, including passing another vessel that sent fireballs into the sky after it was attacked.

"Most people, when they think about the Strait of Hormuz, they think of a shipping lane," he said. "But it is also one of the most beautiful places I have ever been … it's one of the treasure troves of the natural world."
"With all these ships being sunk, this area is under severe threat," he added. "It's going to take years, decades for this area to recover."

Iran has in recent weeks increased attacks on vessels that it claimed traveled along unauthorized routes in the strait as it seeks to impose its control on the crucial waterway, where a fifth of all oil traded passed through before the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Feb. 28.
Several tankers have also struck sea mines laid by Tehran, in some cases exploding and bursting into flames, among them one that was carrying more than 2 million barrels of oil last month.
Pugh warned of how oil leaking from the dozens of tankers damaged since February could create lasting problems for the region's animals, as well as its coastlines, coral reefs and mangrove forests.

He described seeing large numbers of dolphins following his boat as he sailed in, as well as turtles and ospreys. He also marveled at the hundreds of turtles he saw during a swim along the Omani coast before the war.
"When oil gets in there, when chemical pollution gets in there, it becomes very, very difficult to clean up that type of mess," he said. "It lasts for generations."
Pugh has had plenty of experience facing extreme temperatures and predators, including great white sharks. But swimming in a conflict zone presented entirely new dangers.

To stay safe, the challenge was done in sections over three days, with a total of about 6½ hours of swimming. The athlete recalled seeing a gas carrier being struck as he returned to the harbor on the second day.

"I'll never ever forget going past that gas carrier, the smell of the chemicals and then the flames, they were literally like fireballs going up into the sky. Around the ship, the water was on fire," Pugh said.
"And to think of the impact which a casualty like this has on nature — it was very, very acute."

Pugh has spent much of the past 40 years swimming in places from Antarctica to the Red Sea and the English Channel to urge more action to protect marine environments from climate change, pollution and loss of biodiversity.

He was the first athlete to swim across the North Pole and complete a long-distance swim in every one of the world's oceans. In 2023, he swam all 315 miles of the Hudson River to highlight the importance of clean rivers.
His foundation says the challenges have helped secure official agreements to protect more than 1.35 million square miles of vulnerable ocean.
Some have dubbed Pugh's blend of epic swimming and political outreach as "Speedo diplomacy."
"Sport opens doors, it creates dialogue, it enables people to start thinking about these important issues," Pugh said.
"My message is very simple," he added. "We've got to stop the war. We've got to open the strait, and we've got to clean up the pollution."

title: Princess Kate reflects on healing in new documentary: "Cancer does change you"
summary: The princess reflects on her cancer journey in the documentary and speaks to others about their experiences.
story: Britain's Catherine, Princess of Wales, opens up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary exploring life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024.
"Heal" follows 44-year-old Catherine as she attempts the Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours.

The Princess of Wales said at the time she undertook the challenge in support of the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, an organization connected to the hospital where she received her treatment. She was greeted by her husband Prince William, who is heir to the throne, and their children Princes George and Louis and Princess Charlotte, as well as her parents and brother after completing the climb.
In a trailer released Saturday by Prince William and Catherine's Kensington Palace office, the princess reflects on her cancer journey and speaks to others about their experiences.
Catherine announced in March 2024 that she had cancer and was undergoing chemotherapy following major abdominal surgery. She did not reveal what type of cancer she was treated for.

Catherine disclosed in January 2025 that she was in remission about 10 months after announcing her diagnosis. At the time, she said in her post on Instagram that she remains focused on recovery: "As anyone who has experienced a cancer diagnosis will know, it takes time to adjust to a new normal."
She has gradually resumed her public duties, visiting India with William earlier this month.

In the trailer, Catherine says cancer changes people profoundly, and "healing is a journey. How to reconnect with the things you once knew, and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty."
She adds that "it's clear we're not meant to carry life's challenges alone" and "often, it is through pain that we realize there's a greater beauty that lies beyond that."
The film will premiere on the BBC in the United Kingdom on Nov. 29, before airing internationally on NBCUniversal in the United States on Nov. 30.

title: Families frustrated with Pentagon probe of deadly drone strike
summary: The Pentagon is preparing to release findings of its investigation into the attack that killed six U.S. soldiers in Kuwait early in the Iran war.
story: Gold Star families have told CBS News that briefings about a forthcoming U.S. military report on the deadliest strike on U.S. soldiers in the Iran conflict did not, to their satisfaction, address their concerns about the military preparations and response to the attack.

Several of the families said they have been briefed about the unclassified results from the long-awaited internal probe into one of the first attacks on U.S. troops during Operation Epic Fury. Six U.S. Army Reserve soldiers were killed by a drone strike on their command post in Kuwait, known as Port Shuaiba, on March 1.
The official report has not yet been released to the public. The Pentagon has indicated it could be made public in a matter of days.
Over the past week, the Army briefed at least three Gold Star families on the investigation, and several family members told CBS News they were frustrated by what they heard.

Some of those briefed told CBS News the report does little to address the findings of an eight-month CBS News investigation, in which multiple sources said Army commanders ignored repeated warnings about the drone threat in the weeks before the attack.

Witnesses told CBS News that the facilities were not fortified to protect service members from a strike by one-way attack drones, which are a staple of the Iranian arsenal. Soldiers on the site said they had seen U.S. intelligence prior to the war showing the location was on an Iranian target list. And they argued the facilities lacked sufficient medical supplies and a plan for a mass casualty incident.

The briefings were led by Brig. Gen. Peter Glass, the deputy commander of U.S. Army Central, according to those who attended. They were individually held at either military or National Guard posts in locations close to the respective families.

"I wish I felt better," a Gold Star family member told CBS News after her briefing, which she said lasted roughly three hours. "I wish this gave me more than what I had yesterday or what I had the day before."

The briefings come just days after a U.S. Army soldier who survived the deadly Iranian drone attack filed a whistleblower complaint to Congress alleging senior military officials ignored warnings and did not plan properly for anti-drone defenses ahead of the war with Iran.

The whistleblower, Army Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom, spoke exclusively with 60 Minutes' Norah O'Donnell about his complaint, which was submitted to the House and Senate Armed Services Committees on Nov. 13 and obtained by CBS News.

In the complaint, Ramsbottom alleges that Army leaders were warned about drone threats at   the U.S. command post, and alleges the site had "no dedicated protection" against the Iranian drones. In an interview with CBS News, he identified Brig. Gen. Clint Barnes, who commanded the unit, and Maj. Gen. John Hinson, who oversaw logistics for the U.S. command, as dismissing warnings about protection at the location. Ramsbottom called for an independent investigation.
Neither official responded to multiple requests for comment from CBS News.

Another Gold Star family member described the briefing as mostly "cordial" but said the exchange grew tense when family members pressed for more answers about why the unit was moved to Port Shuaiba when most other soldiers were sent out of Kuwait ahead of the launch of Operation Epic Fury.
"We took a couple breaks because it got heavy and I needed some air," one family member said.

Joey Amor, whose wife, Master Sgt. Nicole Amor, was among those killed, told 60 Minutes he believes she might have survived if there was a better plan in place. "I think my wife had a shot, yeah," he said.
He said investigators told him that, no matter what medical resources were present, his wife's injuries were too severe for her to have survived the strike.

The Pentagon for months has declined comment to CBS News, but confirmed its internal investigation into the Port Shuaiba attack concluded in June. Still, it would take until mid-November for the Army to share its findings — another point of contention for some Gold Star family members.
"Going in I had an idea of what I wanted to know," another family member said. "I just knew I wasn't going to get answers — and I was right."

title: Princess Kate announces she's in remission from cancer
summary: Princess Kate made the announcement on social media after visiting the London hospital where she received treatment.
story: Catherine, the Princess of Wales, said Tuesday her cancer is in remission, about 10 months after announcing her diagnosis. Princess Kate made the announcement on social media after visiting the London hospital where she received treatment.

"It is a relief to now be in remission and I remain focused on recovery," she said in her post on Instagram after visiting the Royal Marsden Hospital in London. "As anyone who has experienced a cancer diagnosis will know, it takes time to adjust to a new normal."
The princess had announced last March that cancer was discovered following an abdominal surgery and she was undergoing preventative chemotherapy.

In September, she said she had finished chemotherapy. She spoke about receiving the cancer treatment during her visit Tuesday. "It's really tough,'' she said, according to the Associated Press. "It's such a shock."

Kate spoke with patient Katherine Field about the chemotherapy port that's used to deliver the treatment, saying, "I got so attached to it," and joking that she was almost reluctant to have it removed, according to the AP.
On social media Tuesday, Kate said she visited the hospital to thank the staff "for looking after me so well during the past year."

"My heartfelt thanks goes to all those who have quietly walked alongside William and me as we have navigated everything," she said, referring to her husband, the Prince of Wales. "We couldn't have asked for more. The care and advice we have received throughout my time as a patient has been exceptional."
Kensington Palace also announced that she and William have become patrons of the hospital.

"My hope is, that by supporting groundbreaking research and clinical excellence, as well as promoting patient and family wellbeing, we might save many more lives, and transform the experience of all those impacted by cancer," Kate said on social media.

Since 2007, William has held the role of the hospital's president. His mother, Princess Diana, also held that position, according to the palace. The hospital is known as a world-leading cancer center with three sites in London.
Kate spoke with other patients as well as doctors and nurses during Tuesday's visit, according to Britain's Press Association news agency.
"The body is amazing at telling us 'you need to take time out,'" she said after learning about a man's diagnosis.
She also talked about receiving her cancer diagnosis, according to the news agency.

"It's the uncertainty of that initial diagnosis," she said. "It's such a wealth of information. Understanding the diagnosis, it's a massive amount of information to take on as a patient. Having that continuity, in the clinical setting and outside in the home setting, is so important."

title: Billy Bob Thornton says he’s a holiday ‘purist’ as he brings back ‘traditional’ Thanksgiving at home
summary: Billy Bob Thornton says one restaurant Thanksgiving was enough, as his family returns to traditional cooking, football and holiday rituals at home.
story: "The Mayflower" host Billy Bob Thornton tells Fox News Digital why eating out on Thanksgiving just doesn’t hit the same.
Billy Bob Thornton tried to have Thanksgiving dinner at a restaurant in the past, and he'll never do it again.

During an interview with Fox News Digital about his new Fox Nation series, "The Mayflower," Thornton opened up about his own Thanksgiving traditions and how his newest gig shows the actual events that unfolded in 1621, not what is taught in schools.

"Well, I've always been a little bit of a purist in terms of holidays and, especially when you have kids, you want to kind of, you know, keep that tradition going. So my early thanksgivings were in Arkansas, and then after high school I moved to Texas and Houston," he began. "I've always wanted traditional holidays and particularly Thanksgiving and Christmas. And we have that, my family and I always have a traditional Christmas and Thanksgiving."
Billy Bob Thornton hosts "The Mayflower" on Fox Nation, which premieres on Nov. 23. (Fox Nation)
He continued, "But for Thanksgiving, a couple of times over the last decade, we went to a restaurant, and it just didn't seem right."
BILLY BOB THORNTON PUSHES BACK ON CELEBRITY ACTIVISM: ‘I DON'T KNOW ANYTHING ABOUT POLITICS’
Thornton said his wife and sister-in-law were tired of the mess that Thanksgiving creates in the kitchen, so they proposed the idea that they go out for dinner instead.

"We get there, and it was just like, we do this all the time, what's special about it, you know? And so this year, we're going back to the traditional thing and there's going to be a lot of cooking going on and a lot of football-watching," Thornton said.
Thornton hosts and narrates "The Mayflower," which is a three-part historical docudrama. It premieres Monday, Nov. 23, on FOX Nation.
Thornton said that part of the series was shot on a replica of the Mayflower. (Matei Horvath/Getty Images)

Speaking to Fox News Digital, the Academy Award-winning actor explained that once he was brought on to this project, he learned about the reality of the journey on the Mayflower and the extent of the "pain, suffering and sickness" people endured.
WATCH: BILLY BOB THORNTON SAYS HE REFUSES TO DO THANKSGIVING AT A RESTAURANT

"I would say the fact that not everybody who came over here, they weren't all exactly buddies. You know, there were people who just hitched a ride and all this kind of stuff. And also just learning to what extent there actually was pain and suffering and sickness. By the end of the first winter, half of those people were gone. I mean, that was surprising," he said.
Thornton explained that the Fox Nation series created a replica of the ship, which was much smaller than he expected.
Thornton told Fox News Digital he learned a lot about the first Thanksgiving when creating this series. (Scott Dudelson/Getty Images for Stagecoach)

"We did stuff on the replica of the Mayflower. It's not a big ship, I mean, at all, and to go down below deck there and see where these people were, and they were literally on top of each other – I mean, it was crowded getting the crew down there to film anything. And so it really brings it home to you about how difficult this really was," he said.
Thornton said he wasn't aware of the "bloodshed" that surrounded the Mayflower's journey to America.
WATCH: BILLY BOB THORNTON ON THE DARK HISTORY BEHIND THE FIRST THANKSGIVING

"I mean, I've heard things, but you know, like it says in the documentary, most of us, in terms of Thanksgiving, know what we learned in the third and fourth grade," he continued. "And it was all just like, 'Oh, look, look at the Native people. Let's invite them over for dinner, you know, and make peace.' And it wasn't like that. I mean, there was a war involved in this."
Thornton told Fox News Digital one of the main reasons he signed on to this series was because it was intended to educate people.
Billy Bob Thornton is an Academy Award-winning actor. (Jim Smeal/Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

"To be a part of something like this, to actually host something that educates you – and believe me, it educated me. I learned as I went along – I did not know this story. And so I just love being a part and telling a story that people don't know about," he said.

The actor is really hoping this docudrama hits home with young people, so they can remember the true meaning of Thanksgiving.
Billy Bob Thornton said he loves being a part of something that tells a story "that people don't know about." (Fox Nation)

"I think the more young people that watch this, the better. I think it would be really good for young people to see this and to understand where we come from and exactly how difficult it was and to maybe appreciate their forefathers and even within their own families," he told Fox News Digital.

title: 'Platoon' star Tom Berenger disses Hollywood as a 'company town,' praises Florida life

story: The "Platoon" actor spoke to Fox News Digital about his new docuseries "Ronin 3: The Battle for Sangin."
Tom Berenger said he never liked the idea of living in Hollywood because he always felt that it was like a "company" town where everyone had the same job and talked shop constantly.

"I never lived in Hollywood," the "Platoon" actor told Fox News Digital recently. "I started in New York in the theater, and I always lived there. And I knew all those New York actors, you know, John Heard, Chris Walken. And a few guys are gone: Brian Dennehy, Peter Weller. They all saw Los Angeles as a "company town where all people did was talk about it all the time," he explained. "I guess it'd be like being in Detroit if they all talked about cars constantly. I don't know. But it was boring to us. It was tedious… it wasn't about anything."

Tom Berenger says he always saw Los Angeles as a "company town." (Getty Images for TCM)

These days, Berenger calls Florida home, which he said he vastly prefers to L.A.

"And South Carolina, it was better too," he said of where he lived for three decades. "They have other jobs and real jobs, for one thing, and it's not the same old chit-chat, I guess. They look different. The people are nicer… I could go on probably for hours if I had to."

title: Russell Brand's wife vows to 'honor' prison rules after comedian's 'not guilty' message sparks investigation
summary: Laura Brand says she will honor HMP Littlehey's rules after reading Russell Brand's "not guilty" message, which officials say is urgently investigated.
story: Fox News senior foreign affairs correspondent Greg Palkot reports on Russell Brand's 10-year sentencing after his conviction for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others. The judge criticized Brand's conduct, while his attorneys are expected to appeal the verdict.

One week after Russell Brand's wife, Laura, sparked a government investigation by broadcasting a "not guilty" message from her imprisoned husband, she is pledging to follow prison communication rules while standing by her family.

Laura addressed the incident during the Nov. 22 episode of the couple's weekly Sunday Service YouTube vlog, telling viewers she will "honor" the rules set in place for her husband — who was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for rape and sexual assault.

"Last week’s episode drew a considerable amount of attention," Laura said. "And now that I understand the parameters set by the brilliant and professional staff at HMP Littlehey, I will absolutely honor that."

Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court in London on Oct. 29, 2026, ahead of his trial on rape and sexual assault charges. He has denied all charges. (Getty Images)
RUSSELL BRAND SPARKS PRISON INVESTIGATION AFTER WIFE READS DEFIANT MESSAGE FOLLOWING RAPE CONVICTION

title: John Malkovich recalls losing 'pretty much everything' to Bernie Madoff's Ponzi scheme
summary: John Malkovich opens up to "60 Minutes" about losing his entire fortune to Bernie Madoff's Ponzi scheme and the moment he told his wife the news.
story: FOX Business' Charlie Gasparino joins 'Your World' to discuss the downfall of the former American financier
John Malkovich recalled once losing his entire fortune to disgraced financier Bernie Madoff.
Malkovich, 72, told "60 Minutes" that he had recently returned from directing a play in Mexico City when he found out about Madoff's Ponzi scheme.

"I got home from that and I saw this photograph of Bernie Madoff in handcuffs, and I thought, 'Oh, well that could prove interesting,'" Malkovich said. "I went in and said to my wife, you know, 'I'm just going to go around the corner, buy a pack of cigarettes.'"
FRAUD MASTERMIND BEHIND MULTIMILLION-DOLLAR PONZI SCHEME THAT VICTIMIZED TRAVIS KELCE IS ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT
John Malkovich was one of many victims of late disgraced financier Bernie Madoff's Ponzi scheme. (Swan Gallet)
He added, "I said, 'We have a little problem. Bernie Madoff just got arrested.'"
Malkovich, a previous smoker, hadn't indulged in nicotine "for a while" when he left the house that day, he said.

"That was pretty much everything I'd ever made," he admitted before coming to terms with his situation. "You know, you look to blame, you're going to do this and that, and then you realize, 'Look, why don't you shut up?'"
FORMER DISNEY STAR ERIK VON DETTEN SUED FOR ELDER ABUSE AFTER COUPLE POURED $2.1M RETIREMENT SAVINGS INTO GOLD
"Whatever you lost, most people who were ever born will never have a 10th of that, no matter what they do. No matter what they do. Get on with your life and that's it."
Madoff died in April 2021 while serving a 150-year sentence at the federal medical care center in Butner, North Carolina, where his attorney said he was being treated for terminal kidney failure.

A decades-long force on Wall Street, Madoff shocked the world when he pleaded guilty in 2009 to running a vast Ponzi scheme that prosecutors said swindled thousands out of their life savings. The scheme began in the early 1970s, and by the time Madoff was arrested in December 2008, had defrauded as many as 37,000 people in 136 countries out of up to $65 billion.
His victims included the famous – director Steven Spielberg, actor Kevin Bacon and Nobel Peace Prize winner Elie Wiesel – as well as ordinary investors.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Madoff said he started the fraud, in which he appeared to deliver steady returns to clients, but was actually using money from new investors to pay off existing shareholders, in the 1990s because he felt "compelled" to give investors solid returns despite the recession and weak stock market. Prosecutors contend he started defrauding investors much earlier.
Bernard "Bernie" Madoff pleaded guilty in 2009 to running a massive Ponzi scheme. (Mario Tama/Getty Images)

"When I began the Ponzi scheme, I believed it would end shortly and I would be able to extricate myself and my clients," Madoff told the judge at his plea hearing. "However, this proved difficult, and ultimately impossible, and as the years went by, I realized that my arrest and this day would inevitably come."

Prior to his downfall, Madoff was viewed as a self-made and respected figure among financial professionals as the head of the seemingly successful Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities firm. He also served as the chairman of the Nasdaq Stock Market in 1990, 1991 and 1993.

In addition to being sentenced to the maximum 150 years in prison, Madoff and his family took a major financial hit: A judge issued a $171 billion forfeiture order in June 2009 requiring the disgraced financier to give up his interests in all property, including real estate, investments, cars and boats. Under the arrangement, the government also obtained his wife's interest in all property, including $80 million that she claimed belonged to her, leaving Ruth Madoff with $2.5 million in assets.
Madoff died in April 2021 while serving a 150-year sentence at the federal medical care center in Butner, North Carolina. (Bureau of Prisons)

The decline and fall of Madoff also took a toll on his family. The oldest of his two sons, Mark Madoff, died by suicide on the second anniversary of his father's arrest in 2010. His other son, Andrew, died from cancer at age 48 in 2014.
Mark Madoff's suicide prompted his mother, Ruth Madoff, to cut off all communications with her husband.

"I was responsible for my son Mark's death and that's very, very difficult," Madoff said during a 2013 interview with CNN. "I live with that. I live with the remorse, the pain I caused everybody, certainly my family, and the victims."

title: 'I Dream of Jeannie' star Barbara Eden, 95, still rides exercise bike for 35 minutes to stay fit
summary: Barbara Eden reveals the stationary bike routine and personal trainer workouts keeping her fit as the "I Dream of Jeannie" star turns 95.
story: Barbara Eden, who starred on "I Dream of Jeannie" in the 1960s, still works out with a personal trainer at 95 years old.  (Silver Screen Collection/Getty Images; Franziska Krug/Getty Images for Marcel Remus)
Barbara Eden isn’t slowing down at all — she's actually speeding up.
Despite turning 95 in August, the "I Dream of Jeannie" icon stays fit by working out on her stationary bicycle.
"I go for about, I don't know, 35 minutes on the bike," Eden told Fox News Digital recently of her fitness routine. "It's good."
BARBARA EDEN, 95, SAYS SHE’S ‘OKAY’ AFTER LAST-MINUTE CANCELATION OF FESTIVAL APPEARANCE
Barbara Eden does a workout on a beach in 1964. (Getty Images)
The former sitcom star said that both she and her husband of 35 years, Jon Eicholtz, both have a personal trainer who comes to their home.
"I don't go to the gym anymore," she revealed, adding that when she did, it was "spinning class for an hour, and then I worked with a trainer for a half hour, lifting weights."
DONNA MILLS DOES 100 SIT-UPS A DAY, PLAYS TENNIS FIVE TIMES A WEEK AT 85 BUT WON'T QUIT DORITOS
Eden said she still lifts weights a little. "Not as heavy as I used to." She added that weightlifting is especially good for women and their bones.
"You have to be disciplined about being active when you’re an actor," she laughed when asked. "My husband and I both have a trainer that comes in and helps us out."
4 SIMPLE HABITS CAN HELP SLOW MUSCLE LOSS AS YOU AGE, FITNESS EXPERT SAYS
Eden said she wasn’t sure what to credit for her longevity and energy, "but I'm glad I'm here, and I'm glad I'm still working."
Eden starred as Jeannie on the sitcom, which ran from 1965 until 1970. (Getty)

"I'm careful about what I eat, but I'm not overly stupid about it, you know?" she said when asked about her diet and philosophy on health. "I've never smoked. I don't know if that means anything. But, I think one of the things that's most important in your life is that you recognize other people. You realize that they're not so different than you are and that you have to get along. And when you do that, you find life is much more interesting, and people are much more interesting."
The actress also has a simple beauty routine which she said is what she’s always done. It involves washing her face at night and putting on moisturizer.
"That's about it," she revealed.

One thing the timeless beauty said she wished she had known about when she was younger was "the damage the sun could do to your skin. We didn't know that when I was growing up. And I think it really helps, if you know, to put sunscreen, you know, on your face during the day. Or if you're working."
The actress’ career spans more than 70 years, but she is best known for her titular role in the iconic sitcom "I Dream of Jeannie," which she said she never expected to become a phenomenon.
‘I DREAM OF JEANNIE’ STAR BARBARA EDEN TURNS HEADS AT 94 IN NEW PHOTO WITH HUSBAND
Barbara Eden poses for a photo as Jeannie on "I Dream of Jeannie." (Getty Images)
"It makes me so happy, really so happy that people still enjoy her," Eden said. "I really never expected the show to have the longevity it has."
The "Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea" star said that she gets fan mail from all over the world, including China and Russia.
‘CHARLIE’S ANGELS’ STAR JACLYN SMITH LIVED APART FROM HER HUSBAND FOR 17 YEARS DURING THEIR 35-YEAR LOVE STORY
"I'm just flabbergasted when I get the mail, and very, very proud. I just didn't expect it this long to be around."
Some fans even tell her that the show helped them through a difficult childhood.
WILLIAM SHATNER SAYS HE'S 'TAKING CARE OF BUSINESS' AT 95: 'THE LEAST OF ALL I WANT DO IS DIE'

"People will come up to me and say, ‘Oh, my God, you saved me when I was a child, because I had such a terrible childhood,’ and they just pour out what happened to them during their growing up period," she explained. "And so many of them were hurt either physically or mentally, and the show helped them. And I'm so happy to hear that."
Barbara Eden poses as Jeannie at an event in June. (Getty Images for Project Angel Food's Lead with Love 7)
One fan even revealed that they had turned their bedroom into a bottle as a refuge from the difficulties of life in the opulent style of Jeannie’s — where she slept on the show.
Eden also fondly remembers her "wonderful" co-star Larry Hagman, who played her love interest and "master" astronaut Anthony Nelson on the show.
"You never knew what was going to happen with Larry," she laughed, explaining that he was a bit of a prankster.

"He was just fun and unexpectedly fun, you know, for a lot of people." she added. "He was a dear guy. Yes, he was. He was like working with a 12-year-old boy. That's what it was, yes."

Eden said she rarely hears criticism of the series, but one thing that does bother her is when people wonder: "‘Why did you call him your master? You know, you're not supposed to call him a master.’ You know, and that's so foolish. Look, it's a fantasy, you know, and it's magic. She treasures her five seasons on the show, but the one creative difference she had was Jeannie and Tony getting married in the last season.

title: ‘Dukes of Hazzard’ star Catherine Bach says co-star stripped naked except for cowboy hat to cheer her up
summary: Catherine Bach recalls James Best's hilarious naked prank on the "Dukes of Hazzard" set that lifted her homesickness, ending with 30 crew members bowing to him.
story: Catherine Bach tells Fox News Digital how her "Dukes of Hazzard" co-star James Best surprised her with a naked prank when she was feeling homesick while filming in Georgia.
"Dukes of Hazzard" star Catherine Bach recalled a wild behind-the-scenes prank that her co-star, James Best, pulled on her while they were filming the iconic 1980s sitcom.

The 72-year-old actress recently spoke with Fox News Digital at Cure Addiction Now's third annual Fundraising Evening at the Beverly Hills Hotel, which raised money for research into treatments for substance-use disorder.

During her interview alongside her daughter, Laura Lopez, Bach revealed that Best, who played Sheriff Rosco P. Coltrane on the show, stripped down naked to cheer her up when she was struggling with homesickness on the "Dukes of Hazzard" set.
‘DUKES OF HAZZARD’ STAR CATHERINE BACH STUNS FANS IN NEW PHOTO AFTER REPORTED HOSPITALIZATION
Catherine Bach recalled how her "Dukes of Hazzard" co-star James Best stripped down naked to cheer her up during filming.  (Paul Archuleta/Getty Images; CBS via Getty Images)
"I was a little depressed," Bach remembered. "I was so far away from home. I'm in Georgia and it's all guys."
However, Bach said her spirits were lifted after Best enlisted the help of a makeup artist for an outrageous stunt, which unfolded during what appeared to be a routine touch-up.

"He has the makeup man. He goes, ‘Catherine, we need to get the makeup underneath your eyes. We need to straighten it out,'" Bach recalled. "And I said, ‘OK.' Close my eyes. He goes, ‘No, open your eyes so I can get underneath,' and I was like, ’What are you talking about?' So he goes, ‘Just look at my hat.' And I say, OK.’"
‘LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE’ STAR SAYS BRUTAL FILMING CONDITIONS LEFT CAST MEMBERS UNCONSCIOUS
"And there's Jimmy, naked, except for his cowboy hat and his holster and guns," Bach remembered with a laugh.
WATCH: ‘DUKES OF HAZZARD’ STAR CATHERINE BACH SAYS CO-STAR PULLED NAKED PRANK TO CHEER HER UP
According to the actress, her co-star received an enthusiastic reception from the men on set afterward.
"So then, when he came to set, 30 people were waiting for him, and they all bowed down, all the guys," she said. "But he got a laugh out of me because I hadn't been laughing very much."

"The Dukes of Hazzard" aired for seven seasons on CBS from 1979 to 1985 and initially filmed in Georgia before production moved to California. The action comedy series followed cousins Bo and Luke Duke, played by John Schneider and Tom Wopat, and their adventures in fictional Hazzard County. Bach played their cousin Daisy Duke, while Best's Sheriff Coltrane frequently found himself outmaneuvered by the Duke boys.

The series was a major hit, drawing in as many as 20 million viewers per episode. By its third season, "The Dukes of Hazzard" had become the second-biggest show on TV, according to The Hollywood Reporter.

"The Dukes of Hazzard" catapulted the cast to stardom, especially Bach, whose short shorts made her a sex symbol. The cast members also became genuinely close both on and off set, forming lifelong friendships that have lasted decades after the show ended.

James Best, as Sheriff Rosco Coltrane in "The Dukes of Hazzard," holds Flash, a basset hound, in Los Angeles on Jan. 1, 1982. (CBS via Getty Images)
Best died in April 2015 at age 88 due to complications from pneumonia. While speaking with Fox News Digital, Bach shared how Best's sense of humor remains part of her memories of making the series.
Asked to name the biggest troublemaker on set, Bach declined to limit the distinction to one cast member.
"Everybody, everybody. Jimmy Best, he was hilarious," she said.
The actress has previously said that practical jokes were a regular part of life on the "Dukes of Hazzard set."
"We all became such a family; there were so many pranks," Bach told the audience at a 2025 Hollywood Museum event with Schneider and Wopat, according to Remind magazine.
Bach has previously said that the cast "became such a family." (Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

During her interview with Fox News Digital, Bach also recalled how Daisy's wardrobe became a defining part of the series. The character's denim cutoffs became so closely associated with her that the style became widely known as "Daisy Dukes." During her time on the show, Bach posed as Daisy Dukes for a poster that sold five million copies, and her legs were insured for $1 million.
The actress said she had a hands-on role in creating the clothes audiences saw onscreen, saying that she "made them all," including the Daisy Dukes.
"And the bathing suit and the shirt," she added.

Bach explained that her sewing skills came from her mother's insistence that she learn a practical skill alongside pursuing acting.
"My mother said I needed to have a craft in case I didn't make it as an actress," she said.
Bach's short shorts, known as "Daisy Dukes," became a fashion sensation. (Getty Images)

Bach previously discussed her influence over her character's costume choices in a 2019 interview with Fox News Digital. She said producers initially wanted her to wear a poodle skirt, but she suggested the denim shorts that became a fashion sensation.
However, Bach shared that the Daisy Dukes presented a familiar problem when it came time to put them on, saying that "gaining weight" in between seasons was "impossible."

"Every year I would say, 'Wait a minute, you guys wash these in the washing machine, and you dried them, I know it. You're supposed to dry-clean them,'" she recalled. "They said, ‘No, we did, we do.’ I said, 'No, you didn't. See, I can't zip them up.'"
"It might be me," she admitted with a laugh.
The actress rose to fame starring on the show, which ran from 1979 to 1985. (Silver Screen Collection/Getty Images)
The famed Daisy Dukes are not the only pieces of "Dukes of Hazzard" that remain part of Bach's life.
"I'm building a General Lee," she told Fox News Digital. "A Charger."

The orange 1969 Dodge Charger nicknamed General Lee that was driven by Bo and Luke was a signature part of the series, appearing in the high-speed police car chases and long stunt jumps that helped define the show.

Bach said her own car began as a surprise gift from her husband, although she suspected he had another reason for choosing it.
"I think he wanted it for himself," she said.
She told Fox News Digital that the vehicle has since become connected to her charity activities, with students currently getting an opportunity to work on it.
Bach told Fox News Digital that she owns a "General Lee." (Getty Images)
"Anyhow, I got it, and it's been a continuation of charity events," Bach said. "It's at a college right now, and all the kids are working on it."
Once the work is completed, Bach said she plans to bring the car to a hospital and offer children rides around the parking lot.
"You know, just stuff like that. It's fun," she said.

Weighing in on what she missed about classic television, Bach said "wholesome" entertainment.

"But funny, and a little edgy, but that you can watch with the whole family, because that's what you can do with ‘Dukes of Hazzard’ and with many other shows," she said. "The whole family can sit around without getting, you know, getting ruffled. Grandma, grandpa, the kids, the mom and dad, everybody. That's what I miss."

Catherine Bach and her daughter, Laura Esmeralda Lopez, attend Cure Addiction Now's 3rd Annual Fundraising Evening at The Beverly Hills Hotel in Beverly Hills, Calif., on Nov. 9, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)

While attending the Cure Addiction Now's third annual Fundraising Evening, Bach also shared a health update during an interview with People alongside her daughter, Laura. Bach was hospitalized for an embolism in October 2025, according to multiple reports.
"I’m good... Everything’s on the up and up," she said. "It was very serious. Yeah. It was a very serious situation."

PHOTOS SHOW AFTERMATH OF RIOTS AS MASKED GROUPS CLASH WITH POLICE ACROSS FRANCE

title: Robert Pattinson becomes seventh actor to play James Bond in franchise's 60-year history
summary: Robert Pattinson becomes the seventh James Bond, joining a legacy from Sean Connery's 1962 "Dr. No" to Daniel Craig's 2021 "No Time to Die."
story: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos said the team was "slightly biased a little against" Robert Pattinson because of his fame before screen tests made it "so obvious."
Robert Pattinson officially stepped into cinema’s most famous tuxedo as the seventh actor to play James Bond, joining a group of Hollywood legends who defined 007 for generations.
The casting marks the latest chapter in a more than 60-year cinema legacy that began with Sean Connery in 1962 and most recently saw Daniel Craig retire the tuxedo in 2021's "No Time to Die."

Before Pattinson takes his first sip of a shaken martini, we are looking back at every actor who previously held the iconic license to kill — from the modern-day action stars to the original 1960s trailblazers.
Robert Pattinson will take over the James Bond role from Daniel Craig. (Getty Images)
ROBERT PATTINSON NAMED NEXT JAMES BOND
Daniel Craig (2006-2021)
Daniel Craig was unveiled as legendary British secret agent James Bond 007 in the film "Casino Royale." (Greg Williams/Eon Productions via Getty Images)

Daniel Craig took over as James Bond in "Casino Royale" in 2006, delivering one of the franchise's most dramatic reinventions. The English actor's casting initially sparked debate among the spy's fans, but his intense physical performance and emotionally layered portrayal helped establish a new direction for the iconic spy.

Craig starred in five Bond films: "Casino Royale," "Quantum of Solace," "Skyfall," "Spectre" and "No Time to Die." His version of Bond was more vulnerable and psychologically complex, with an interconnected storyline exploring the character's relationships, personal losses and loyalty to MI6.
Craig concluded his 15-year run with "No Time to Die," marking one of the most consequential endings in the franchise's history.
Pierce Brosnan (1995-2002)
Pierce Brosnan stars as 007 in the 1999 James Bond film "The World Is Not Enough." (Keith Hamshere/Getty Images)
Pierce Brosnan became James Bond in 1995 with the release of "GoldenEye." The Irish actor helped introduce the legendary spy to a new generation of moviegoers.

Along with "GoldenEye," Brosnan starred in "Tomorrow Never Dies," "The World Is Not Enough" and "Die Another Day." Following his departure from the franchise, Brosnan continued his Hollywood career with projects including "Mamma Mia!," "The Ghost Writer" and "Black Adam."

Timothy Dalton (1987-1989)
Timothy Dalton poses as 007 in a publicity still for the 1987 James Bond film "The Living Daylights." (Keith Hamshere/Getty Images)

The year 1987 brought yet another James Bond, played by Timothy Dalton. The Welsh actor brought a darker and more serious tone to the franchise. Dalton developed his acting career through theater, television and film before becoming 007.

Dalton appeared in two Bond films, "The Living Daylights," and "Licence to Kill." His portrayal moved away from the humor associated with Roger Moore and focused more heavily on espionage, revenge and realistic action.
Roger Moore (1973-1985)
Sir Roger Moore as James Bond. (Keith Hamshere/Getty Images)

Roger Moore took over the role in 1973 with the premiere of "Live and Let Die." The British actor brought a lighter, more humorous approach to the spy, differing from Connery's original tougher interpretation.

Moore portrayed Bond in seven films, more than any other actor in the franchise. In addition to "Live and Let Die," he starred in "The Man with the Golden Gun," "The Spy Who Loved Me," "Moonraker," "For Your Eyes Only" and "Octopussy"
His final appearance as Bond came with "A View to a Kill" in 1985.

George Lazenby (1969)
George Lazenby aiming a gun for the James Bond film "On Her Majesty's Secret Service," directed by Peter Hunt, 1969. (United Artists/Getty Images)

George Lazenby took over the role of James Bond after Sean Connery left the franchise. The Australian actor appeared in "On Her Majesty's Secret Service." At 29 when the film premiered, he became the youngest actor to portray Bond in the official film franchise.
Lazenby's portrayal of Bond focused more on his romantic side, particularly through Bond's relationship with Tracy di Vicenzo.

Although the film received mixed reviews upon release, it has since developed a strong following among Bond fans. Lazenby chose not to return for another installment, making him the only actor to portray Bond in just one official film.

Sean Connery (1962-1971)
Sean Connery as James Bond in 1964. (Screen Archives/Getty Images)

Sean Connery became the first official James Bond when he starred in "Dr. No" in 1962. The Scottish actor helped turn Ian Fleming's fictional British spy into Hollywood's most recognizable action star.

Connery starred in six official Bond films, including "From Russia with Love," "Goldfinger," "Thunderball," "You Only Live Twice" and "Diamonds Are Forever." He also appeared in the unofficial Bond film, "Never Say Never Again."

title: Kate Middleton's unexpected house rule for George, Charlotte and Louis: author
summary: Like Queen Elizabeth II, who washed dishes at Balmoral, Kate Middleton uses chores, baking and gardening to keep her royal children grounded in normalcy.
story: Royal boadcaster Ian Pelham Turner discusses Kate Middleton's love for freezing cold water swimming and late-night birthday cake baking as part of her modern royal family life.
Being born into royalty doesn't mean getting a free pass at home.

Kate Middleton is reportedly determined to make sure Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis don't grow up expecting everything to be done for them. And the future queen consort has a surprisingly ordinary way of keeping her three children grounded.
It all starts in the family kitchen.
PRINCE LOUIS' 8TH BIRTHDAY PORTRAIT SHOWS 'RELATABLE' FAMILY VACATION MOMENT: EXPERT
The Prince and Princess of Wales are seen with their three children on April 5, 2026, at St. George's Chapel in Windsor, England. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"When it comes to household chores, Kate is extremely organized," Christopher Andersen, author of "Kate!," told Fox News Digital, citing his own sources. "She wants to impart her ingrained sense of normalcy to the children by having them do all their own chores. There is a schedule that she draws up and posts in the kitchen, dividing up daily tasks among the kids."
Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.
"Kate!: The Courage, Grace, and Power of the Woman Who Will Be Queen" by Christopher Andersen is available now. (Gallery Books)

"They make their own beds every morning, prepare their own breakfasts and clean up after themselves," said Andersen. "It’s a good thing that Prince George was accustomed to making his own bed at home, because that’s one of the chores he’s expected to do at Eton College. It’s a valuable lesson for any child growing up under such abnormal circumstances."
Fox News Digital reached out to Kensington Palace for comment. A palace spokesperson previously told Fox News Digital that the palace does not comment on books.
Royal experts told Fox News Digital that Kate Middleton loves to garden and she gets her family involved. (Getty Images)
Kate has made no secret of her fondness for one household chore in particular.
"I love washing up. I really do," the princess said during a visit to a community transport organization in West Sussex.

Prince George, Prince Louis, Catherine, Princess of Wales and Princess Charlotte watch a flypast from the balcony of Buckingham Palace to mark the 80th anniversary of VE Day on May 5, 2025, in London, England. (Getty Images)
When asked whether William lends a helping hand, Kate replied, "He does the drying. We are a good double act. And we get the children involved," The Times of London reported.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Catherine, Princess of Wales laughs as she talks with Lynda Jones at a weekly lunch club at Pulborough Village Hall in Pulborough, southern England, on Sept. 30, 2026. West Sussex Minibus, a volunteer-led community transport group and member of the Community Transport Association, transported attendees to the event. (Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
Andersen wasn't surprised.

"Kate and William have been a dishwashing duo since their days rooming together at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland," he explained. "They bonded over simple domestic chores like making beds, taking turns doing the laundry, whipping up simple pasta dishes and shopping at the local supermarket. It's really part of their DNA as a couple — a bit of normalcy in an otherwise very high-pressured, anything but normal life."

New graduate Kate Middleton wears a traditional gown to the graduation ceremony at St. Andrews University to collect her degree on June 23, 2005, in England. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)
William was no stranger to getting his hands dirty before meeting his future wife.
Prince William cleans a lavatory during his Raleigh International expedition in Tortel, Chile, on Dec. 7, 2000. (Getty Images)

During his gap year in Chile, the prince took part in charity work that involved chopping wood, making beds, washing dishes and doing laundry, Andersen said. The experience may have helped prepare him for the everyday household responsibilities he would later share with Kate.

For William and Kate, those everyday household habits didn't end when they married. In 2024, a source told the U.K.'s Daily Mail that giving their children daily chores was important to the Prince and Princess of Wales.
Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales, smile as they attend The Earthshot Prize Awards Ceremony at the Jio World Convention Centre on Nov. 17, 2026, in Mumbai, India. (Getty Images)

"I think it would surprise people to see how ordinary things are at home," the insider told the outlet. "The children help with laying the table, clearing their plates when they’re finished eating and helping with tidying up. There is no preferential treatment."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Prince Louis pulls on Prince William's uniform aiguillettes as they attend a military procession down The Mall to mark the 80th anniversary of VE Day on May 5, 2025, in London. (Getty Images)
The source also said the couple rely on daytime staff to "manage their busy working schedules" and help during "after school" time.
But it's not all work and no play for the royal children, British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital.
Catherine, Princess of Wales visits the Nowrosjee Wadia Maternity Hospital in Mumbai, India, on Nov. 18, 2026. (WireImage)

"Princess Catherine cooks regularly and is known to bake birthday cakes, pizza dough and other family meals," said Fordwich. "She also gardens. She declared, while at a Welsh denim factory last year, that she 'loves making things,' referring to knitting and sewing."

Prince William and Theresa Connor, owner of The Welsh Cake Shop, watch as Catherine, Princess of Wales, places rolled and cut Welsh cakes onto a tray for baking during a visit to Pontypridd Market in south Wales on Feb. 26, 2025. (Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

William and Kate want their children to grow up with a sense of normalcy. Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital that the couple's down-to-earth approach reflects the kind of royal family they believe the British public wants to see.
WATCH: KATE MIDDLETON EMBRACES COLD WATER SWIMMING, LATE-NIGHT BAKING: EXPERT

"The reality these days is that William and Kate are a modern family," he said. "And the children do chores at the same time. William makes sure that they understand exactly what life is like in modern-day Britain. So, the children will do things like gardening. They'll do things like baking cakes. They'll do things like other household chores as well, keeping the house clean and tidy. Prince George, who is now at Eton, has learned that domesticity is necessary."
Kate Middleton and Prince William walk with their 13-year-old son, Prince George, as he arrives for his first day at Eton College on Sept. 8, 2026. (Getty Images)
Kate isn't the first royal to find satisfaction in an ordinary household chore.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Princess Catherine and Queen Elizabeth II watch part of a children's sports event while visiting Vernon Park during a Diamond Jubilee visit to Nottingham on June 13, 2012, in Nottingham, England. (Phil Noble/WPA Pool/Getty Images)
The late Queen Elizabeth II was also known to roll up her sleeves and wash dishes at Balmoral, her beloved Scottish retreat, according to royal experts who previously spoke with Fox News Digital.

Dickie Arbiter, a former Buckingham Palace press secretary who worked for Queen Elizabeth II and the then-Prince Charles, recently published a book, "On Duty with the Royals." He told Fox News Digital that one encounter with the queen left a lasting impression.
"On Duty with the Royals" by Dickie Arbiter is available now. (W. F. Howes Ltd.)

"After I joined Buckingham Palace, I was invited up to Balmoral," Arbiter recalled. "We went for a picnic. It had been raining. The picnic was in a log cabin and she got everything ready. I was left outside with Prince Philip. And the lunch was really four people: the queen, Prince Philip, the lady-in-waiting and myself."
WATCH: FORMER PALACE AIDE DETAILS QUEEN ELIZABETH'S OFF-DUTY LIFE

"At the end of it, we had to clear up," said Arbiter. "At least I had to clear up, being the newbie. She didn't tell me to, but I took it upon myself, and I started washing up. And I heard these footsteps behind me, thinking it was the lady-in-waiting coming in to give me a hand."
Prince Philip, Queen Elizabeth II's "strength and stay," died in 2021 at age 99. The queen passed away in 2022 at age 96. (Ray Collins - WPA Pool/Getty Images)

"I said casually over my shoulder, 'OK, I'll wash. You dry.' And this very familiar voice said, 'No. I'll wash. You dry.' It was the queen. And she plunged her hands into soap suds, did the washing up and I did the drying up. That's the sort of person when she was off-duty. Different person when she was on-duty."
Andersen said the late queen viewed washing dishes as "a kind of therapy."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
A view of Balmoral Castle in Scotland. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)
"It reminded her that, in addition to being the monarch, she was a wife, mother and grandmother," said Andersen. "The same applies to William and Kate. These are the tasks that keep them grounded."
Fordwich said the couple's approach to parenting reflects more than a desire to keep their children grounded. It also offers a glimpse into the kind of monarchy William and Kate hope to represent.

Prince William, Princess Charlotte, Catherine, Prince George, and Prince Louis wave from the balcony of Buckingham Palace during Trooping The Colour in London on June 13, 2026. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)
"This is in lockstep with so many members of the public and bodes well for the future of the monarchy remaining connected to everyday life rather than fully insulated from it," she said.

title: Sammy Kershaw responds to 'sellout' critics after attending 2026 CMA Awards red carpet
summary: Sammy Kershaw says talks with the Country Music Association went in a positive direction after he claimed he and wife Mendy were denied red carpet access.
story: At the 2026 CMA Awards, Sammy Kershaw opens up about his private sit-down with the CMA, addressing critics who accused him of selling out and explaining why walking the red carpet meant ‘more than a carpet walk’ for country music fans.

"Well, it went great, and I'm not going to tell you all the details of what was said. All I can tell you is that I know things were going in a positive direction. So, when we decided that I was going to come to the show and walk the carpet, there's a few people out there that said things like, 'Oh, he sold out' and this and that. But that's not how I look at it," Kershaw began.

title: Ty Pennington calls out 'excessive' home renovation trend people do in kitchens
summary: Ty Pennington calls renovation trend overkill, while sharing why kitchens and baths still build equity.
story: Ty Pennington, who suffered from an abscess in his throat that nearly took his life in July 2023, told Fox News Digital that it allows you to "really appreciate the people that love you, because sometimes we take that for granted."
Ty Pennington has built and maintained a successful career with his extreme home makeovers, but there's one renovation trend he believes homeowners are taking a little too far these days.

In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, Pennington — who has recently partnered with Insmed on the "Suspect BE" campaign to encourage people with unresolved respiratory symptoms to pursue further testing — weighed in on where homeowners should and shouldn't put their renovation budgets, calling out oversized kitchen islands packed with redundant appliances as a trend that has crossed into overkill.

"I would probably say the island with three dishwashers," the veteran HGTV star, 62, said when asked about renovation trends that go overboard. "It's maybe a little excessive. This is coming from somebody who was a personal dishwasher for many years of my life."
JOANNA GAINES REVEALS WHY SHE AND CHIP WALKED AWAY FROM 'FIXER UPPER' AT THE HEIGHT OF ITS SUCCESS
Ty Pennington attends the "Americans With No Address" red carpet premiere at Harmony Gold in Los Angeles on Oct. 3, 2024. (Getty Images for Robert Craig Films)

"There is a point that you almost get too big," he continued. "Is there an island that's almost the size of a small court? Possible. So I think sometimes we may be sort of outgrowing things. We may be just going too big. I know that's hard to believe, but I think sometimes we've got to scale back not only in budget, but also maybe in size. Cozy is cool."
Ty Pennington left "Trading Spaces" after the show launched his career in 2000. (Mark Peterman/WireImage)
While Pennington advocates for dialing back the scale, he still acknowledges that kitchens and bathrooms remain the smartest investments for homeowners looking to build equity.
"The most expensive are the kitchens and the bathrooms, but I do think they're kind of necessary if you plan on selling, because that's what people look at first," he explained.
