title: States rally behind Catholic church in first-of-its-kind Supreme Court fight over prayer shrine
summary: A Kentucky Catholic community's Virgin Mary prayer grotto sparked a neighbors' zoning fight now at the Supreme Court in a RLUIPA religious liberty case.
story: First Liberty senior counsel Ryan Gardner explains to Fox News Digital why the Kentucky dispute could shape religious land-use protections nationwide.

FIRST ON FOX: A Catholic religious community's plans to build a small shrine to the Virgin Mary on its own property have triggered a years-long legal battle with two neighbors, drawing a coalition of state attorneys general into a potential landmark religious liberty showdown before the U.S. Supreme Court.

Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman is leading an 18-state coalition urging the justices to reverse a ruling that blocked the roughly 600-square-foot prayer grotto in Park Hills, Kentucky, despite the project initially receiving approval from local zoning officials.

The dispute pits the Missionaries of St. John the Baptist against neighboring property owners Joel and Elizabeth Frederic, who challenged the city's approval of the outdoor shrine and ultimately prevailed in Kentucky's appellate courts.
YOU SHOULDN’T NEED A PERMIT TO PRAY IN YOUR OWN HOME — THE SUPREME COURT SHOULD AGREE
St. John Church in Park Hills, Ky., is at the center of a Supreme Court case over plans to build a prayer grotto on its property. (First Liberty Institute)

"I’m proud to stand with other Attorney General colleagues from across the country in defense of these Kentuckians’ religious liberty," Coleman said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital. "This fundamental American freedom cannot be brushed away simply by a heckler’s veto, and I’m confident the justices will agree."

The coalition's intervention comes as the Supreme Court prepares to consider whether blocking a religious structure on an organization's property constitutes a "substantial burden" on religious exercise under the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA).

The case marks the first time the Supreme Court is considering the federal law's land-use protections, according to Coleman's office, raising the stakes for churches and religious organizations nationwide.
The controversy began in 2021 when the Missionaries sought permission to construct a 16-by-39-foot grotto honoring the Virgin Mary's apparition to Saint Bernadette in Lourdes, France.
SUPREME COURT SHOWDOWN LOOMS OVER ST MICHAEL STATUE BLOCKED FROM PUBLIC SAFETY BUILDING
The property near St. John Church in Park Hills, Ky., where the Missionaries of St. John the Baptist have sought to build a prayer grotto. (First Liberty Institute)
The proposed structure would include a shrine, plaza, walking path and retaining wall, offering a quiet place for prayer and meditation.
The church building has stood on the property for nearly a century, predating Park Hills' zoning ordinance adopted in 1974, according to previous Fox News Digital reporting.
The Park Hills Board of Adjustment approved the project in April 2021. But the Frederics challenged the approval in court, arguing that the proposed construction violated local zoning requirements.
A trial court initially upheld the city's decision before the Kentucky Court of Appeals reversed, finding that the zoning board exceeded its authority in granting the necessary permits.
SUPREME COURT TO HEAR CATHOLIC PARISH'S CHALLENGE AFTER COLORADO BARRED SCHOOLS FROM UNIVERSAL PRE-K PROGRAM
The Kentucky Supreme Court affirmed the rejection of the Missionaries' federal religious land-use claim in December 2025.
Coleman previously defended the religious organization's position before Kentucky's highest court and led a 20-state effort in April urging the U.S. Supreme Court to take up the dispute.
The justices agreed in October to hear the case, with oral arguments scheduled for Jan. 20, 2027.
Ryan Gardner, senior counsel at First Liberty Institute, which represents the Missionaries, previously told Fox News Digital that the stakes extend far beyond the proposed Catholic shrine.
"This is a massive case for religious liberty because it has the potential to impact every single zoning law in this country," Gardner said in an October Fox News Digital exclusive.
The Supreme Court is seen on Capitol Hill in Washington, Dec. 17, 2024. (J. Scott Applewhite, File/AP Photo)
Gardner compared the grotto's footprint to a swimming pool, underscoring the modest size of a project that has since reached the nation's highest court.
"RLUIPA is at the intersection of two very critical rights in this country: the rights of religious liberty and property rights," Gardner said.
Congress enacted RLUIPA in 2000 to protect religious institutions from certain burdens imposed through zoning and land-use regulations.
The Missionaries argue that preventing them from constructing a religious structure on their property substantially burdens their religious exercise.

The Frederics, however, have disputed that interpretation, arguing in their Supreme Court opposition brief that the religious organization failed to demonstrate why alternative locations for the grotto were unavailable.
They also challenged claims that lower courts are fundamentally divided over the legal standard for determining substantial burdens under RLUIPA.
The Supreme Court agreed to consider the substantial-burden question, rather than every issue raised in the underlying zoning dispute.
Kentucky Solicitor General Matt Kuhn, Principal Deputy Solicitor General Jack Heyburn and Deputy Solicitor General Jacob Abrahamson prepared the multistate brief, according to Coleman's office.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

What began as a proposal for a quiet place to pray has become a national battle over religious liberty, property rights and how far neighbors can go in challenging religious construction on private property.
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: Dems brush off Elon Musk's anti-MAGA pivot, warn DOGE probe still coming
summary: Democratic lawmakers call Elon Musk an "opportunist" and a "chameleon" after his MAGA remarks, warning of possible DOGE oversight probes in January.
story: Democratic lawmakers react to Elon Musk saying he’s "not MAGA," speaking on his role in DOGE, potential investigations and whether they could work with him. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

Democratic lawmakers are labeling Elon Musk an "opportunist" after the billionaire denied being "MAGA" last week and shared his regret for putting roughly $450 million toward the GOP in the midterm elections.
"I think that Mr. Musk is an opportunist," Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, told Fox News Digital. "I think he's a chameleon. I think he will be whatever benefits him and his business."
"It sounds like buyer's remorse to me," Rep. Christian Menefee, D-Texas, said. "Maybe he should spend his time focusing on his businesses instead of trying to buy politicians."
I SAW THE REAL DOGE FROM THE INSIDE. WHY THE MEDIA GOT DOGE AND ELON ALL WRONG

Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk speaks at a rally for former President and Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump at Madison Square Garden in New York, Oct. 27, 2024. (Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images)

The political flip-flop callout comes after Musk made comments distancing himself from President Donald Trump and Republicans on Wednesday during The New York Times' DealBook Summit. Musk has put millions of dollars toward Trump, has previously campaigned with him and worked for the administration.
"Whatever," Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., said when asked about Musk’s comments. "That’s my response. Whatever."
Musk has also been facing wrath from Democratic lawmakers as a potential target of oversight investigations for his time as the head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).

"You're the architect of DOGE," Carter continued. "You wreck people's lives. You tear people's opportunities and their careers apart in a reckless effort to so-called save money when nobody's pocket's been padded with his. If he really wants to do the right thing, demonstrate it, not in word, but in deed."
"I’m certain that he will be the subject of investigations," Rep. Sanford Bishop Jr., D-Ga., said. "We’ll deal with it when we deal with it."

An investigation into Musk and DOGE seems to be at the top of the list for many Democrats as the party pushes for investigations to look into alleged corruption under the Trump administration after the party took back majorities in both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections.

"I've not seen anything that he's done to reach out to Democrats or help or anything else in that regard," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., said when asked if Democrats would reach out to Musk to work together.
He continued, "What he's done is destroy the State Department [and] destroy diplomacy."
THE TOP TRUMP OFFICIALS DEMOCRATS ADMIT ARE ON THEIR HIT LIST FOR INVESTIGATIONS IN THE NEW CONGRESS
Elon Musk denied being "MAGA" last week and shared his regret for putting roughly $450 million toward the GOP in the midterm elections. (Getty Images)

Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Ala., urged Democrats to not make oversight investigations the center of their party’s agenda over the next two years with a majority in both the House and the Senate. He said the upcoming years should be focused on "leveraging this majority" to bring results to Americans.

"I think there will obviously be some degree of oversight into what happened with DOGE, and I think rightfully so," Figures said. "But I don't believe that sort of oversight can become the North Star of what the party is all about over the next two years."

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who was just elected by his party to serve as speaker of the House, also recently left the door open to potential investigations into Musk when asked by Fox News Digital about the conversations surrounding oversight. He deferred leaving investigation decisions up to Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif. — the party’s expected leaders of oversight work.
The Republicans whom Fox News Digital spoke with were not totally convinced that Musk’s recent comments meant he was backing out of supporting Republicans.
"I think Musk is about fiscal responsibility," Rep. Glenn Grothman, R-Wis., said. "And the Republican Party, while it lets you down some of the time, is still the party of fiscal responsibility."
JEFFRIES BRUSHES OFF OPPOSITION FROM FAR-LEFT DEMS WHO VOTED NO: 'WE’RE GOING TO WORK TOGETHER'
Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., acknowledged that Republicans in Congress "fell short," excusing the American people for being upset with her party.

"It's totally in his hands, whether he supports [Republicans] or not," Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., said. "But I don't think that there's any question that this Congress fell short, specifically the Senate, and people have a right to be angry. Hell, I'm angry."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Congressional oversight into Musk could come as soon as January, when Democrats officially take control of Congress and leadership of the House Oversight Committee.
Fox News Digital's request for comment from Musk was not immediately returned.
Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: Trump accused of 'socialism, communism' after helping scandal-plagued Nvidia CEO reclaim top job
summary: Sen. Ruben Gallego calls Trump's role in Jensen Huang's Nvidia return "as close to socialism, communism as I've ever seen."
story: President Donald Trump predicted that Nvidia and its CEO, Jensen Huang, wouldn't be diminished by the scandal during an interview on Monday and said, "sex sells," when responding to a question about how the company would move forward.

FIRST ON FOX: Republicans blasted Democrats on the campaign trail for pushing a socialist and communist agenda, but President Donald Trump’s involvement in getting Jensen Huang’s old job back has some lawmakers claiming hypocrisy.
"This is as close to socialism, communism as I've ever seen," Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., told Fox News Digital.

"I mean, it's essentially state planning of private economies, and it's a whole new level of hypocrisy," he continued. "But the Republican Party definition of socialism is any government program, or government power, as long as the president doesn't like it or use it."

Nvidia’s board reinstated Huang Tuesday morning after allegations that the tech executive had a handful of affairs, notably with an alleged Chinese spy, placing him back at the top of the chip juggernaut after two weeks out of the gig.
TRUMP ‘DIRECTLY AND INDIRECTLY’ INTERVENED TO GET NVIDIA’S CEO REINSTATED, POTUS SAYS

President Donald Trump stands with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after presenting him with the National Medal of Science during the "A New Golden Age" summit at the U.S. Institute of Peace, renamed The Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace by the Trump administration, in Washington, D.C., Oct. 8, 2026. (Evan Vucci/Reuters)

The company’s chips power myriad technologies that the Trump administration has pinned as critical to national security, including data centers and artificial intelligence, which lawmakers fear would be disastrous to fall into the hands of the Chinese government.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who has been hawkish on China’s access to Nvidia’s chips, told Fox News Digital that the company’s board was "free to vote however they want, but the federal government owes the American people answers about what actually happened."

"This looks terrible on its face, and it drives home the need for Congress to be informed on the full impact of Jensen Huang’s actions on our national security and economy," Scott said. "Congress needs to be fully briefed on this as soon as possible, so we can take appropriate action if need be."
TRUMP OFFICIALS TOLD 'NOT TO STAB EACH OTHER' AMID DEMANDS NVIDIA DISPUTE BE PUT UNDER OATH IN CONGRESS

The company’s stock spiraled and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle raised national security concerns about China’s access to Nvidia’s chips. They have since pushed for stricter export control legislation and demanded that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify on the Hill.
Trump, in an appearance on CNBC shortly after the board’s announcement, said he didn’t believe Huang would have been reinstated without him as he lauded the stock market’s upward trend.
"The answer is no," Trump said. "I believe my intervention was very important."

The Trump administration has not been shy about turning the government into a pipeline to the corporate world. The Cato Institute found in a report released in October that the administration has equity stakes in about 40 companies — though Nvidia is notably not on the list.
TWO TOP TRUMP CABINET OFFICIALS GO TO WAR OVER CHINA SPY SCANDAL AMID EXPLOSIVE ACCUSATIONS: REPORT
Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said Trump's involvement in getting Jensen Huang’s old job back "looks terrible on its face." (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

And Trump’s intervention did not stop Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., from plowing ahead with a scheduled hearing with Huang. He announced that the embattled, newly reinstated CEO would appear before the panel on Dec. 3.

Gallego, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, told Fox News Digital in a brief interview that "it really frightens me about what's happened with our national security," and questioned whether Trump had engaged "in stock market manipulation before making these announcements."
"All these things, you know, are really now up in the air," he said. "And at the core, the question is, what's going to happen to our national security?"

And Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who has made AI safeguards a center of his challenge against Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., told Fox News Digital that Huang was "at the center of this political corruption and political rot, and he seems to have been given a free hand by President Trump when it comes to formulating the Trump administration's AI and chips policy."

The lawmaker is also a member of the Banking Committee, and said he was keenly interested in Huang's "efforts to increase and accelerate the export of high-end chips to China, how he's been accomplishing that, how he's been getting his way with the administration."

"And then obviously, the concern is that it is undermining our national security interests. After all, high-end chips can be used by the military in China," Van Hollen said. "And it's completely it's just completely hypocritical for the Trump administration, on the one hand, to say the reason we have to take off all the brakes on AI development here at home is because China will leap ahead, if we don't, when in fact, it's the Trump administration that's helping China leap ahead."

Senate Republicans are equally uneasy about the national security implications of the move, despite Trump assuring in a post on Truth Social that "the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security."
"No national security risk? Based on what," Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, said on X.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., a member of the Senate Banking Committee, also told Fox News Digital that it was Nvidia’s right to reinstate Huang, but that the CEO needed to answer for what happened.

"Jensen Huang’s actions raised national security concerns, and he must answer for them," Britt said. "The Commerce Department also has a responsibility to explain the role it played in allowing for potentially serious threats to our national security."

"I look forward to having both Jensen Huang and Secretary Lutnick in front of the United States Senate Banking Committee, where my colleagues and I can ask questions and conduct necessary oversight," she continued.
The White House did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Jeffries faces online fury over cryptic answer when asked if Dems would risk gov't shutdown: 'Political games'
summary: Hakeem Jeffries declined to rule out a government shutdown to advance the Democratic Party's agenda, citing the appropriations process before Dec. 11.
story: In a recent interview with The New York Times’ Lulu Garcia-Navarro, Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., refused to say "one way or the other" whether Democrats would pursue a government shutdown to advance their agenda.

Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., triggered online backlash after declining to say "one way or the other" whether the Democratic Party would pursue a government shutdown to advance its agenda during an interview with The New York Times.
When asked by The New York Times' Lulu Garcia-Navarro if he would be willing to risk shutting down the government to achieve Democrats' goals, Jeffries declined to rule out the possibility.
"I'm not going to say that one way or the other because we got to figure out right now what's possible in terms of the appropriations process," he said.
Jeffries said Democrats are now weighing possible restrictions on funding for the Iran war "to make clear that this [war] has to end" ahead of the Dec. 11, 2026, federal funding deadline.
HAKEEM JEFFRIES CALLS TRUMP CHIEF OF STAFF STEPHEN MILLER A ‘STONE-COLD RACIST,’ REFUSES TO SIT DOWN WITH HIM

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) holds a press conference on the fourteenth day of the U.S. government shutdown on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., Oct. 14, 2025. (Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters)

"It needs to be over," he said. "In fact, Donald Trump can end it right now. That doesn't mean there's not going to be a lot of work ahead, because Iran is in a stronger position now than they were before this reckless and costly war of choice started."
He added the 43-day government shutdown that began in October 2025 was an example of Democrats "not going to go along simply to get along."
"That was the longest complete shutdown in American history, and at the end of it, we actually were successful in forcing a vote to extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits," he said.
SCHUMER, JEFFRIES SIDESTEP QUESTIONS ON NUKING FILIBUSTER, LAUNCHING ELON MUSK PROBE AFTER BLUE WAVE
President Donald Trump delivers an address to the nation about the Iran war at the White House in Washington, D.C., on April 1, 2026. (Alex Brandon/Pool via Reuters)
Social media users were quick to criticize Jeffries' open-ended answer in the viral exchange on Saturday.

"Bookmark this video," Shane Schaetzel, a religious influencer, posted on X. "The Democrats said it first and in advance. They're going to shut down the government. Now when they do this, they always blame the Republicans, and the Legacy Media always dutifully backs them on this. Yet here it is, they're announcing they THEY (the Democrats) are going to do it."
ASRA Q. NOMANI: OLD-GUARD DEMS FACE FRANKENSTEIN MOMENT AS LEFTISTS COME FOR THEM

U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., arrives onstage during "The New Power Structure: Black Politics in the Age of Resistance" panel during the 2026 National Association Of Black Journalists Convention at the Atlanta Marriott Marquis on Aug. 13, 2026 in Atlanta, Ga. (Paras Griffin/Getty Images)

In another post on X, conservative influencer Josh Fulfer, who runs the social media account Oreo Express, wrote, "Democrats are responsible for all the shutdowns that have cost our economy billions of dollars, and left people homeless because they were not paid. They are planning to do it again."

"Federal funding set to expire on December 11 and we know that they are willing to do it to get their way," conservative account Defiant L's posted on X. "People shouldn't suffer because of political games."
"Hakeem Jeffries won't rule out shutting down the government to enact Democrats' agenda," RNC Research posted on X.

Conservative commentator Paul Szypula also posted on X, writing, "Everyone saw this coming. Democrats already forced shutdowns while in the minority. With a majority they'll have an easier time doing it."

Democrats secured several midterm victories this month, taking back control of both the Senate and the House beginning in January. Some Republicans and conservatives worry the shift could lead to future shutdowns and bitter standoffs.

Fox News Digital reached out to Jeffries' office for comment.
Kiera McDonald is a Production Assistant for Fox News Digital.

title: Trump admin announces sweeping measure to cut Iran’s ‘last financial lifeline’
summary: The Treasury Department blacklisted Iranian exchange houses and front firms in Dubai, Hong Kong and Turkey accused of moving billions for Iran.
story: Tensions escalate in the Middle East as President Donald Trump signals his willingness to resume military strikes against Iran next year following recent drone attacks. Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst reports live from Tel Aviv on the retaliatory claims, while retired Navy SEAL officer Mike Sarraille discusses the conflict during 'The Faulkner Focus.'

FIRST ON FOX: The Treasury Department on Monday imposed sweeping new sanctions against more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, overseas front companies and financial operatives accused of moving billions of dollars through a global "shadow banking" network to keep Iran connected to international trade.

The action, carried out by the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), targeted "financial plumbing" spanning Iran, Dubai, Hong Kong and Turkey that officials say enables Tehran to bypass U. S. restrictions, sell oil and petrochemicals, and settle transactions in Russian rubles and Chinese yuan.

"Iran’s economy is underwater, and its leaders are panicking," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wrote in a statement Monday before the news release. "Iran’s shadow banking system is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime. Treasury will continue dismantling these illicit networks until we have buried the head of the snake."
TRUMP’S IRAN CRACKDOWN ‘SUFFOCATING’ REGIME AS OIL WELLS COULD SHUT WITHIN DAYS, BESSENT SAYS

Monday’s designations mark the latest escalation under Operation Economic Outcast, a maximum financial pressure campaign Bessent launched on Aug. 24, to cut off the regime's remaining revenue streams and heighten secondary sanctions risks for foreign banks and brokers that continue doing business with Tehran.
TRUMP'S FIRST IRAN WAR ESCALATION POST-MIDTERM LOSSES SEEKS TO CHOKE OFF TEHRAN’S TRADE

According to the Treasury Department, Iran's "shadow banking" apparatus is overseen by the Central Bank of Iran and relies on domestic currency exchange houses paired with bank-affiliated "rahbar companies" that manage sanctions-evasion networks through thousands of foreign shell firms. As declining oil revenues and existing sanctions squeeze the Iranian economy, Treasury said shadow banking facilitators have increasingly failed to repatriate export earnings while enriching themselves with state funds.

The Treasury also revealed Monday that its Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) "identified approximately $14.7 billion of financial activity from January 2025 to August 2026 potentially linked to Iranian shadow banking."
MILLIONS OF BARRELS OF IRANIAN OIL SIT BEYOND TRUMP BLOCKADE AS HE VOWS ‘ZERO LEAKAGE’

Among the highest-profile targets in Monday’s package is the Iran-based Iran Center for Exchange of Currency and Gold, which matches Iranian exporters holding foreign currency with importers seeking to buy goods abroad across tens of billions of dollars in annual trade. Treasury noted that the Central Bank of Iran also uses bonds issued by the exchange center to facilitate cross-border trade in Russian rubles and Chinese yuan without relying on the U.S. dollar.
BESSENT WARNS IRAN'S OUTSIDE BACKERS TO 'STAY AWAY' AS TRUMP SEEKS TO 'ASPHYXIATE' TEHRAN'S ECONOMY

The OFAC package sanctions Rahbar Bazargani Nesim Baharan Qeshm Company — the rahbar affiliate for Iran’s Bank Sarmayeh — along with three of its senior officials, Sayyed Mohammad Jalali, Valiollah Hemmati and Ali Kalhor, for facilitating transactions on behalf of major Iranian oil companies. Two Iran-based currency dealers, Mina Fashki and Partners Exchange Company and Mellat Exchange Company, were blacklisted alongside five of their owners and officials.
US TARGETS CHINESE REFINERY IN SWEEPING IRAN OIL CRACKDOWN, SANCTIONS ‘SHADOW FLEET’ TANKERS

To choke off Tehran's overseas payment channels, Treasury targeted 10 exchange house front companies across the United Arab Emirates, Turkey and Hong Kong accused of moving billions of dollars for Iranian clients. Those include Dubai-based Recaz Star General Trading LLC, which sent and received hundreds of payments totaling more than $170 million tied to Sadaf Exchange, and OGA Global General Trading L. L. C, which oversaw millions of dollars in payments for the state-owned National Iranian Tanker Company.

Other newly sanctioned front companies include Hong Kong-based Grandez Trading Limited, Turkey-based Bogazici Gumrukleme Ithalat Ihracat Turizm Petrol Urunleri Sanayi Ve Ticaret Limited Sirketi and several Dubai-based trading firms — including Gespl International General Trading LLC, which Treasury alleged was used by the National Iranian Oil Company to launder oil and petrochemical proceeds, and Robust Trading LLC for processing payments for the sanctioned National Iranian Copper Industries Company.
IRANIAN ‘GHOST FLEET’ FILMED EVADING US BLOCKADE EN ROUTE TO CHINA, UANI SAYS

Treasury also invoked counterterrorism authorities to sanction Dubai-based H N B Trading Co LLC, alleging it received hundreds of thousands of dollars from a front company tied to Iran’s Armed Forces General Staff to help pay for the charter of a vessel alongside sanctioned shipping firm Dragon Road Ltd.

Under Monday's order, any U.S.-based assets or property interests belonging to the designated individuals and entities — as well as any businesses 50% or more owned by them — will be frozen, and Americans are barred from transacting with them.

Treasury also warned that foreign financial institutions risk losing access to U.S. correspondent accounts if they knowingly facilitate significant transactions for the sanctioned networks.
Whistleblowers who report sanctions violations resulting in penalties exceeding $1 million might ultimately qualify for federal awards.

title: Federal appeals court clears Army to detonate volatile Iowa explosives as Dem gov-elect refuses to sign off
summary: President Donald Trump said earlier Monday the military won't detonate unstable explosives in Middletown without sign-off from both the Eighth Circuit and Iowa's incoming governor.
story: The 'Fox & Friends Weekend' panel discusses a legal battle after a court blocks the U.S. Army's plan to detonate tons of hazardous bomb-making chemicals in Iowa, sparking local fears of a toxic lead dust cloud.

A federal appeals court on Monday cleared a key legal hurdle for the U.S. Army to detonate degrading explosives in Iowa, leaving the next step uncertain after President Donald Trump said the blast would not move forward unless Gov.-elect Rob Sand also agrees to it.

Earlier Monday, Trump declared on Truth Social that he ordered the military to hold off on detonating degrading lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant unless both the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals and Sand signed off.

"I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation," Trump said in a lengthy post.
He warned that if either "do not agree," he would be forced to "hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation."
ARMY DELAYS CONTROLLED DETONATION OF UNSTABLE BOMB-MAKING CHEMICAL IN IOWA
A federal appeals court on Monday cleared a key legal hurdle for the U.S. Army to detonate degrading explosives in Iowa. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)
Hours later, the Eighth Circuit denied an emergency request from the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club to block the blast, lifting a temporary pause it issued last week.

"Here we are faced with a situation in which the risk is between a controlled detonation and an unplanned explosion, not between the risk of a controlled detonation and no explosion at all," the Eighth Circuit said.
In a Monday evening post on X, Sand declined to approve or reject the blast.

"The Administration should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks," Sand wrote. "Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward."
Sand added that he asked the federal government to publicly release the same briefing details he received "as soon as possible."
The Army had already delayed its plan to detonate the material until Wednesday, postponing the explosion expected to send "lead-containing particles" into the air.

The detonation was previously scheduled for Friday but was then rescheduled for Monday, with Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle noting in a Thursday statement, "This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material."
But the Army on Sunday announced another postponement until Wednesday in order "to allow for more optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced."
An environmental assessment prepared by the Army explains the reason for the plan to detonate the material in Iowa rather than relocating it.

"In March 2026, during a proactive facility safety review, IAAAP identified a stockpile of lead azide, a highly sensitive primary explosive used in munitions detonators, that had degraded and crystallized over time," the assessment noted.
IOWA RESIDENTS NEAR AMMUNITION PLANT TOLD TO VACATE BEFORE ARMY DETONATES 5 TONS OF BOMB-MAKING CHEMICALS

The Army had already delayed its plan to detonate the material until Wednesday, once more postponing the explosion expected to send "lead-containing particles" into the air. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

"Due to its chemical degradation, the material’s legal status transitioned from a viable production component to an unserviceable hazardous waste. Lead azide in a crystallized state becomes extremely shock-and-friction sensitive presenting a serious safety hazard to plant personnel and preventing safe physical transport of the material to standard off-site demilitarization facilities," the document explains.
But the detonation will impact local communities, an advisory issued last week explained.

"Extensive modeling efforts predict that the potential level of lead particles in the air may be elevated but well below the level at which EPA would require protective actions be taken. The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground," according to the advisory.

"While safety measures will be fully enforced, the controlled detonation will cause temporary noise, ground vibrations, and a dust plume that will contain some lead. Residents in Middletown will hear a loud noise; feel vibrations from two consecutive, rapid detonations; and see a plume of dust which is expected to linger for no more than one hour after the detonation, depending on wind speed," the notice stated.

A legal challenge was lodged last week and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit order on Thursday declared, "An administrative stay of the emergency permit issued by the Environmental Protection Agency is granted until the emergency motion for stay is ruled upon by this court."
But the U.S. government in a document on Saturday alerted the court that the Army planned to proceed with the detonation anyway.
TRUMP'S EPA REFORMS ARE A HUGE BOOST TO MANUFACTURERS, BUT THERE'S MORE RED TAPE TO CUT: EXPERT
The detonation will impact local communities, an advisory issued last week explained. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

"The Government notifies the Court that the Department of the Army ("Army") intends to invoke the emergency munitions and explosives exclusion to EPA’s regulatory and permitting Resource Conservation and Recovery Act ("RCRA") requirements, under which the Army may perform treatment by controlled detonation of the lead azide waste without the Emergency Permit that is challenged in this petition," the filing noted. "The Army must perform a controlled detonation to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion, and the Army intends to act by November 24, 2026."

While the Army had announced on Sunday that the detonation would be delayed until Wednesday, Nov. 25, Trump, issued his Truth Social post on Monday declaring that the project would not move forward without the approval of the court and the governor-elect.

"Iowa is a very special place to me, a place that I won, by substantial margins, in all three Elections but, whether I won or lost, would never deter me from making a correct decision. As everyone knows, there is a Military ‘clean up’ operation, without which, a very dangerous situation exists. In 2009, the Obama Administration improperly stored a vast number of explosives, and the Experts, who know it well, and have been studying it for many years, feel there is a substantial chance that this material will explode of its own volition, perhaps sometime in the near future," Trump wrote in the post.
Sand and the White House could not immediately be reached by Fox News Digital for comment.
Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Federal judge blocks blue state’s ICE mask mandate and other rules targeting federal officers
summary: A judge's injunction blocks enforcement of state use-of-force standards and investigations, along with rules on federal officers’ masks and identification.
story: New York City sanctuary laws are upheld after a federal judge dismisses a Department of Justice lawsuit, drawing sharp criticism from Joe Abraham, whose daughter Katie was killed in a hit-and-run crash. Meanwhile, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul deflects questions on migrant crime during a gubernatorial debate.
Connecticut’s effort to impose state rules on federal immigration officers hit a major legal obstacle after a federal judge ruled that the provisions are likely unconstitutional.

In a preliminary ruling Friday, U.S. District Judge Vernon D. Oliver blocked Connecticut officials from enforcing certain sections of SB 397 against federal officers while the federal government’s lawsuit over the law continues.

The blocked provisions of the law, passed in May, set statewide use-of-force standards, gave state officials authority to investigate and prosecute certain cases involving federal officers — such as excessive use-of-force incidents — and restricted federal officers’ use of face coverings. Oliver wrote that the sections likely violate the Constitution’s supremacy clause, which limits states’ ability to control federal operations.
DHS, DEM OFFICIALS CLASH AFTER ICE ARREST AT SEATTLE AIRPORT
An FBI agent watches over an immigrant after he was detained outside the Connecticut Superior Court on July 3, 2025, in Stamford, Connecticut. (John Moore/Getty Images)
The case underscores a broader legal fight over how far states and cities can go in regulating federal officers who operate within their borders.

Federal judges have already blocked state and local restrictions on federal officers in Virginia, New York and Philadelphia. Most recently, a federal judge in California entered a permanent injunction barring enforcement of challenged state mask and identification laws against federal officers. The cases, however, vary in scope, and none resolves Connecticut’s separate dispute over state use-of-force standards.

"It is un-American to allow masked, secret police to detain our residents and I am hopeful that this ruling will be overturned on appeal and the law will survive it its entirety when the case is heard on the merits," Democratic state Sen. Matt Lesser, the deputy majority leader in the Connecticut State Senate, said following the court's ruling.
BORDER DEM POISED TO WIELD ICE PURSE STRINGS REJECTS SOCIALIST 'DEFUND' PUSH
Federal agents conduct immigration enforcement operations, Feb. 5, 2026, in Minneapolis. (AP Photo/Ryan Murphy, File)

Oliver's ruling gives the Justice Department a win, but it is not a final decision on the matter. The federal lawsuit also did not challenge a separate section of SB 397 allowing people to sue over alleged constitutional violations, so that provision was outside the injunction.

"I want Connecticut residents to know that the majority of this law still stands, and it still provides them the right to sue for violations of their constitutional rights," Lesser continued in his remarks about the ruling. "It also provides protections from ICE activity without a warrant in sensitive locations like schools, hospitals, and places of worship."

State Rep. Steven Stafstrom, D-Bridgeport, a key backer of the law as co-chair of the Judiciary Committee, also criticized the ruling, saying he feared it would leave Connecticut less safe because it blocks state tools to investigate deaths involving federal officers. He said he would work with colleagues and the attorney general’s office on next steps.
Connecticut State Capitol (Getty)

Fox News Digital reached out to Gov. Ned Lamont’s office and Attorney General William Tong’s office to ask whether Connecticut plans to appeal and for comment on the ruling. Neither office responded by publication.
Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: Trump officials told 'not to stab each other' amid demands Nvidia dispute be put under oath in Congress
summary: Sen. John Kennedy wants Howard Lutnick and Scott Bessent to testify under oath over claims Commerce let China circumvent chip export controls.
story: Rep. Rick Crawford, R-Ark., discusses his letter with Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., asking Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify about AI chips allegedly diverted to China. Crawford also weighs in on the alleged Chinese spy scandal.

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., is among the lawmakers who want Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to put their dispute on the record amid the ongoing Nvidia affair scandal tied to the company's chip sales to China.

Tensions are reportedly running high among two of President Donald Trump's top Cabinet officials, so Kennedy says he hopes the two can not "stab each other" if they testify before the Senate Banking Committee.

Asked about Nvidia founder reportedly Jensen Huang agreeing to appear amid claims he placed U.S. national security at risk by having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Kennedy said he is "more interested" in speaking with Lutnick and Bessent.
"I’m less interested in talking to Mr. Huang," Kennedy said during NBC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday. "You know, he did what he did."
Sen. John Kennedy, a Republican from Louisiana, speaks during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, March 3, 2026. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
TWO TOP TRUMP CABINET OFFICIALS GO TO WAR OVER CHINA SPY SCANDAL AMID EXPLOSIVE ACCUSATIONS: REPORT

"I’m more interested in talking to Howard Lutnick and to Scott Bessent. It appears to me — I emphasize, 'appears' — that the Department of Commerce has allowed the Communist Party of China to circumvent our export controls on advanced chips, either that or they didn’t know what they were doing."
"They’re so incompetent, you wouldn’t put them in charge of a food truck."
But, the sharp-tongued Republican senator argued that those in charge are not incompetent but rather "knowingly allowed this to happen."

"Scott Bessent has been saying, 'Stop it.' So I want to get both of them in front of a committee, put them under oath, ask them not to stab each other because I realize they don’t like each other, and let’s get to — let’s answer some hard questions," Kennedy concluded.
He claimed that if Lutnick "is giving our chips away, he needs to stop it."
Kennedy's comments came right before Nvidia's board reinstated Huang as CEO on Monday following his resignation.
The Commerce Department and Treasury Department did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick testifies during a Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies hearing on the Commerce Department 2027 budget request in Washington, DC on April 22, 2026. (Photo by Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Kennedy has called on Lutnick and Bessent to testify before the Senate Banking Committee regarding China reportedly accessing restricted Nvidia chips — even after the Commerce Secretary was warned of U.S. intelligence that Huang was involved in an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
Lutnick is anticipated to appear before the committee following the request.

Kennedy's recent comments come after reports Bessent clashed with Lutnick over the Commerce Department's failure to add major Nvidia customer Megaspeed to a list of companies that may pose risks to U.S. national security. Alice Huang is the Megaspeed executive with whom the Nvidia chief is suspected of having an affair, and is a suspected spy for the CCP.

Sources familiar with the matter told Axios that Lutnick has spent the last year "undoing" other Trump administration officials’ attempts to hold Megaspeed accountable for allegedly illegally diverted U.S. chips to China, citing concerns that such a move could cause U.S.-China trade tensions to surge.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent speaks with reporters at the White House, Wednesday, in Washington, D.C. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)
Amid intense public scrutiny, Huang resigned on Nov. 12.
Following a sharp decline in value following Huang's departure, Trump on Sunday called for Nvidia to reinstate its CEO.
JD VANCE SAYS HE AND TRUMP STILL 'DON'T KNOW' WHETHER ALICE HUANG WAS A CHINESE SPY

Nvidia's board of directors announced Monday morning it is reinstating Huang as president and CEO of the tech giant effective immediately, citing the board feeling "confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk."

title: Rubio ducks questions on Nvidia CEO's reinstatement after reportedly sounding alarm over suspected Chinese spy
summary: President Donald Trump said he spoke directly and indirectly with Nvidia’s board to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang, insisting his return poses no national security risk.
story: Rubio’s silence comes as Trump describes administration’s intervention as key to the NVIDIA board’s decision to bring Huang back.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio declined to address President Donald Trump’s efforts to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive officer at NVIDIA, exiting a press conference without taking any questions on Monday.

"Is Jensen Huang’s reinstatement a national security risk?" Rubio was asked by reporters as he met with the Qatari prime minister at the State Department. He turned around and walked away without answering.

His abrupt departure comes on the heels of statements from Trump, confirming that the president and the vice president had helped persuade NVIDIA to reinstate Huang — despite reported lingering concerns among some of the administration's cabinet members about the company’s efforts to safeguard sensitive intelligence.

A source familiar told Fox News that President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance worked over the weekend to reinstate Huang after they received security briefings and became convinced that Huang did not present a national security threat in his role as CEO. In recent days, Vance worked with figures in Silicon Valley and higher-ups at Nvidia to urge the board to reinstate him, the source said.

The source also said the administration viewed Huang's support for open-source AI as a backstop against major AI companies accruing uncontested capabilities behind closed doors — a rare position among AI executives.
ELON MUSK ISSUES 5-WORD REACTION TO JENSEN HUANG'S REINSTATEMENT

President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio conduct a news conference on Trump's recent trip to China, the Iran war, and other issues, in the White House briefing room on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

"Yeah, the answer is no," Trump told CNBC in an interview when asked about the development and whether Huang could have been reinstated without his input. "I believe my intervention was very important. And I worked with other people, you know, in the administration, JD and Scott and, you know and [Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick]."

Nvidia's board decided to bring back CEO Jensen Huang after he resigned earlier this month following reports of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom The New York Times reported U.S. intelligence identified as a suspected Chinese intelligence asset operating under corporate cover.
But even before that development, Rubio, who also serves as national security advisor, had already singled out Huang and NVIDIA as a possible liability.

According to The New York Times, Rubio oversaw a highly classified memorandum in the spring warning senior administration officials that Huang was in a close relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The Washington Post later reported that Rubio had recast a CIA report in more assertive terms to warn Trump about the relationship, and that a leak of the memo's findings helped set off the chain of events leading to Huang's resignation earlier this month.
In the wake of his resignation, Trump has personally pushed back against the characterization of any threat tied to Huang.

"The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security," Trump wrote in a statement Monday. "The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."

In interviews explaining his reasoning, Trump noted that replacing Huang would have been difficult for the company, likely setting it back in a similar way to other companies that have lost top executives to scandal.
NVIDIA SPY CASE EXPOSES HOW FOREIGN AGENTS TARGET AMERICA’S CORPORATE ELITE: 'HE IS COMPROMISED'
President Donald Trump listens during a news briefing in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House on Nov. 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

"I have watched for a long time the different, you know, scandals and problems and everything. And I've seen some unbelievably talented CEOs get thrown out because, they were kissing somebody inappropriately at a game or something, you know, and I've seen them lose their job, and I've seen the company go through hell for ten years. 15 years. They never got somebody back who was this good, you know?" Trump told CNBC.
"If I didn't get involved, you'd probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come. I've seen it," Trump added.

Trump’s account of his role in Huang’s return clashes with concerns from members of his own Cabinet who have questioned the company’s efforts under Huang’s leadership to implement the security needed to safeguard its sensitive AI information.

In addition to developing cutting-edge AI processing chips used by top U.S. companies, Nvidia also partners closely with the U.S. intelligence community. Earlier this year, Nvidia secured a Department of Defense contract to help develop and deploy classified network capabilities.

"This effort supports the Department's AI Acceleration Strategy by enabling new capabilities across its three core tenets of warfighting, intelligence and enterprise operations," the Pentagon stated in May.

Even as the partnership between Nvidia and the U.S. government has grown, figures like Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have cast doubt on the company’s information safeguards. Bessent has raised concerns about China’s acquisition of some of NVIDIA’s chips against U.S. restrictions, characterizing the company to Fox as having a "culture of noncompliance."
Ahead of Trump’s intervention, Bessent had recommended the company bring on their next CEO from outside the organization.
"We have been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers and we do need answers," Bessent said in a recent interview.

"It behooves NVIDIA to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was. Was there a promiscuous attitude towards this? If it happened, where were the faults? And then they can move on."
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks at Dreamforce 2026 summit in San Francisco, Calif., on Sept. 15, 2026. (Carlos Barria/Reuters)
Bessent and the White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment on whether their concerns about NVIDIA's security scrutiny remain.
Similarly, outgoing Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, also took to social media to wonder if the FBI had evaluated Trump's claim that Huang would not pose a national security threat.
"Again, did the FBI do a defensive briefing of Huang? If not, why not? If so, what did they tell him about the risk? Did he ignore it?"  Cornyn wrote.
Newt Gingrich, the former Speaker of the House, called for lawmakers to exercise an ongoing scrutiny on Huang and NVIDIA.

"There is something profoundly wrong about Jensen Huang having a relationship with a Chinese Communist Spy and helping China get a huge number of very advanced computer chips when that was specifically against the policy of the United States Government and now he is being reinstated as CEO of the most advanced chip-making company in the world," Gingrich wrote in a post of his own.
"Congress should really dig into this as a national security issue of enormous proportions and also a significant failure in the federal bureaucracy."

Democrats cited similar concerns as Bessent, criticizing the president for, in their view, hastily putting his thumb on the scale of Nvidia’s internal deliberative process to benefit a political ally.
Nvidia pledged $25 million to support Trump’s White House ballroom project.

"Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., wrote in a social media post on Monday.
HOUSE DEMS TARGET TRUMP FAMILY, JD VANCE IN SWEEPING NEW INVESTIGATION PUSH

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., turns to an aide during a news conference where he commented on Elon Musk's criticism of President Donald Trump's spending and tax bill, at the Capitol in Washington, Tuesday, June 3, 2025.  (J. Scott Applewhite/AP)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Schumer promised to investigate the relationship between Huang and Trump when Democrats retake control of the Senate in January.

"Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain," Schumer added.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., also criticized Trump's involvement, anticipating Huang's continued influence in Washington, D.C. amid talks on AI legislation.

"This reckless decision to bring back Jensen Huang does not change the fact that Huang and NVIDIA still owe Congress answers. The Trump Administration needs to explain what 'input' was given and by which senior officials to support Huang’s reinstatement. Huang’s return only increases the urgency to pass bipartisan export control bills and make sure NVIDIA does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk," Warren wrote on social media.
Fox News Digital reached out to Nvidia and Huang for additional comment.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Democrats unveil 2028 debate rules with new dark money restrictions — but there's a catch
summary: The DNC's 2028 Democratic primary rules require candidates to denounce dark money from super PACs and 501(c)(4) groups to qualify for 12 debate stages.
story: Democratic strategist John McCarthy discusses the DNC’s new mandatory pledge for 2028 candidates to swear off of dark money in the primary.
The 2028 election season is already off to the races.

The Democratic Party released its rules of engagement for the next presidential primary season on Monday morning, outlining a framework for 12 debates and setting barriers for candidates hoping to compete.
One key rule will have Democratic presidential hopefuls swear off dark money during the course of the primary election.

"In the wake of the Citizens United Supreme Court decision, dark money and independent spending have exploded, increasing the influence of special interests in politics," a press release by the Democratic National Committee (DNC) said. "While the DNC does not have the legal authority to ban super PACs or dark money groups, we are requiring our candidates to denounce their involvement in the Democratic presidential primary, in line with Democratic Party values and our 2024 Platform, in order to qualify for the debate stage."
HOUSE COMMITTEE PASSES FOREIGN FUNDING TRANSPARENCY ACT TO EXPOSE FOREIGN DONATIONS TO NONPROFITS
Democratic presidential candidates arrive on stage for the Democratic presidential primary debate at the Charleston Gaillard Center on Feb. 25, 2020, in Charleston, S.C. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)
That includes money earned by both super PACs and 501(c)(4) nonprofit organizations during the course of the entire primary.
And the rule, according to a framework obtained by Fox News Digital, will rely largely on Democrats' own self-reporting.
Each campaign must designate a go-between with the DNC whose job is to specifically identify and report spending by outside dark money groups.
DEM FUNDRAISING GIANT MAKES DAMNING ADMISSION AS GOP PROBES FOREIGN DONATION ALLEGATIONS
If outside groups spend money on a specific candidate that said candidate did not approve, they must denounce the action to still qualify for primary debates.
Democratic presidential candidates debate each other on NBC News in June 2019 in Miami. (Drew Angerer/Getty Images)
If the candidate does approve or request the spending, they are required to refund those dollars and provide proof of doing so.

"This is a framework, and it's the first step. There's going to be more granularity that comes over the next few months as the field takes shape. So this is kind of the opening of a conversation," Democratic strategist John McCarthy told Fox News Digital on Monday. "I think it's good that we're having this opening of a conversation because it will put pressure on all of the candidates internally to sit and say, we're going to lock arms and embody our values as Democrats."
Asked about whether the emphasis on self-reporting will be a strong enough guardrail given the lack of laws around dark money spending, McCarthy suggested pressure from the party base will help.
"I think if someone doesn't wanna make that pledge, I don't think that they're going to be rewarded by our primary voters as someone who they want to move forward as our nominee," McCarthy said.
And while the pledge explicitly talks about the primary, it leaves open the question of dark money spending in the general election.
DNC Chair Ken Martin makes a speech during the press conference for the DNC site visit at Ball Arena in Denver on May 6, 2026. (Hyoung Chang/The Denver Post via Getty Images)
But McCarthy suggested that it would not hurt whoever the Democrats' eventual nominee will be.
"I think that Democrat-on-Democrat fighting is not going to enhance us for the general election," he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"There needs to be a meaningful debate over ideas. But we need to be the party that's for getting money out of politics. I think any Democrat who you talk to wants to come to the general election as strong as possible and ready to fight with anything it takes. So, you know, I think that people are comfortable with doing whatever it takes to win the general election."
Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

title: 'Failed socialist state': Deep blue state’s lone GOP congressman reveals secret to winning as Democrats sweep
summary: Rep. Cliff Bentz told Fox News Digital that Oregon voters rejected failed progressive policies, blaming high taxes and regulation for hurting business.
story: Rep. Cliff Bentz, R-Oregon, told Fox News Digital that the high cost of living in his state, coupled by what he claims are failed socialist policies ravishing through his communities, drove voters to back him one more in his re-election efforts.

EXCLUSIVE: Oregon's lone Republican congressman told Fox News Digital that voters in his district rejected what he described as the state's "failed" progressive policies, offering the GOP a roadmap for winning back voters after Democrats' midterm sweep.

Rep. Cliff Bentz, R-Ore., who won his fourth term in Congress by over 70,000 votes, with a total of 61% of the vote, made his remarks after securing re-election despite a nationwide Democratic wave that handed Republicans significant losses in Congress and state elections.

"My folks wanted someone that they could depend upon when it comes to protecting business and trying to reverse this horrible trend toward more, in this you have a failed state than anything else," Bentz told Fox News Digital.
FLORIDA CONGRESSMAN DIAGNOSES GOP'S BLUE TSUNAMI LOSSES: 'WE FAILED TO MAKE THEM THINK WE CARED ABOUT THEM'
Rep. Cliff Bentz suggested that "When you're in the minority, you can start calling out the stupidity of the opponent's approach to the economy and to regulation." (Cliff Bentz)

The congressman argued that his continued electoral success stems from highlighting what he considers the economic consequences of Democratic leadership in Oregon, particularly policies enacted in the state capital.
"Crazy, crazy Democrat policies emanating out of Salem, the capital of Oregon," Bentz said, pointing to what he described as "the ridiculous impact of these policies."

Bentz blamed high taxes and progressive regulations for hurting businesses and contributing to Oregon's declining quality of life, arguing that voters are increasingly frustrated with the state's political direction.

Oregon has a 9.9% state income tax rate, a top corporate income tax of 7.6% and a 0.57% corporate activity tax rate, which he believes has driven the local economy to a near collapse. The state legislature has recently enacted policies such as ones that require certain large employers in retail, hospitality and food service to provide advance work schedules, which critics argue limits scheduling flexibility.
REPUBLICANS NEED HISTORY LESSON ABOUT THEIR PARTY IF THEY WANT TO MOVE ON FROM DEFEAT
The Republican also suggested that his party could regain ground nationally by adopting a similar approach, particularly as Republicans prepare to enter the minority in Congress.
Democrats outnumber Republicans by nearly 100 seats in the House, and 10 seats in the Senate.

Ronald Ross, Multnomah County outreach supervisor with the 4D Recovery Center, speaks to a person in a tent about services for those experiencing homelessness and efforts to offer mental health support and treatment for fentanyl addiction in Portland, Oregon on January 24, 2024. (Photo by Patrick T. Fallon/AFP/Getty Images)
"When you're in the minority, you can start calling out the stupidity of the opponent's approach to the economy and to regulation," Bentz told Fox News Digital.
"So you start out by saying, 'Hey, if you want more of this, well, just keep voting for it,'" he continued.
Bentz argued that Republicans should use their time in the minority to highlight the economic consequences of Democratic policies and present themselves as an alternative to progressive governance.
Voters cast their ballots at official ballot boxes on November 8, 2022, in Portland, Oregon. (Photo by Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty Images)

"I think that's hugely important, and that's what I'll be doing in these next two years," Bentz added.

title: GOP senator 'not likely' to mount presidential bid, but continues leaving door open to possibility
summary: Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana is continuing to leave the door open to the possibility of mounting a 2028 bid for the presidency.
story: While Sen. John Kennedy says that he plans to seek re-election, he is leaving the door open to potentially run for president in 2028. (NBC News)

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., is continuing to leave the door open to the possibility of mounting a 2028 presidential bid, though he said that such a move is "not likely" and that he plans to seek re-election.
"My plan right now is to run for re-election," Kennedy told Kristen Welker during an interview that aired on NBC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday.

"If I get fed up with things and catch a wild hair and have a, I don't know, a spontaneous moment of ... questionable genius, if I get really fed up I could run. But it's not likely," he said, noting that he plans to pursue re-election.
DEMOCRATS SIZE UP 2028 IN DENVER. WE ASKED WHO'S READY TO RUN
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Kennedy has served in the Senate since early 2017. His current term ends in early 2029, so if he wants to seek a third Senate term, he will need to run in 2028.
President Donald Trump, who is currently serving his second term, is constitutionally barred from being elected president again.
REPUBLICAN SENATOR OPENS DOOR ON POSSIBILITY OF A PRESIDENTIAL BID, IN SHIFT FROM PAST POSITION
President Donald Trump listens during a news briefing in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House on Nov. 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
During a "Meet the Press" interview that aired last month, Kennedy also told Welker that he planned to seek re-election.
"But as I've said before," he told Welker last month regarding the idea of a presidential run, "if I don't think I can be effective in the Senate anymore I would consider it."
