He said during that appearance in October that if a group of "goobers" runs on his side of the aisle, "and I think I could do a better job, I would consider runnin'. But right now I'm runnin' for re-election."
Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Trump vows to seek death penalty for child killers, rips Newsom’s plan to spare 548 death row inmates
summary: Marc Klaas and other victims' relatives joined President Donald Trump at the Justice Department, urging action against California Gov. Gavin Newsom's plan.
story: The Trump administration vows to implement the death penalty for anyone who murders a member of law enforcement. The administration also honors the families of victims and pledges no compromise on public safety.

FIRST ON FOX — President Donald Trump vowed Monday to direct the Justice Department to seek the death penalty for child murderers and speed up federal executions, as victims’ relatives spoke out at the Justice Department against California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s plan to spare 548 death row inmates.
"We’re here today to talk about one of the most shocking acts of injustice our country has ever seen," Trump said at the Justice Department.
He called the inmates "548 of the most evil monsters on the face of the Earth" and said Newsom "stole away the only closure those families might ever have."
Newsom responded in a video posted on X, telling victims’ families that the inmates would remain behind bars for life under his plan and accusing Trump of using presidential pardons to reward allies.
NEWSOM'S BID TO EMPTY CALIFORNIA'S DEATH ROW COLLIDES WITH VOTERS' REPEATED REJECTION OF ABOLITION
"To the families standing with him today, your grief is real," Newsom said. "That’s why every person, every person on California’s former death row will die in prison. No one walks out."
Newsom called for federal pardon reform, accusing Trump of turning "the power of mercy into a business." He added, "Justice is not for sale, not in California and not in America."

Polly Klaas’ father, Marc Klaas, was among several victims’ relatives who spoke. He told Trump his family had spent three decades believing the death sentence handed down to Richard Allen Davis, who kidnapped Polly from a sleepover at her Petaluma home in 1993, would stand.
According to the White House, family members of these 10 California murder victims attended the press conference alongside President Donald Trump. (Courtesy of the White House)
"While nothing can bring Polly back, her life mattered," Klaas said. "The pain inflicted on our family was real, and the pursuit of justice should not become a political exercise."

Trump said he would sign a presidential directive that would also order federal prosecutors to seek the death penalty for rapists and human traffickers who kill their victims. "Once juries have spoken, capital punishment will be swift and certain," he said.

Among those who would be spared execution under Newsom’s plan are Marcus Wesson, who murdered nine members of his family, Richard Allen Davis, who killed 12-year-old Polly Klaas, and Isauro Aguirre, who tortured and killed 8-year-old Gabriel Fernandez.

Trump said Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, had introduced the Just Punishment for Murder Act at his request. Trump said the bill would write parts of the directive into law and expand federal death penalty policy to cover murderers in the country illegally.
NEWSOM ORDERS CALIFORNIA’S MOST REVILED KILLERS OFF DEATH ROW – 10 OF THE WORST WHO COULD BENEFIT
Newsom released a letter to the victims and their families defending his controversial decision earlier this month. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu, File)
"I’m calling on Congress to send me that bill without delay, and I will sign it," Trump said.

Newsom announced Nov. 5 that he intended to replace all 548 death sentences with life in prison without parole, arguing that capital punishment is incompatible with the state’s values. Trump and several speakers described the commutations as already granted, but the plan has yet to take effect.

Under California’s Constitution, 382 of the proposed commutations require a recommendation from the state Supreme Court because the inmates were convicted of more than one felony. Newsom’s administration has said it will wait for the court to act before proceeding with any of the commutations.
Chester Turner, convicted of murdering 14 women in Los Angeles, and Cary Stayner, convicted of four murders near Yosemite National Park, were also named.

Some of the cases involved the slaughter of entire families. Ramon Salcido was convicted of killing seven people during a Sonoma County rampage, including his wife and two young daughters, while former school administrator Vincent Brothers was convicted of murdering his wife, three children and mother-in-law in Bakersfield.

The White House's intervention comes as Newsom faces mounting opposition from California prosecutors and victims' advocates who argue that his sweeping clemency plan disregards the verdicts of juries and the suffering of families who spent years pursuing justice.
CALIFORNIA DA SAYS GAVIN NEWSOM'S 'CRUEL' DEATH ROW CLEMENCY STABS CRIME VICTIMS 'IN THE HEART'

Convicted murderer Charles Ng enters the Orange County Superior Court in Santa Ana, where a jury recommended that he be put to death for killing 11 people in Northern California in 1984. (Al Schaben/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

Ahead of the event, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital, "Governor Newsom is failing the victims and their families by refusing to carry out justice against these barbaric child killers and serial killers. These murderers raped, tortured and terrorized innocent victims. Governor Newsom must stop playing politics with public safety."

Asked by Fox News Digital about the proposed commutations, Newsom’s office referred reporters to his previously published letter defending the decision. The office did not directly address the individual cases highlighted by the White House. The governor acknowledged that some victims’ families strongly oppose the plan, and his office pointed to other survivors who support ending capital punishment.

"California voters have voted to keep the death penalty on the books, and I respect that," Newsom wrote. "But the constitution also gave every governor clemency authority, and that power exists for moments when law as applied cannot be squared with justice. For me, this is that moment."

At the Justice Department, Sandy Friend recalled how her 8-year-old son Michael Lyons loved fishing, Ninja Turtles, telling campfire stories and bringing her flowers. Michael was walking home from school in Yuba City in 1996 when Robert Boyd Rhoades abducted, tortured and killed him.

Gavin Newsom’s plan to commute California’s 548 death sentences to life without parole drew sharp criticism from President Donald Trump and victims’ relatives at the Justice Department. The proposed commutations have not taken effect and remain subject to legal steps. (Tayfun Coskun/Getty Images)
"Governor Newsom, we deserve to be heard," Friend said.

Placer County Sheriff’s Lt. Jason Davis said his brother, Detective Michael Davis, had been his patrol partner before he was killed in a 2014 crime spree that also took the life of Sacramento County Sheriff’s Deputy Danny Oliver. He told the audience he had forgiven the man who murdered his brother.
"But forgiveness does not eliminate accountability or erase consequences," Davis said.

Gloria Vega told Trump her father, Palm Springs police Officer Gil Vega, was months away from retirement when he and fellow Officer Lesley Zerebny were killed responding to a domestic disturbance in 2016. Trump announced that he would contribute $5,000 to a Trump Account for Vega’s 17-year-old granddaughter in the officer’s honor.

Trump told Friend that people in the room were working "to get this travesty overturned in some form." He gave no specifics about what action his administration might take against the state plan in that exchange.
Later in his remarks, Trump said his administration could find common ground with Democrats on issues such as lowering drug prices and improving health care.
"But when it comes to defending the lives and safety of American people, there can be no compromise," Trump said. "We’re not going to compromise. We’re going to take this right to the end."

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said Monday that he led 14 attorneys general in condemning the plan, arguing that Newsom had overridden juries, courts and California voters. "We stand with victims’ families," Uthmeier wrote on X.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, who introduced Trump, said the Justice Department had sought the death penalty 49 times since Trump returned to office in January 2025. Trump directed the department on his first day back in office to prioritize seeking and carrying out lawful death sentences.
In April, the department announced that it would reinstate its previous lethal injection protocol and expand the available methods for federal executions.

The father of Polly Klaas, Marc Klaas, heavily criticized California Gov. Gavin Newsom amid reports that he is considering a mass commutation of the state's death row inmates. Richard Allen Davis, who was convicted for the 1993 death of Polly Klaas, was sentenced to death by a judge. (Polly Klaas Foundation; AP)

Trump also said he was directing the Department of Housing and Urban Development to require public housing authorities to tighten tenant screening and make it easier to remove tenants who pose a danger. He said the Justice Department would award nearly $150 million in public safety grants to help hire more than 1,000 additional officers and speed up responses to reports of domestic violence and sexual assault.

San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow previously told Fox News Digital he was "just sickened, frankly, for the crime victims in California who were slapped in the face by our governor." Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer accused Newsom of extending "mercy for the wolves … while inflicting the ultimate act of cruelty on the sheep."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

A coalition of California prosecutors and victims’ relatives asked the state Supreme Court last week to halt the plan, arguing that Newsom failed to give families a chance to be heard before pursuing the commutations. The court invited additional briefs through Tuesday, Nov. 24, and Newsom asked the justices to act before his term ends in January.

California voters rejected measures to abolish the death penalty in 2012 and 2016. The state last carried out an execution in 2006, and Newsom imposed a moratorium shortly after taking office in 2019.Fox News Digital's Louis Casiano contributed to this reporting.
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: Trump's Thanksgiving turkeys arrive at luxury DC hotel as Americans vote on their names
summary: Two turkeys raised on a West Virginia farm strutted a red carpet at the Willard InterContinental Washington, D.C., ahead of Tuesday's pardon.
story: ‘Fox & Friends Weekend’ dives into the historical tradition of pardoning turkeys before Thanksgiving.
Talk about talking turkey.

Two feathered VIPs have checked into one of Washington's most luxurious hotels, complete with plush beds, a red-carpet welcome and a crowd of eager photographers, ahead of President Donald Trump's annual Thanksgiving turkey pardon at the White House.

The presidential hopefuls arrived Sunday at the historic Willard InterContinental Washington, D.C., where they were photographed strutting across a red carpet, posing for pictures and standing atop the hotel's beds before their big day on the South Lawn.
THE PENNSYLVANIA FARM BEHIND A WHITE HOUSE THANKSGIVING TURKEY TRADITION

Two Thanksgiving turkeys make themselves at home on separate beds at Washington's luxurious Willard InterContinental hotel ahead of President Donald Trump's annual White House turkey pardon on Nov. 24, 2026. (Courtesy of USDA via X)

The U.S. Department of Agriculture celebrated their arrival on X, announcing a "SPECIAL DELIVERY TO WASHINGTON, D.C.!" and describing the birds as "two VERY special guests" receiving the presidential treatment.

Photographs shared by the USDA, credited to the White House and National Turkey Federation, showed the plump white birds making their grand entrance before an audience of hotel guests and photographers. One turkey was even pictured riding through the hotel's ornate hallways inside a travel crate perched on a brass luggage cart.
The pair appeared equally comfortable with the accommodations, with one bird spreading its feathers atop a neatly made bed while its companion stood nearby.
But before the turkeys meet the commander in chief, Americans have been invited to settle a pressing matter of national importance: What should they be called?
SOCIAL MEDIA USERS ARE EATING HUGE AMOUNTS OF CARROTS AND SHRIMP FOR A NATURAL TAN

Two Thanksgiving turkeys strut down the red carpet at the historic Willard InterContinental hotel in Washington, D.C., on Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026, ahead of President Donald Trump's annual White House turkey pardon. (Courtesy of USDA via X)
The White House launched an online contest offering three possible combinations: "Commander & Chief," "Freedom & Feathers" and "Honey & Ham."

Voting on the names closed Sunday at 5 p.m. ET, with the winning pair expected to be announced before a second round of voting opens Monday at 8 a.m. That final vote will determine which turkey receives the official ceremonial pardon.
The birds, raised by American turkey farmers Scott and Becky Rightsell at Deans Gap Farm in West Virginia, have already received their own playful presidential biographies.

Both hatched July 15, but their tastes apparently differ. According to the White House, one enjoys Golden Delicious apples and scenic country drives, while the other prefers Dr Pepper and dreams of vacationing in Aggieland.

The pair was selected from a larger flock based on appearance and temperament, according to West Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey's office. Their preparations included getting accustomed to crowds, camera lights and noise.

And for Americans who cannot get enough turkey-related excitement, the White House has unveiled "Gobble Getaway," an online game challenging players to help a turkey dodge a chef armed with a net and roasting pan while making its way across the South Lawn to the pardon podium.
The annual Thanksgiving tradition dates back to 1947, when the National Turkey Federation first presented a holiday bird to President Harry Truman.
FOX NEWS MEDIA KICKS OFF HOLIDAY SEASON WITH SEVENTH ANNUAL ALL-AMERICAN CHRISTMAS TREE LIGHTING

One of President Donald Trump's Thanksgiving turkeys gets a ride on a hotel luggage cart at the Willard InterContinental in Washington, D.C., ahead of Tuesday's presidential turkey pardon. (Courtesy of USDA via X)
President John F. Kennedy spared a gift turkey in 1963, while President George H.W. Bush established the formal presidential turkey pardon in 1989.
Trump and first lady Melania Trump are scheduled to participate in this year's ceremony on Tuesday, Nov. 24, at 2 p.m. ET on the White House South Lawn.
Although the public gets to vote on which turkey receives the ceremonial pardon, both birds are traditionally spared the Thanksgiving dinner table.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
For now, the pair can enjoy their luxury accommodations and newfound celebrity status, knowing their next stop is 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue rather than the oven.
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: New York Dem addresses bizarre 'lizard people' claims after viral clip behind Mamdani
summary: New York Assemblyman Jordan J.G. Wright breaks silence on viral reptilian claims after a clip showed him rolling his eyes behind Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
story: A clip showing New York Democratic Assemblyman Jordan J.G. Wright making an unusual eye movement while standing behind Zohran Mamdani during a press conference has sparked wild "lizard people" conspiracy theories online. (Credit: Mayor Mamdani)

A Democratic New York City assemblyman addressed bizarre "lizard people" conspiracy theories after a viral video appeared to show his eyes rolling backward while standing behind Mayor Zohran Mamdani during a press conference.
Jordan J.G. Wright was spotted during a press conference behind Mamdani on Friday, when the city announced plans to eventually shut down Rikers Island.
As Mamdani spoke, Wright appeared to flash a slight grin before blinking and rolling his eyes in a circular motion toward the back of his head, prompting a wave of bizarre speculation online.
"I have no idea what was going on in that video. I’m really not sure," Wright told the New York Post in a statement.
NYC MAYOR MAMDANI ANNOUNCES DELAYED PLAN TO CLOSE CITY'S LARGEST JAIL
A New York City assemblyman is addressing bizarre speculation about his humanity after an unusual eye movement behind Mayor Zohran Mamdani went viral. (ABC 7)

He added that his work as an assemblyman speaks to his human character, pointing to a project he championed in Harlem that serves as the city's first community-based center dedicated to climate action. The five-story hub provides residents with environmental education and advocacy.

"Obviously I’m a human being, and my humanity can be seen through my legislation like the $4 million for the WE ACT environmental justice center in Harlem," he said. "I can’t speak to any reptiles or aliens."

The video sent social media users into a frenzy over the weekend, reigniting a decades-old conspiracy theory that extraterrestrial reptilians secretly control the Earth by disguising themselves as world leaders and celebrities to manipulate society.

"This is how lizards blink… I am pretty sure there is full-blown ‘Men in Black’ aliens walking among us disguised as human beings, and they are hiding in plain sight," one social media user said, according to the Post.
NYC SUSPECT IN CHINATOWN FATAL BEATING HAD 5 OPEN CASES AS MAMDANI PUSHES PLAN TO CLOSE RIKERS
Jordan Wright says he is human after a viral video from Zohran Mamdani’s Rikers Island press conference sparked a bizarre reptilian conspiracy. (ABC 7)
Another X user suggested the clip showed that aliens were becoming increasingly brazen about revealing themselves to the public.
"The ‘reptile’ is standing right behind Mamdani, as he announces a full scale-release of dangerous prisoners from NYC jails," the X user said.
"The aliens are not even bothering to hide themselves anymore. They intend to create so much chaos on Earth, that we will be unable to defend ourselves," the user added.
The discussion also spilled onto Reddit, where some users questioned whether Wright was human.
"Yes, the guy in the back is a reptilian, 100%" the Reddit user said.
MAMDANI IGNITES ONLINE FIRESTORM AFTER MOURNING DEATH OF INMATE CHARGED IN GRISLY MURDER: 'WTF ARE WE DOING?'

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks with inmates on Rikers Island on July 15, 2026, in New York. Mamdani announced plans to close Rikers Island by 2032 and move remaining detainees to four smaller borough-based jails. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig)
Wright, the son of former Assemblyman Keith L.T. Wright and grandson of former New York Supreme Court Judge Bruce Wright, represents New York's 70th Assembly District in Harlem.

He was reelected without opposition in November after defeating Democratic socialist Conrad Blackburn in the Democratic primary in June. His legislative priorities include affordable housing, health care access and public safety, according to his profile.
A lifelong New Yorker and Central Harlem resident, Wright graduated from Syracuse University in 2017 with a degree in psychology.
Wright stood behind Mamdani on Friday as the mayor announced plans to cut New York City's jail population by 2,500 inmates over the next five years and close the city’s largest jail by 2032.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The remaining inmates, estimated at 4,100 detainees, will be moved to four new, smaller borough-based jails opening in Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens and the Bronx.
Fox News Digital reached out to Jordan J.G. Wright for comment.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Democrats clinch historic House majority as Chuck Hubbard defeats longtime GOP Rep. Virginia Foxx
summary: Democrats secured their largest House majority since 1992, setting up clashes with Trump over investigations, health care and Republican policies.
story: President Donald Trump expresses surprise at the results of the 2026 midterm elections after it is projected Democrats will take control of the U.S. House and Senate on ‘FOX News Democracy 26.’

Democrats have stormed back into power in the House, securing the largest majority of any party since 1992 in a sweeping midterm victory that will reshape the balance of power in Washington and leave Republicans with significantly less influence over the chamber.

The victory was cemented after Democrat Chuck Hubbard was elected to the House from North Carolina, according to The Associated Press (AP). He defeated longtime Republican incumbent Rep. Virginia Foxx, who chaired the powerful House Rules Committee, which determines which bills reach the House floor for a vote.

With several general election results still being called, Democrats have picked up 44 seats so far, giving them at least 258 seats in the House, their largest majority in more than three decades, according to The AP.
STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE
FILE — Democrats secured at least 258 House seats, their largest majority since 1992, with four races still undecided. (Chip Somodevilla)
Meanwhile, Republicans have been left with at least 173 seats.
Four House races remain undecided in Minnesota, Tennessee and two December runoffs in Louisiana, according to The AP.

The party's projected majority will surpass its post-election totals in every election since Bill Clinton first won the presidency in 1992, when Democrats secured 258 seats, the outlet said. The party's next-largest showing reportedly came in 2008, when Barack Obama was elected president and Democrats won 257 House seats.
The shift in the 435-member House will set the stage for a dramatic power struggle in Washington.
WHAT THE 2026 MIDTERM RESULTS MEAN FOR CAPITOL HILL
Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated longtime Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx (pictured), who chaired the powerful House Rules Committee. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
Democrats are also poised to take control of the Senate, where they secured a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their largest advantage in more than a decade.

Democrats scored some of their biggest victories in traditionally competitive states and Republican strongholds alike, including Texas, Georgia, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina.
BLUE WAVE NEARLY SWALLOWED SOME OF AMERICA'S REDDEST STATES AS ELECTION DATA EXPOSES GOP'S CLOSE CALLS
FILE — President Donald Trump faces a Democratic-controlled Congress poised to investigate his administration and challenge his legislative agenda. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images)

President Donald Trump will face a new legislative reality when the next Congress convenes in January, with Democrats preparing to launch a flurry of investigations targeting his administration and its Republican allies in Congress.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The party's 100-day agenda will also focus on rolling back Republican policies, with top priorities including reversing GOP Medicaid cuts and restoring Affordable Care Act tax credits that Republicans allowed to expire, The AP said.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Trump warns of new strikes against Iran after new year, calls negotiators ‘professional tap dancers’
summary: President Donald Trump calls Iran's negotiators "professional tap dancers" and dismisses talks with Tehran as meaningless while the naval blockade holds.
story: Fox News Chief Congressional correspondent Trey Yingst joins 'Fox News Live' to weigh in on President Trump's remarks after new Iran aerial attacks targeted U.S. military facilities.

President Donald Trump is warning that he is inclined to order military strikes against Iran after the new year if the two countries fail to reach an agreement, dismissing ongoing diplomatic talks with Tehran as meaningless.
In exclusive comments Sunday to Fox News, the president accused Iranian negotiators of stalling while continuing to escalate hostilities following the U.S. elections.
TRUMP KEEPS SIGNALING AN END TO IRAN WAR, BUT EXPERT WARNS A CRUCIAL PIECE OF HIS STRATEGY IS MISSING

If negotiations with Iran collapse, the U.S. is likely to move quickly to degrade Tehran’s military capabilities — a campaign analysts say would begin with missile systems, naval assets and command networks before escalating to more controversial targets. (Yuri Gripas/Abaca/Bloomberg via Getty Images:  Sasan / Middle East Images / AFP via Getty Images)
"They’re more aggressive now than before the election," Trump said, characterizing Iranian officials as "professional tap dancers."
"They talk all the time, all they do is talk, but it’s all b------," he added.

The remarks come as the U.S. maintains a naval blockade of Iranian ports amid broader conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, and as Trump predicted that tit-for-tat strikes will continue between American and Iranian forces.
PROTESTERS CALL FOR REGIME CHANGE IN IRAN FOLLOWING DEADLY CRASH THAT KILLED 13 OIL AND GAS WORKERS
Trump also dared Tehran to challenge the U.S. naval siege.
"I hope they do, they’ll all be at the bottom of the sea like the rest of the navy," Trump said regarding the possibility of Iranian forces testing the blockade.

Meanwhile, anti-government demonstrations have flared up again in several Iranian cities. Asked about the renewed unrest inside the country, Trump offered a direct message to demonstrators on the ground: "Keep protesting."

title: Trump says it would be 'hard' to work with Chuck Schumer: 'He will fail again'
summary: President Donald Trump says it will be "hard" to work with Chuck Schumer as Senate majority leader, claiming the Democratic leader will "fail again."
story: Political strategists Tiffany Smiley and Al Mottur join 'The Faulkner Focus' to analyze the growing progressive push for a sweeping legislative agenda on Capitol Hill. The panel debates whether Sen. Chris Van Hollen's challenge against Sen. Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader exposes deep fractures within the Democratic Party or represents a routine internal disagreement.
President Donald Trump predicted it would be "hard" to work with Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., if he is chosen to continue leading Senate Democrats next year.

Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sunday that Schumer is likely to "fail again" if he is elected. Schumer is running for Senate majority leader once again, but opposition to his leadership is gaining steam.

"It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader. He failed badly as 'Leader' once before, one of the worst in history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again," Trump wrote.
DEMOCRATS TURN ON SCHUMER AFTER HISTORIC ELECTION WINS AS POTENTIAL CHALLENGER EMERGES

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., speaks during a press conference at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 4, 2026, a day after Democrats claimed a majority in the Senate following the midterm elections. (AFP via Getty Images)
"All he did was perpetuate the Russia, Russia, Russia Hoax, and many other Hoaxes and Scams, making my victory in 2024 an easy and glorious one. Here we go again!" he added.
CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER'

Schumer's main challenger is Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who represents a more radical wing of the party. His base of support includes Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who caucuses with Senate Democrats; Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., and Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan, both progressives whom Schumer did not initially back in their respective races.
President Donald Trump
SCHUMER'S FORMER ALLY MOUNTS LEADERSHIP CHALLENGE AS DEMOCRATS FACE RARE INTERNAL POWER STRUGGLE
Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., also threw her support behind Van Hollen last week.
Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade as both minority and majority leader, so far has 15 senators in his camp, according to previous Fox News Digital reporting.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., speaks as he campaigns for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed during a campaign rally in Ferndale, Michigan, July 25, 2026. (Rebecca Cook/Reuters)

The longtime Democratic leader has remained confident, but quiet, about his chances of retaining his job, posting shortly after Van Hollen’s announcement last week that he welcomed "discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead," and that he has "the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader."
Fox News' Hanna Panreck contributed to this report.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: Progressives unveil $25 minimum wage push to solve affordability crisis despite economist inflation warning
summary: House Democrats push a $25 minimum wage to fight the affordability crisis, but Heritage economist E.J. Antoni warns it could raise costs and unemployment.
story: Reps. Everton Blair, R-Ga., and Delia Ramirez, D-Il., told Fox News Digital that raising the minimum wage to $25 is a crucial step in solving the affordability crisis, while dismissing concerns that their desired minimum wage could raise inflation.

House Democrats are pushing to raise the federal minimum wage to $25 an hour, calling the current hourly pay a "remnant of slavery" to "oppress women," despite warnings from conservative economists that the proposal could drive up costs and threaten jobs.

The proposal from the Congressional Progressive Caucus would more than triple the current $7.25 federal minimum wage, raising questions about its potential impact on businesses and workers in states with significantly lower living costs than major cities.

"We should be rallying around (a minimum wage of) $25 at minimum, and it should be cost adjusted for inflation, so that people can have a job that enables them to survive and thrive," Rep. Everton Blair Jr., D-Ga., told Fox News Digital.
The push for higher federal wage mandates is fueling debate among economists over potential trade-offs that could harm American workers and businesses. (Kathleen Flynn/Bloomberg/Getty Images)
AOC-BACKED $25 MINIMUM WAGE PLAN SOUNDS GREAT — BUT AT WHAT COST?
Asked whether a nationwide $25 minimum wage could hurt workers and businesses in lower-cost states, Blair argued that the proposed rate should serve as a national baseline.
The congressman said $25 an hour should be "the floor" and "should be higher in places with a higher cost of living."
Blair acknowledged concerns that raising the minimum wage could contribute to inflation but said lawmakers must find a way to increase workers' earnings while "keeping people afloat."
Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., echoed Blair's support for the proposal, pointing to the high cost of living in cities such as Seattle and Washington, D.C., as justification for raising wages.
Rep. Delia Ramirez attends a news conference on June 30, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
DEMOCRATS SEIZE ON MIDTERM WINS TO PUSH MASSIVE MINIMUM WAGE HIKES, BUT ECONOMISTS SEE TROUBLE AHEAD
"The truth is that the boogeyman, the corporations, don't want to pay their workers liveable wages," Ramirez told Fox News Digital.

Heritage Foundation chief economist E.J. Antoni warned that a $25 federal minimum wage could increase costs and unemployment, arguing that the economic consequences would extend beyond major metropolitan areas.
"Whenever a price floor on labor is set above the market equilibrium, a surplus of labor is created. In this case, we call that surplus unemployment," Antoni told Fox News Digital.
DEMOCRATS PLOT MASSIVE SPENDING SPREE AFTER MIDTERM ROUT — AND TRUMP COULD HELP THEM PULL IT OFF

Despite those warnings, progressive lawmakers expressed confidence that the proposal could gain support from Democratic leadership in both chambers and potentially reach President Donald Trump's desk.
"There's a widespread coalition of folks in the Democratic caucus who have long been saying that one job should be enough to pay the bill," Blair told Fox News Digital.
Ramirez also expressed cautious optimism about the possibility of Trump signing the legislation, pointing to his previous willingness to discuss bipartisan immigration reform.
She said she "never knows what the president might or might not be willing to do."
SANDERS-AOC BACKED PROGRESSIVE DEBUTS FEDERAL $25 MINIMUM WAGE BILL WITH COALITION OF 100+ ORGANIZATIONS
The strategy reflects a broader push to drive loyalty as consumers pull back on discretionary spending, according to reports. (Eric Thayer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The Living Wage for All coalition, which joined lawmakers in unveiling the proposal, says support for a $25 minimum wage extends beyond Democratic voters.

"Not a blue wave," the coalition said, citing polling it claimed showed 63% of Republicans support a $25 federal minimum wage. "There is a blue collar demand that says that this is how we address the affordability crisis."

Coalition members also drew comparisons between the history of minimum-wage policies and slavery-era labor practices, arguing that the current wage system has historically disadvantaged women and marginalized workers.

The proposal comes as Democrats prepare to advance their affordability agenda in the 120th Congress, with progressives seeking to make higher wages a central component of the party's economic platform.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Neither House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., nor the White House responded to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

title: DHS, Dem officials clash after ICE arrest at Seattle airport
summary: DHS says a passenger threw hot coffee at ICE officers during a Seattle airport arrest of a visa overstay, as Washington Democrats blast the operation.
story: Video shows federal officials detaining illegal immigrants who allegedly overstayed their visas, leading to Democrat Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson saying enforcing the law is "out of control."  (John Gaedeke via Storyful; KOMONEWS via AP)

Federal officials and Washington state Democrats are at odds after ICE officers arrested two prospective airline travelers – both accused of overstaying visas and one accused of throwing hot coffee at agents – on a Seattle airport jetway Saturday morning.
"This violence must end," the Department of Homeland Security fired back on X, responding to Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson saying, "ICE is completely and totally out of control."

The operation began around 8:05 a.m. PT as travelers boarded an Alaska Airlines flight, according to the Department of Homeland Security. DHS says ICE officers targeted Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, whom the agency described as a Mexican national "who overstayed his visa." During the arrest, other travelers began getting in the officers' way, and one passenger threw hot coffee at the agents, DHS said.
TLAIB MOVES TO BLOCK ICE AIRPORT ARRESTS, SAYS TSA HELPING TARGET IMMIGRANTS

At his Saturday news conference, Democrat Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called video of the incident "horrific" and "chilling," adding that he told Alaska Airlines representatives that "they need to call on ICE to get out of our airports." (John Gaedeke via Storyful; KOMONEWS via AP)

"The individual who threw the hot coffee was identified as Sofia Hernandez Mejia, an illegal alien from Mexico and visa overstay," DHS wrote on X. "She was subsequently arrested as well. She will be charged with assaulting a federal officer."

The attorney representing Mejia disputed DHS' characterization in a statement shared with Fox News."She is not a U.S. citizen and was in the process of adjusting her status. It is pending with USCIS," Olia Catala said in a statement. "Yes, her entry into the United States was lawful. She subsequently had pending asylum status, later married a U.S. citizen, and was undergoing the legal process to adjust her status."
The post came in response to Ferguson, who claimed law enforcement removing suspected illegal immigrants from flights is "creating chaos in our communities."

"ICE is completely and totally out of control," Ferguson wrote on X, making no mention to the alleged assault of the officers. "Like many Americans, I’m outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities."
BORDER CZAR TOM HOMAN FIRES BACK AFTER DEMOCRAT CHRIS MURPHY CLAIMS ICE IS ‘TERRORIZING LITTLE KIDS’

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., has designs on using her leverage in Congress to curb federal immigration law enforcement, while Republicans and Trump administration officials have long rebuked Democrat efforts to curb enforcement versus changing the laws already on the books. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Ferguson even suggested airlines should push federal immigration agents out of the airport, which has been under stress from this month's nationwide ground stop and rooting out security threats during the busy holiday travel season.

"This morning, masked ICE agents terrorized our community, dragging at least one woman on the ground and arresting her as she was in line to board her flight," Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., wrote on X. "This behavior is totally unacceptable. Violent arrests are the hallmark of fascist states, not a democracy."

At his Saturday news conference, Ferguson called video of the incident "horrific" and "chilling," adding that he told Alaska Airlines representatives that "they need to call on ICE to get out of our airports." He said he plans to make the same request of every other airline operating out of the Seattle and Tacoma airport.

DHS and Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials have been agitated by protesters and efforts to halt the Trump administration's detention efforts, sometimes creating deadly circumstances and exchanges between federal officers and agitators.
DEMS SHAMED AS DHS BRINGS ICE SHOOTING RECEIPTS AFTER POLITICIAN CALLED ICE OFFICERS ‘LIARS WITH MASKS’
DHS defended the agents and pointed to what it described as a surge in violence against federal officers, citing DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin's directive on prosecutions.

"Assaulting and obstructing law enforcement is a crime and a felony," the DHS X post continued. "Secretary Mullin has been clear: anyone who assaults or obstructs law enforcement will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. Our brave law enforcement is facing more than a 1,600% increase in assaults, 300% increase in vehicular attacks, and an 8,000% increase in death threats against them. This violence must end."

Democrats ran on affordability in the midterm elections, but Jayapal vows to work to end immigration enforcement operations, taking the fight from American streets and airports to the House and Senate.
'SQUAD' DEMOCRAT SLAMMED BY TRUMP ADMIN FOR MOST 'RADICAL' PLAN TARGETING ICE YET

"Soon, Democrats will take back control of Congress and we will continue the critical work to rein in these out of control agents and hold them accountable," her X post continued, expressing concern for the illegals who overstayed their visa versus the law enforcement officers attacked during an obstruction. "My heart goes out to those directly affected, and the passengers and airline workers whom ICE traumatized today."
Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson, a democratic socialist, called efforts to enforce immigration law "un-American."
"I am outraged by videos of masked ICE agents causing chaos and dragging a woman off the jetway at Sea-Tac airport," she wrote Saturday on X. "These tactics are unacceptable and un-American."
Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., called federal law enforcement "a profound threat to our community."

"This morning, masked ICE agents detained at least one passenger waiting to board an Alaska Airlines flight at Sea-Tac Airport," he wrote on X. "The masked agents forcibly dragged the individual off the jet bridge, taking them into custody. Let me be clear: this is absolutely unacceptable.

"ICE’s conduct across our country is putting people in harm’s way, undermining public trust, and stoking fear in our communities. I am incredibly concerned about the conduct of immigration enforcement and believe that ICE is operating as a paramilitary force that is a profound threat to our community. There is no question that this agency needs to be reined in before causing more chaos and fear."
DEMOCRAT COMPARES ICE TO 'DOMESTIC TERRORISTS' AS 111 HOUSE DEMS DEMAND TEXAS DETENTION CENTER CLOSE
Alaska Airlines said it had no advance warning of the enforcement action and moved many affected passengers onto other flights.

"Alaska Airlines was not provided advance notice of the enforcement action and we are working to understand the circumstances surrounding what occurred," the airline said in a statement, adding it is "concerned" by the federal action.

Union leaders representing airport workers also criticized the timing of the arrests ahead of a busy travel week. April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, called the operation a "smash-and-grab" action that injected fear and chaos into the terminal.

title: 'Crazy': Moderates fear Dem leadership promised far-left reparations and ICE demands in turn of votes
summary: House Democrats are split as progressives' push to abolish ICE and reparations for descendants of slavery, while moderates warn it may hurt affordability.
story: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., told Fox News Digital she hopes to work with President Donald Trump on a stock trading ban and healthcare, while leaving the door open to a potential presidential run.

Progressive House Democrats believe party leaders could use their newly won majority to back their far-left agenda on such matters as reparations and abolishing ICE, despite pushback from moderates concerned about the party's direction.

Newly elected Democratic Caucus Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., and progressive lawmakers told Fox News Digital that proposals to abolish ICE, expand deportation protections and pursue slavery reparations will be part of the party's legislative discussions under Speaker-nominee Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., despite concerns from moderates that the agenda could distract from affordability.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and other House Democrats attend the hearing on "Americans impacted by service cuts, mass firings and healthcare price hikes," due to the government shutdown in the Capitol Visitor Center on Oct. 22, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
‘SQUAD’ MEMBER ANNOUNCES ‘MAJORITY PRIORITIES’ INCLUDING REPARATIONS, ABOLISHING ICE AFTER BLUE WAVE
"Jeffries has been very clear, he wants to make sure everyone in the caucus is well represented," Rep. Sara Jacobs, D-Calif., a member of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, told Fox News Digital.
Lieu told Fox News Digital that he is "excited" to have "discussions on everything" with members of the caucus, including proposals involving reparations and abolishing ICE.

The California Democrat said he would also be willing to consider other priorities of Rep. Ayanna Presley, D-Mass., including Medicare for All, "abortion justice" and extending Temporary Protected Status for Third World migrants.
Rep. Ted Lieu speaks during a press conference at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Feb. 3, 2026. (Matt McClain/The Washington Post)
'SQUAD' MEMBER URGES DEMS TO TAKE ADVANTAGE OF MIDTERM SWEEP BY PASSING FAR-LEFT POLICIES

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., a prominent supporter of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), told Fox News Digital that progressives and Jeffries have found common ground on several priorities outlined in Pressley's agenda, including expanding healthcare access and public housing.

"Of course, there are going to be areas where leader Jeffries and DSA are going to be in strong opposition, but there are also areas like expanding Medicaid, public housing, and housing issues in general, where there are shared values that unite everybody," Ocasio-Cortez, a potential 2028 presidential contender, told Fox News Digital.

Ocasio-Cortez has also begun working with Democratic leadership on the House Energy and Commerce Committee to advance her healthcare priorities, a senior congressional democratic staffer told Fox News Digital.

However, moderate Democrats were skeptical that party leadership would embrace the progressive agenda, with some questioning whether Jeffries and other leaders had promised to consider those demands in exchange for support during the leadership elections.

"Our agenda is to focus on costs," Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., told Fox News Digital. "What's clear is we had an overwhelming majority. I think some of my colleagues seem to be unhappy with winning in a place we've never won before."
Gottheimer accused progressive colleagues of wanting to "squawk and complain and make their demands" rather than focus on the issues that helped Democrats win the midterm elections.

The New Jersey Democrat also rejected proposals to "defund police, have open borders, or get rid of the United States Senate," arguing that neither he nor Democratic leadership would support such policies.
HAKEEM JEFFRIES REJECTS MEDICARE FOR ALL, DSA AGENDA AS RO KHANNA CALLS HEALTH PLAN 'MOST IMPORTANT PRIORITY'
Rep. Ayanna Pressley takes to the stage at an election night party for Gov. Maura Healey and Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll on Nov. 3, 2026. (Jessica Rinaldi/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)

"The DSA, they have their own agenda," Gottheimer said.
RADICAL SOCIALIST WING'S HUGE NIGHT REVEALS ASCENDING CLOUT WITHIN DEMOCRATIC PARTY
Another Democratic lawmaker, who requested anonymity, told Fox News Digital that they and a longtime colleague viewed the prospect of leadership adopting the progressive agenda as "crazy."
The lawmaker also speculated that Lieu and Jeffries were expressing openness to progressive proposals to avoid opposition during Wednesday's leadership elections.

title: Google AI smartwatch could flag high blood pressure
summary: Google's AI used smartwatch sensors to spot hypertension without a blood pressure cuff, but the Nature study found it missed about 1 in 3 cases.
story: Eko Health co-founder and CEO Connor Landgraf discusses how their AI-powered stethoscope is revolutionizing cardiac care and improving patient outcomes. This innovative device amplifies heart and lung sounds, analyzes them in real-time and detects early signs of heart disease and arrhythmias in just 15 seconds. The technology offers physicians consistent, reliable insights, enhancing early diagnosis and intervention.

When was the last time you checked your blood pressure? If you're like a lot of people, it probably happened during your last doctor's appointment. And if you feel perfectly healthy, you may not give it another thought. That's what makes high blood pressure so concerning. You can have it for years without noticing anything wrong.

Now, Google researchers are exploring a way to uncover that hidden danger using something many of us already wear on our wrists. In a new study recently published in Nature, researchers demonstrated an artificial intelligence system that can identify signs of hypertension using standard smartwatch sensors. It works in the background without requiring calibration with a traditional blood pressure cuff.

The technology uses sensors that already exist in consumer smartwatches. That could make early detection much more accessible. However, the research also reveals a limitation that anyone relying on a smartwatch for health information should understand.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. SMARTWATCH AFIB ALERT SENDS DAD TO ER BEFORE HEART SURGERY
Google's Health Guardian feature tracks blood pressure trends over time and can flag potentially elevated levels without providing actual blood pressure readings. (Google)
How Google AI detects high blood pressure using a smartwatch
Your smartwatch already knows quite a bit about your body. It can track your heart rate throughout the day. Depending on the model, it may also detect irregular heart rhythms.

Google's new AI takes the information collected by those sensors and looks for signs of something harder to detect: ongoing high blood pressure. According to Google Research, the system analyzes two types of sensor data.

The first sensor uses light to detect changes in blood volume beneath your skin. It's the same basic technology many watches use to monitor your pulse. The second sensor measures movement. Researchers found that it can also capture incredibly small vibrations caused by your heart pumping blood. You wouldn't notice those vibrations. However, the AI can analyze them alongside your pulse patterns to look for signs associated with hypertension.

The system collects information over multiple days. It then combines those patterns with your height to estimate the likelihood of sustained high blood pressure. Unlike a traditional monitor, the smartwatch doesn't produce a reading such as 120 over 80. Instead, it looks for signs that your blood pressure may be consistently elevated. What's interesting is that you wouldn't have to do anything differently. You could go about your day while your smartwatch quietly looks for potential warning signs.
Google's smartwatch AI study reveals promising results

Google worked with researchers from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School to develop and test the system. First, researchers trained the underlying AI using nearly 500,000 hours of smartwatch sensor data collected from 2,109 consenting participants. They then evaluated the hypertension detection system in a clinical study involving 196 participants across five U.S. locations. None of those participants had known cardiovascular disease or were taking blood pressure medication.

During the study, participants wore a consumer smartwatch for seven days. Researchers compared the AI's findings with results from 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring. That medical test uses a cuff to measure blood pressure repeatedly throughout the day and night. Doctors use it to help confirm hypertension.
During initial screening, the results showed:

65.8% sensitivity: The AI correctly identified nearly two-thirds of participants who had hypertension.90% specificity: The system correctly classified 90% of participants who did not have hypertension.80.6% positive predictive value: Among participants the AI flagged as having hypertension, about four out of five actually had the condition.
65.8% sensitivity: The AI correctly identified nearly two-thirds of participants who had hypertension.
90% specificity: The system correctly classified 90% of participants who did not have hypertension.
80.6% positive predictive value: Among participants the AI flagged as having hypertension, about four out of five actually had the condition.

For comparison, initial blood pressure screenings performed in medical offices identified 55.3% of participants with hypertension in the study. That's an encouraging result. However, the difference between the smartwatch and office screening was not statistically significant, according to a Nature Portfolio summary of the findings. There's another number worth paying attention to.
The AI missed roughly one in three participants who had hypertension during initial screening.
That's a number worth paying attention to. After all, we're talking about a condition that can lead to a heart attack or stroke, often without any warning signs.

Researchers also looked at a smaller group of 48 people who had elevated blood pressure readings during their initial doctor's visit. In that group, the AI correctly identified 78.4% of those with ongoing hypertension. It also correctly ruled out the condition in 90.9% of those who didn't have it. Those results are encouraging, but there's still work to do. Google needs to test the technology on more people before we can know how reliably it can detect high blood pressure.
MICROSOFT AI BEATS DOCTORS IN SIMULATED DIAGNOSIS TEST

Google's AI analyzes pulse patterns and tiny vibrations from the heart using smartwatch sensors to identify possible signs of high blood pressure. (Andreswd via Getty; Justin Chin/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Can your Pixel Watch detect high blood pressure today?

Here's where things get interesting for people who already own a Google smartwatch. Google introduced its Health Guardian features in September 2026. Among them is a blood pressure trends feature available through the Google Health app.

According to Google's September announcement, blood pressure trends are available at no additional subscription cost on eligible Pixel Watch 3, Pixel Watch 4 and Pixel Watch 5 devices. Availability depends on your region.

The feature analyzes pulse and movement patterns over time. Then, it provides a monthly assessment of whether your blood pressure trend appears high. Google says these existing Health Guardian capabilities are informed by clinical research, including work connected to its newly published findings. However, there's an important difference between the experimental system described in Nature and the feature available on your watch today.

The existing Pixel Watch feature is intended for general wellness. Google specifically says it cannot diagnose hypertension or serve as a medical screening tool. It also cannot tell you your actual systolic or diastolic blood pressure numbers. According to Google's support documentation, the feature provides a monthly trend assessment such as "High" or "Not high."

And a "Not high" result doesn't guarantee your blood pressure is normal. Google also warns users against relying on these estimates to change medications or treatment plans. Meanwhile, the newly published research remains exploratory. Google has not announced that the experimental hypertension screening system will become a commercial diagnostic feature.
Apple Watch already offers hypertension alerts

Google has some competition in this area. Apple has already introduced FDA-cleared hypertension notifications for compatible Apple Watch models. As we previously reported in Apple Watch gets FDA-approved hypertension alerts, the feature looks for patterns associated with chronic high blood pressure. It uses information gathered by the watch's optical heart sensor over 30-day periods.

The feature supports Apple Watch Series 9 and later models, along with Apple Watch Ultra 2 and later models, subject to software and regional availability. If the watch detects concerning patterns, it can notify you. However, Apple also makes clear that the feature cannot diagnose hypertension. And it may miss cases. Apple recommends checking your blood pressure with a traditional cuff and discussing the results with a healthcare professional if you receive an alert.

So, while Apple and Google are approaching this technology differently, the current guidance remains clear. A smartwatch alert can give you useful information, but you still need an accurate blood pressure measurement.
Why detecting high blood pressure earlier could save lives

High blood pressure has earned the nickname "silent killer" for a reason. According to the World Health Organization, more than one billion adults worldwide live with hypertension. Many have no idea they have it.

Meanwhile, untreated high blood pressure can damage blood vessels and increase the risk of a heart attack or stroke. Younger adults can be particularly vulnerable to missed diagnoses because they may feel healthy and see little reason to get checked. Now, consider what could happen if a smartwatch noticed concerning patterns before someone developed symptoms.

That person might decide to schedule an appointment and have their blood pressure checked. If doctors confirm hypertension, earlier treatment could help reduce the risk of complications. Of course, researchers still need to determine whether smartwatch-based screening actually improves diagnosis rates and long-term health outcomes.
COULD A PAINT-ON ELECTRONIC TATTOO SPOT HEART ATTACKS?

Smartwatches can alert users to possible signs of high blood pressure and encourage them to check their readings with a traditional cuff and discuss the results with their doctor. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
What should you do if your smartwatch flags high blood pressure?

If your smartwatch warns you about possible high blood pressure, don't ignore it. But don't assume the watch has diagnosed you, either. The next step is to check your blood pressure using a validated upper-arm cuff.

The American Heart Association recommends automatic upper-arm monitors for home measurements because they provide more reliable readings than typical wrist or finger monitors. If you're using Google's blood pressure trends feature and receive a "High" result, Google recommends checking your blood pressure twice a day for seven days and sharing those readings with your doctor.

Make sure you follow your monitor's instructions and use the correct cuff size. Also, keep an eye on how you're feeling. If you experience emergency warning signs such as chest pain or difficulty breathing, seek immediate medical attention rather than waiting for another smartwatch assessment.

And remember, even if your watch never sends an alert, you should continue getting your blood pressure checked. For another way to track your readings, see our article on how to monitor blood pressure with your Apple Watch using a compatible blood pressure monitor.
The biggest challenge Google's smartwatch AI still faces

One of my biggest questions about this technology comes down to how much confidence people will place in the results. Let's say your smartwatch tells you everything looks normal. Would you still bother checking your blood pressure? That's where the research raises an important concern.

In Google's initial screening study, the AI missed a meaningful number of people who actually had hypertension. And while the results compared favorably with initial office screening, the study was relatively small. Researchers will need more evidence before the technology can become a dependable part of routine medical screening.

Google's findings suggest that everyday wearables could eventually help identify people who might otherwise go undiagnosed. For now, though, a reliable blood pressure cuff and a conversation with your doctor remain essential.
Kurt's key takeaways

I like where Google is going with this. Most of us probably don't think about our blood pressure until we're sitting in a doctor's office with a cuff around our arm. So the idea that a smartwatch could spot a potential problem before we even know something's wrong is pretty exciting. But there's one number in this study that concerns me. The AI missed roughly one in three people who actually had high blood pressure. That's a lot, especially when you consider the serious health risks involved. I think this technology has tremendous potential, and I'm looking forward to seeing how Google improves it. But for now, I wouldn't rely on my smartwatch to tell me whether my blood pressure is normal. I'd still want to check it with a traditional cuff.

title: FBI warns AI hackers can breach systems in under 3 hours
summary: The FBI warns the ARTEX AI hacking tool can give criminals privileged access in under three hours, targeting Microsoft 365 and financial firms.
story: James Gagliano, retired FBI supervisory special agent, warns about the rising threat of artificial intelligence in global cyberattacks. This follows a string of disruptive tech outages impacting major financial institutions including Chase and Bank of America.

Your bank could spend millions protecting its computer systems. Your employer might have an entire cybersecurity team watching for suspicious activity. Yet hackers now have an AI-powered tool that can help them break into some organizations in less than three hours.

The FBI is warning that criminals are using the ARTEX AI hacking tool to automate cyberattacks against businesses around the world. Some attacks have moved from initial targeting to powerful administrator-level access in under three hours. That leaves companies very little time to recognize an attack and stop it.

If hackers reach a business that stores your personal information, you could end up dealing with the consequences. Here's how ARTEX works, why the FBI is concerned and what you can do to protect yourself.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
AI-POWERED CYBERATTACKS FUEL 'BLACK OCTOBER' FEARS
Strong passwords and multifactor authentication can help protect your personal accounts if criminals obtain sensitive information through a company data breach. (Pornyot Palilai via Getty Images)
What is the ARTEX AI hacking tool?

ARTEX started as a legitimate penetration testing framework. Cybersecurity professionals use these tools to find weaknesses in computer systems before criminals discover them. However, hackers have found ways to turn ARTEX against organizations without permission. The framework uses artificial intelligence to handle tasks that previously required significant hacking expertise. It can search for security weaknesses and attempt to exploit them. Once inside a system, ARTEX can work toward gaining higher levels of access and extracting sensitive information. What makes ARTEX particularly concerning is its ability to operate with limited human involvement. Attackers can give the software instructions, then let AI agents carry out much of the work automatically.

ARTEX also connects to external AI models, including OpenAI's GPT and Anthropic's Claude. It supports DeepSeek and several other models. These integrations allow the framework to process instructions and automate complicated hacking operations. Their availability does not mean the AI companies are directing the attacks. According to the FBI, the technology allows criminals with relatively little technical knowledge to launch sophisticated attacks against multiple organizations simultaneously.
FBI warns ARTEX hackers can gain access in under 3 hours

In a November 13, 2026, security advisory, the FBI warned that criminals have used ARTEX in cyberattacks since at least August 2026. The agency identified campaigns targeting financial institutions and healthcare organizations. Government agencies and technology companies have also appeared among the targets. The speed of these attacks is especially troubling. According to the FBI, some intrusions progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours. That means hackers obtained powerful permissions that could allow them to make changes inside compromised systems.

ARTEX can also identify weaknesses in systems that companies sometimes overlook. These include employee portals and older business applications. Criminals may exploit vulnerable third-party connections to reach organizations with stronger security. Although automated attacks can trigger security alerts, their speed creates another challenge. A company's security team might detect suspicious activity only after criminals have already gained access.
How hackers used ARTEX to attack Microsoft 365

One of the clearest examples involves Microsoft 365, the service millions of employees rely on for work email and company files. In October 2026, hackers exploited compromised application credentials associated with ConnectWise Cloud Backup. The service, formerly known as SkyKick Cloud Backup, helps businesses back up Microsoft 365 information. Here's why that attack is so concerning. The compromised applications already had permission to access customer environments. Hackers took advantage of those existing permissions to authenticate without needing an employee to sign in. In an October 21 investigation, Microsoft attributed the campaign to a China-state-aligned hacking group it tracks as Storm-0940.

The group used ARTEX to speed up its operations and attempt access to more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 customer environments. Cybersecurity company Huntress reported unauthorized sign-ins across at least 162 customer environments during its initial investigation. However, the number of environments targeted does not represent the number where criminals stole information. Microsoft specifically warned that successful authentication does not automatically mean customer data was accessed or taken. The attack also did not result from a vulnerability in Microsoft's own systems or services. Hackers exploited permissions associated with a trusted third-party application. For businesses, that's a serious concern. Employees could have strong passwords and multifactor authentication enabled, yet criminals might still gain access through a compromised application the company already trusts.
ARTEX cyberattacks have already exposed personal information

The Microsoft 365 incident represents only part of the FBI's warning. In South Korea, hackers used ARTEX in attacks against financial institutions. Those attacks exposed personal information belonging to approximately 67,000 people, according to the FBI.

In a separate investigation, South Korean authorities arrested seven suspects connected to attacks against more than 90 organizations. Police said the group stole approximately 8.2 million data records, with ARTEX reportedly used in many of the attacks. Researchers have also identified a separate international cyberespionage campaign.

Cybersecurity company CrowdStrike reported that a China-linked hacking group known as Vapor Panda used ARTEX in attacks targeting more than 200 organizations across 14 countries. The campaign compromised at least nine organizations. The AI agents helped criminals identify vulnerabilities and obtain credentials. When one attack method failed, the software could attempt another approach. These incidents show how quickly AI-assisted hacking has expanded from individual targets to coordinated attacks against organizations around the world.
Why the ARTEX warning should concern you

You probably have never heard of ARTEX before now. But the businesses you depend on could become targets. Think about the information your employer keeps on file. It may include your Social Security number and banking details for direct deposit. Your healthcare provider holds sensitive medical information, while financial institutions maintain records connected to your identity. If criminals steal information from those organizations, they could use it to attempt identity theft or target you with convincing scams. A hacker who obtains your email address and details about your employer could create a phishing message that looks legitimate. A message mentioning a company you actually do business with may be harder to recognize as fraudulent.

There's another concern. Your personal information could be exposed through a company you barely remember giving it to. The FBI has not warned that ARTEX automatically compromises personal phones or home computers. Its advisory focuses on attacks against organizations and the systems they operate. Still, you don't have to be the direct target of a cyberattack to feel its effects.
NEW AI MALWARE RANKS VICTIMS BY HOW MUCH THEY'RE WORTH
The FBI warns that hackers using the ARTEX AI hacking tool can gain privileged access to company systems in under three hours. (Craig Hudson For The Washington Post via Getty Images)
Why removing ARTEX from GitHub hasn't stopped the attacks

The original ARTEX developer released the framework publicly in July 2026. After reports emerged that criminals were abusing it, the developer removed the original GitHub repository on October 8. However, the software remains available through archived copies and modified versions. The FBI also identified a commercial version called ARTEX PRO. As of early November, researchers had identified more than 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles. That figure refers to accessible framework interfaces, rather than 1,600 confirmed criminal operations. Removing the original project did little to eliminate copies already circulating online.
How to protect yourself from AI-powered cyberattacks
While companies are responsible for securing their systems, you can still take steps to protect your personal information and limit the damage if a business you trust gets hacked.

If criminals steal login credentials from one organization, they may test those credentials against other accounts. Reusing passwords makes that easier. Use a strong, unique password for every important account. A reputable password manager can generate secure passwords and store them for you. Start with your primary email account because criminals who gain access to it may be able to reset passwords for other services.

Multifactor authentication adds another security check when someone tries to sign in to your account. Enable it for your email and financial services whenever available. Choose a passkey or authenticator app when supported. Passkeys can provide stronger protection against phishing than traditional passwords. Keep in mind that these protections cannot prevent every attack. The ConnectWise incident involved compromised application credentials rather than someone entering an employee's password.

You may have granted third-party applications permission to access your Google or Microsoft account without thinking much about it. Review those connections periodically. Remove permissions for unfamiliar services or applications you no longer need. For personal Microsoft accounts, visit account.microsoft.com. For Google accounts, review your connected apps through myaccount.google.com. Look for unfamiliar sign-ins while you're there. If something seems suspicious, secure the account and revoke any sessions you don't recognize. For work accounts, contact your IT department before changing business application permissions.

Cybercriminals often use major security incidents to create convincing phishing messages. You might receive an email claiming your bank was hacked and asking you to verify your password. Another message could direct you to a fake account recovery page. Avoid clicking unexpected links or opening unfamiliar attachments. Instead, visit the company's official website or open its app directly to check for alerts. Never share verification codes with someone who contacts you unexpectedly, even if the person claims to work for your bank.

Install security updates on your computer and phone. These updates frequently address vulnerabilities criminals could exploit. Strong antivirus software with real-time protection can also help identify malicious downloads and suspicious programs. Some security tools offer additional protection against phishing websites. However, antivirus software on your personal computer cannot prevent criminals from compromising a company's cloud systems. Check your financial accounts regularly and enable transaction alerts. These notifications can help you spot unauthorized activity quickly. Review your credit reports for unfamiliar accounts or credit inquiries. You can request free reports through AnnualCreditReport.com. If your Social Security number has been exposed, consider freezing your credit with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A credit freeze is free and can make it harder for criminals to open new credit accounts using your identity. A freeze will not prevent fraud involving accounts that are already open, so continue monitoring those accounts.
VISA, MASTERCARD AND JPMORGAN CUSTOMER DATA LEAKED

ARTEX uses artificial intelligence to automate cyberattacks, allowing criminals to identify security weaknesses and attempt to break into multiple organizations at once. (Philip Dulian/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Know what to do if your information is exposed
If a company notifies you about a breach, find out exactly what information was compromised. Then take action based on the type of data involved.

Change exposed passwords immediately. Update any other accounts where you reused the same password.Secure your email account. Check for unfamiliar forwarding rules or recovery information. Sign out of suspicious sessions.Contact your bank if financial information was exposed. Ask whether your accounts need additional protection.Consider a credit freeze. This can help protect against fraudulent new credit accounts if sensitive identity information was stolen.Watch for follow-up scams. Criminals may use stolen details to make fake security alerts more convincing.Report identity theft. Visit IdentityTheft.gov for a recovery plan if someone has misused your personal information.
Change exposed passwords immediately. Update any other accounts where you reused the same password.
Secure your email account. Check for unfamiliar forwarding rules or recovery information. Sign out of suspicious sessions.
Contact your bank if financial information was exposed. Ask whether your accounts need additional protection.
Consider a credit freeze. This can help protect against fraudulent new credit accounts if sensitive identity information was stolen.
Watch for follow-up scams. Criminals may use stolen details to make fake security alerts more convincing.
Report identity theft. Visit IdentityTheft.gov for a recovery plan if someone has misused your personal information.
You can also report suspected internet crime to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov/.
Kurt's key takeaways

A backup service is supposed to help protect a company's information. In the ConnectWise attack, hackers abused that trusted connection to gain access to customer systems. That's especially concerning because employees could have followed every security recommendation and still been exposed through a service their company depended on. The speed of these AI-powered attacks also worries me. Three hours gives security teams very little time to stop criminals who know exactly where they're going. I think companies need to take a much harder look at the outside applications they trust and how quickly they can detect unauthorized access. For you, the best approach is to secure your own accounts and pay attention when a company reports a breach. You shouldn't have to become a cybersecurity expert to feel confident that businesses are protecting your information.

title: FDA clears tiny surgical robot to remove bladder tumors
summary: The FDA-authorized Virtuoso Endoscopy System uses needle-sized robotic arms to remove bladder tumors intact, helping pathologists assess detrusor muscle.
story: CEO of Sellas Life Sciences Angelos Stergiou explains how AI is revolutionizing medicine by enabling precision medicine in cancer treatment.

If a doctor finds a tumor in your bladder, you want to know what you're dealing with. Is it cancer? Has it reached the bladder muscle? The tissue removed during surgery helps answer those questions. Now, a tiny surgical robot could give doctors a clearer view of what's happening inside the bladder.

The FDA has authorized the Virtuoso Endoscopy System, developed by Nashville-based Virtuoso Surgical. It uses two needle-sized robotic arms to remove bladder lesions through the urethra, without cutting through the skin. The technology allows surgeons to remove many tumors in one piece, potentially giving pathologists better tissue samples to examine. This new approach to robotic bladder tumor removal could help doctors make more informed treatment decisions.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
