title: Congress reacts with anger and skepticism about Jensen Huang reinstatement
summary: Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle vowed to press ahead with investigations into the once-again Nvidia CEO, who’s scheduled to meet with them next week.
story: The stock market was thrilled with the announcement that Jensen Huang was returning as CEO of Nvidia, but lawmakers on both sides of the aisle reacted with shock — and said they still expect him to answer questions next week on Capitol Hill.

“You gotta be kidding me,” Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told MS NOW when he learned of Huang’s reinstatement 11 days after he resigned in the wake of revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese spy.
In its announcement, the board said it reached the decision after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that his “reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
“No national security risk? Based on what?” Cornyn asked in a post on X.
President Donald Trump told CNBC he’d spoken to the board “directly and indirectly.”

“One of the things the board wanted to know, is there a national security problem?” Trump said. “And after a lot of research, we — you know, we’ve been looking at this for more than a couple of days, right? This has been a story for a few weeks. We said no, it’s not a problem.”
Lawmakers made clear they still need answers.
The Senate Banking Committee, chaired by Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., announced that Huang was scheduled to testify publicly Dec. 3.

“The national security concerns and adherence to export controls will be central to the committee’s oversight and the congressional hearing. Our markets demand transparency. Americans deserve the truth. Our committee will deliver answers,” Scott said in a statement.

A spokesperson for the House Intelligence Committee told NBC News that Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO “changes nothing” for the three House committees that are set to conduct a closed-door transcribed interview with Huang on Dec. 1.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“There are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers. Seems like the only thing that is consistent these days on this issue is our three Committee’s commitment to oversight,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

In a joint statement later Monday, the chairs of the House Select Committee on China, the Intelligence Committee and the House Foreign Affairs Committee said Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter “have confirmed they will appear for their transcribed interviews on December 1 and December 2 as previously planned.”

“We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of NVIDIA products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities,” said the three Republicans, Reps. John Moolenaar of Michigan, Rick Crawford of Arkansas and Brian Mast of Florida.

The speedy reinstatement and assurances of the lack of a security risk came after the Justice and Commerce departments last week shared details about their investigation into Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company tied to Alice Huang, the suspected spy with whom Huang was allegedly involved.
Megaspeed reportedly acquired billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips and is also being investigated over concerns that it — and its subsidiaries — smuggled chips to China.

Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said in an X post that “the legal and reputational risk of hiring a CEO who may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws is now born by the board of Nvidia, but the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens. The risk of extortion by a Chinese asset who’s been banned by Singapore is risk enough to not rehire Huang.”
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told NBC News in a phone interview “It’s not my job as a public official to tell a private company who to pick for their CEO. That’s up to the board of directors.”

But, he added, “What I want to know is whether Nvidia violated the export controls of our country with respect to advanced chips. And I want to know if the Department of Commerce did. That will be the purpose of the Banking Committee hearing.”

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said in a statement that the administration appears to have known about the Chinese espionage efforts targeting the Nvidia CEO for the past year and his reinstatement “without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation.”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said the administration’s “rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act.”

“Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat,” Schumer said in a statement. He added that “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain.”
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., called the board’s decision “indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible.”

“Congress will not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce,” Jeffries said.
Lutnick agreed earlier this month to testify before Congress about the Huang scandal amid lawmakers’ scrutiny of China’s access to advanced AI chips.

Democrats pointed Trump’s financial ties to Nvidia, with Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the ranking member on the Oversight Committee, noting the president has a sizeable amount of Nvidia stock. “No president who has invested in a private company should be involved in their board decisions,” Garcia said.
Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill., cited Nvidia’s donation to Trump’s White House ballroom project as a reason to give the board’s decision extra scrutiny.

“Trump’s assurances cannot be taken at face value, especially after Nvidia’s $25 million donation to his ballroom. Huang must testify at a full public congressional hearing, with every member of the relevant committees allowed to question him,” he posted on X.
Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., questioned the Nvidia board’s decision in a post on social media.

“Jensen Huang had multiple affairs including with subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy,” Ricketts wrote. “His own board described his behavior as lacking ‘candor.’ I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement.”

“Nvidia’s decision today doesn’t excuse Jensen Huang from testifying before Congress,” he continued. “It also doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips. I look forward to Mr. Huang coming to the Senate in December.”

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., called the president’s actions “Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration’s big tech and AI policy.” He told reporters it was a “good sign” that Republican senators and lawmakers have spoken out because they “realize this is a threat to national security.”

title: Court allows Army to go forward with planned detonation of toxic drums in Iowa
summary: A U.S. appeals court said Monday that it would allow the Trump administration and the Army to move forward with the detonation of lead azide in Iowa, denying an emergency request by environmental groups to halt the Army’s permit.
story: A U.S. appeals court said Monday that it would allow the Trump administration and the Army to move forward with the detonation of lead azide in Iowa, denying an emergency request by environmental groups to halt the Army’s permit.
It is not clear when the detonation, which was most recently set for Wednesday, will happen.

“We are mindful of the very real risks presented by the Army’s planned detonation of the stores of degraded lead azide,” the order from the 8th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals said. “However, we must acknowledge the realities of the situation: the degraded explosives present a risk of an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion, which would occur without the benefit of the safety measures that the Permit puts in place.”
The court said that the Environmental Protection Agency had adequately incorporated safeguards to minimize the dispersal of lead and that the Army had considered a full range of alternatives.

“A controlled detonation with attendant safety measures better alleviates the risk of irreparable harm than the risk of an uncontrolled explosion,” the court said in lifting an administrative stay on the permit.
The detonation, which would send a plume of lead dust across Iowa and likely into neighboring states, has raised fear and concern from residents who said they had not had enough time to prepare.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Earlier Monday, President Donald Trump ordered the Army to pause its planned detonation until the court weighed in.

“I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation,” Trump said in a Truth Social post.

The detonation was initially scheduled for Friday. After public outcry and a lawsuit from environmental groups last week, the Army delayed the detonation until Monday and then later pushed it again to Wednesday. The court last week gave an administrative stay in the case, putting the Army’s environmental permit to detonate on hold. But the Army told the court it could go forward with a detonation in an emergency without the court’s ruling. The Eighth Circuit ruling, released on Monday afternoon, will clear the way for the Army to go forward with the court’s blessing.

The outcry over the federal government’s handling of the situation and the decision of whether to detonate had become something of a political football earlier on Monday afternoon. In his Truth Social post before the appeals court ruling, Trump seemed intent on deferring responsibility to Sand, who has not taken office yet.

“If he or the Courts do not agree,” Trump said of Sand, “we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation.”
Trump said military leaders had advised him that detonating the material soon was the safest option and that the weather forecast for Wednesday was optimal.

“The Experts, who know it well, and have been studying it for many years, feel there is a substantial chance that this material will explode of its own volition, perhaps sometime in the near future,” Trump wrote. “The weather, right now, is optimal for this planned response to take place.”

The Army has said it must detonate the 68 drums of deteriorating, toxic lead azide — a chemical used to make bomb triggers — at the Iowa ammunition plant because the chemical has undergone a process of “recrystallization” that has made it highly unstable and dangerous. The Army has said that it is unsafe to move the drums and that cold weather will further destabilize the material and could cause a spontaneous explosion.

The Army had told Middletown residents that the blast could break windows and shake their homes. But residents elsewhere in Iowa — and in the plume’s potential path outside the state — said they didn’t learn about it until last week and were concerned for their families’ well-being, crops and pets.

Lead is a potent neurotoxin for which there is no safe level of exposure. Airborne lead is an acute health risk, experts said, and once the metal gets deposited in soil or on surfaces, it can remain there forever unless it’s physically removed.

Exposure to lead is associated with learning disabilities, reproductive problems, mental health issues and increased risk of hearing loss, among other effects. The long-term risks are particularly pronounced for young children.

The Army said it had covered the bunker with two stories of sand in collapsible, modular barriers to dampen the effects of the explosion. Meanwhile, scientists, politicians and residents have been trying to figure out how the situation got so sideways and why the Army feels its only choice is a detonation, whether planned or unplanned.

In a statement on X before the court’s ruling, Sand said the administration should make its decision “based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago” and who have been in Middletown for weeks. Sand implied that the administration might have information about the urgency of the situation that is not known publicly.

“Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward,” Sand said. “That means they should have the same access to the information I’ve received in briefings from the administration, straight from the source. I’ve asked the federal government to share that information with the public as soon as possible.”
An Army spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Iowa residents said they were growing frustrated with the twists and turns of the detonation saga.

Debra Ott, who works at Fat Annie’s August Tap, which is about a quarter-mile from a gate that leads into the ammunition plant, said she was planning to stay inside for a full day if and when the detonation takes place.

“I have some heart issues, and I have a hard enough time breathing anyway. So whenever they do it, I plan on staying in the house 24 hours because I don’t want to be out,” Ott said. “The bean dust and corn dust around here is bad enough without lead.”
Ott, who lives in Augusta, Iowa, about 5 miles from Middletown, said she was growing tired of the scheduling changes for detonation and increasingly concerned about a spontaneous explosion.

“I don’t want to be sitting at home at midnight and have it go off and not have a clue what’s going on without anybody up there to try to control it. If they’re going to do it, I wish they just do it and quit changing it every day,” she said.
Ott lives with her granddaughter and her granddaughter’s three young children, who are 13, 4 and 2.

“We’ll hose down all the outside stuff and wipe off, you know, wipe down the doorknobs and anything the vehicles, anything the kids can touch with their hands, where they could get it in their mouth,” Ott said. “We just don’t know what to expect because we don’t know when they’re going to do it.”
The trajectory of the dust plume depends on the direction and strength of the wind, so each delay puts a new group of people in the path of the expected hazard.
“It’s just very frustrating,” said Jill Holler, who lives about 50 miles from Middletown, in Muscatine, Iowa, which could be in the path of the lead dust plume, depending on the wind.

Holler, whose family has a farm about 20 miles west of Middletown where they raise cattle and grow soybeans and corn, said she was racing to gather soil samples ahead of the blast Sunday night. Understanding the lead content present in soil before the blast could help determine if a property is affected and what remediation might be needed.

“We thought it would be tomorrow. So I was down in the dark getting the soil samples and it just, it’s frustrating,” Holler said on Monday. “It’s just strange, and you just never know what the next day is going to bring, and so you never. You’re, you’re pretty confident there’s going to be something else changing, and we can’t really believe what the next thing they say is going to happen.”
Holler said she was most sympathetic to the people of Middletown, who are essentially living with a threat in their backyards that the Army has indicated could spontaneously explode.

“If there really is an imminent threat and it’s very dangerous to explode at any time,” Holler said. “But it seems like they’re delaying, so it just isn’t adding up. It doesn’t make sense. So I think there’s going to have to be some explanation of what’s been going on.”

title: Judge unseals documents related to search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home
summary: A federal judge unsealed more than 160 pages’ worth of court documents Monday night pertaining to the warrant authorizing a federal search of Rep.
story: A federal judge unsealed more than 160 pages’ worth of court documents Monday night pertaining to the warrant authorizing a federal search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home in Washington, D.C.

Chief U.S. District Judge James E. Boasberg ruled that some of the documents could be released with redactions after a coalition of news publications, including NBCUniversal News Group, sought access to the sealed records. The released documents do not include the search warrant.

Boasberg agreed with the Justice Department in its efforts to keep the majority of the records sealed, but said a back-and-forth regarding the protection of Omar’s “speech or debate” rights — a clause that shields lawmakers from criminal and civil liability tied to legislative acts — should be made public.

About half of the pages are mostly or entirely redacted from public view, but what is clear from the unredacted portions is the length to which a magistrate judge worked to ensure the Trump administration was following proper procedures for executing a search warrant on a member of Congress.

Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh asked the Justice Department several times for briefings explaining its theory of probable cause, and the DOJ said the process included “several rounds” of affidavit revisions. Sharbaugh ultimately found that the speech or debate clause was at least in part relevant, because it was a search of Omar’s home.
As a result, “special search procedures” were carried out at Omar’s home, according to the unsealed documents.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The list of property the government planned to seize from Omar’s home is largely redacted — and the list of property they took is entirely redacted — but unredacted documents  indicate it included “All records and information that constitute fruits, contraband, evidence, and instrumentalities of violations of (REDACTED).”

The government also planned to seize papers, records, photographs, documents, thumb drives, external hard drives, computers, or other electronic media devices holding any of the above records or documents, along with cellphones and any digital device owned, used or controlled by Omar that could have contained evidence of wrongdoing.
Omar previously said that federal agents took 17 items from her home, including old phones which she said belonged to her and one of her daughters.

The filings unsealed Monday also make clear the length of time the government believed violations of the law took place — between 1980 to the present. Omar’s congressional bio page says she was born in October 1982.

“The United States believes ILHAN has committed (REDACTED) crimes over decades — beginning long before she was ever in Congress,” another filing submitted to the court by Associate Deputy Attorney General Alessandra Serano reads. “Nothing in the search warrant affidavit, briefing, or oral argument indicates that the United States’s case has anything to do with ILHAN’s professional life.”
Omar’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment regarding the released documents.
The congresswoman’s home was searched in October, within weeks of the midterm elections, an unusual move to take against a sitting lawmaker seeking re-election.

The DOJ has kept the charges against the Minnesota Democrat under wraps, but people familiar with the investigation previously told NBC News that they revolve around potential immigration-related crimes. Omar is a naturalized citizen, who immigrated to the U.S. from Somalia when she was a child.
Omar has called the search “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”

President Donald Trump has repeatedly taken political shots at Omar, and at Somalis more generally. When speaking about the congresswoman at his rallies, crowds of Trump’s supporters have sometimes erupted into chants of “lock her up.”
The president has denied any involvement with the search of Omar’s house.

title: $98 million civil judgment awarded in Ohio rape that could not be prosecuted
summary: An Ohio woman who survived a brutal rape that went unsolved for decades was awarded a $98 million civil judgment against her attacker, a doctor who admitted to the assault but could not be prosecuted for it because the statute of limitations had expired.
story: An Ohio woman who survived a brutal rape that went unsolved for decades was awarded a $98 million civil judgment against her attacker, a doctor who admitted to the assault but could not be prosecuted for it because the statute of limitations had expired.

Hamilton County Court of Common Pleas Judge Christopher McDowell awarded $48.2 million in compensatory damages and $50 million in punitive damages on Thursday to Dana Beatty in connection with the 1989 rape at her Cincinnati home, documents filed Friday show.

McDowell described the punitive damages — which are meant to address especially egregious conduct — as “warranted and constitutionally proportionate” because the conduct of Frederick Tanzer was “intentional, violent, prolonged, and extraordinarily reprehensible.”
Although Tanzer, 67, could not be prosecuted for the rape, he pleaded guilty to lying to federal authorities about it and was sentenced in January to 15 years in prison.
In an interview with “Dateline” earlier this year, Tanzer admitted to the rape and said he was “working on the why.”

Beatty filed the complaint against Tanzer in January 2025, alleging battery and intentional infliction of emotional distress. Tanzer did not respond to the complaint, McDowell wrote, nor did he appear at a Nov. 17 hearing on the matter. He did not have an attorney in the proceedings, according to McDowell.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

In an interview Monday, Beatty said she was shocked by the massive judgment but grateful to McDowell for his understanding of the “complex, lifelong ramifications the crime had on my life and my family’s.”
The size of the judgment, she said, demonstrated that understanding.

“Unless you have been through a crime of this magnitude, it’s hard to comprehend the lifelong and massive repercussions that the victim and her family have to live with the rest of their lives,” she said.
Beatty said she would be pleasantly surprised if she were to recover any of the damages.

Beatty was assaulted for hours on Aug. 1, 1989, by a masked man armed with a knife and wearing a black lycra bodysuit. He wrapped her face in tape, lashed to her to a bed and left an ominous note, telling Beatty — who at the time worked for IBM — “no police, or I’ll be back, Miss IBM,” authorities have said.
The case remained cold until 2023, when DNA recovered from Beatty’s dress was matched to Tanzer. At the time of the attack, Tanzer was married to Beatty’s best friend.

Tanzer could not be prosecuted for the rape since Ohio’s statute of limitations was just six years in 1989. But in 2024, local and federal authorities began pursuing what one investigator described as a last-ditch effort to hold Tanzer accountable: They planned to catch him in a lie about his role in the crime.

When investigators questioned Tanzer about the assault, he told them that he hadn’t had sex with Beatty or gone to her apartment on Aug. 1, 1989. He was arrested on suspicion of making false statements to a federal agent, a charge he pleaded guilty to in September 2025.

Ohio’s statute of limitations for rape is now 25 years, and it can be extended an additional five years if a DNA match is made with a possible suspect. But Beatty’s case highlights the often-uneven manner in which time limits are applied to some of the most serious sexual assault cases in the United States.

An NBC News analysis from all 50 states and Washington D.C. found that time limits for adult victims differ dramatically among the more than 30 states that have them. While nearly a dozen states eliminate statutes of limitations if DNA evidence comes into play, 14 either offer limited DNA extensions of five years or less or no extension at all.

In Montana, the statute of limitations for aggravated sexual intercourse without consent — that state’s most serious rape charge — is five years, with a one-year DNA extension. In New Hampshire, the time limit is six years, with no DNA extension.
Beatty said Monday that she hopes to use the civil judgment as momentum to help other victims change statute of limitations laws.

title: Trump uses backdrop of DOJ to bash Gavin Newsom on death row commutations
summary: President Donald Trump gave his speech at the Justice Department headquarters — a rarity for a president — and invited victims’ family members to speak onstage.
story: President Donald Trump on Monday delivered remarks at the Justice Department’s headquarters in Washington, denouncing Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s plan for commuting the death sentences of more than 500 convicted murderers.

It is rare for a president to speak at the Justice Department. Trump last did so in March 2025, when he called for jailing his perceived political foes. This time, he took swipes at Newsom, a potential 2028 presidential contender, whom he called a “terrible” governor.

“He stood with the murderers and the child slayers, but today we say the American people stand with you. We stand with you. We’re not going to let this happen,” Trump said, without elaborating on how his administration could intervene.
The death row sentences being commuted by Newsom all stem from state cases.

Trump also announced several new executive actions, including a presidential directive that he said ordered the DOJ to seek the death penalty for “child murderers, as well as rapists and human traffickers who kill their victims.” He added that the order would direct the attorney general to expedite the execution of federal death row inmates.

The president brought relatives of several victims onstage, who at times became emotional when describing how their loved ones had died. Some who spoke were the parents of victims whose killings made national news for years and sparked changes to the law.

Marc Klaas, whose 12-year-old daughter Polly was abducted from her home in Petaluma in 1993 before being killed, said he was “outraged” by Newsom’s actions. Actress Winona Ryder had offered a $200,000 reward for information at the time Polly went missing. The man convicted in her death, Richard Allen Davis, had a record and was previously released from prison — his conviction helped lead to California’s “three strikes” law that increased prison sentences for repeat offenders.
Another speaker, Sandy Friend, whose 8-year-old son Michael Lyons was killed by Robert Boyd Rhodes, asked Newsom to “face” her as she described her son’s death.

“His most feared thing was the dark. That night, Michael learned that the boogeyman was real. Mikey was raped, sodomized and tortured for 10 hours, from the very first inflicted stab wound to the last,” Friend said, choking up at one point while adding, “Sorry, this is so very hard.”
“Governor Newsom erased that with the swipe of a pen, without notifying the families,” Friend said of Rhodes’ death sentence.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Newsom responded to the DOJ event in a video message on social media, accusing the president of “selling” pardons and benefiting his associates.

“To the families standing with him today, your grief is real. That’s why every person, every person on California’s former death row will die in prison. No one walks out. Donald Trump’s criminals, they walk out,” Newsom said.

“A Justice Department that prosecutes his enemies and pardons himself and his friends — that’s not law enforcement. That’s a protection racket,” the governor added. He previously said, in announcing his plan, that “state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values.”

Trump wrapped up the somber event by shaking hands with the victims’ family members, some of whom had been in tears only minutes before. But the tone quickly shifted when his campaign anthem — the upbeat “YMCA” — played as he left the stage.

Newsom and Trump’s back-and-forth comes amid a series of botched executions across the country. Last week prison staffers in Texas struggled to find a vein on Reinaldo Dennes, resulting in an execution that lasted over an hour as Dennes cried out in pain. And in September, Christa Pike, the sole woman on Tennessee’s death row, became the first person to survive a lethal injection. She was placed on a ventilator and regained consciousness days later.
Support for the death penalty in the U.S. has generally been declining since a high of 80% in 1994, but Americans have complicated feelings about capital punishment.

A Gallup poll this month found that 49% of U.S. adults favored the death penalty for those convicted of murder, with 45% opposed. But a Pew Research Center survey in August found that 66% of Americans were in favor of the death penalty for those convicted of murder, though 59% said the death penalty was not a crime deterrent. There is also a partisan gap, with Democrats increasingly opposing the death penalty.

title: Amazon drone delivering shampoo snags on wire and tumbles onto Michigan man’s garage roof
summary: James Brennan, of Huntington Woods, Michigan, near Detroit, said he had not requested a drone delivery and assumed his package would arrive at his doorstep as usual.
story: When James Brennan was waiting for his shampoo delivery last week, he didn’t realize an Amazon drone would hit a wire and tumble onto the roof of his garage.

Brennan, of Huntington Woods, Michigan, near Detroit, said he had not requested a drone delivery and assumed his package would arrive at his doorstep as usual. But on Friday, he received a notification from Amazon telling him to keep an eye out for the unmanned aircraft, so he went outside to take a video.

“I just thought it would make amusing, amusing conversation over Thanksgiving or at work or whatever,” Brennan said in an interview. “And I was just going to get a shot of it. I never expected this to happen.”

He went to the front yard and heard the unmistakable whirling of a drone as it neared. The rotors kicked up leaves, debris and dust, Brennan said, before the drone set the package down and began its ascent again.
Video taken from across the street shows the drone hitting a cable, wobbling and ultimately plopping down on Brennan’s roof.
“It swayed a couple of times, and then it swayed over the top of the garage,” Brennan said. “It kind of laid down and died. And as soon as it laid down, the motors shut off, and that was it.”
Amazon workers responded to the incident quickly and retrieved the problem drone, but the ordeal did cause neighbors to temporarily lose internet access, he said.
In a statement, Amazon spokesperson Jack Stelzner said safety is the company’s “top priority” and that “incidents are extremely rare.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
“Anytime a delivery does not go as planned we investigate what happened and use the findings to further improve the service,” he said.
A spokesman for the National Transportation Safety Board said officials are gathering information and have not decided whether to launch an investigation.
Brennan said the damage to his garage roof was “very minor,” comprising only a few scuffed shingles. He said he and some neighbors also got a $100 Amazon gift card for their troubles.
Brennan now hopes Amazon will continue to refine its drone delivery system to prevent future accidents.
“Until they develop better technology to spot these these kinds of things, this is going to continue to happen,” he said.

title: How will voters respond to divided government?: From the Politics Desk
summary: In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur digs into how an electorate that is hungry for results may collide withe the realities of divided government.
story: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur digs into how an electorate that is hungry for results may collide withe the realities of divided government. Plus, we look ahead to the governor’s races on the ballot in the South next year.
— Adam Wollner
Which party is expected to deliver in divided government? The last 3 presidential elections provide clues.

With Democrats poised to claim historic majorities in the House and Senate come January, the biggest substantive question is what they’ll be able to accomplish with President Donald Trump in the White House over the next two years.
And the biggest political question: If little is done, who will pay the price?
A common theory after midterm elections is that the party that just won needs to prove it can govern — and deliver tangible results — in order to be successful in the next presidential election.

But is that actually true? History says no — voters tend to punish the president’s party, not the party that captured one or both chambers of Congress in the previous midterm, when they’re unhappy with the status quo.
Let’s review what happened after the last three midterms.
2014: Republicans flipped the Senate and expanded their House majority for President Barack Obama’s final two years in office.

But what happened next? Not much. Congress passed 172 substantive bills (not including ceremonial ones like renaming federal buildings), according to the Pew Research Center, well below the average of 236 substantive bills over the last four decades. Highlights included a surface transportation bill, unwinding “No Child Left Behind” and a Medicare bookkeeping resolution known as the “doc fix.” There was plenty of fighting, including the rebellion that led to Speaker John Boehner’s resignation and countless Affordable Care Act repeal show votes.
So, did voters punish Republicans? No. They won the trifecta in 2016, with Trump becoming president for the first time.
2018: Two years later, Democrats flipped about 40 House seats and took control of the chamber, although Republicans kept the Senate.

Just 150 substantive bills passed in the next session of Congress, the Pew Research Center found. Key pieces of legislation included the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement and several emergency Covid relief measures once the pandemic hit. But as was the case after the 2014 midterms, divided government led to several high-profile clashes, including a 35-day government shutdown and Trump’s first impeachment.
Were Democrats punished for the lack of productivity? No. They won full control of Washington in 2020, with Joe Biden taking the White House.
2022: Biden’s first midterm saw Republicans regain control of the House while falling short in the Senate.

But it was a similar story as the previous two midterms, with just 84 substantive bills passing during the next congressional session, according to Pew. That included a spending agreement following a debt ceiling fight that spooked the markets and led to a downgrade of the U.S. credit rating. Republicans also fought bitterly with each other, eventually deposing Speaker Kevin McCarthy mid-session.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
But did Republicans pay a political price? Not quite. The GOP again won a trifecta in the 2024 election, with Trump returning to the White House.
2026: And two years later, voters ushered in huge Democratic majorities after deciding, according to NBC News exit polling, that Trump failed to fulfill his promises to make life more affordable.
Will Democrats deliver on that? And if they don’t, will they suffer politically for it in the 2028 presidential election?

Based on the lessons of the last dozen years, the onus is on the president and his party to work with the new majorities in Congress, because voters have shown that they’ll punish the party in the White House for dysfunction and paralysis in Washington.
📺 Related: Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., said on “Meet the Press” that he’s open to working with Trump to bring down costs and improve healthcare for Americans. Read more →
Democrats look to 2027 races for governor to build on gains in the South
Democrats calling on their party to invest in the South after historic victories this year won’t have to wait until 2028, with races for governor in Mississippi, Louisiana and Kentucky ahead in 2027.

These contests will come just one year after Democrats flipped Senate seats in Mississippi and South Carolina, governorships in Texas and Georgia and House districts across the South for the first time in decades. And Southern Democrats are confident their party has taken notice.

“The South is competitive for Democrats,” Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who chaired the Democratic Governors Association this year, told NBC News. “As a Southern Democrat, we were often overlooked, underfunded, sometimes even looked down upon. But we have scrapped our way back to the table.”

Beshear, a possible presidential candidate, won a second term by 5 points two years ago and cannot run again due to term limits. In 2023, Democrat Brandon Presley lost in Mississippi to GOP Gov. Tate Reeves, who is term-limited, by 3 points. And former Democratic Gov. John Bel Edwards won two terms in Louisiana in 2015 and 2019 before Republican Gov. Jeff Landry won the office in 2023.
This year, Democrat Scott Colom notched a historic Senate victory in Mississippi and Democrat Jamie Davis came close to winning Louisiana.

title: Appeals court gives Trump another chance to move his hush money conviction case to a federal venue
summary: The 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found a federal judge “erred” when he ruled that President Donald Trump had waited too long to raise his immunity defense.
story: An appeals court on Monday opened the door to moving to federal court President Donald Trump’s New York state criminal case that resulted in a felony conviction.

In a brief two-page order, the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found that a lower court judge had “erred” when he ruled Trump’s legal team had waited too long to raise a presidential immunity defense.
“We disagree with the district court,” the three-judge panel said, directing a lower court judge to reconsider Trump’s motion to move the case from state court.
U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein in August had denied Trump’s request to consider moving the case, finding his arguments were not “legally sufficient.”
A spokesperson for Trump’s legal team praised the appeals court’s “prompt and correct ruling.”

“As today’s order highlights, the Supreme Court’s historic decision on Immunity, the Federal Constitution, and other established legal precedent mandate that the Witch Hunt perpetrated by the Manhattan DA be removed to federal court, and immediately overturned and dismissed,” his statement said.
“President Trump will keep defeating the Liberal Hoaxes at every turn,” it added.
For Subscribers
A spokesperson for the Manhattan district attorney’s office, which prosecuted the case, declined to comment.

Trump was convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records in 2024 as part of a scheme to cover up a hush money payment that his attorney had paid to an adult film star during the 2016 presidential campaign.

Trump managed the repayment to his attorney while he was president, and his lawyers have contended that a 2024 Supreme Court ruling that expanded the parameters of presidential immunity after he’d already been convicted should have resulted in the conviction being overturned.
Trump, who has denied any wrongdoing, had been separately appealing the conviction in state court, but Monday’s order effectively freezes that case while it’s being decided in federal court.
For Subscribers

“In order to preserve the status quo, the district court shall also respectfully request that no further proceedings occur in the state courts while the removal question is pending,” the judges wrote.
Judges Raymond Lohier, John Walker and Jose Cabranes also found that if the lower court decides the case should be moved to a federal venue, the “court should adopt the state court judgement.”
That would allow Trump to make his case for the conviction to be tossed out by the 2nd Circuit.
It’s unclear who will hear the case at the lower federal court level. Hellerstein died last month at age 92, and the case has yet to be reassigned.
Hellerstein had previously rejected other attempts by Trump to move the case, finding “hush money paid to an adult film star is not related to a President’s official acts.”

During arguments before the 2nd Circuit last week, Steven Wu of the district attorney’s office argued Trump had been prosecuted for falsifying business records, not for official presidential conduct, and that challenges to the conviction should go through the state courts.

Trump attorney Robert Giuffra acknowledged to the appeals court judges last week that it was unusual for a defendant to try to move a case after he’d already been convicted, but noted, “Everything about this case is unprecedented.”

Trump was sentenced to an unconditional discharge in the case 10 days before he was sworn in for his second term as president. The sentence meant that the conviction is on his record, but with no further penalties.

title: Democratic Rep. Jimmy Gomez to resign after Ethics Committee finds he engaged in sexual misconduct
summary: Gomez — who lost his re-election bid this month — said that while he cooperated with the investigation, he had “strong disagreements” with the committee’s conclusions.
story: Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., said Monday he will resign next week after the House Ethics Committee found that he engaged in sexual misconduct with a House staffer and said that his behavior could constitute “criminal misdemeanor sexual abuse.”

“I recognize the seriousness of the Ethics Committee’s report, and as I previously stated I take full responsibility for the personal mistakes I committed outside of my marriage,” Gomez said in a statement.
He said he cooperated with the Ethics investigation but added he has “strong disagreements with the Committee’s report and its conclusions.”

“Among other significant deficiencies and omissions, the report does not include key portions of my testimony that are essential to a full and fair understanding of what occurred,” Gomez said in his statement. “I also have serious concerns about the process. In my interview, I answered the Committee’s questions only to see my statements selectively quoted, disparaged, and disregarded throughout the final report, to which I was given no opportunity to respond.
“With this in mind, I see no other alternative than to resign, effective December 1, to allow for my staff to close out important constituent casework and needs,” he said.

His resignation will speed up his departure from Congress by about one month. Earlier this month, Democratic socialist Angela Gonzales-Torres defeated Gomez in California’s 34th District, as he faced the ethics investigation.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The development comes months after Gomez’s close friend, former Rep. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., dropped his bid for governor and resigned from office following sexual assault allegations from multiple women, including a House staffer.
The Ethics panel had launched an investigation into Gomez in the wake of the Swalwell saga after news reports that the married Gomez was observed at a party kissing a House staffer.

Gomez disclosed to the Ethics panel he had interactions with two women, including “consensual kissing.” But one of the women, identified as “Witness 1” in the new Ethics report, described the interactions with Gomez as unwanted sexual advances. Witness 1 was in her mid-20s and worked for a House leadership office and not for Gomez, according to the committee. She left her job as a House staffer in 2025.

During the first incident, while celebrating an unidentified member of Congress’ birthday in 2024, the woman told the committee that Gomez groped and sexually assaulted her at Rocket Bar in Washington, D.C., according to the report. When they went outside, she told investigators he pushed her against the wall and began kissing her.

The congressman told the committee that he did kiss the woman outside the bar and that there was sexual contact but that she gave him consent. Witness 1 later told another person her account, that second witness told investigators.

During a second incident, Witness 1 said she went to Gomez’s congressional office during late votes and that he tried to kiss her and was “forceful” with her; she said his actions were nonconsensual, according to the report. Gomez, speaking to the Ethics panel, rejected that characterization and said there was no indication she was uncomfortable and that he did not try to prevent her from leaving.

The Ethics panel did not issue a recommendation for the full House, such as censure or expulsion, presumably because Gomez was slated to leave Congress in January. But the panel said it issued its report as a warning to the entire House of Representatives.

“There must be zero tolerance for unwanted sexual advances toward House staff. The Committee is tasked with investigating alleged misconduct and, where appropriate, holding Members accountable for conduct that does not reflect creditably on the House or puts other Members and staff in danger,” the Ethics panel wrote in its report.

“Having determined that Representative Gomez made unwanted sexual advances toward a House staffer, the Committee adopted this Report to hold Representative Gomez accountable and to serve as a warning to the entire House community that this conduct will not be tolerated,” the committee added.

Responding to Gomez’s resignation, the top three House Democrats, Hakeem Jeffries, Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar, said in a joint statement: “The report of wrongdoing and abuse of power by Rep. Gomez is serious and deeply troubling. It is appropriate that he is stepping down. Decisive action to set a new standard for reform is an urgent priority for House Democrats.”

The Gomez report comes just days after the Ethics Committee formally adopted six changes to its procedures aimed at speeding up investigations and increasing transparency, particularly in cases involving sexual misconduct.
All six proposed changes were adopted without amendment following a rare public meeting, a source familiar with the matter confirmed to NBC News.

The changes include formally requiring public disclosure of substantiated sexual misconduct findings while protecting victims’ identities; allowing the chairman and ranking member to jointly issue subpoenas without a full committee vote; and streamlining disciplinary proceedings.

The reforms follow longstanding scrutiny over the pace and secrecy of congressional misconduct investigations, including cases in which lawmakers resign before investigations conclude. The changes come amid a separate bipartisan congressional workplace reform effort announced earlier this year.
Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., the top Democrat on the Ethics panel, said the reforms followed bipartisan deliberations and collaboration with the Congressional Women’s Caucus.

“The House of Representatives must have a zero-tolerance policy for sexual harassment and misconduct and the Committee on Ethics is committed to ensuring that its practices and processes sufficiently hold perpetrators accountable and deliver justice for survivors,” DeSaulnier said.

title: Tyson Fury, former boxing champ, reveals schizophrenia diagnosis
summary: Former heavyweight champion Tyson Fury said he was diagnosed with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder after his life was plunged into “darkness,” fearing at one point he’d “end up in a padded room with the door locked.”
story: Former heavyweight champion Tyson Fury said he was diagnosed with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder after his life was plunged into “darkness,” fearing at one point he’d “end up in a padded room with the door locked.”
The boxing star made the revelation about his mental health in the new Netflix documentary “Tyson Fury,” set to hit the streaming service on Friday.
The former champ described to the filmmakers how his life spiraled after reaching the pinnacle of the sport, when he defeated longtime champ Wladimir Klitschko in 2015.
He’d spent so much of his life dreaming of a defeating Klitschko that once it happened, there was nothing left to do.
“I achieved all my childhood dreams,” said Fury, now a 38-year-old father of seven. “And then when I finally beat this man, it was like my whole point of existence had been taken away.”

The next year, Fury was rushed to the hospital for what was initially believed to be a heart attack. Instead, doctors determined it was anxiety attack and told the fighter that he was suffering from depression, bipolar disorder and mild schizophrenia.

“Words can’t explain the darkness I was in,” Fury, 38, said in the documentary. “It’s like a living version of  the pits of hellfire. And I 100% thought at times I’d end up in a padded room with the door locked, and that scared me so much.”
For Subscribers
His wife, Paris Fury, said in the film she couldn’t understand any of the medical terms coming from doctors. But once they explained the symptoms, she understood completely.

“I’d never heard of ‘bipolar,’” she said. “Somebody actually explained it to me, like some days you’d be as happy as anything, ‘Oh yeah, yeah, yeah, let’s go, let’s go’ and then something can switch in it, like, ‘No, I can’t go outside today.’  Like wow, that’s him to a T.”
Fury, nicknamed the Gypsy King in honor of his Irish nomadic lineage, also revealed the voices in his head were telling him that the Illuminati was out to harm his family.

“The radio starts talking to me, literally having a full conversation with me,” Fury said. “‘No one’s untouchable. We can get you at any time. You don’t behave yourself, we’re going to kill your father.’ So I’m thinking, ‘OK, you’re all involved.’”
For Subscribers
The fighter’s dad admitted in the film he’d probably seen his son in pain for years, but just didn’t grasp the illness.

“I can tell you this: When I look back, it’s always been there,”  said John Fury, who named his son after the heavyweight champ Mike Tyson. “Me being who I am and no understanding of anything, I didn’t want to see a depressed kid — and if I did see it, I paid no mind to it. But I understand now. It’s an illness, a terrible illness. I suffer with it myself.”
Fury said he didn’t make any effort to get well until going out to party on Halloween night 2017.
“I thought I’d had the world in my hands. I threw it all away and now I’m just a fat mess addicted to alcohol,” he said.
Fury took about 2 1/2 years off to get back into shape. His memorable comeback consisted of two wins and a draw against fearsome American Deontay Wilder.
Fury regained titles until dropping consecutive bouts to Ukrainian Oleksandr Usyk in 2024.
Fury announced his retirement in early 2025, but has since returned to the ring, winning two bouts earlier this year.
The 36-2-1 fighter will next be in the ring on Dec. 11 fighting Anthony Joshua at Principality Stadium, Cardiff.

title: Court allows Army to go forward with planned detonation of toxic drums in Iowa
summary: A U.S. appeals court said Monday that it would allow the Trump administration and the Army to move forward with the detonation of lead azide in Iowa, denying an emergency request by environmental groups to halt the Army’s permit.
story: A U.S. appeals court said Monday that it would allow the Trump administration and the Army to move forward with the detonation of lead azide in Iowa, denying an emergency request by environmental groups to halt the Army’s permit.
It is not clear when the detonation, which was most recently set for Wednesday, will happen.

“We are mindful of the very real risks presented by the Army’s planned detonation of the stores of degraded lead azide,” the order from the 8th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals said. “However, we must acknowledge the realities of the situation: the degraded explosives present a risk of an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion, which would occur without the benefit of the safety measures that the Permit puts in place.”
The court said that the Environmental Protection Agency had adequately incorporated safeguards to minimize the dispersal of lead and that the Army had considered a full range of alternatives.

“A controlled detonation with attendant safety measures better alleviates the risk of irreparable harm than the risk of an uncontrolled explosion,” the court said in lifting an administrative stay on the permit.
The detonation, which would send a plume of lead dust across Iowa and likely into neighboring states, has raised fear and concern from residents who said they had not had enough time to prepare.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Earlier Monday, President Donald Trump ordered the Army to pause its planned detonation until the court weighed in.

“I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation,” Trump said in a Truth Social post.

The detonation was initially scheduled for Friday. After public outcry and a lawsuit from environmental groups last week, the Army delayed the detonation until Monday and then later pushed it again to Wednesday. The court last week gave an administrative stay in the case, putting the Army’s environmental permit to detonate on hold. But the Army told the court it could go forward with a detonation in an emergency without the court’s ruling. The Eighth Circuit ruling, released on Monday afternoon, will clear the way for the Army to go forward with the court’s blessing.

The outcry over the federal government’s handling of the situation and the decision of whether to detonate had become something of a political football earlier on Monday afternoon. In his Truth Social post before the appeals court ruling, Trump seemed intent on deferring responsibility to Sand, who has not taken office yet.

“If he or the Courts do not agree,” Trump said of Sand, “we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation.”
Trump said military leaders had advised him that detonating the material soon was the safest option and that the weather forecast for Wednesday was optimal.

“The Experts, who know it well, and have been studying it for many years, feel there is a substantial chance that this material will explode of its own volition, perhaps sometime in the near future,” Trump wrote. “The weather, right now, is optimal for this planned response to take place.”

The Army has said it must detonate the 68 drums of deteriorating, toxic lead azide — a chemical used to make bomb triggers — at the Iowa ammunition plant because the chemical has undergone a process of “recrystallization” that has made it highly unstable and dangerous. The Army has said that it is unsafe to move the drums and that cold weather will further destabilize the material and could cause a spontaneous explosion.

The Army had told Middletown residents that the blast could break windows and shake their homes. But residents elsewhere in Iowa — and in the plume’s potential path outside the state — said they didn’t learn about it until last week and were concerned for their families’ well-being, crops and pets.

Lead is a potent neurotoxin for which there is no safe level of exposure. Airborne lead is an acute health risk, experts said, and once the metal gets deposited in soil or on surfaces, it can remain there forever unless it’s physically removed.

Exposure to lead is associated with learning disabilities, reproductive problems, mental health issues and increased risk of hearing loss, among other effects. The long-term risks are particularly pronounced for young children.

The Army said it had covered the bunker with two stories of sand in collapsible, modular barriers to dampen the effects of the explosion. Meanwhile, scientists, politicians and residents have been trying to figure out how the situation got so sideways and why the Army feels its only choice is a detonation, whether planned or unplanned.

In a statement on X before the court’s ruling, Sand said the administration should make its decision “based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago” and who have been in Middletown for weeks. Sand implied that the administration might have information about the urgency of the situation that is not known publicly.

“Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward,” Sand said. “That means they should have the same access to the information I’ve received in briefings from the administration, straight from the source. I’ve asked the federal government to share that information with the public as soon as possible.”
An Army spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Iowa residents said they were growing frustrated with the twists and turns of the detonation saga.

Debra Ott, who works at Fat Annie’s August Tap, which is about a quarter-mile from a gate that leads into the ammunition plant, said she was planning to stay inside for a full day if and when the detonation takes place.

“I have some heart issues, and I have a hard enough time breathing anyway. So whenever they do it, I plan on staying in the house 24 hours because I don’t want to be out,” Ott said. “The bean dust and corn dust around here is bad enough without lead.”
Ott, who lives in Augusta, Iowa, about 5 miles from Middletown, said she was growing tired of the scheduling changes for detonation and increasingly concerned about a spontaneous explosion.

“I don’t want to be sitting at home at midnight and have it go off and not have a clue what’s going on without anybody up there to try to control it. If they’re going to do it, I wish they just do it and quit changing it every day,” she said.
Ott lives with her granddaughter and her granddaughter’s three young children, who are 13, 4 and 2.

“We’ll hose down all the outside stuff and wipe off, you know, wipe down the doorknobs and anything the vehicles, anything the kids can touch with their hands, where they could get it in their mouth,” Ott said. “We just don’t know what to expect because we don’t know when they’re going to do it.”
The trajectory of the dust plume depends on the direction and strength of the wind, so each delay puts a new group of people in the path of the expected hazard.
“It’s just very frustrating,” said Jill Holler, who lives about 50 miles from Middletown, in Muscatine, Iowa, which could be in the path of the lead dust plume, depending on the wind.

Holler, whose family has a farm about 20 miles west of Middletown where they raise cattle and grow soybeans and corn, said she was racing to gather soil samples ahead of the blast Sunday night. Understanding the lead content present in soil before the blast could help determine if a property is affected and what remediation might be needed.

“We thought it would be tomorrow. So I was down in the dark getting the soil samples and it just, it’s frustrating,” Holler said on Monday. “It’s just strange, and you just never know what the next day is going to bring, and so you never. You’re, you’re pretty confident there’s going to be something else changing, and we can’t really believe what the next thing they say is going to happen.”
Holler said she was most sympathetic to the people of Middletown, who are essentially living with a threat in their backyards that the Army has indicated could spontaneously explode.

“If there really is an imminent threat and it’s very dangerous to explode at any time,” Holler said. “But it seems like they’re delaying, so it just isn’t adding up. It doesn’t make sense. So I think there’s going to have to be some explanation of what’s been going on.”

title: Congress reacts with anger and skepticism about Jensen Huang reinstatement
summary: Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle vowed to press ahead with investigations into the once-again Nvidia CEO, who’s scheduled to meet with them next week.
story: The stock market was thrilled with the announcement that Jensen Huang was returning as CEO of Nvidia, but lawmakers on both sides of the aisle reacted with shock — and said they still expect him to answer questions next week on Capitol Hill.

“You gotta be kidding me,” Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told MS NOW when he learned of Huang’s reinstatement 11 days after he resigned in the wake of revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese spy.
In its announcement, the board said it reached the decision after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that his “reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
“No national security risk? Based on what?” Cornyn asked in a post on X.
President Donald Trump told CNBC he’d spoken to the board “directly and indirectly.”

“One of the things the board wanted to know, is there a national security problem?” Trump said. “And after a lot of research, we — you know, we’ve been looking at this for more than a couple of days, right? This has been a story for a few weeks. We said no, it’s not a problem.”
Lawmakers made clear they still need answers.
The Senate Banking Committee, chaired by Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., announced that Huang was scheduled to testify publicly Dec. 3.

“The national security concerns and adherence to export controls will be central to the committee’s oversight and the congressional hearing. Our markets demand transparency. Americans deserve the truth. Our committee will deliver answers,” Scott said in a statement.

A spokesperson for the House Intelligence Committee told NBC News that Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO “changes nothing” for the three House committees that are set to conduct a closed-door transcribed interview with Huang on Dec. 1.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“There are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers. Seems like the only thing that is consistent these days on this issue is our three Committee’s commitment to oversight,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

In a joint statement later Monday, the chairs of the House Select Committee on China, the Intelligence Committee and the House Foreign Affairs Committee said Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter “have confirmed they will appear for their transcribed interviews on December 1 and December 2 as previously planned.”

“We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of NVIDIA products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities,” said the three Republicans, Reps. John Moolenaar of Michigan, Rick Crawford of Arkansas and Brian Mast of Florida.

The speedy reinstatement and assurances of the lack of a security risk came after the Justice and Commerce departments last week shared details about their investigation into Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company tied to Alice Huang, the suspected spy with whom Huang was allegedly involved.
Megaspeed reportedly acquired billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips and is also being investigated over concerns that it — and its subsidiaries — smuggled chips to China.

Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said in an X post that “the legal and reputational risk of hiring a CEO who may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws is now born by the board of Nvidia, but the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens. The risk of extortion by a Chinese asset who’s been banned by Singapore is risk enough to not rehire Huang.”
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told NBC News in a phone interview “It’s not my job as a public official to tell a private company who to pick for their CEO. That’s up to the board of directors.”

But, he added, “What I want to know is whether Nvidia violated the export controls of our country with respect to advanced chips. And I want to know if the Department of Commerce did. That will be the purpose of the Banking Committee hearing.”

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said in a statement that the administration appears to have known about the Chinese espionage efforts targeting the Nvidia CEO for the past year and his reinstatement “without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation.”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said the administration’s “rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act.”

“Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat,” Schumer said in a statement. He added that “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain.”
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., called the board’s decision “indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible.”

“Congress will not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce,” Jeffries said.
Lutnick agreed earlier this month to testify before Congress about the Huang scandal amid lawmakers’ scrutiny of China’s access to advanced AI chips.

Democrats pointed Trump’s financial ties to Nvidia, with Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the ranking member on the Oversight Committee, noting the president has a sizeable amount of Nvidia stock. “No president who has invested in a private company should be involved in their board decisions,” Garcia said.
Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill., cited Nvidia’s donation to Trump’s White House ballroom project as a reason to give the board’s decision extra scrutiny.

“Trump’s assurances cannot be taken at face value, especially after Nvidia’s $25 million donation to his ballroom. Huang must testify at a full public congressional hearing, with every member of the relevant committees allowed to question him,” he posted on X.
Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., questioned the Nvidia board’s decision in a post on social media.

“Jensen Huang had multiple affairs including with subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy,” Ricketts wrote. “His own board described his behavior as lacking ‘candor.’ I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement.”

“Nvidia’s decision today doesn’t excuse Jensen Huang from testifying before Congress,” he continued. “It also doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips. I look forward to Mr. Huang coming to the Senate in December.”

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., called the president’s actions “Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration’s big tech and AI policy.” He told reporters it was a “good sign” that Republican senators and lawmakers have spoken out because they “realize this is a threat to national security.”

title: U.S. Army veteran mauled to death by pack of dogs in Georgia
summary: A Georgia family on Monday was preparing to bury an Army veteran and mother of three who was mauled to death last week by a pack of dogs.
story: A Georgia family on Monday was preparing to bury an Army veteran and mother of three who was mauled to death last week by a pack of dogs.

Allison Lynn Anderson, 36, was found naked and lying face down on the ground and “the top and back of the scalp were missing,” according to a Bartow County Sheriff’s Office report dated Nov. 16 which described the incident as a “murder.”
Anderson’s niece told NBC News they’re still coming to grips with “this horrible crime.”

“My aunt was about to become a grandmother for the first time when she was murdered,” the niece, Samantha Evans, 26, said when reached by telephone at a funeral home in Jasper, Georgia. “We want justice.”
In a statement released to Atlanta First News, Anderson’s daughter said her mother died before she could tell her that she was about to become a grandmother for the first time.

“If my mom knew that I was carrying her first grandchild she would be over the moon and full of excitement... ... I am so disgusted and absolutely heartbroken that the owners of these dogs did not have control over them,” Miley Garner said in the statement. “What my mom went through was torture.”

The Georgia Bureau of Investigation is leading the inquiry into the  death of Anderson, who was found dead around 9:00 a.m. on November 16 in the yard of an apparently abandoned house in Cartersville, a small city some 45 miles northwest of Atlanta.
For Subscribers

Preliminary autopsy results indicated she “sustained fatal injuries after being attacked by dogs,” the GBI said in a press release. “Several of the dogs involved in the attack have been located and are in the custody of Bartow County Animal Control.”
Also, in the incident report, a sheriff’s deputy wrote that he interviewed a person who lives in the area and who said “his dogs did bark last night, but he did not know what time that occurred.”
That person’s name was blacked out in the report obtained by NBC News. And it wasn’t clear if this person’s dogs were involved in the deadly attack.
For Subscribers
But as of Monday, nobody has been arrested in connection with the death of Anderson, a GBI spokesperson said.
Evans said she was told that at least two of the three dogs being held by animal control are “pit-bull mixes.”
“They are waiting for the DNA results to confirm that these dogs were involved in the attack,” Evans said. “After that happens, they will be put down.”
Anderson joined the Army 2007 and served as a combat medic, her family told 11 Alive, the NBC affiliate in Atlanta. At the time of her death, she was living with another woman in Cartersville.
Still unclear is what Anderson was doing at the property on Dogwood Trail Southwest when she was attacked by the dogs.
The GBI has appealed to members of the public to call them at 1-800-597-TIPS (8477) if they have any information or witnessed the attack.
“Someone took the life of a Mother, daughter, sister, aunt,” Evans posted on the Justice for Allison Lynn Facebook page. “Somebody took her from our entire family forever. She was an innocent woman.”
In addition to her daughter, Anderson is survived by two sons Lathem and Jaxon, her mother, and extended family, according to her obituary. She will be laid to rest on Tuesday.

title: Bo Derek and John Corbett adopted Gene Hackman’s dog, Bear, after actor’s death
summary: Hollywood power couple Bo Derek and John Corbett adopted Gene Hackman’s dog after the actor and his wife were found dead last year at their New Mexico home.
story: Hollywood power couple Bo Derek and John Corbett adopted Gene Hackman’s dog after the actor and his wife were found dead last year at their New Mexico home.

Derek told The Hollywood Reporter that when they were asked to adopt the German shepherd, named Bear, they initially declined because they already had two other dogs and thought it would be too much to handle. But after seeing a picture of the dog, they changed their mind.
“I was a goner,” Derek said.
Derek — the star of “10” and “Tommy Boy” — has been married to Corbett — the star of “Sex and the City” and “My Big Fat Greek Wedding” — since 2020.

The bodies of Hackman and his wife, Betsy Arakawa, were found in separate rooms of their Santa Fe home in February 2025. A maintenance worker at the home became concerned after the couple failed to answer the door and contacted a security officer in the subdivision, who went to the residence and discovered the couple inside, the sheriff’s office said.
Arakawa, 65, died from hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, a virus found in rodents. Hackman, 95, died about a week later from heart disease with Alzheimer’s disease as a contributing factor.

Hackman’s adult daughters, Elizabeth and Leslie Hackman, told investigators that his health had declined and that on Jan. 30, 2024, they had to remind him three times that it was his birthday, according to documents related to the investigation into the couple’s deaths.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The daughters also said that they had not seen rodents at the home but had seen mouse traps. State health inspectors noted mouse traps at the residence, as well as live rodents, dead rodents, and rodent feces in a detached garage and in two guest houses, the documents state. There was also a rodent nest, a live rodent, and a dead rodent among working vehicles, abandoned vehicles or farm machinery on the property, according to the documents.
The report said the main house was clean with no signs of rodent activity.

Body camera footage released along with the documents showed that one of the couple’s three dogs was near Arakawa’s body when she was found. Another dog was located outside and the third was found dead in a crate, likely from a lack of food and water.
Corbett told The Hollywood Reporter that the dog found near Arakawa’s body was Bear. Derek said that since she adopted him, Bear has been the “perfect gentleman.”

title: Appeals court gives Trump another chance to move his hush money conviction case to a federal venue
summary: The 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found a federal judge “erred” when he ruled that President Donald Trump had waited too long to raise his immunity defense.
story: An appeals court on Monday opened the door to moving to federal court President Donald Trump’s New York state criminal case that resulted in a felony conviction.

In a brief two-page order, the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found that a lower court judge had “erred” when he ruled Trump’s legal team had waited too long to raise a presidential immunity defense.
“We disagree with the district court,” the three-judge panel said, directing a lower court judge to reconsider Trump’s motion to move the case from state court.
U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein in August had denied Trump’s request to consider moving the case, finding his arguments were not “legally sufficient.”
A spokesperson for Trump’s legal team praised the appeals court’s “prompt and correct ruling.”

“As today’s order highlights, the Supreme Court’s historic decision on Immunity, the Federal Constitution, and other established legal precedent mandate that the Witch Hunt perpetrated by the Manhattan DA be removed to federal court, and immediately overturned and dismissed,” his statement said.
“President Trump will keep defeating the Liberal Hoaxes at every turn,” it added.
For Subscribers
A spokesperson for the Manhattan district attorney’s office, which prosecuted the case, declined to comment.

Trump was convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records in 2024 as part of a scheme to cover up a hush money payment that his attorney had paid to an adult film star during the 2016 presidential campaign.

Trump managed the repayment to his attorney while he was president, and his lawyers have contended that a 2024 Supreme Court ruling that expanded the parameters of presidential immunity after he’d already been convicted should have resulted in the conviction being overturned.
Trump, who has denied any wrongdoing, had been separately appealing the conviction in state court, but Monday’s order effectively freezes that case while it’s being decided in federal court.
For Subscribers

“In order to preserve the status quo, the district court shall also respectfully request that no further proceedings occur in the state courts while the removal question is pending,” the judges wrote.
Judges Raymond Lohier, John Walker and Jose Cabranes also found that if the lower court decides the case should be moved to a federal venue, the “court should adopt the state court judgement.”
That would allow Trump to make his case for the conviction to be tossed out by the 2nd Circuit.
It’s unclear who will hear the case at the lower federal court level. Hellerstein died last month at age 92, and the case has yet to be reassigned.
Hellerstein had previously rejected other attempts by Trump to move the case, finding “hush money paid to an adult film star is not related to a President’s official acts.”

During arguments before the 2nd Circuit last week, Steven Wu of the district attorney’s office argued Trump had been prosecuted for falsifying business records, not for official presidential conduct, and that challenges to the conviction should go through the state courts.

Trump attorney Robert Giuffra acknowledged to the appeals court judges last week that it was unusual for a defendant to try to move a case after he’d already been convicted, but noted, “Everything about this case is unprecedented.”

Trump was sentenced to an unconditional discharge in the case 10 days before he was sworn in for his second term as president. The sentence meant that the conviction is on his record, but with no further penalties.

title: ‘The Traitors: New Blood’ Finalist Katie Reveals if She Regrets Recruiting Shane After Win
summary: Katie Fites and Victor Vollbrechthausen discuss “The Traitors: New Blood” season finale, fruit-gate and Shane’s recruitment with TODAY.com.
story: Although they didn’t win “The Traitors: New Blood,” Katie Fites, the tiny Traitor, and Victor Vollbrechthausen, “the boy who cried fruit,” still had a lasting impact on the game and fans.
The first all-civilian season of the NBC competition show ended Nov. 19 with Shane Beatty being crowned the sole winner, and Victor and Katie coming in fourth and fifth place, respectively.

Shane became a Traitor near the end of the game after Katie recruited him to the turret. Shane and the other finalists, including Victor, voted Katie out in the last stage of the game — the Fire of Truth.
More about the 'Traitors' finale

‘The Traitors: New Blood’ Finalists Wyatt and Abbey on the ‘Shocking’ and Tear-Filled Finale: ‘Out of Body Feeling’‘The Traitors: New Blood’ Winner Shane Beatty on His Victory: ‘I Played It Flawlessly’
‘The Traitors: New Blood’ Finalists Wyatt and Abbey on the ‘Shocking’ and Tear-Filled Finale: ‘Out of Body Feeling’
